events.event_narrative: Daytime high temperatures ranged from 105-115 degrees each afternoon. In addition, overnight lows remained in the mid to upper 60s, and even low 70s in some locations.

A wind gust of 68 mph was recorded at the Glacier Park International Airport. The thunderstorm resulted in a couple hundred customers without power in West Glacier and near Coram, according to Flathead Electric COOP. Numerous reports of downed trees were also received.
The Montana Department of Highways reported that multiple large trees were down, and crossed the road along US Highway-12, near Lolo Pass. Inbound velocities on radar reached 60 mph.
Reports of large trees down near Lolo Pass were received. Radar velocity data indicated winds over 60 mph.

Radar velocity data indicated wind speeds over 50 knots. An emergency manager reported a tree falling on a house in Target Range. A wind gust of 51 mph was recorded at the Missoula International Airport.
The forest service reported that over 200 trees were blown down across a 22 mile stretch of road from Spring Creek to Long Tom Lookout.

A weather spotter reported that a large tree, approximately 18 inches in diameter, fell down one mile east of Seeley Lake. Trees were also reported down on Morrell Creek Road and 13 miles south of Condon, on Highway-83. A couple hundred customers lost power near Condon.

Multiple car crashes were reported on Interstate-90 near Missoula as a thunderstorm with strong winds and heavy rain moved through. A wind gust of 52 mph was recorded at the Missoula International Airport, with the main core of the storm passing to the east of the airport.
Between 4 and 8 inches of snow fell between Happy's Inn and Kila during the event.

Heavy snow and gusty winds occurred and caused roads to be slick with ice underneath the snow. A weather spotter in Hungry Horse and COOP in West Glacier both reported 9 inches of snowfall during the event.

Light snow between 1 and 3 inches fell across the Flathead and Mission valleys with slick roads reported by a weather spotter. MDT reported 6 to 8 inches of lake effect snow fell on the southeast side of Flathead Lake on the 27th and 28th. A large arctic steam devil as high as 300 feet tall was reported and photographed near Wood's Bay on the 29th by a person from the public.
Flash freezing of roadways developed as 1 to 2 inches of snow fell on already wet roads and temperatures fell into the 20s.

Rain followed by snow, along with falling temperatures into the 20s and gusty easterly winds to 30 mph caused flash freezing of the roadways. A CoCoRaHS observer in the South Hills reported 0.25 inches of ice underneath the 3.1 inches of snow. Other snow amounts include 3.8 inches Lolo and 6 inches on the grass 2 miles north of Wye. A secondary storm brought very heavy snow rates of 1 to 2 inches per hour to the Darby area during the evening of the 25th. A person from the public reported 10 inches of total snowfall in Darby.

Rain developed on the evening of the 24th which set the stage for a flash freeze situation as rain changed to snow and temperatures fell into the low to mid 20s by daybreak on the 25th. Lolo Pass received 9 inches of total snowfall.

Rain changed to snow as temperatures fell into the 20s and winds gusted to 35 mph which caused flash freezing of the roadways. A COOP in Potomac reported 4 inches of snow. A semi rolled over east of Clearwater Junction and caused Highway 200 to closed for a period during the afternoon of the 25th.

Flash freeze of roadways occurred as rain changed to snow with falling temperatures into the teens. Gusty north to east winds between 20 and 40 mph caused periods of blowing snow with reduced visibility along and west of the Divide. Snow amounts include 6 inches in Ovando, 8 inches west of Anaconda and Philipsburg through the morning of the 25th. A secondary storm brought an additional 11 inches of snow to Anaconda and the 2 day total of 19 inches became the 2nd highest on record.  Butte received a total of 7.3 inches out of both storms. A plethora of vehicle accidents and semi jackknifes occurred during this time period.

The Savage Pass SNOTEL picked up 8 inches of snow while Lolo Pass received 9 inches. Mountain Meadows which is located south of Red River Hot Springs picked up 3 inches of snow. Temperatures fell into the 20s from Lolo Pass to Powell on US-12 which could have produced black ice on the 25th.

Light freezing rain was reported at Glacier International Airport beginning at 6:20am. Minor ice accumulations were reported with several car accidents in the Flathead Valley related to slick conditions.

Light freezing rain fell along the Interstate 90 corridor west of Missoula. Black ice was reported with several car accidents near the Cyr Bridge. Icy conditions also occurred on Highway 200 near Noxon.

Light freezing rain was reported at Missoula Airport beginning at 6:15am. Icy conditions were reported on many roads and highways in both the Missoula and Bitterroot valleys. A significant accident occurred on Highway 93 just north of Stevensville which blocked the road for several hours.

Light snow accumulated on roadways in the Flathead Valley with an inch of snow falling at Glacier International Airport. Light freezing rain in the Mission Valley caused icy conditions on roads and sidewalks with related accidents.
A wintry mix caused icy roadways for the morning commute. Alberton schools were delayed 2 hours due to slick conditions.

Light snow fell across the area with amounts generally in the one to two inch range. Roads were snow covered and slick, likely contributing to a fatal crash that occurred around 0700 MST near Rollins. A school bus, with two occupants, collided with two passenger trucks on northbound Highway-93, leading to a fatality of one of the passenger truck drivers.

Moderate to heavy snowfall occurred, leading to snow covered roads at Lookout Pass. A number of vehicle crashes were reported, while chains were required over the pass for periods of time. Traffic cameras also showed periods of greatly reduced visibility with falling snow.

Heavy snow fell for locations like Lolo Pass and Lost Trail Pass. Lost Trail Pass received 21 inches of snowfall, as reported by the ski resort. Lolo Pass also received 21 inches of snowfall, as recorded by the SNOTEL.

Moderate to heavy snow occurred, causing widespread snow-covered roads. Difficult travel conditions were reported by the Idaho Transportation Department on Highway 12 near and over Lolo Pass. Elk River picked up over 15 inches of snow accumulation.

Difficult travel conditions were reported on Highway 12 at Lolo Pass by the Idaho Transportation Department. Chains were required over the pass for a period of time. Lolo Pass picked up around 17 inches of total snow accumulation.
Heavy wet snow occurred with 10 inches reported in Headquarters and Pierce. A report of 11 inches was received from Elk River. Roads were snow covered across the area.

A mix of light snow and freezing rain fell, leading to slick roadways. Gusty winds combined with the falling precipitation decreased visibility. The public reported slick road conditions and multiple accidents along Highway 95 between Whitebird Hill and Grangeville.

Dense fog formed at the Missoula International Airport around 22:25 MST on December 15, with visibility below one quarter statute mile. Visibility briefly improved to one half mile between 11:53 MST and 15:30 MST on December 16, before returning to one quarter mile after 15:30. Dense fog lasted through 0910 MST on December 17, with visibility continuing to move between one half mile and one quarter mile through 0625 MST on December 18. In total, Missoula International Airport was below airport landing minimums for around 28 hours. This led to multiple days of flight delays, cancellations, and diversions.
Dense fog developed at the Glacier Park International Airport, with visibility dropping to one quarter statute mile. The fog led to 5 flight diversions and at least one cancellation.
Freezing fog led to ice formation on area roadways. Icy roads were considered a factor in a fatal crash that occurred on Highway 200 between Lincoln and Ovando.

Freezing fog led to the formation of ice on area roadways. A propane truck tipped onto its side on railroad tracks at the intersection of Mullan Road and Beckwith Street in Frenchtown. Icy roads were believed to be a contributing factor to the crash. There were also multiple flights delayed and one flight diverted at Missoula International Airport due to the dense fog.

Freezing fog led to ice formation on area roadways. Icy roads were likely a contributing factor to a three vehicle collision on Highway 93 near Evaro. The crash resulted in five injuries and two fatalities.

Estimated snow totals of 12-20 inches occurred in the West Fork drainage with 10 inches observed at Lost Trail Pass. Snow covered roads were common, with chains required at Lolo Pass for a time. Intense snow showers were observed on the evening of the 15th,  with sudden reduced visibility leading to difficult travel.

Snow totals ranged from 6 to 8 inches in Hamilton with 8-12 inches on the benches around Hamilton and in the southern end of the Bitterroot Valley. Lesser amounts of 1 to 3 inches occurred in the northern Bitterroot Valley. Travel conditions were difficult on the morning of the 15th and again during the evening commute as bands of snow brought dramatic reductions in visibility.

Prefrontal winds were strong at Gilmore Summit with a 67 mph gust. The front itself brought a brief period (1 to 2 hours) of gusty winds and heavy snow. Snow accumulations were generally an inch or less for valley locations.

Several power outages were reported due to gusty winds with a total of 150-200 customers without power. Areas impacted by the outage included Thompson Falls, Ashely Lake, Heron, and Hot Springs. Very little snow fell in the valleys.

Winds gusted to 53 mph at Marias Pass and 52 mph at Hungry Horse RAWS with a higher elevation gusts of 104 mph at Tunnel Ridge. Periods of snow fell with 1-3 inches at lower elevations, and up to 7 inches fell at Marias Pass.  Travel was difficult at times.
There was a 58 mph wind gust at Somers with a 59 mph gust near Creston. Power outages occurred for 61 customers. Only a dusting of snow fell.

Snowfall near 7 inches was reported at Lookout Pass by the morning of the 26th, with rates averaging around 0.5 inch per hour. Snow covered roads at times, especially near Lookout Pass.  Chains were also required at times over the pass. Lower valleys experienced only light snow amounts.
Lost Trail Pass is estimated to have received around 10 inches of snow in 4 hours between 7am and 11am.  Severe driving conditions were observed at Lolo Pass with 10 inches of new snow as well.
Up to 3 inches of snow fell at lower elevations with 6 inches for Discovery Ski leading to slick roads at times. Wind gusts generally stayed below 40 mph but a 55 mph gust occurred at MacDonald Pass.
Two hundred customers were without power due to strong winds.  No other damage was noted.
Three hundred and seventy eight customers lost power. Wind blew a tree over on Highway 35 near Creston and east of Pablo.
Snow amounts of 6 to 7 inches fell in Gibbonsville, while Salmon recieved 3 inches of new snow.

Slow moving thunderstorms produced 1 to 2 inches of rain over 3 hours on Highway 162 just southwest of Kamiah. Flash flooding occurred along Fort Misery Road just south of Highway 162 with 1.5 to 2 miles of roadway destroyed. Debris from Fort Misery Road washed on to Highway 162 with the highway closed around 12 hours. One car was caught in the debris flow but no injuries were reported. Also, one power pole was lost in the debris slide causing 8 customers to lose power. Seven Mile Creek came out of its banks, and began forming a new channel just upstream from its confluence with Lawyer Creek. Water and some debris also washed over Highway 12 in several places between mile markers 63 to 66 (mostly Lewis County) requiring brief mitigation.
Snow Squall. Heavy snow showers with up to 3 inch per hour rates led to numerous cars and semis in the ditch at Lookout Pass, which caused Interstate 90 to be closed for a period of time.
Heavy snow showers brought an estimated and unconfirmed 9 inches of snow to Libby. Other snow amounts include 4 inches in both Yaak and Eureka, 3 inches in Noxon and 1 inch in Marion.

Snow Squall. Heavy snow combined with falling temperatures and wind gusts near 30 mph contributed to a flash freeze along US-12 from Garrison Junction to MacDonald Pass. The squall had a history of lightning leading up to the event.

There was a gust of 49 mph measured at Missoula airport (KMSO).  An NWS employee took a photo of a  large, mature tree blown down at the corner of Bancroft and Brooks streets in Missoula.  There were 77 locations without power in Missoula, MT (zip code 59807) according to Northwest Energy.
There was a measured gust of 58 knots near Clearwater Junction on the Blackfoot River (site MTM08).  Northwest Energy reported 29 locations without power.

There was a measured wind gust at Bert Mooney airport (KBTM) in Butte of 52 knots, and 58 knots was observed at Montana Tech in Butte (MTM46).  Northwest Energy reported 552 customers without power just south of the airport. The Walmart reportedly had no power as of 4 pm MST.

Showers brought gusty winds to the Flathead Valley with a peak gusts of 47 mph at KGPI. The gusty winds caused a few trees to fall on power lines with just over 800 electric customers without power for a short time.
From 0.3 to 0.7 inch of snow water equivalent fell, estimated at 2 to 6 inches of snow. Backcountry travel was difficult.
From 0.4 to 0.8 inch of snow water equivalent fell, estimated at 3 to 7 inches of snow. Backcountry travel was difficult.
Generally 0.4 to 0.5 inch of snow water equivalent fell, estimated at 3 to 4 inches of snow. Backcountry travel was difficult.
Generally 0.5 to 1.0 inch of snow water equivalent fell, estimated at 4 to 8 inches of snow. Backcountry travel was difficult.
Generally 0.5 to 1.0 inch of snow water equivalent fell, estimated at 4 to 8 inches of snow. Backcountry travel was difficult.
From 0.6 to 1.1 inch of snow water equivalent fell, estimated at 5 to 9 inches of snow. Backcountry travel was difficult.
From 0.1 to 0.4 inch of snow water equivalent fell, estimated at 1 to 3 inches of snow.

A witness described multiple living, mature Douglas Fir and Grand Fir trees snapped in half. After reviewing the radar data, it appears a microburst occurred. After the thunderstorm pulsed up over the headwaters of the American River basin, north of Elk City, it then dropped over the Selway River between Selway Falls and Glover Campground. For these healthy trees to be snapped in half, the wind speeds could have exceeded 70 mph. It was reported that some of the trees were positioned towards the west-southwest direction.

Flash flooding and mudslides occurred along Salmon River Road from just above Ebenezer Campground to just below Owl Creek. Radar estimates of up to 1.25 inches of rain fell over a half hour period across the southern half of the Owl Creek Basin. There were three major slides along the Salmon River Road, near Poverty Flat, Skull Gulch, and one roughly 0.3 miles in length where the road bank collapsed into the river. The Skull Gulch slide destroyed at least one outbuilding. There were also 30 to 50 additional small slides across the Salmon River Road that didn't cause structural damage.

Missoula and Ravalli Counties had about 12,500 customers without power.  A downed tree closed U.S. Highway 93 south of Conner, MT.  Although no snow was recorded in Missoula or Hamilton, three to six inches of wet, heavy snow fell throughout the Bitterroot Valley.

Saddle Mountain SNOTEL on Lost Trail Pass recorded 10 inches of snow as of 02:00 MST May 23. A person from the public reported an estimated 3 feet of snowfall in the Sapphire Mountains, east of Florence.  There were about 1500 people without power from Painted Rocks to Sula according to Ravalli County Electric.

The Montana Department of Transportation (MDT) closed Interstate 90 over Homestake Pass east of Butte at 0530 MST May 23 due to multiple stuck vehicles.  At least two semis were jackknifed at 0500 MST.  MDT also reported 'Severe Driving Conditions' on Interstate 15 north of Butte at 2315 MST May 22.  MDT required chains to travel on US Highway 12 over MacDonald Pass west of Helena at 0138 MST May 23.  A weather spotter in Melrose reported 6 inches of snow in 3.5 hours from 0530 MST until 0900 MST. In the Porter's Corner and Georgetown Lake areas, total snowfall reports ranged from 18 to 23 inches of snowfall.
Utility company reports 173 without power due to heavy snow as of 00:28 MST May 23 along Interstate 90.
The Ravalli County Sheriff's Office reported U.S. Highway 93 south of Hamilton between mile marker 38 and mile marker 39 was closed due to downed power lines.
Several large, mature trees were uprooted.  One tree landed on a car in Johnsrud Park and completely crushed it.  Windspeed estimated from Beaufort Scale.

The Dworshak Reservoir saw 6 days of highs in the 100s with lows in the low to mid 60s. The hottest day was the 9th when the high reached 106 degrees at Dworshak and the unofficial reading at the Dent RAWS reached 105 degrees.
The Fenn RAWS hit 100 or higher five times during this heatwave. The highest readings occurred on the 9th when Fenn was 105 degrees, and on the 10th when the Moose Creek RAWS hit 107 degrees.

Orofino saw 6 days of temperatures in the lower 100s. The hottest day occurred on the 10th when the high reached 107 degrees. The warmest low temperature was 66 degrees on the morning of the 11th. While the Camas Prairie saw highs in the mid 90s, the Kamiah area was similarly as hot as Orofino.

events.cz_name: LOWER HELLS CANYON / SALMON RIVER REGION
events.event_narrative: Very hot temperatures were observed in both the Snake River and Salmon River valleys. The Pittsburg Landing RAWS saw its highest reading of 111 degrees on the 9th and 10th. Its low temperatures were in the low to mid 70s with a 76 low on the morning of the 11th. The Riggins COOP station saw its highest temperature of 104 degrees on the 14th.

A strong ridge of high pressure resulted in Excessive Heat Watches and Warnings.  The Heat Risk was rated Major to Extreme.  An observing site in Orofino, ID reached a high of 104 degrees on August 1.

events.cz_name: LOWER HELLS CANYON / SALMON RIVER REGION
events.event_narrative: A strong ridge of high pressure resulted in Excessive Heat Watches and Warnings.  The Heat Risk was rated Major to Extreme.  A RAWS observing site in Slate Creek, ID reached a high of 113 degrees on August 2 with low temperatures only getting down to about 78 degrees.
A trained spotted called in to report one inch hail at 17:06 PDT from Cottonwood, ID.
An NWS employee reported one inch hail in Missoula.
An NWS employee reported one inch hail in Frenchtown at 17:04 MST.

The Sheriff's Office reported downed powerlines over the Eastside Highway south of Stevensville.  There were 113 people reported without power.  Strong winds knocked over a camper and truck camper 8 miles east of Florence.
A severe thunderstorm produced golf ball sized hail.
Thunderstorm winds pushed over a 20 foot tall tree along Eastside Highway.

Missoula County reported eastbound traffic closed at Reserve Street as well as westbound at Paxon St for a tree in the road.  The power company reported over 1000 customers without power.   The ASOS at Missoula Airport measured a gust of 72 mph.
An NWS employee measured 1 inch hail near Frenchtown.
The public reported two rounds of hail in and around the Bison Range.  They reported wind gusts to 53 mph with the first round of hail.
The public measured 1.5 inch hail near Ferndale east of Big Fork.
A trained spotter measured one inch hail near Columbia Falls.

A severe storm knocked over several trees along Highway 93 from south of Hamilton through Victor.  The Soft Rock mesonet station in Corvallis recorded a gust of 72 mph.  The power company reported about 2800 without power.

A severe thunderstorm produced a gust of 67 mph at the ASOS at the Missoula Airport.  An NWS employee estimated a gust to 90 mph in Frenchtown.  A mesonet site in Turah measured a gust of 54 mph.  There were reports of trees across the roads in Missoula.  The power company showed a few thousand without power.
A lot of trees down around St. Ignatius.  The wind picked up a turkey pen and flipped it upside down.  Trees and power lines were also downed in Kicking Horse and Polson.
Flathead Electric reported about 15,000 without power due to downed power lines and downed trees.  There was a social media post reporting  a 64 mph gust near Badrock.

Social media reported lots of damage in Seeley Lake.  Essential travel only was declared at about 5:17pm MST and lifted on Aug 24 at 5:46pm MST.  Social media produced several images of trees down on houses and decks.

Glacier Park rangers reported 10 to 12 inches of snow.  The Logan Pass snow measuring site recorded 11 inches in 24 hours.  The Park closed the Going to the Sun Road.  The storm stranded park visitors, and buses slid off the road.  One person was killed in a slip and fall accident on Sperry Trail on August 28.  Media sources identify the deceased as a 65 year old male who slipped and hit his head.

The hottest temperature readings were reported as follows: Libby Dam Base was 102 degrees on the 10th, Eureka was 101 degrees on both the 10th and 11th, and both the Troy RAWS and COOP reported 103 degrees on the 10th.

The high of 97 at Kalispell on the 11th broke the previous daily record of 95 set back in 1975. The SKQ Dam also reported a record high of 98 on the 11th which broke the previous record of 97 degrees set back in 1953. The hottest temperature reported was 103 degrees in Hot Springs on the 10th.
The hottest temperature readings in degrees were as follows: 102 in Alberton, and 101 at Thompson Falls.

The Missoula International Airport reached 101 degrees on the 10th. The Stevensville COOP reported an official high of 98 degrees which interestingly enough, was five degrees lower than the nearby unofficial RAWS station.
Dworshak Reservoir reported five straight days with temperatures in the low 100s. The highest reading was 109 degrees set on the 20th. The airport in Grangeville hit 103 degrees on the 21st.

events.cz_name: LOWER HELLS CANYON / SALMON RIVER REGION
events.event_narrative: The observer in Riggins reported 104 degrees on the 20th, 22nd and on the 24th. The Pittsburg Landing RAWS saw its highest reading of 114 degrees on the 21st. Highest low temperature reported was 75 degrees at Pittsburg Landing on the 22nd.
During the heatwave, the hottest temperatures reported were 101 degrees in Pierce on the 21st, and 106 degrees at the Dent RAWS along Dworshak Reservoir on the 21st.
Lowell saw its highest reading of 105 degrees on the 18th. Other readings include 101 in Powell, 107 at the Moose Creek RAWS and 99 degrees in Elk City.
Salmon saw four days of 100 degree temperatures and the highest reading was 102 degrees set on the 24th. Leadore reached 95 degrees on the 24th.
The Indianola RAWS located west of Shoup recorded its highest temperature of 105 degrees on the 23rd.

Gusty outflow occurred throughout the Bitterroot Valley but a localized area from just south of Corvallis to near Quast Lane experienced damaging winds. A few downed trees and numerous downed branches were noted.  A peak gusts of 63 mph occurred at Soft Rock RAWS which was supported by radar velocities with 2000-3000 customers losing power.
Strong cold front triggered thunderstorms and caused the temperature to drop from 59 degrees to 46 in an hour. Wind gust occurred with thunderstorm outflow. No storm damage noted.

A strong cold front initiated a thunderstorm over the mountains to the west. Radar imagery revealed the thunderstorm dropped its core by 6:13 pm which triggered the high winds. No storm damage noted around the town of Salmon.
Thunderstorm outflow winds were observed, with a radar estimated time of 2:47 pm MDT. Minor structural damage to the Incident Command Post for the Johnson Fire but no injuries.
Thunderstorm outflow wind gusts. No damage noted in Butte.
Thunderstorm outflow wind gusts, no damage noted. Mesocyclone/wall cloud observed from MacDonald Pass webcam with this thunderstorm.

On July 21, Libby saw a high of 104 degrees, while the Libby Dam COOP reported 103 degrees, and Eureka experienced a reading of 100 degrees. The Troy area saw highs in the low 100s for three days straight.
On the 21st Kalispell reached 100 degrees, SKQ Dam saw 96 degrees and Hot Springs reached 100 degrees.
The Alberton COOP reported temperatures ranging from 98 to 102 for eight days straight. Other locations including St. Regis, and Trout Creek reported multiple days of temperatures in the low 100's.
The Missoula International Airport reported five straight days of low 100s. The Stevensville COOP reported two days of 100 degrees. Low temperatures were in the upper 50s to mid 60s.
Private weather stations in both the Fish Creek and Rock Creek areas reported temperatures from the upper 90s as high as 101 degrees.

The Potomac observer reported low 100s with up to 102 as the highest reading. An unofficial and private weather station in Clinton saw highs up to 103 on the 24th and also reported warm low temperatures of 68 degrees.

Hurricane force winds caused hundreds of trees, of all types, and diameters up to 2 feet wide, to be either uprooted or snapped in half along the track of the derecho from between Grangeville and Pollock, east and north towards Lolo Pass. Much of the Lochsa Corridor east of Kooskia sustained massive wind damage, and blocked access to many main and side roads. Multiple people were trapped for hours until people came to cut up the trees with chainsaws. Around 58 trees had to be cut along Forest Service road 221 southeast of Grangeville. A large willow tree fell on a house in Pollock and totaled it. A woman was injured from falling trees near Moose Creek where trees snapped off 20 feet above the ground and some damaged the ranger station there. Multiple vehicles, campers and infrastructure were either damaged or totaled at the Powell, Wendover, and Whitehouse campgrounds. The forest service estimates that 1 out of every 6 leave trees were uprooted in portions of their forest. Other impacts include: widespread power outages that lasted for days, multiple power poles damaged, at least 69 lightning-caused wildfires, 911 call center was inundated with 100s of calls, a motorcyclist was run off the road on U.S. Highway 12, and rock slides between mileposts 128 and 133 on U.S. 12. One of the lightning strikes triggered the Wye fire which turned into a large, 11,000 acre Moose Creek Complex. The emergency manager of Idaho County mentioned that some areas saw some of the worst damage they had ever experienced.

A state of emergency was declared by both the Missoula County Commission Chair and Missoula Mayor because of the unprecedented wind damage that occurred. The 80 to 100 mph winds brought thousands of trees down across the county. It wasn't just a quick gust, but rather high winds that lasted for a couple of minutes. This led to power and transmission poles breaking in half and triggering power outages that lasted for up to a week after, affecting close to 40,000 customers, many of which had to toss out spoiled food. One utility reported 80 power poles were broken across their service area with 42 of those knocked down or shattered along Mullan Road, located approximately 7 miles west of US-93. Many traffic lights did not work until two days after the event. The Missoula County 911 call center received over 600 calls with many people not getting through. The main repeater on Horseback Ridge, located southwest of Missoula, went down because of the wind and firefighters could only use line-of-sight radio communication throughout the night. Natural gas meters and natural gas lines were damaged. The DNRC gave a conservative estimate that 1,000 city trees were uprooted, splintered at the truck or suffered some other total failure. Their Missoula Campus lost 52 mature ponderosa pines, and over 25 tree species. Water conservation restrictions were put up in place because the Missoula Water was running on generators. Many parts of the city were shut down including parks and mainstem rivers due to downed power lines. Live power lines trapped many people traveling through the city, including two teenagers who sat in their car for over an hour until rescue personnel could reach them in the Lower Miller Creek area. Over a hundred homes had some sort of shingle or siding damage, and many could not get roofers to fix it until 2 months later. Portions of the Blackfoot River were closed due to downed power lines and damaged power poles and lines were also reported in the Clinton, Salmon Lake, Condon and Seeley Lake areas.

A weather station at the Stevensville Airport reported the gust to 66 mph originating out of the northwest. Multiple power line and pole issues were reported in the northern Ravalli County due to the winds. It appears that the Stevensville area was the furthest south extent of the derecho winds, while the Missoula area took a direct hit.

Frenchtown Rural Fire District rpeorted a structure fire after a pine tree crashed onto a power line in Alberton, causing the lines to arc. The Mineral County Disaster and Emergency Services reported that its phone lines were down. The severe winds of the derecho clipped the southeastern third of Mineral County.
A person from the public reported that there were dozens of trees down on forest service roads east and northeast of Arlee.
Widespread freezing temperatures occurred with readings from the upper 20s to lower 30s observed. Damage occurred to unprotected sensitive vegetation.
Widespread freezing temperatures occurred with readings from the upper 20s to lower 30s observed. Damage occurred to unprotected sensitive vegetation.

Widespread freezing temperatures occurred with readings from the upper 20s to lower 30s observed.  Typical cold spots dropped into the upper teens.  Damage occurred to unprotected sensitive vegetation.
Temperatures dropped to freezing on the Camas Prairie with upper 30s for Orofino. Damage occurred to unprotected sensitive vegetation.
Morning temperatures ranged from the upper 20s to lower 30s. Damage occurred to unprotected sensitive vegetation.
Morning temperatures ranged from the upper 20s to lower 30s. Damage occurred to unprotected sensitive vegetation.
Morning temperatures ranged from the upper 20s to lower 30s with typical cold spots in the mid 20s. Damage occurred to unprotected sensitive vegetation.
Morning temperatures ranged from the upper 20s to lower 30s with typical cold spots in the mid 20s. Damage occurred to unprotected sensitive vegetation.
Morning temperatures ranged from the upper 20s to lower 30s with typical cold spots in the mid 20s. Damage occurred to unprotected sensitive vegetation.
Widespread power outage in Thompson Falls with up to 4000 thousand customers without power. There was also a downed tree at the bottom of Cherry Creek Road around 7:20pm.
Morning temperatures ranged from the upper 20s to lower 30s with typical cold spots in the mid 20s. Damage occurred to unprotected sensitive vegetation.

Radar and local mesonet observations indicate 0.75 to 1.00 inch of rain fell over 30 minutes across the Elkhorn burn scar. Large debris flows and scour paths occurred across the Salmon River Trail #096 for about 2.5 miles between Bargamin and Rattlesnake creeks. Multiple flow paths scoured at least 30 feet deep and 35 to 80 feet across where the trail crossed small draws.

A utility company reported over 500 people without power northwest of Thompson Falls to the Noxon area. The Montana Department of Transportation reported a tree that blocked U.S.-2 and S-482, located just south of Libby.

Glacier National Park reported multiple trees down including 12 trees along the North Fork Road, trees down near the Walton Ranger Station near Essex and mile-marker 182 on U.S. Highway 2, trees down along Camas Road, near Lake MacDonald and in Apgar.

At least three trees fell due to estimated 60 mph winds in Moiese. The largest tree fell onto a house and cause considerable damage. Over two thousand customers were without power during the event. A large pine tree fell onto a yard located north of Polson. The Glacier Park International airport ASOS recorded a peak gust to 59 mph at 1719 PM MDT.

Several private weather stations between Lolo and Victor, on the west side of US-93 reported wind gusts between 66 and 83 mph. The Stevensville RAWS recorded a peak wind gust to 64 mph. The winds were strong enough to push over both a porta john and watch for wildlife road sign. Several mature ponderosa pine trees were uprooted west of Bell Crossing. Close to one thousand people were without power due to trees on power lines.
Frequent wind gusts between 50 and 60 mph were recorded by the Deer Mountain, Tepee Point and Point 6 RAWS stations.

A large Western Larch tree fell down next to a tent in the Big Larch campground in Seeley Lake. A large tree fell onto two cars in the Turah area. Over 1500 people were without power between Seeley Lake and Condon.

A private weather station located 5 miles north-northeast of Garrison Junction recorded a peak wind gust of 63 mph at 1929 MDT. Wind gusts between 49 and 55 mph were common from Avon to Wise River. An unknown quantity of power outages were reported from Drummond to Butte.
The Red Rock Complex wildfire took a 11 mile run due to the 50 to 60 mph winds and dry conditions.
Multiple trees were blown down along the Salmon River, west of the North Fork area. Wind gusts over 50 mph were common at a lot of weather stations in the valleys.
Lookout Pass SNOTEL picked up 6 inches of snow in 3 hours.
Lookout Pass SNOTEL recorded 8��� snow depth and 0.70��� of snow water equivalent.

Elk Butte SNOTEL received an estimated 8 inches of snow and 1.20 inches snow water equivalent.  Crater Meadows SNOTEL, located in the Clearwater Mountains in eastern Clearwater County at 5960 feet, received 7 inches of snow and recorded 1.10 inches of snow water equivalent.
Lolo Pass SNOTEL recorded 7 inches of snow and 0.60 inches of snow water equivalent.  Savage Pass SNOTEL recorded 5 inches of snow.

At 0048, chain requirements were enacted for Interstate 90 at Lookout Pass as webcams confirmed snow-covered roads. The hazardous conditions were driven by heavy snow, with the KMLP ASOS station above the Lookout Pass summit reporting snowfall rates of approximately one inch per hour.

There were multiple reports of heavy, wet snow and freezing rain causing motor vehicle accidents, broken tree limbs, and downed power lines.  The snow primarily fell from Yaak to Olney in this zone, 8-10 inches as of the morning of the 23rd.  Rain resulted in Boorman Creek to breach its banks (no damage from flooding was reported).  A major power outage was reported in Lincoln County lasting 24 to 36 hours.

Montana Department of Transportation reported about a foot of snow at Java (east of Essex). MDT stated there has been blowing and drifting east of Java, and described the situation as a nightmare for them to keep up the roads the last 36 hours. They were fighting with ice, especially when people pull off in the wet dense snow. This was mainly a problem between West Glacier to Essex, where it has been warmer. They  said the worst timeframe for them was November 23 between 4am and 10am MST when precipitation was transitioning from rain to snow.  Social media conveyed several reports of motor vehicle accidents, downed trees, and power outages.  Flathead Electric   reported several thousand without power.

KPAX news media station reported about 15,000 people were without power at 19:00 MST on November 24.  Wet, heavy snow combined with rain broke branches and resulted in the power outage.  Snow reports varied from about two to four inches.

Chicago Ridge SNOTEL, located at 5800 feet northeast of Noxon, received 1.30 inches of snow water equivalent and 13.0��� estimated snowfall.  Poorman Creek SNOTEL at 5100 feet in the Cabinet Mountains received 1.60 inches of snow water equivalent and 10.0 inches estimated snowfall.  Stahl Peak SNOTEL at 6030 feet, east-northeast of Eureka, received 1.40 inches of snow water equivalent and 10.0��� estimated snowfall.

Noisy Basin SNOTEL at 6040 feet recorded 2.00 inches of snow water equivalent and  11.0��� estimated snowfall.  Marias Pass SNOTEL recorded 0.43��� snow water equivalent and an estimated 4-5��� of snow.

Twin Lakes SNOTEL at 6400 feet on the Bitterroot spine, recorded 1.20 inches of snow water equivalent and 10 inches of snow.  Saddle Mountain SNOTEL near Lost Trail Pass recorded 0.40 of snow water equivalent and 5 inches of snow.
Elk River recreation district reported penny sized hail.
Ten inch diameter trees were blown over along Montana Highway 37. Hail 0.5 to 0.75 inches in diameter was also reported.
Public reported 0.75 inch hail just north of Garrison, MT.
Public reported shingles knocked off the roof of a building due to thunderstorm winds.
There were several reports of icy roads and sidewalks, especially between Trout Creek and Thompson Falls.

Icy conditions were reported around the Camas Prairie and on Highway 14 to Elk City. There were numerous slide offs and disabled vehicles on Highway 95 from mile marker 257 to 261 which closed the highway for several hours the evening of the 7th.

Snow showers just after sunset brought only light snow but a localized high impact as Interstate 90 closed due to accidents at mile makers 229 and 232. Ice and slush developed after the showers passed, resulting in difficult travel conditions.

Light freezing rain in the early morning hours resulting in icy conditions on Highway 2 between Libby and Happys Inn. Precipitation turned to snow with 6 to 8 inches near Crystal Creek during the daylight hours.

Light snow fell over the Flathead Valley but the far eastern part of the Valley along the foothills of the Swan Range received locally heavy snow.  Areas near Lake Blaine and Echo Lake picked up 8 to 14 inches of new snow. An interesting note, Noisy Basin SNOTEL had 4.6 inches of precipitation over 48 hours, making it the second highest 48 hour total on record for that station during the winter season.
Rain on snow along with gusty winds to 40 mph caused power outages from Olney to Stryker with isolated outages along Therriault Creek Road.

Rain on snow caused icy conditions. Winds gusted up to 55 mph near Marias Pass and up to 82 mph on the higher mountain ridges. Localized power outages were observed near Swan Lake with 171 customers losing power.

Numerous power outages were reported from the south side of Flathead Lake to the Mission Valley. Frequent wind gusts over 50 miles per hour and even gusts over 60 miles per hour were reported with a peak gust of 67 miles per hour in Ronan. At least 2000 to 3000 customers were without power in the Mission Valley from multiple outages.

Precipitation started as snow then turned to rain and eventually back to snow with slick roadways and multiple accidents on Highway 200 and Interstate 90. Snow amounts were light, generally less than two inches.
Peak gusts of 66 miles per hour at MacDonald Pass, 62 mph at Warm Springs Pond and 55 mph at Elliston were observed during the wind event.

Up to a quarter inch of ice accretion for many valleys of Lincoln County, including the towns of Libby and Troy. Untreated roads and sidewalks were very icy with many slide offs reported. Side roads were the worst but even primary highways had periods of ice cover. There were reports that some people avoided travel because of the conditions. There was also a power outage in Libby that was related to the weather event.

The total snowfall from the storm included 8.3 inches in Kila, 6 to 7 inches in Marion, 5.5 inches in Eureka, and 4 inches in Libby. The Cabinet Mountains received 10 to 14 inches of snowfall from this event. On Friday afternoon, the 3rd, rain fell along US-2 west of Marion. After dark, black ice developed in some areas.

Roads became slick by Friday evening, February 3, in the Swan Valley and along US-2 from Columbia Falls to West Glacier. The fresh snowfall of 4 to 8 inches, combined with strong winds gusting up to 35 mph, caused blowing and drifting snow, reducing visibility along the US-2 corridor���especially east of West Glacier to Marias Pass. Wind chills dropped to the negative single digits Friday night. The surrounding mountains received 0.60 to 1.00 inches of snow water equivalent which could equate to 6 to 12 inches.

Multiple reports of icy roads appeared on social media, including references to white-knuckle driving in the Mission Valley. One person mentioned that their truck began sliding, and they saw another truck in a ditch near Bigfork. Multiple slide-offs were also reported across the Flathead Valley. The icy roads developed after dark as sub-freezing air, with gusts up to 20 mph flowing out of the Glacier Region, solidified the wet roads. Snowfall totals ranged from 4 to 7 inches in the Flathead Valley and 6 to 8 inches in the Mission Valley.

Snow intensity became heavy at Lookout Pass by the afternoon but decreased by late evening. The combination of wet roads re-freezing at sunset, falling snow, and rain likely contributed to very slick conditions and a double fatality(indirect) on Evaro Hill. A semi-truck jackknifed, rotated into the oncoming lane, and slid down US-93, crashing into a truck and killing a 19-year-old man and a 17-year-old woman. Traffic was blocked for three hours, from 5 to 8 p.m. MST, on Friday evening. Snowfall totals included: 3 to 6 inches along Highway 200 west of Thompson Falls and around 10 inches at Lookout Pass.

Light snow fell intermittently until the morning of February 3, when it intensified in the Bitterroot Valley. A spotter on the west side of Stevensville reported 7 inches of total snowfall over 36 hours from the event. By late afternoon, a mixture of freezing rain, ice pellets, and snow was reported and continued into the evening. After dark, reports indicated that side roads had frozen over, with snow accumulating on top. Total snowfall from the event ranged from 4 to 7 inches.
Slick roads were reported via webcams and total snowfall amounts ranged from 4.5 inches in Turah, to 6.4 inches in Seeley Lake to 6.8 inches in Potomac.

Winter driving conditions were reported across the region. The conditions worsened at night due to re-freezing roads. The arctic intrusion was not particularly strong along and west of the Divide. At MacDonald Pass, northeast winds reached up to 14 mph, but wind chills dropped to around 12 below zero. Total snowfall was approximately 4 inches in Anaconda, while the mountains generally received 6 to 10 inches.
Snow covered the roads across Lemhi County during the morning of the 3rd. A weather spotter in Gibbonsville reported 5 inches of snowfall and the COOP in Salmon reported 2 inches.
Between 6 and 12 inches of snow fell in the mountains, including at Lolo pass. The COOP in Dixie reported a total snowfall of 6.6 inches.
Mountain locations reported 20 to 30 below zero wind chills in the Glacier Region.

Roads refroze by sunset on the 17th and caused very slippery conditions in the Missoula Valley. The coldest air temperatures on January 20 include 16 below zero in west Florence, 10 below by the Ranch Club in Missoula, 3 below at the Missoula International Airport and 8 below in Hamilton.
Wind chills were as low as 40 below in Seeley Lake. The coldest air temperatures include 24 below in Potomac and 21 below at Seeley Lake.

The coldest wind chills observed included 44 below Fahrenheit in Avon and 32 below at MacDonald Pass. The coldest air temperatures reported were 33 below zero between Feely and Divide near Interstate 15, south of Butte; 24 to 28 below in Elliston; 29 below at Georgetown Lake; and 27 below at Bert Mooney Airport, located just south of Butte.

Multiple accidents occurred in the Libby area Friday evening due to rain that iced up side roads. Between 0.10 to 0.20 of an inch of rain fell between Marion and Libby. A wrestling team headed to Eureka on Saturday morning had to turn around because Highway 37 was icy and MDT had hoisted severe driving conditions there. This event continued into February 1.

Severe driving conditions was hoisted Saturday morning along Highway 83 from Ferndale south towards Condon. This event continued into February 1. Storm total snowfall included 2.5 inches in West Glacier and 5.6 inches in Essex.

There were numerous reports of accidents and slide-offs due to icy roads. At one point, an observer counted 22 vehicles in the ditch between the Flathead County landfill and the turn onto Highway 40 just before 4 pm MST Friday afternoon. This event continued into February 1.

Multiple reports of icy roads, and driveways due to the freezing rain. MDT hoisted severe driving conditions for Highway 135. A person reported that it was a sheet of ice with multiple cars losing control, including a semi-truck that had crossed the center line and ended up in the wrong lane.
The City of Missoula issued an emergency travel only message Friday evening due to the icy roads. There were multiple reports of freezing rain across Missoula County.
MDT reported that roads had ice on them. Lolo Pass received 14 inches of snow with 1.40 inches of snow water equivalent. Lost Trail Pass received around 7 inches of snow.

Freezing rain fell during the evening and overnight hours and brought slick conditions, especially to side roads. MDT hoisted severe driving conditions on Highway 83 north of Seeley lake Saturday morning February 1. The mountains received 8 to 10 inches of new snowfall.
Icy roads contributed to a vehicle roll-over on Cascade Drive in Orofino during the early morning hours of February 1.

Heavy snow, ranging between 8 and 16 inches in total, fell in the mountains and around 3000 feet near and west of Pierce. The Grangemont sensor reported rain with a surface temperature of 29 degrees from 2100 to 0600 February 1, which infers that freezing rain fell.
Lolo Pass received 14 inches of heavy snow during the event. Freezing rain caused slick surfaces in the lower elevations.

Multiple accidents were reported in the Libby area Friday evening after rain caused side roads to become icy. Between 0.10 to 0.20 of an inch of rain fell between Marion and Libby. A wrestling team headed to Eureka on Saturday morning had to turn around because Highway 37 was icy and MDT had hoisted severe driving conditions there.

Severe driving conditions were hoisted Saturday morning along Highway 83 from Ferndale south towards Condon. This event continued into February 1. Storm total snowfall included 2.5 inches in West Glacier and 5.6 inches in Essex.

There were numerous reports of accidents and slide-offs due to icy roads. At one point, an observer counted 22 vehicles in the ditch between the Flathead County landfill and the turn onto Highway 40 just before 4 pm MST Friday afternoon.

Multiple reports of icy roads and driveways were received due to the freezing rain. MDT hoisted severe driving conditions for Highway 135. One person reported that the road was a sheet of ice, with multiple vehicles, including a semi-truck, losing control.
MDT reported that roads had ice on them. Lolo Pass received 14 inches of snow with 1.40 inches of snow water equivalent. Lost Trail Pass received around 7 inches of snow.
The City of Missoula issued an emergency travel only message Friday evening due to the icy roads. There were multiple reports of freezing rain across Missoula County.

Freezing rain fell during the evening and overnight hours and brought slick conditions, especially to side roads. Montana Department of Transportation hoisted severe driving conditions on Highway 83 north of Seeley Lake on Saturday morning, February 1. The mountains received 8 to 10 inches of new snowfall.
Lolo Pass received 14 inches of heavy snow during the event. Freezing rain caused slick surfaces in the lower elevations.

Heavy snow, ranging between 8 and 16 inches in total, fell in the mountains and around 3,000 feet elevation near and west of Pierce. The Grangemont sensor reported rain with a surface temperature of 29 degrees from 2100 to 0600 February 1, which infers that freezing rain fell.
Icy roads contributed to a vehicle roll-over on Cascade Drive in Orofino during the early morning hours of February 1.

Periods of heavy snow fell at and around Lookout Pass in the mid-afternoon on the 21st, causing a full full blockage of Interstate 90 due to accidents and stuck vehicles. Periodic road closures continued through the morning of the 22nd with reports of 9 to 10 hours wait times for motorists attempting to cross Lookout Pass. The Lookout Ski resort reported 10 to 16 inches of snow over the 24-hour period ending on the morning of the 22nd.

Moderate snow of 2 to 5 inches fell across southwest Montana, but became locally heavy on Homestake Pass from the mid-evening of the 29th through the early morning of the 30th. The Basin Creek SNOTEL, located just south of Homestake Pass, reported 14 to 16 inches of snow over 12 hours. Interstate 90 was closed for about 5 hours due to the heavy snowfall rates.
Moderate snow of 2 to 4 inches was common. Chains were required on Homestake Pass for several hours due to lane blockages from an accident that lasted into the morning of April 1.

From the evening of the 31st into the morning of April 1, wet snow of 1 to 4 inches caused power outages across eastern sections of the Flathead Valley as branches and trees fell onto power lines. Up to 1,600 customers were without power at one point, according to the local electric cooperative. The Noisy Basin SNOTEL, located in the Swan Range just east of the Flathead Valley, picked up 4 inches of snow water equivalent in the form of 22 inches of snow.
Nine inches of snow fell near Happy's Inn, accompanied by easterly winds that caused significant drifting from Marion to Kalispell. Schools in Olney and Marion were closed on the 5th.

The Montana Department of Transportation reported 8 to 9 inches of new snow, along with strong easterly winds that made it difficult to keep Highway 2 open.  Very cold temperatures accompanied the snow and wind, resulting in wind chills of -30 to -40 degrees Fahrenheit. The Swan Valley received a foot of snow during the event.

The Montana Department of Transportation (MDT) and Flathead County Roads reported stranded vehicles and road closures. There were multiple school closures and delays. One public report mentioned whiteout conditions on US-93, north of St. Ignatius, while another described blowing and drifting snow on Highway 28 near Lonepine, along with 8 inches of snow.  Snowfall reports varied: one from Columbia Falls noted 6.5 inches with deep snowdrifts along Highway 2; another indicated 19 inches southeast of St. Ignatius; and Polson reported 12 inches.  MDT also reported accidents along Highway 93 west of Flathead Lake.

The Montana Department of Transportation reported multiple incidents along Interstate 90 west of Superior. Ten to fourteen inches of snow were reported, including: 8-10��� Plains, 12��� St. Regis, 14��� in Ninemile, 9��� Trout Creek, and 8��� at Lookout Pass. School closures on February 5 included Thompson Falls, Trout Creek, Noxon, and Superior. Easterly winds gusting to about 30 mph, combined with cold temperatures in the lower teens, resulted in wind chills of approximately -7 to 0 degrees. Webcams depicted blowing and drifting snow.

Ravalli County Sheriff's Office requested emergency travel only in the Bitterroot Valley due to blowing snow.  Multiple schools were closed on February 5 including Corvallis, Hamilton, Missoula, Darby, and Stevensville. Public snow measurements included 14 inches in Hamilton, 16 inches in South Grantsdale, 20 inches north of Florence, 12 inches in Darby, and nearly 2 feet on the west side of Hamilton up Dutch Hill. A local resident remarked that even though she had great tires and drove an SUV, the intersections in the Bitterroot Valley were very slick.

Lolo Pass SNOTEL reported 1.30 inches of snow-water equivalent and 20 inches of new snow.  Lost Trail Pass reported a 48-hour total of 24 inches. The Saddle Mountain SNOTEL reported 0.90 inches of snow-water equivalent.  Chains were required over Lolo Pass during the early morning hours of February 4.

The Montana Department of Transportation reported severe driving conditions on State Highway 83 and State Highway 200 on February 4. Clinton Schools had a delayed opening. Measured snowfall in Seeley Lake was 8.2 inches, and about a foot was reported in Potomac. Winds gusted to 35 mph.

Public reports included wind gusts up to 38 mph with blowing snow near Garrison Junction, a two-hour delay for Drummond Public Schools, eight inches of snowfall near Ovando, and solid ice beneath the snow on Montana Highway 1.
The Pierce COOP reported 8.7 inches of snowfall, while the Shanghai Summit SNOTEL recorded 12 inches of snow.

Idaho County Sheriff's Office declared emergency travel only for U.S. Highways 95 and 12 due to winter driving conditions on February 4 at 1805PST.  They reported 'several accidents' and stated that visibility was limited due to snow.  The power company reported 692 customers without power on February 5 at 0337PST.  Lolo Pass SNOTEL received 1.30 inches of snow-water equivalent, likely corresponding to well over a foot of snow accumulation.

Idaho County Sheriff's Office declared emergency-only travel for U.S. Highways 95 and 12 on February 4 at 1805 PST. They reported 'several accidents' due to snow.  One power company reported 1,239 customers without power on February 4 at 2222PST. The CoCoRAHS site at 3 NNE Clearwater reported 18 inches of snow on February 5 at 0800PST, while another site reported 10 inches at 5 NNE Orofino. The Grangeville COOP recorded 13 inches of snow with 1.18 inches of precipitation. Kamiah and Grangeville schools were closed on February 5.

events.cz_name: LOWER HELLS CANYON / SALMON RIVER REGION
events.event_narrative: Idaho Transportation Department cameras on Whitebird Hill showed intense snowfall reducing visibility to less than one-quarter mile on the night of February 4. They also reported a semi crashed on U.S. Highway 95, milepost 196 at 1803PST on February 4.  A trained spotter on Whitebird Hill measured 18 inches of new snow.

Heavy snow fell initially, with up to 10 inches of accumulation near Gibbonsville and 8 inches in Salmon. During the day, melting snow caused water to accumulate on roadways, which turned to ice after dark due to ground temperatures remaining well below freezing. A weather spotter northeast of Carmen reported that all side streets were icy. He measured 7 inches of snow with 0.55 inches of water between February 2-3. Lemhi County also reported icing on county roads. Lost Trail Pass recorded 24 inches of snow in the  48-hour period ending at 0500MST on February 5. A snow squall produced wind gusts up to 45 mph and heavy snow around 1000MST on the 5th, impacting northern Lemhi County.
Law enforcement reported multiple crashes and slide-offs in the Kalispell and Columbia Falls areas.

Local law enforcement declared essential travel only within Missoula city limits due to very slick conditions caused by snow falling on refrozen surfaces. Several auto accidents were reported in the Missoula Valley.

Posts on social media showed difficult driving conditions along the Bitterroot Valley, with blowing and drifting snow causing whiteout conditions. Five inches of snow was reported at Dutch Hill. There were multiple reports of school buses stuck in the snow, one west of Hamilton and another near Bell Crossing on U.S. 93. Numerous reports also came in of vehicles off the road in the Missoula and Bitterroot valleys along U.S. 93 and Interstate 90. The Missoula County Sheriff's Office declared emergency travel only on Interstate 90.

A trained spotter in Silver Bow County reported approximately 6 inches of snow in just 90 minutes around 0800MST, and a storm total of 8.5 inches by 1135MST, along with one-quarter mile visibility due to blowing snow and wind gusts near 20 mph. The COOP observer in Philipsburg reported 7 inches of snow. Interstate 15 south of Butte was closed due to an accident at 0843MST, and chains were required over Homestake Pass on Interstate 90.

events.cz_name: LOWER HELLS CANYON / SALMON RIVER REGION
events.event_narrative: Idaho Transportation Department (ITD) reported 10 to 12 inches of snow at Whitebird Grade and 3 to 4 inches towards Riggins. ITD cameras showed heavy snow accumulating on U.S. Highway 95 between 0600 and 0730PST. Riggins also experienced tree damage and power outages that lasted 12 to 24 hours after the storm.

The Lemhi County Roads Department described the storm as a 'high-end event'. They reported 3 inches of snow overnight in Salmon, followed by another 4 inches between 0600 and 1000, for a storm total of 7 inches. Snow falling on already icy roads made travel very difficult, prompting the declaration of emergency-travel-only status. They also reported a 30-minute period of intensified winds, resulting in near-zero visibility. Additionally, a road grader flipped on the ice, though the driver was not injured.

events.cz_name: LOWER HELLS CANYON / SALMON RIVER REGION
events.event_narrative: The Idaho Department of Transportation reported 6 inches of snow from Whitebird Hill to Riggins at approximately 0900PST on February 10.
Public reports of snowfall over 5 days was 3 inches for Eureka, 8 inches for Libby, 5 inches for Troy.  Upwards of 20 inches were recorded in the Cabinet Mountains.

Montana Department of Transportation reported severe driving conditions on State Highway 83 at 0530 on February 17.  Law enforcement reported a motor vehicle accident  on Highway 2 east of West Glacier.  Four to 8 inches of snow fell in the Glacier Region, but closer to 18 inches fell at Swan Lake. Nightly black ice brought slick conditions. In the Swan Range, an estimated two feet of snow fell.

On the evening of February 16, fresh snowfall quickly covered icy roads, making travel treacherous. Many drivers struggled to maintain control, leading to multiple accidents with unknown injuries. Heavy snow fell in the eastern Mission Valley and Mission Mountains, with a Pablo resident reporting 4 inches of snow in 3 hours. As a result, many schools in the Mission Valley were closed on the 17th. Road conditions remained hazardous throughout the day, with additional accidents and jackknifed vehicles reported. By evening, new snow bands formed, creating more slick travel conditions. Total snowfall reached 1 to 2 feet in the Mission Valley, while the Flathead Valley received 8 to 16 inches.

Very slick roads contributed to multiple accidents, with one that caused multiple injuries. Snow became heavy at times during the evening of the 17th due to banding. Snow amounts ranged from 6 to 9 inches along Highway 200, 7 to 12 inches between Alberton to Haugan, and up to 20 inches at Lookout Pass.  Chains required on Interstate 90 at 0200 on February 16.

Severe driving conditions were reported by Montana Department of Transportation due to slick roads on the morning of February 16. Very slick conditions were reported again during the next two nights with fresh snow falling. An accident during the early morning hours of February 18 occurred near Frenchtown on the eastbound lanes of Interstate 90, resulting in three fatalities.

Periods of moderate to heavy snow fell at the passes while valley locations experienced slick conditions from black ice. Total snowfall included 2 feet at Lolo Pass, 17 inches at Lost Trail Pass and a foot in Rock Creek.

Severe driving conditions due to very icy conditions occurred the evening of February 16 along Interstate 90. Periods of heavy snow occurred the evening of February 17 due to snow bands. Total snowfall amounts include: 15 inches in Potomac, 14 inches in Seeley Lake, and 13 inches in Clinton.

The combination of falling snow and roads refreezing caused very slick conditions at times. Multiple crashes were reported along Highway 200 and Interstate 90. A large snow band brought 2-inch-per- hour snow rates, very low visibility and gusty winds nearing 30 mph at MacDonald Pass and Elliston the evening of  February 17th. Interstate 90 near Butte was reported to be very icy after dark on February 17th and contributed to multiple accidents in a small area. Snowfall amounts ranged from near 5 inches in both Butte and Deer Lodge to around a foot west of Anaconda. Ovando received 14.5 inches, and the Georgetown Lake area received two feet of snow.
Heavy snow fell at times across Clearwater County. Total snowfall amounts were consistent between 13 and 15 inches near Pierce and close to 2 feet of snow fell in the mountains.

Very heavy wet snow fell at times and brought slick conditions to U.S. Highway 12. Power outages were reported the morning of the 18th due to the heavy snow rates from snow bands. Snowfall ranges include: 9 inches in Syringa, 2 feet at Lolo Pass, a foot at Dixie and 3 feet fell near Red River Hot Springs Idaho.
Periods of heavy snow caused power outages in the northeastern part of the Camas Prairie. Total snowfall ranged from near 9 inches in Grangeville up to 16 inches in Woodland.

events.cz_name: LOWER HELLS CANYON / SALMON RIVER REGION
events.event_narrative: Idaho Transportation Department cameras indicated periods of moderate snow fell at times at Whitebird Hill.  Idaho County Sheriff reported a rock slide on Highway 95 at mile post 202.

Light freezing rain resulted in icy conditions on U.S. Highway 2. Unplowed side roads turned to sheets of ice. An avalanche measuring 20 to 30 feet high and 75 feet wide, completely blocked Going-To-The-Sun Road. Higher elevations above 7000 feet gusted as high as 78 mph early on the 24th.

Rain fell with cold subsurface ground temperatures and gusty winds, resulting in icy conditions. Road crews had to treat roads even with air temperatures in the 40s. Several accidents were noted. Ponding water also blocked roadways. Gusty winds to 55 mph also occurred in the Mission Valley early on the 24th.

Icy conditions were noted on Highway 83 and 200 the mornings of the 23rd and 24th. Traffic accidents were noted including a fatality related to icy conditions near Potomac. A rock and snow slide blocked the northbound lane of Highway 200 near Bonner around 1620MST on the 22nd.
Snow slide blocked the right lane of Highway 1 in the Flint Creek Canyon, northwest of Georgetown Lake.
Up to 2.00 inches of rain fell from Bull Lake to Noxon, heaviest on the evening of the 23rd.
An avalanche blocked the eastbound lane of Highway 12 near Elk Summit Road and Powell Junction. The avalanche was estimated to be 8 feet tall and 30 feet long.
Minor power outages were noted in the Bull Lake and Libby areas due to gusty winds estimated near 45 mph. Thunderstorms in the Idaho Panhandle may have enhanced winds as well.

Snow Squall. A snow squall brought near-zero visibility and wind gusts up to 45 mph across northwest Deer Lodge County and southern Granite County. Dangerous driving conditions ensued due to the snow squall.

At least two crashes involving injuries were reported by the Montana Department of Justice crash webpage: one near Clinton and another near Seeley Lake. Snowfall was light, with only 1 to 2 inches reported by observers, but breezy north to east winds between 10 and 20 mph caused blowing snow and reduced visibility, making the morning commute slower than usual.
Several crashes and slide-offs were reported along Interstate 90. Two of the crashes had unknown injuries. The COOP observer in Alberton measured 1.3 inches of snow.

The Saddle Mountain SNOTEL reported 0.50 inches of snow water equivalent, which at temperatures in the teens, could equate to 6 to 10 inches of snowfall. Lost Trail Pass experienced northerly winds between 10 and 22 mph, resulting in blowing and drifting snow.
The Grangeville COOP reported 4.8 inches of snowfall, while the airport recorded north winds between 10 and 13 mph. The webcams showed snow-covered roads.

Nine to ten inches of snow were reported on Williams Creek Summit. Given that high elevation stations like the Red Rock Peak RAWS recorded westerly winds of 15 to 31 mph, blowing and drifting snow were likely occurring at the summit.

The coldest morning was the 11th, with lows ranging between the single digits below zero to teens below zero, except for readings of 30 to 36 below northwest of Marion, and to 25 below near Happy's Inn and Olney.
Low temperatures in the Glacier Region generally ranged between 10 and 20 below zero, with the coldest reading observed at 28 below in Polebridge.

The coldest readings observed included 25 below at Hot Springs on the 11th and 12th, and 23 below in West Valley, located northwest of Kalispell. Wind chills neared 30 below in the northeastern part of the Flathead Valley and along Highway 28 on the morning of the 11th.

Low temperatures ranged from the single digits below zero down to 17 below, with the coldest reading reported at 17 below in Plains. The lowest wind chill was 22 below in Thompson Falls on the 12th, due to a stiff easterly gap wind of 10 to 20 mph.
The coldest morning was the 13th, when temperatures dipped down to 24 below at the Ravalli County Airport, 21 below in Stevensville, and around 20 below northwest of Missoula.

Among the three mornings when temperatures plummeted well below zero, the coldest readings were observed on the 11th: Seeley Lake reached 30 below, and Potomac dipped down to 32 below. During the morning hours of the 12th and 13th, canyon-accelerated gap winds along I-90 south of Clinton contributed to dangerously low wind chills between 30 and 40 below zero.

The coldest low temperatures reported were 45 below in Drummond, 33 below at Georgetown Lake, 32 below at Elliston, and 31 below at the Bert Mooney Airport near Butte and in Bearmouth. Wind chills between 30 and 46 below were observed at multiple stations along and west of the Continental Divide, including Butte, Avon, and Elliston.
Generally, 1 to 2 inches of snow fell with this event, except for locally higher amounts of up to 4.5 inches in the Marion area.

Total snowfall ranged from 2 inches in West Glacier, to 5.4 inches in Essex, and up to 6 inches at both Swan Lake and Marias Pass. Easterly winds between 8 and 13 mph, with gusts up to 24 mph between Essex and Marias Pass, caused blowing and drifting snow.

Multiple social media reports indicated that roads became very slick during the evening of the 14th. One individual noted that while at the ER, three or four separate people were being treated for serious injuries from vehicle accidents that evening. Another person stated, 'Highway 2 between Evergreen and Columbia Falls is pure ice.' Light snow, combined with northerly winds gusting up to 24 mph at times between the GPI Airport and Columbia Falls, contributed to deteriorating conditions. Snowfall totals included 4 to 5 inches in the Kalispell area and Mission Valley, 9.5 inches at Creston, and 6 inches near Bigfork.
Snowfall amounts generally ranged between 1 and 2 inches, except near Heron, where a report of 3.5 inches was received.

Multiple reports on social media remarked that the roads became slick Friday evening the 14th. One person remarked that the roads became much worse after 1800MST. Snowfall totals ranged between 2 and 3 inches.

The Montana Department of Transportation reported severe driving conditions on Highway 200 between Potomac and Helmville, from 2100 to 2305MST on February 14. They also issued severe driving conditions on Interstate 90 between Clinton and Drummond for two hours starting at 2300MST on the 14th. Law enforcement reported several crashes and slide-offs east of Missoula on Interstate 90.

The Montana Department of Transportation reported severe driving conditions on Interstate 90 west of Gold Creek towards Clinton on the night of February 14. Multiple crashes and slide-offs were reported, particularly west of Drummond, where a crash with unknown injuries occurred just before midnight on the 14th. Snowfall was generally light, with accumulations of 1 to 2 inches across the region.
A weather spotter reported 2.1 inches of snowfall in 1.5 hours, ending at 0700MST. The Marion CoCoRaHS observer reported 3.0 inches of snow with 0.25 inches of snow-water equivalent.

At Marias Pass, 7 inches of snow fell, accompanied by northeast winds between 7 and 12 mph, with gusts to 25 mph. Temperatures fell to 4 below zero the following morning. Java East, located at the U.S. Highway 2 bend southeast of Essex, received 3.4 inches of snow. During the morning of the 3rd, Java East picked up an additional 2.6 inches of snow between 0500 and 0600MST. Up to 10 inches fell in the mountains of Glacier National Park.

The combination of gusty northeast winds near 30 mph, air temperatures near freezing, and falling snow contributed to slick roads from the Flathead Valley to Flathead Lake. There were multiple reports of vehicle slide-offs along U.S. Highway 93 on the west side of Flathead Lake during the late morning and early afternoon hours. Snow fell in the Mission Valley, bringing low visibility and slushy accumulations.
A CoCoRaHS observer located west of Anaconda received 1.2 inches of snowfall. The mountains along and west of the Continental Divide, including Georgetown Lake, received 1 to 2 inches of snow.

Showers formed along the cold front as it slowly shifted southwards, producing strong, gusty winds over 40 mph. Power outages were reported from near Happy's Inn eastward to Marion along U.S. Highway 2. Snow was reported at Olney and Crystal Creek, but didn't accumulate on the roads.

Heavy snowfall rates of 1 to 2 inches per hour occurred during this event between Essex and Marias Pass along U.S. Highway 2. Marias Pass received 7 inches of snow, accompanied by northeast winds gusting to 25 mph. The COOP observer at Essex measured 5.1 inches of snow.
The Heron COOP observer reported significant limb damage and one fallen tree. The utility company reported 259 customers without power during the early evening hours.

Georgetown Lake, MacDonald Pass, and Homestake Pass all experienced snow-covered conditions at times during the event. Strong winds up to 45 mph occurred along and west of the Continental Divide. A few power outages were reported in the Philipsburg and Butte areas.
A trained spotter reported 0.88 inch diameter hail.
A trained spotter reported one inch diameter hail. A flight into Kalispell was diverted to Spokane due to the storm.
A trained spotter reported pea to golf ball sized hail.
Trained spotter 5 miles west of Butte reported 1.25 inch hail.
Trained spotter in Anaconda reported 1.00 inch hail.
Trained spotter in Anaconda reported 0.75 inch hail.
State employee 14 miles south of Philipsburg near Georgetown Lake reported 1.75 inch hail.
Public reported 1.75 inch hail 1 mile east of Jens along Interstate 90.
Public reported widespread tree damage near Lion Creek northeast of Condon. Many spruce trees 1.5 feet in diameter snapped.
Sheriff reported 30 trees blown down over Highway 83 10 miles northwest of Condon.
Car dealership 5 miles south of Ronan reported 0.88 inch hail and damage to vehicles in the car lot.
Trained spotter in Essex reported 0.75 inch hail.
Fire lookout at 6629 feet reported 0.75 inch hail.
Spotter reported 1.50 inch hail 7 miles south of Ronan.
Trained spotter reported up to 1 inch hail with winds up to 45 mph and damage to a camper.

Destructive thunderstorms swept through the Leadore area, unleashing estimated wind gusts of 80 mph. A local motel and a double-wide mobile home had their roofs ripped off by the violent winds. The storm also toppled trees, damaged home siding, pushed over 300 feet of fencing, and rolled a 300-gallon fuel tank.

Snowfall reports of 4 to 8 inches were common for Leadore and Gilmore Summit.  Ten inches of snow occurred at North Basin, located just north of Watson Peak. While paved roads remained clear overall, backcountry routes were snow-covered.

Snow began on the afternoon of the 21st and continued through the morning of the 22nd. Going-to-the-Sun Road was closed due to hazardous driving conditions going over Logan Pass during this period. New snowfall was estimated at 10 inches at Logan Pass, with accumulation reported as low as the Big Bend area around 4,300 feet. The top of Big Mountain Ski Area reported about 4 inches of new snow, which disrupted outdoor activities.

A very heavy downpour on Fiddle Creek, dropped approximately 0.75 inches of rain in one hour. The heavy rainfall triggered a substantial mud and debris flow that closed the highway near milepost 201 for nearly two days. Despite the intensity of the storm, no lightning occurred ��� an unusual feature for the region. No vehicles were trapped.
A wind gust of 70 mph was measured by the National Park Service.
Local emergency manager reported trees down across Montana Highway 200 partially blocking traffic. Downed trees estimated to be 1 to 2 feet in diameter.
Snowslip automated weather station reported a wind gust up to 80 mph.
A trained spotter reported several trees down over power lines. Downed trees estimated to be 1 to 2 feet in diameter. One tree also tore aprt a fence when it fell and another landed on a house.
A tree was blown down over a power line and knocked out power to 4500 customers in Whitefish and Columbia Falls.
A power line was blown down and knocked out power to much of the town of Libby.

Mud and debris flows reported along the Middle Fork of the Salmon River at mile markers 13, 15 and 58. At mile marker 15, a significant log jam occured which backed up the river and flooded Greyhound Camp.
Salmon AWOS reported 66 mph wind gusts.
Trained spotter in Leadore reported numerous downed trees along Highway 28.
A trained spotter reported hail that was a quarter to half dollar size near Elk Bend.
A trained spotter reported penny sized hail and 1.50 inches of rain in 40 minutes at Leadore.
A trained spotter reported 1 1/2 inch diameter hail with a passing storm.
A member of the public reported 1 inch hail size with hail accumulation to 4 inches deep at Holland Lake.
The Saddle Mountian lookout reported up to penny size hail and heavy rain.
A trained spotter reported up to quarter size hail.
Automated observation station at Logan Pass reported 80 mph wind gusts.
A public report described torrential rain of approximately 20 minutes in duration and  roadway ponding near Bernice���s Bakery around 1600MST; additionally, the roof of new annex started leaking.

The Bitterroot National Forest has issued a safety alert for a debris flow across Forest Road 724 near the East Fork Trailhead. The debris flow occurred within the 2024 Johnson Wildfire burn scar after a short, intense storm dropped a radar-estimated 0.41 inches of rain in just 15 minutes, and around 0.51 inches in less than an hour.
Multiple debris flows blocked Skalkaho Highway (Highway 38) in three locations. Two slides occurred south of Skalkaho Falls, with an additional flow reported west of the winter gate.

Local media received reports of minor debris flows along the North Fork of the Salmon River in and around the town of North Fork, ID and westward towards Shoup, ID from heavy rainfall that fell on the unstable slopes.
Trained spotter reported several debris flows which resulted in closing of a 10 mile stretch along Highway 93 between Salmon and Ellis from a half inch of rainfall in 30 minutes.
Ravalli County dispatch received several reports of downed trees due to thunderstorm winds in the Bitterroot Valley from Florence to Hamilton.

A measured wind gust of 43 mph was recorded at the Crystal Lakes Resort airport, south of Grave Creek. It was noted that winds could have been stronger in canyons, with estimates closer to 50 mph. The winds caused scattered power outages, with specific reports of an outage in the town of Troy and another outage affecting Montana Highway 56 north of Noxon.
National Weather Service employee reported 2 tree tops blown off with structural damage to a neighbor's roof. Winds estimated to be 53 mph.

The RAWS station at Mount Aeneas (7120 ft) recorded a peak wind gust of 88 mph. Within Glacier National Park, an estimated 10 trees were downed, many of them large Lodgepole Pines with diameters up to 24 inches wide. One of these trees fell onto a parked car at the Lake McDonald Lodge, causing damage. The downed trees also contributed to an 18-hour closure of the Inside North Fork Road and the Quarter Circle Bridge Road leading to Apgar Lookout. The observer at the Thoma Lookout by the Canadian border at 7,112 feet, reported wet snow falling during the early morning hours. Numerous trees were reported on the east side of Swan Lake.
National Weather Service employee reported the metal roof on the Rock Creek Lodge was blown off from thunderstorm winds.
National Weather Service employee reported several cottonwood trees blown down along Interstate 90, 4 miles west of Nimrod. The trees fell onto the highway obstructing traffic.
National Weather Service employee reported that heavy rainfall from a thunderstorms caused a rock and debris slide with some overwash onto the frontage road near Bearmouth Lodge.
National Weather Service employee reported 1.25 inch diameter hail on Interstate 90 between Clinton and the Rock Creek Road exits.
A trained spotter reported an estimated wind gust to 60 mph from a passing thunderstorm.
A trained spotter reported damage to a boat dock and several boats at the Dworshak Reservoir. Numerous trees were also reported blown down, causing a power outage in Orofino with fire starts.
A trained spotter reported penny size hail and numerous trees and branches blown down from downtown Orofino to 5 miles northwest of Orofino.
A trained spotter reported penny size hail. The Dent, ID RAWAS observation station recorded a wind gust of 54 MPH.

Strong sustained and wind gusts were reported by the Snowslip and Logan Pass automated observation stations. Between these two stations sustained winds ranged between 25 to 40 mph with gusts ranging between 50 mph to 84 mph.
A trained spotter reported 0.75 inch hail with a passing thunderstorm.
A trained spotter reported 0.75 inch hail from a passing thunderstorm.
A trained spotter reported 0.75 inch hail from a passing thunderstorm.
A trained spotter reported 0.75 inch hail from a passing thunderstorm.
A trained spotter reported 0.75 inch hail from a thunderstorm.
A trained spotter reported 0.75 inch hail from a thunderstorm.
Police Officer reported to Silver Bow County Dispatch penny sized hail in downtown Butte.
A trained spotter reported 0.5 to 0.75 inch hail.
A trained spotter reported nickel sized hail.

The ASOS station at Kalispell (KGPI) measured a peak gust of 58 mph, with unofficial estimates of frequent gusts near 50 mph along the east shore of Flathead Lake. The winds led to extensive power outages, with over 2,500 customers without power at the peak of the event and at least eight separate instances of downed power lines reported. The winds also caused a pile burn to get away from the owner and cause a shed to catch fire, and a photo showed roof damage to a structure in Yellow Bay.
