Several orchards between Blue Bay and Yellow Bay sustained damage in the form of bruising and cherry, plum and leaf drop. At least three powerline-related wildfires were started: northeast of Bigfork on Highway 83 near Echo Lake, northeast shore of Whitefish Lake as a tree fell onto a line, and near Hilltop Road in Columbia Falls. Flathead Lake exhibited confused seas, with swells arriving from multiple directions. A boat broke loose in the Lakeside area. A 58-year-old male drowned after taking a rowboat out with friends Tuesday morning near Rocky Point July 15.

At 5:35 pm, the Hamilton AWOS reported southerly winds of 41 mph gusting to 49 mph. These damaging gusts caused significant disruption, leading to three separate power outages in the area. At the Hamilton Brewfest, a participant sustained a significant injury when a large tree branch broke and fell onto them. The associated storms also produced dangerous lightning, which ignited at least six new wildfires in the Bitterroot National Forest.
A large Cottonwood tree was downed near mile-marker 27 on Rock Creek Road. The Missoula International Airport(KMSO), recorded peak wind gusts of 60 mph at 1902 and 1909 MDT.

In East Missoula, a wedding tent was collapsed by the winds. Northwest of the Wye, gusts were estimated to be over 50 mph. The University of Montana campus also sustained damage, with several downed trees, one of which fell onto a roof.
Radar estimated 1.41 inches of rain had fallen over the western portion of the Daly burn scar, located west of Skalkaho Pass. A few days later, a rock slide was reported in the vicinity.
Radar-estimated rainfall of 1.77 inches fell in one and a half hours and triggered a debris flow that covered the East Fork Road, east of Sula, at Mile-marker 4.

A thunderstorm over Butte produced hail estimated close to one inch in diameter and caused flash flooding near Schley Avenue. Over an inch of rain fell in one hour, overwhelming local storm drains and leading to a flooded basement, an overflowing manhole, and significant water ponding on streets and in nearby parking lots.

A slow-moving thunderstorm impacted the area northwest of Missoula, producing both large hail and heavy, localized rainfall. Quarter-sized (1.00 inch) hail was estimated via photos near the Frenchtown Mill. The storm's torrential downpour resulted in an official measurement of 0.92 inches at the Missoula International Airport (KMSO), with radar estimating up to 1.40 inches nearby. This intense rainfall overwhelmed drainage systems on Broadway, causing water to flood the eastbound lane. A downed tree was reported on the northbound lane of Highway 83 near milepost 31, north of Summit Lake.
Hail estimated slightly over one inch in diameter was reported in Lolo, an event confirmed by at least two separate photos submitted by local residents.
In Darby, at least two trees were felled, power lines were damaged, and a lightning strike started a grass fire on Gorus Loop.

Strong outflow winds swept through the northern Flathead Valley, with the Elmo MDT station reporting a peak gust of 59 mph. Nearby, the Glacier Park International Airport (KGPI) recorded gusts up to 38 mph. Approximately 100 people were without power. Conditions on Flathead Lake were also hazardous, where a boater near Wildhorse Island reported high winds, white caps, and three-foot swells. Confirming the turbulent weather, a mesonet at the Flathead Lake Biological Station's Narrows site registered a peak wind speed of 45 mph.
Flooding was reported on the Highline Trail. People needed to be rescued, but ongoing thunderstorms prevented helicopter operations.

A line of thunderstorms marched northward across west-central Montana with gusty outflow winds. A gust of 59 mph occurred between Avon and Finn along Highway 141. Similar gusts occurred across the Windy Rock Fire southwest of Finn. No damage was noted.
Thunderstorm outflow winds marched northward through the Bitterroot Valley, resulting in about 20 utility customers losing power. General gusts were 35 to 45 mph topping out near 50 mph.

Low temperatures dropped to 30-33 degrees at Elk City and Powell for the first time in the fall season leading to significant frost and damage to area gardens. Frosty mornings continued through the rest of the week.

Low temperatures dropped to 28-32 degrees at Libby, Marion, and similar-elevation locations for the first time in the fall season, leading to significant frost and damage to area gardens. Frosty mornings continued through the rest of the week.

Morning low temperatures dropped to 28 degrees at typical cold spots such as Polebridge and Condon for the first time in the fall season leading to significant frost and damage to area gardens. Frosty mornings continued the rest of the week.

Morning temperatures dropped to 32-35 degrees in low-lying areas and river bottoms for the first time in the fall season leading to significant frost and damage to area gardens. Frosty mornings continued the rest of the week.
A hail size of one inch in diameter was reported 3 miles north-northwest of Kamiah by a trained spotter.

The Idaho County Sheriff's Office Facebook page reported washouts and subsequent closure on Reservation Line Road near Cottonwood Creek due to heavy rainfall from thunderstorms. A Flood Advisory for the area was issued on the evening of the 11th. The Sheriff's office reported that the road reopened by 1320 PST on the 12th.
Icy conditions necessitated the closure of the Going-to-the-Sun Road within Glacier National Park. The hazardous surface was a direct result of up to 4 inches of snow that fell across the area.

The road report for Highway 2 between Happy's Inn and Kalispell highlighted snow and ice conditions resulting from 2 to 5 inches of total accumulation. Mountain areas received a total snow accumulation of 4 to 8 inches. Below-freezing temperatures and persistent north-to-east winds, with gusts up to 20 mph, were key factors in the rapid and widespread formation of black ice.

A high-impact early-season snow and strong east wind event resulted in the closure of Going-to-the-Sun Road (GTTSR) at Logan Pass due to hazardous ice development beneath 6 to 8 inches of snow and was confirmed by plow operators. Mountain zones across the region (above 5,000 feet) received widespread snowfall ranging from 6 to 25 inches, with the highest accumulations, including 25 inches at Moss Peak, concentrated through the Swan and Mission Ranges. Several crashes and slide-offs were reported by Montana Highway Patrol. Additionally, the event was accompanied by strong winds with gusts to 50 mph along the foothills of the Swan Range, while gusts to 72 mph were recorded at Mount Aeneas.

Strong easterly winds periodically gusted over 50 mph at times in the Flathead Valley, resulting in a few reports of wind damage. A local power company reported a tree fell onto a power line in the Lakeside area, which caused a power outage affecting 1,015 members. An additional power outage was reported in the Lake Blaine area. Meanwhile, up to 3 inches of snow fell on a bench above Lakeside and 1.3 inches was reported in the city of Kalispell.

A combination of snow and ice-covered roads and plummeting temperatures after the passage of an Arctic cold front in the evening hours on the 12th, led to widespread impacts across the area. Public reports indicated multiple accidents between Butte and Anaconda, and several power outages were reported in Deer Lodge County. On the morning of 13th spun-out vehicles blocked the southbound lanes of Interstate 15. Total snow accumulations ranged from 4 inches in Butte, to 6 inches falling west of the city. Winds gusting over 20 mph brought blowing and drifting snow at the passes.

Between Potomac and Ovando, 1 to 2 inches of snow fell, with a maximum of 2.5 inches recorded at Drummond. Conditions rapidly deteriorated as temperatures fell to freezing and below by 2030MDT, contributing to slick road surfaces. Separately, strong gusty winds caused a downed tree in Bonner that blocked the lanes of Highway 200.

The ASOS at Bert Mooney Airport in Butte recorded gusts to 30 mph and visibility of less than one quarter mile with periods of heavy snow and fog from 1020 to about 1050 MST.  The Montana Department of Transportation reported icy, snow-covered roads.  They required chains over Homestake Pass along Interstate 90.  Web cameras showed heavy snow falling at Homestake Pass.  The Missoula Weather Forecast Office issued a Snow Squall Warning.
Web cameras indicated heavy snow falling around West Glacier.  Marias Pass received 0.4 inches of snow-water equivalent.
Social media indicated reports of icy roads on US Highway 35 east of Flathead Lake.  Multiple power lines were down near Somers.

Snotel sites measured 2 inches of snowfall at Hawkins Lake, 6 inches at Banfield Mtn, 3 inches at Grave Creek,  7 inches 1 mile SSE Eureka, 5 inches at Hand Creek, 6 inches at Poorman Creek, and 3 inches at Blacktail Mountain.

Montana Department of Transportation in West Glacier reported 6 to 8 inches, with high amounts in isolated areas. He said they had a little bit of wind, with gusts around 30 mph, with a little blowing and drifting.

There were reports of slick driving in the Mission Valley in the morning, but only saw a couple of slide-offs and accidents.  Ravalli Hill got very slick, enough for 2 tractor trailers to jack-knife.  Five inches of snow fell northeast of Ronan.  Power outages reported by local news.  Wind gusts of 35 mph reported by ASOS at KGPI near Kalispell.
Snotel sites recorded 3 inches of snowfall at Lolo Pass, 5 inches at Black Pine, 5 inches at Skalkaho Summit, and 8 inches at Twin Lakes.
Montana Department of Transportation reported multiple motor vehicle accidents including a jack knifed truck from heavy snow and a flash freeze.

Montana Department of Transportation reported multiple accidents, several of them with injuries. Severe driving conditions from Elliston to MacDonald Pass along US Highway 12.  Observers reported four to six inches of snow.  Winds gusted to 33 mph at Helmville.  Visibility at Bert Mooney Airport (KBTM) in Butte was below one-half mile from 1235 to 1320 MST.
Snotel measured 7 inches of snowfall at Crater Meadows, 5 inches at Hemlock Butte, and 3 inches at Elk Butte.
Snotel reported 3 inches of snowfall at Lolo Pass, 3 inches at Mountain Meadows, and 6 inches at Savage Pass.

Snow accumulations varied across northwest Montana, with 1 to 2 inches reported in Yaak and heavier amounts between 3 to 5 inches from Libby east to Marion. The Montana Department of Transportation reported severe driving conditions on U.S. Highway 93 from Eureka to Dicky Lake and on Highway 37 west towards Lake Koocanusa.

Snowfall amounts in the valleys ranged from 5 and 6 inches between Hungry Horse Dam and West Glacier, with up to 7 inches at Essex. The mountains received 8 to 12 inches of new snow. Along U.S. Highway 2 between Devil���s Creek and Marias Pass, wind gusts between 30 and 40 mph caused blowing and drifting snow, thereby reducing visibility.

Snowfall totals of 2 to 5 inches created icy and hazardous conditions across the region. At Lookout Pass, a crash was reported at 1518MST, with webcams showing vehicle slide-offs by 1630MST. Chains were required at the pass by 1650MST. Later that evening, a crash blocked both eastbound lanes of Interstate 90 east of Alberton starting at 2100MST, where road conditions showed ice. Near the Idaho border, a crash blocked both lanes of Montana Highway 200 between mileposts 0 and 2 near Heron at 2253MST.

Although snowfall totals were modest, ranging from 1.0 to 1.7 inches in Missoula and less than an inch east of Florence, the societal impact was high due to a rapid transition from wet to icy roads. Early afternoon sunshine had warmed pavement temperatures above freezing, causing the initial snowfall at 1620MST to melt on contact. This created a layer of slush and water that was quickly packed down by heavy rush-hour traffic. As the sun set and temperatures continued to fall, this compacted slush froze into a solid, bonded sheet of ice.||The Missoula City Police Department issued a MEANS alert at 1915MST for emergency travel only due to hazardously icy conditions. By 2016MST, the Missoula County Sheriff's Office alerted drivers to avoid Upper Miller Creek Road as it became impassable. Conditions gradually improved as road crews treated the ice, and emergency travel alerts were lifted by 2314MST.

Snowfall totals generally ranged from 4 to 6 inches. Numerous reports of very slick road conditions were received during the evening commute on December 1, particularly from the Flathead Valley south along the shores of Flathead Lake. At one point, an accident blocked U.S. Highway 93 near Somers due to the icy conditions.

Snowfall totals across the Potomac and Seeley Lake regions were light, generally ranging from 0.8 to 2.5 inches. While road temperatures at Bonner reached the mid-30s during the afternoon, northwest winds cooled surfaces toward the freezing mark before snow began. Road temperature sensors at Greenough Hill and Bearmouth remained near or below freezing through the afternoon. Because pavement temperatures had stabilized closer to the air temperature, the widespread melt-refreeze cycle seen in lower valleys was avoided. Impacts were limited to scattered slick spots and standard snow-covered surfaces.
Snowfall totals ranged from 3.8 inches in Pierce to 4 to 6 inches in the mountains. Road temperatures were above freezing before snow began which could have brought localized slick spots.
Snowfall totals were variable across the mountains, ranging from 3 inches at Lolo Pass to 12 inches at Mountain Meadows.

Snowfall totals included 2.2 inches at Woodland and 1.5 inches in Cottonwood. Road temperatures at Greer Grade were 36 degrees before snow began at 1530PST on December 1, creating a risk for localized slick spots.

While valley locations saw 2 to 3 inches of snow before transitioning to rain overnight, sub-freezing surface temperatures created hazardous pockets of freezing rain. The Cabinet Mountains bore the brunt of the storm, recording over two inches of snow water equivalent, equating to approximately 2 feet of new snow; however, because the moisture plume was so narrow, accumulations decreased sharply to the north, with mountains near the Canadian border receiving only 6 to 10 inches. Snow-covered roads were observed during the onset of the snow, particularly at Yaak Hill, Bull Lake, and Crystal Creek.

While lower elevations saw moderate snow accumulations of 2 to 7 inches, including 2.3 inches in West Glacier and 7 inches at Marias Pass, the higher terrain received 1 to 2 feet of new snow. The most hazardous travel conditions were experienced at Marias Pass, where southwest winds gusted to 40 mph, creating blowing and drifting snow until temperatures finally rose above freezing by mid-morning December 6.

Moderate to heavy snow rates quickly overcame warm road temperatures, resulting in widespread snow-covered roads by late afternoon. Total accumulations ranged from 1 to 4.7 inches across the Flathead Valley, with up to 3 inches observed at the SKQ Dam near Polson.

Between 12 and 18 inches of snow fell in the mountains and at Lookout Pass. The Montana Department of Transportation required chains at Lookout Pass. Other snow amounts include 1.5 inches at Heron and 3.6 inches near Trout Creek.

A burst of moderate to heavy snow marked the onset of the event, transitioning to freezing rain overnight. Snowfall amounts were highly variable, with only 1.7 inches measured at Missoula International Airport while up to 5.5 inches near Kelly Island. A CoCoRaHS observer located southeast of Florence reported 2.9 inches of snow. Subsequent showers on the evening of December 6 led to the formation of black ice the following night as temperatures fell to freezing.

Total snow amounts ranged from approximately 16 inches at Lost Trail Pass to 2 feet at Lolo Pass. The immense weight of the wet snow caused temporary power and communication failures for local radio and television stations.

Heavy snow rates developed across the Seeley Lake and Potomac areas on the evening of December 5. While valley accumulations included 7.4 inches in Clinton, 7.5 inches in Seeley Lake, and 9.4 inches at Lindbergh Lake, the surrounding mountains were buried under 2 to 3 feet of new snow. The immense weight of this heavy, wet snow resulted in power outages across the Seeley Lake area during the morning and afternoon of December 6.

Valley snowfall amounts varied, with 4.5 inches reported in Drummond, 2 inches in Butte, and a notable 8.2 inches measured by an observer located 7 miles west of Anaconda. Higher elevations saw even greater totals, including 7 inches at Nevada Ridge, 8 inches at Copper Camp, and up to 10 inches across the Anaconda Range. Severe driving conditions were declared east of Butte including Homestake Pass at 2331MST December 5.

The period of highest impact occurred between 0900PST and 1515PST on December 4, when snowfall rates near 1 inch per hour frequently reduced visibility to less than one mile. The Grangemont area received an estimated 8 inches of new snowfall during that period. The snow changed to freezing rain at night in the lower elevations. The surrounding mountains received 8 to 14 inches of new snowfall.

Between 6 and 7 inches of snow fell between Elk City and Dixie, while the mountains, including both Lolo Pass and Red River Hot Springs, saw much heavier totals of 1 to 2 feet. Precipitation changed to freezing rain at Elk City during the evening of December 5, but air temperatures rose above freezing by midnight.

A period of light to moderate snow resulted in widespread minor accumulations across the lower elevations, including 1.8 inches in Cottonwood, 3.5 inches near Orofino, and 4.4 inches in Woodland. As the system progressed, snow transitioned to rain, causing temperatures to fluctuate and potentially leading to the formation of black ice on road surfaces.

Snowfall totals ranged from 1.5 inches in Salmon, to 6.7 inches in Gibbonsville, to over a foot of snow at Lost Trail Pass. Snowfall changed to rain in the Salmon area at night while low temperatures were below freezing which implies black ice issues.

Power outages affected approximately 400 customers across the Yaak, Bull Lake, Noxon, Libby, and McGregor Lake areas. Additionally, MDT reported a tree in the roadway on Montana 37 (milepost 9), just east of Libby.

Strong winds impacted the canyon regions early on December 6, with valley gusts reaching 50 to 55 mph and mountain peaks seeing gusts between 60 and 80 mph. At 0255MST, a tree was blown into a power line in the Coram area, contributing to outages for approximately 400 customers between Martin City and Essex.

Multiple power poles and lines were knocked down near Jacob���s Island Dog Park, leaving parts of  Missoula and the University of Montana district without power for approximately three hours. The outage delayed the first-ever UM vs. Salish Kootenai College basketball game and impacted traffic lights and businesses along East Broadway. Additionally, a large tree was reported down across US-93 in Darby at milepost 31 at 1616MST.
Power outages were reported from Clinton south to Rock Creek during the early evening hours. Winds were gusting 50 to 60 mph in the higher terrain above.

Notable infrastructure losses included the Farm-to-Market Road state bridge over Libby Creek, the Granite Creek county bridge, Ramsey Creek Bridge at milepost 8.9, Old Town/Libby Creek Bridge 8.1 miles up Libby Creek Road(NFS Road Number 231), West Fisher Road bridge over Lake Creek at about the 5.5 milepost, the Lower Granite Creek Bridge at milepost 2.5 on National Forest Service(NFS) Road 4791, Whoopie Creek Bridge(NFS Road 384) near Spar Lake in the Troy District, and Keeler Creek took out the Lake Creek Road county bridge(NFS Road 473) and the county levee in Troy. Additional washouts occurred on Libby Creek Road (NFS Road 231) at mileposts 0.9 and and about 25.0 and along NFS Road 384 where it was washed out due to a landslide past the Whoopie Creek Bridge. The Hiatt Creek Bridge(NFS Road 384) near Spar Lake sustained damage. While the Ross Creek bridge survived the flood, the creek bed beneath it rose significantly. Floodwaters deposited so much rock and gravel that the space under the bridge was reduced from 8 feet to 6 inches, leaving no room for water to pass. The West Fisher Road lost about 600 feet of road at milepost 25.5, and the Poorman Creek culvert washout on NFS Road 278/Bear Creek Road. The Upper Young Creek Road, NFS Road number 7202, located northwest of West Kootenai, was made impassable between milepost 3.5 and 3.6 due to a landslide. The Kootenai National Forest Service remarked that there were other bridges that incurred minor damage and they will have to repair some of the abutments. ||In the Ross Creek Cedars recreation area, the newly reconstructed facilities and trails���completed just months prior at a cost of approximately $1.9 million���sustained major damage. The access route, NFS Road 398, was compromised by multiple landslides and debris deposits, including a large slide that taken half the road and a compromised bridge where Ross Creek Road crosses Ross Creek. ||In Libby, Cherry Creek jumped its banks to flood subdivisions along Cherry Creek Drive and Claire Avenue, while Libby Creek inundated homes near Champion Haul Road and Riverdale Drive, cutting off residents and submerging properties under nearly a foot of water on Vicks Lane. The Lower Flower Creek Diversion Dam was nearly compromised by debris and high sediment, resulting in a long-term boil water advisory for the City of Libby. For a time, the 5th Street Bridge in Libby was under water. Water was also across the road on West 2nd Street Extension by Parmenter Creek. ||In Troy, Callahan Creek washed away a 15-foot rock barrier, and Iron Creek caused flooding in multiple residences. Road 427/Callahan Road had 2 washouts (3.4 mile and 6 mile). Washout on road 473/Keeler Road.  The Poorman Creek SNOTEL, located in the Cabinet Mountains south of Libby, reported 5.10 inches of rainfall in 24 hours. This marked the wettest 24-hour period within the month of December, and the third highest for any time of the year. The Yaak River near Troy crested at 8.3 feet(7,940 cubic feet per second) at 1130MST on December 11, while the Fisher River near Libby reached 7.67 feet(4,710 cubic feet per second) at 2115MST.

Heavy rain in the mountains caused flooding and significant erosion of forest service roads in western Mineral County.   In the Superior Ranger District, the Deer Creek Bridge was compromised as the St. Regis River eroded the north bank, severely damaging the surrounding roadbed. Further west, reports from the Ward Creek drainage (National Forest Service Road 889) confirmed a complete washout, forcing the closure of a 7-mile stretch from Milepost 4.5 to 11.9.  A hunter driving out of the mountains along Big Creek reported driving through feet of water at times and encountering falling trees that blocked the road. A plugged pipe at Milepost 1.5 up the East Fork of Big Creek caused the road to be completely covered with rock and debris.

Multiple power outages were reported throughout the Yaak area, as well as the corridor extending from Bull Lake south to Noxon. Strong winds also downed a tree on U.S. Highway 2 at milepost 9.0, resulting in the closure of both lanes. The Montana Department of Transportation reported the blockage began at 2143 MST on the 15th.

Strong winds late on the 15th resulted in widespread tree damage between Columbia Falls and Pinnacle, with dozens of trees snapped or uprooted. The Hungry Horse Fire Department remained on scene overnight to clear debris from secondary roads. Significant structural and property damage was reported: one tree pierced a vehicle, and another demolished a residence. The occupant of the home narrowly escaped with minor bruises and scrapes. Approximately 4,000 customers across the region lost power during the peak of the event.

At approximately 0400MST on December 11, a massive landslide occurred near Eagle View Lane, roughly 2 miles south-southwest of Bull Lake. The debris flow significantly damaged a residential garage, and the residents were unharmed. An Emergency Declaration was issued to address the lowland flooding and debris removal. Highway 56 near Bull Lake was forced to close between mileposts 16.7 and 17.2 after overwhelmed culverts allowed stream overflow to inundate the roadway. The emergency manager reported that over a dozen properties were isolated from Highway 56, either by a foot of water over access bridges or by an approximate 50-yard-wide flow of sediment-laden water separating residences from the main road. |A bridge on Montana Highway 471/Thompson Pass Road, near milepost 15, was washed out by Prospect Creek, resulting in a road closure. Prospect Creek also flooded the Prospect Creek campground at the Wild Coyote, located 7 miles up Prospect from Highway 200.

At 0940 MST, the Lincoln County Sheriff���s Office issued an Emergency Travel Only order as downed trees and power lines rendered major routes���including US-2 and MT-56���impassable. In Libby, a failure of the cellular network created a communications gap for emergency services during the peak of the event.||Property damage was widespread; numerous homes and structures were struck by falling timber, including a home 4 miles NW of Troy and a garage up Pipe Creek. Private losses were notable, including multiple totaled greenhouses and several vehicles crushed by falling Ponderosa pines, such as a late-model truck near the Libby airport and another at Bull Lake. Utility infrastructure was hit hard; numerous downed poles resulted in a total system outage for Lincoln Electric, while Northern Lights and Flathead Electric reported extensive damage to lines, with some Libby-area customers remaining without power for nearly a week. Blacktail Mountain Ski Area was forced to suspend lift operations due to storm-related complications with lift lines.|Due to mild temperatures and additional precipitation, the Yaak River nearly reached minor flood stage on December 17.

Glacier National Park reported that at least 50 trees fell down along the Going-To-The-Sun Road, Camas Road and bike paths. Multiple trees were reported down 10 miles northwest of Essex, laying against power lines and several had blocked U.S. Highway 2 at Milepost 171. Trees were also blown down on Big Mountain Road leading up to the ski resort. Flathead Electrical COOP reported that over 30,000 members were without power by mid-day of the 17th. They restored most of the power by Christmas Eve.

The Lemhi River exceeded action stage on the 27th and reached minor flood stage on the 28th. This caused yard flooding south of Tendoy, between Mabee Lane and McDevitt Creek Road, though no homes were impacted. The river crested at 7.07 feet at 2:00 PM MST on the 29th at the Lemhi River near Lemhi gauge, then receded that evening as ice broke up.

Social media reports indicated widespread black ice resulting in hazardous driving conditions across the area. Multiple vehicle accidents and slide-offs occurred on Highways 93 and 35, as well as at local intersections including KM Ranch Road. At least one vehicle was totaled.
Widespread 1 to 2 inch snow amounts brought slick roads to many valley locations.

Light to moderate snow fell across the region, with the heaviest accumulations of 2 to 3 inches occurring across the Flathead Valley. These totals resulted in slick road conditions for much of the area. Further south, the Mission Valley saw only minor accumulations, with totals generally remaining under 1 inch.
Snow covered roads brought moderate travel impacts with 1 to 3 inches of snow common for lower elevations.
Slick roads occurred with lane blockage for a time near Lookout Pass on Interstate 90 as 1 to 3 inches of snow fell.
A light wintry mix brought very slippery conditions to area roadways. Snow amounts were generally less than an inch with up to a tenth of ice accumulation from freezing rain.
A light wintry mix brought changeable and slippery roads. A crash blocked a lane on Interstate 90 for a time west of Drummond.

A light wintry mix resulted in slick road conditions across the area. On Homestake Pass, chain requirements were put into effect due to the conditions. A vehicle crash associated with the weather blocked both westbound lanes of Interstate 90 just west of the Pass.

A light wintry mix resulted in road conditions described as slick as can be on Highway 14 in Elk City. Light rain fell while temperatures remained near freezing for several locations, including Elk City and near Syringa.
Mountain SNOTEL gauges reported 1.8 to 2.1 inches of precipitation, which fell as 12 to 14 inches of snow. Below approximately 4000 feet, a wintry mix occurred, resulting in slick roadways.

Wet snow caused power outages for approximately 900 customers near Fenn and southwest of Elk City. SNOTEL measurements at Lolo Pass recorded 1.3 inches of moisture, resulting in 13 inches of new snow. These conditions led to chain requirements at Lolo Pass for a period during the evening of the 6th.
Heavy, wet snowfall of 3 to 5 inches fell in the valleys, resulting in localized power outages near Heron. Icy roads led to at least one car accident and numerous reports of slick conditions.

Lookout Ski reported heavy snow with 16 inches of new accumulation.  Dispatch reported that semi-trucks blocked Interstate 90 at Lookout Pass, where 7 to 8 vehicles spun out and some travelers remained stuck overnight. In fact, between 4:00 AM and 5:00 AM on the 7th, the Mullan Pass ASOS estimated intense snowfall rates of 2 to 3 inches per hour. Additionally, the Heron 2 NW COOP station reported 6.7 inches of new snow, and power outages were noted in Haugan for a period of time. An additional 2 inches of new snow fell at the Lookout SNOTEL site on the 8th.
Lolo Pass SNOTEL reported 13 inches of new snow with webcams showing snow covered roadways.

Snow Squall. The main event was a snow squall that marched through parts of southwest Montana, specifically the Butte area, between 9:30 AM and 10:00 AM MST. During this time, visibilities dropped below a quarter mile with peak wind gusts reaching 33 mph. A few weather-related accidents were reported during the squall.

A historic high wind event impacted the Flathead and Mission Valleys on December 17, 2025, as a powerful cold front brought high winds acting on soils super-saturated by a preceding atmospheric river. Peak gusts frequently exceeded 60 mph across the valley floors, including 67 mph at 0855MST at Glacier Park International Airport, 64 mph at 0915MST at Elmo, and 62 mph at 0900MST at the Creston Agrimet station. The Flathead County Sheriff's Office issued a travel advisory at 1000MST due to hazardous conditions and widespread disruptions. Significant transportation impacts included the closure of US-93 near Somers after a semi-truck was blown across the roadway, and multiple lane blockages on MT-35, MT-200, and Big Mountain Road between 0740MST and 1313MST due to fallen trees and power lines.||Utility infrastructure sustained damage that Flathead Electric Cooperative described as unprecedented and one of the most challenging in their 88-year history. At the 1200MST peak, over 30,000 meters were without power. The combination of high winds and unstable root structures sent trees into lines, causing over 150 individual outages. In Lake County, 5,166 Mission Valley Power customers remained without power as late as 1500MST, with some outages persisting past 1800 MST. These extended outages forced many grocery stores and residents to dispose of all fresh and frozen inventory after being without power for over eight hours.||Property damage was widespread; falling timber caused roof damage to homes in Polson and significant structural damage at the historic Conrad Mansion in Kalispell, where a tree destroyed a gazebo. Public and recreational icons were also affected; the iconic Bigfork cross was destroyed. Flathead County officials described the aftermath as devastating, and final power restoration for the last Flathead Electric members was not completed until 1000MST on December 24.

Extreme gusts battered Sanders and Mineral Counties on December 17, with peak wind reports including 69 mph at 0800MST at the Plains AWOS and 57 mph at the Thompson Falls RAWS. The dangerous conditions prompted an urgent Do Not Travel alert from the Community Ambulance Service of Western Sanders County at 0830MST because live power lines and falling trees completely blocked roadways. Major transportation corridors were heavily impacted: a downed tree blocked a lane of I-90 Westbound at 0725MST, fallen trees blocked the Eastbound I-90 Tarkio exit at 0845MST, a semi-truck crash completely blocked MT-200 at 0940MST, and downed power lines forced the closure of Highway 10 West near Huson at 1120MST.||Utility infrastructure suffered catastrophic damage from falling timber. In Mineral County, over 80 percent of tracked customers (4,002 meters) lost power. Sanders County experienced similar devastation, with 4,481 customers, roughly 47 percent of the county, losing electricity. The power outages were so widespread and prolonged that approximately 250 residents utilized a warming shelter in Mineral County two days after the initial event. High-elevation recreation was also impacted, with Lookout Pass Ski Resort losing power by 0735MST, alongside reports of widespread timber blowdowns across its ski runs.||Structural and property damage was severe and widespread across the zone. At 0930MST, severe winds ripped sections of the roof off Thompson Falls Elementary School. In Haugan, falling timber struck the Savenac Historic Tree Nursery and Visitor Center, causing significant roof damage. In Huson, an uprooted tree lifted a camper and twisted it entirely off its jacks. Meanwhile, at Quinn's Hot Springs south of Paradise, an estimated 75 large trees were toppled by the winds, compounding the massive cleanup efforts required across the region.

Peak wind reports across the Missoula and Bitterroot Valleys included 88 mph at the Stevensville Airport at 0956MST, 68 mph at the Little Rock Creek RAWS at 1009MST, 66 mph at the Stevi RAWS at 1014MST, and 61 mph at the Missoula Airport at 0853MST. Hazardous conditions and flying debris severely impacted travel. The Missoula Police Department advised against all unnecessary travel at 0933MST. At 0915MST, fallen trees blocked the left lane of S-203 Southbound, and at 1026MST, US-93 was completely blocked by fallen trees between mile markers 4 and 5. In Missoula, a massive tree fell across West Broadway at Birch Street, pinning a driver inside a vehicle, though they were not injured. Downed trees and power lines also forced the sustained closure of Gharrett Street around 1345MST. In Ravalli County, the Sheriff's Office issued an Emergency Travel Only order as power outages disabled traffic lights and debris blocked numerous roads, including Daly Avenue and Old Corvallis Road. ||Falling timber caused catastrophic damage to utility infrastructure. By 1500MST, approximately 30 percent of Ravalli County (7,433 customers) and nearly 7,000 customers in Missoula County were without power. A prominent transmission pole was left leaning precariously over North Reserve Street near Costco in Missoula. Critical services were interrupted; the Ravalli County Airport lost power around 0914MST, and the Hamilton VA Clinic was forced to close completely due to a lack of power and water. Outages were so extensive that they persisted for thousands of customers well into December 19, and final power restoration for Missoula Electric Cooperative members was not completed until 0300MST on December 24. ||Structural and property damage was severe. Around 0930MST, intense winds ripped sections of the roof off Jefferson School in Missoula. In Frenchtown, a community pavilion near the elementary school was destroyed. Numerous massive trees crashed into homes and vehicles, including a large pine striking a house between Stevensville and Florence, massive fir trees landing on homes on South Third and Fourth Streets in Hamilton, and a spruce tree crushing two trucks on Pine Street in Stevensville. Schools across the region, including in Frenchtown and Hamilton, were forced to close or issue shelter-in-place holds as conditions deteriorated and phone lines failed.

Extreme winds battered the higher elevations, with a weather station atop Mount Sentinel (5,026 feet) serving as a proxy for the surrounding peaks.  This station recorded a sustained wind of 76 mph and a staggering peak gust of 99 mph from the west-northwest at 0900MST, with gusts consistently exceeding 70 to 90 mph throughout the morning and into the afternoon. Along Highway 12 between Lolo and Lolo Pass, the Montana Department of Transportation warned motorists to limit travel as strong winds blew trees, debris, and rocks onto the roadway around 0820MST west of milepost 32.6. Widespread power outages were reported throughout the area, including significant disruptions up Petty Creek noted by emergency services on the evening of December 17.||Recreational areas experienced staggering timber blowdowns, with snowmachine and cross-country trails covered by hundreds of fallen trees. The Bitterroot Cross-Country Ski Club described it as one of the biggest windstorms they had experienced in years. At the Lolo Pass Visitor Center, officials noted extensive damage with trees completely blocking all cross-country trails. At Chief Joseph Pass, the Bitterroot Cross-Country Ski Club reported hundreds of downed trees; crews had to clear over 150 trees on December 18 just to reopen three main skiable trails. The massive cleanup efforts extended for months; the Missoula Snowgoers Snowmobile Association reported removing 62 trees from a single trail near Lolo Hot Springs as late as February 17, 2026. In the Bitterroot National Forest, Lost Horse Road had multiple trees down across the road and sustained damage to campgrounds.

Peak wind gusts included 60 mph at 0846MST at the Bonner I-90 weather station near milepost 110.3. Hazardous conditions and falling timber severely impacted travel corridors throughout the region. East of Hellgate Canyon, a fallen tree partially blocked the westbound off-ramp of I-90 at milepost 107.0 at 1126MST. Highway 200 was closed east of Bonner for a couple of hours due to trees down across both lanes. Along Highway 83, the Montana Department of Transportation issued an obstruction warning for falling trees from milepost 12.0 to 51.0 at 0920MST. Specific blockages on MT-83 included a downed tree causing a partial southbound blockage at milepost 38.5 at 0850MST, and a complete lane blockage at milepost 19.0 near Seeley Lake at 1330MST due to trees and power lines down. The Missoula County Sheriff's Office issued an alert at 1426MST noting traffic delays in both directions from the 19-mile marker. In Clinton, trees were reported down on the roadway at Wallace Creek Road around 1200MST.|Utility infrastructure sustained massive damage. Around 1200MST, power was reported out on Wallace Creek Road in Clinton. By 1800MST on December 17, emergency services reported that a substation was down in the Helmville area, and utility crews were responding to outages in Condon, Placid Lake, and Double Arrow. Thousands of customers remained without power, with the last customer gaining power by 0300MST December 24.

Extreme wind gusts battered the region, including 76 mph near Avon at 1017MST, 62 mph at the Yankee Flat RAWS at 1040MST, and 58 mph at the Bearmouth MDT at 1132MST. MacDonald Pass on US-12 experienced prolonged severe conditions following a cold front passage at 0847MST, which delivered an initial peak gust of 62 mph, then a maximum sustained wind of 51 mph recorded at 1430MST and gusts peaked at 75 mph at 1700MST. Bert Mooney Airport recorded a peak gust of 67 mph at 1353MST. ||Butte-Silver Bow Emergency Management issued a severe weather alert at 0925MST, urging residents to remain indoors, limit travel to emergencies only, and avoid windows due to flying debris, downed trees, and live power lines. By 1330MST, reports indicated high winds left trees either sheared mid-trunk or completely toppled throughout the Butte area. The top half of a massive fir tree snapped on Quartz Street in Uptown Butte, and a spruce tree planted in the 1930s crushed and totaled a parked car in the same neighborhood. The storm compromised the power grid with live downed lines triggering several small ground fires. The destruction was so severe that a representative from the Montana Standard described it as the worst wind damage they had ever witnessed. Law enforcement maintained an emergency-only travel advisory as crews worked throughout the day to clear streets of fallen trees and debris. Also a downed power substation was reported in the Helmville area.

SNOTEL reports showed 5 to 12 inches of new snow, while webcams and road reports indicated snow-covered roadways. These conditions led to chain requirements near Marias Pass on the morning of the 7th, where a vehicle crash resulted in blocked lanes.

The Dent RAWS, located at 1,700 feet, reported wind gusts up to 55 mph between 0508PST and 0608PST, and 57 mph between 0608PST and 0708PST. Fallen trees completely blocked roads and access points throughout the county. Widespread tree damage was noted across central and eastern Clearwater County, including North Fork Road, which was completely blocked by fallen timber between Quartz Creek and Washington Creek. |The storm caused severe, localized utility impacts. At 0710PST on December 17, 2,613 out of 5,960 tracked customers (nearly 44 percent) were without power in Clearwater County. Across Clearwater Power's broader network, power was eventually restored to over 10,750 members, but at least 250 members remained without power through the Christmas holiday.

A falling tree struck a semi-truck at milepost 96 on US-12, just one mile west of Lowell. In an accident near Elk City, a truck was struck by mud and trees sliding down a hillside, while a motorist on SH-13 had a tree fall through their vehicle windshield. Blockages including multiple downed trees, rocks and landslides were reported along State Highway 14. ||Utility infrastructure was devastated, leading to massive and prolonged power outages. By 0637PST on December 17, over 27 percent of tracked customers in Idaho County (1,638 meters) had lost power. To address the widespread outages, Avista deployed more than 45 line crews, 36 contract crews, and 30 vegetation management crews, supported by hundreds of additional employees. Through this massive response, 86 percent of Avista accounts across the region were restored by December 18. Restoration efforts for remote locations like Elk City and Dixie, as well as the Cove area east of Grangeville, safely extended into subsequent days.||Property and infrastructure damage extended deep into the backcountry. At Red River Hot Springs, multiple trees were reported down. Public lands agencies reported significant storm-related damage to facilities. The Nez Perce-Clearwater National Forests noted catastrophic damage at the Fish Creek Recreation Area outside Grangeville, where multiple trees crushed the pit toilet building, pavilion, and parking lot.

An Idaho Transportation Department weather station at Concrete Section recorded a peak gust of 75 mph at 0700PST and multiple instances of sustained winds between 40 and 44 mph between 0600 and 0815PST. The top of Greer Grade measured a 73 mph gust between 0600PST and 0615PST. The Idaho County Sheriff's Office reported that most county roads were blocked or partially blocked by downed trees. Travel was highly discouraged, and official travel not recommended advisories were issued by 1100PST. Emergency responders dealt with multiple highway blockages, including State Highway 13 which was completely shut down between mileposts 6 and 11 due to power lines lying across the roadway, as well as large rocks and trees, and the stretch between Orofino and Peck was described as horrible with trees down everywhere.||In Cottonwood, police reported extreme damage including missing roofs and doors blown completely off a Primeland grain elevator. Downed trees crushed a parked car on 3rd Street, and blocked both King and Myrtle streets, and another massive tree crashed through the roof of a house just moments after a child had left their bed. Near Orofino, a large tree branch pierced the roof of a trailer home in Hidden Village, displacing the residents who were subsequently assisted by the Red Cross. In Grangeville, shingles were blown off roofs, and between Fenn and Tolo Lake, the wind lifted a 40x60 foot open alley barn, moving it 6 to 8 feet off its foundation.||Nearly 4,000 customers lost power in the Idaho County area alone, with regional afternoon totals exceeding 4,600 without power. Broken phone poles, large branches in power lines, and widespread infrastructure damage led to prolonged, multi-day outages, with over 1,000 Clearwater Power customers still without electricity by the evening of December 19. Due to the severe hazards and power loss, numerous regional school districts were forced to cancel classes, including Grangeville, Kamiah, Cottonwood, Orofino (SD 171), and several private academies.

events.cz_name: LOWER HELLS CANYON / SALMON RIVER REGION
events.event_narrative: Power outages were reported across the region due to strong winds.
The Skull Gulch RAWS at 5,878 feet recorded gusts between 60 and 73 mph between 0851MST and 1051MST. Utility companies reported power outages due to trees down across southeastern Idaho.

Lemhi County County dispatch reported at least 3 trees were down. There were multiple weather stations that reported wind gusts above 70 mph for multiple hours. The Idaho Power station on Sandy Creek Road recorded a sustained wind speed of 48 mph with a peak gust of 76 mph at 0900MST.

The Hungry Horse RAWS recorded a peak wind gust of 66 mph between 0311MST and 0411MST, followed by subsequent gusts of 55 mph and 57 mph through 0611MST.||The high winds caused immediate and severe utility disruptions. Flathead Electric Cooperative reported that the main lines feeding West Glacier and the Canyon were down. By 0730MST, approximately 8,600 members across their service territory had lost power. While crews made significant progress throughout the day, the Flathead County Sheriff's Office reported that approximately 3,000 electric meters remained without power by 1600MST.||Additional property and infrastructure damage was reported within Glacier National Park and the surrounding corridors. Park dispatch reported two 12-inch diameter trees fell at the foot of Lake McDonald, and another tree blocked a local bike path. In the Apgar area, a large fir tree crashed onto a cabin, requiring a crane for removal. Travel was also impacted, with the Montana Department of Transportation reporting 8 to 9 downed trees blocking the route between Essex and Goat Lick.
The Flathead Electric Co-op reported that several poles on Blacktail Mountain were snapped from the strong winds.

Heavy snow and strong winds brought blizzard conditions to the backcountry, severely impacting mountain passes on December 18 and 19. SNOTEL sensors recorded massive gains, including a 17-inch snow depth increase at Lolo Pass and 12 inches at Saddle Mountain. |Travel conditions deteriorated rapidly on the afternoon of December 18 as intense snowfall rates���including 1 inch per hour near West Fork���led to rapid accumulation on roadways despite ongoing mitigation efforts. Wind gusts of 25 to 35 mph at Lost Trail Pass created localized blizzard-like conditions with near-zero visibility. The treacherous weather caused severe transportation disruptions on US-12, triggering a chain requirement between mile markers 0 and 4 by 1913MST. The following morning, an incident completely blocked both lanes at milepost 2.0, leading to an official declaration of Severe Driving Conditions that lasted through midday on December 19.

As conditions rapidly deteriorated on the afternoon of December 18, highway officials issued a chains required restriction at 1530MST. Just fifteen minutes later, at 1545MST, a semi-truck spun out in the hazardous conditions, completely blocking the westbound lanes of the highway. The Lookout Pass SNOTEL reported a 5-inch snow depth increase.

The Idaho side of the Bitterroot crest absorbed heavy moisture from the atmospheric river, leading to high-impact winter conditions right along the Lolo Pass border. Further down the Highway 12 corridor at Powell, intense snowfall rates dropped 5 inches of snow in just a 6-hour period during the afternoon and evening of December 18. In Dixie, 6.5 inches of snow fell.

In Salmon, the COOP observer reported 5 inches of snowfall. Lost Trail Pass saw periods of heavy snow and blowing snow at times. The Moose Creek SNOTEL, located just south of the pass, reported 14 inches of snow depth increase during the storm.

Snowfall totals were generally light across the zone, ranging from 1 to 3 inches in the Libby and Yaak areas. Roadways including Highway 2, Highway 37, and Highway 56 became covered in snow, slush, and ice, leading to slick travel during the morning commute.

While total snowfall accumulations remained low, the primary impact was dangerous icing on regional roadways. Black ice was reported on Highway 93 near Polson, and icy patches were noted along Highway 28, creating slick travel conditions throughout the area.

Light wintry precipitation, including probable freezing rain, led to slick travel along Interstate 90 west of Alberton and near St. Regis. Additionally, a hazardous layer of black ice formed on the Highway 200 bypass between Thompson Falls and Plains, causing vehicles to slide and lose traction at highway speeds.

Initially, the region received 0.5 to 0.7 inches of snow before the precipitation transitioned to freezing rain during the early morning hours of December 22. Scattered slick conditions led to a couple of accidents, including a fatal crash on US-93 at the Stevensville bridge, forcing the closure of the bridge. An additional accident was reported at the cross streets Eastside and Wheatland near 3 Mile.
Observers reported of 10 inches of snow at Lost Trail Pass. Meanwhile, possible freezing rain was reported along US-12 west of Lolo.
Slick roads were reported east of Greenough Hill to Helmville on Highway 200. A CoCoRaHS observer reported 1.7 inches of snow in Seeley Lake.

Periods of freezing rain occurred from Drummond to Butte and created very slick conditions along Interstate 90. The icing contributed to a rollover accident near the Philipsburg/Drummond exit, completely blocking the eastbound lanes of Interstate 90 and causing significant travel delays. Less than an inch of snow fell west of Anaconda, Drummond, and in Ovando.
While 4 to 6 inches of snow fell at both Lolo Pass and Dixie, the higher elevations of the Bitterroot Mountains received over a foot of snowfall.
The Gibbonsville COOP reported a 2-day snow total of 13 inches of snow. A CoCoRaHS observer in Salmon recorded 5.8 inches of snow.

Along Interstate 90 between Drummond and Garrison Junction, freezing rain contributed to at least 6 accidents. At 1125MST a small car lost control, slid into the eastbound lane and crashed into a tractor trailer. All three people in the car were declared dead(indirect) on the scene. The road conditions were described as wet and icy.

Snow Squall conditions developed along the Interstate 90 corridor extending from Lookout Pass to St. Regis. Lookout Pass enacted a chains required restriction for towing units at 2117MST. Severe travel impacts with poor visibility and life-threatening driving conditions were subsequently noted near Taft (mile marker 6.4) by 2145MST. A brief period of severe driving conditions along Highway 200, northwest of Thompson Falls, was  reported by the Montana Department of Transportation around 0200MST on the 27th.

Snow Squall: The Missoula International Airport (KMSO) recorded a rapid drop in visibility to one-quarter mile in heavy snow, accompanied by wind gusts up to 39 MPH. The intense squall deposited 0.9 inches of new snow in just 30 minutes.

Snow Squall impacted Interstate 90 from east Missoula to Bearmouth. This prompted the activation of a Wireless Emergency Alert (WEA) for communities including Clinton, Potomac, and Greenough due to continued whiteout visibilities and dangerous, life-threatening travel conditions. Earlier on the 27th, strong winds associated with the frontal passage brought trees down north of Seeley Lake, blocking Highway 83 near mile marker 26.

A strong Pacific cold front brought periods of heavy snow showers, depositing between 1 and 4 inches of snow. Travel along Highway 2 from Libby to Marion became hazardous and was described as awful. Additionally, a tree fell into power lines along the Highway 2 corridor west of Kalispell, causing an outage for approximately 1,000 Flathead Electric Cooperative members.
The COOP observer in Essex reported 4.8 inches of snow, while 3.7 inches of snow fell in West Glacier. A power outage impacted over 300 customers due to strong winds in the Essex area.

A strong cold front brought snow and rapidly dropping temperatures, leading to slick roadways. Snowfall amounts varied from 1 to 3 inches. Traffic going north on Highway 93 outside of Whitefish was stopped after several vehicles slid off the road. A weak Arctic cold front brought enhanced snowfall across the east side of Flathead Lake during the afternoon hours of the 27th.

Heavy snow showers combined with gusty winds to 36 mph brought slick conditions and low visibility, especially from Helmville to Elliston and MacDonald pass. An Arctic cold front pushed westwards and caused temperatures to drop to the single digits below zero.

A weather spotter 7 miles west of Anaconda reported 5 inches of total snowfall. During the morning of the 9th, several vehicle accidents occurred across the region. A rollover was reported at mile-marker 4 on US-12 near MacDonald Pass, followed by a second rollover near Garrison Junction. A jackknifed truck was reported at MacDonald Pass and a separate crash blocked Montana Highway 1 near Philipsburg.

Multiple traffic incidents were reported, including a vehicle rollover on Highway 93 south of Missoula near the Buckhouse Bridge. An additional accident was reported on Highway 93 near Lolo, resulting in a temporary lane closure. Local observers reported heavy snow in the Lolo area at approximately 0700MST, with temperatures hovering near 29 degrees Fahrenheit.

On the morning of February 15, 2026, a head-on collision involving two SUVs occurred on Highway 200 just west of Bear Creek. The accident resulted in three injuries requiring hospitalization and a two-hour closure of the highway. Precipitation totals in the vicinity of the accident ranged from 0.10 to 0.22 inches.

Heavy snowfall impacted the US-93 and US-2 corridors. Eureka received 5 inches of snow, and a nearby location, southeast of Eureka, reported 7.5 inches of snow. A CoCoRaHS observer in Marion reported 3.8 inches. Arctic air seeped south after midnight, leading to slick roads and a flipped truck reported north of Eureka at 0855MST.

Intense overrunning mechanisms led to high snowfall rates, with Hungry Horse receiving 8 inches of snow in only 7 hours.  At the Essex MDT sensor, the primary Arctic cold front passed between 0700MST and 0800MST producing gusty winds and snowfall. A secondary Arctic surge between by 2200MST on the 17th caused temperatures to drop to 6 degrees Fahrenheit, with wind gusts up to 33 mph creating wind chills as low as 15 degrees Fahrenheit below zero. Nearby, the Summit station recorded approximately 2 inches of snow in less than one hour between 1400MST and 1500MST on the 17th.

Snow Squall. Multiple accidents occurred as heavy snow fell during the morning commute in the Flathead Valley. At 0850MST, an accident was reported in Ferndale, followed by a spun-out semi-truck that blocked both lanes of travel north of Yellow Bay at 0915MST. A crash at 1138MST also blocked both directions of MT-83 at milepost 87.4. For snow amounts, between 3 and 5 inches fell in the Flathead Valley, and between 1 and 5 inches of snow fell in the Mission Valley. |On the afternoon of February 18, a snow squall developed as the Arctic cold front caused temperatures to drop from 34 degrees to 23 degrees over Ravalli Hill, located south of St. Ignatius. This squall produced whiteout conditions and rapid icing as snow accumulated on road surfaces that were previously above freezing. Multiple high-impact accidents were reported along US-93, including a head-on collision at  1550MST near mile marker 11 and a multi-vehicle crash at 1831MST that blocked both lanes between mile markers 26 and 29 on Ravalli Hill. Observers reported semi-trucks sliding sideways and traffic backed up for over half an hour on the icy grade of Ravalli Hill.

Snow showers combined with breezy south winds less than 20 mph brought slick conditions and low visibility to the Butte area. These conditions led to multiple injury crashes on I-15 and I-90. Incidents included a crash with injuries just west of Butte on I-90 between 1330MST and 1430MST, and three injury crashes on I-15 just inside Silver Bow County between 1400MST and 1500MST.

Widespread snowfall amounts of 4 to 8 inches were estimated across the zone, with the highest totals near Headquarters. ITD sensors near Grangemont recorded 0.60 inches of liquid equivalent, with roughly 0.45 inches falling as snow after temperatures dropped below freezing at 2115MST on the 16th.
Moderate snowfall impacted the region, with Grangeville recording 6 inches of snow and Woodland received 3 inches.
Homestake Pass eastbound over Interstate 90 was closed from roughly 0500 to 0800MST.  About 10 inches of snow was reported at Discovery Ski Area.

There were 328 without power in the Troy area and Montana Department of Transportation reported a tree blocking part of US-2 north of Troy. There were 159 without power due to a tree on a power line in the Ashley Lake area. There were 48 without power north of Libby.
About 400 people were without power along Highway 2.
Montana Department of Transportation reported on Highways 2 and 37.  The crash on Highway 37 resulted in a fatality.  An observer reported a storm total of 17 inches in Marion.

Montana Department of Transportation in West Glacier reported 10 downed trees.  They received 2 feet of snow in Essex, 14 inches at Marias Pass.  Chains were required on Marias Pass on March 11 at 21:12.  Winds gusted to 49 mph near the Marias Pass summit.

From the afternoon on the 12th through the afternoon on the 14th snow amounts ended up being impressive, in the 6-12 inch range.  Power outages were reported and lasted into Sunday the 15th. Multiple trees had fallen in the Flathead and Mission Valleys especially by Friday and Saturday (March 13-14) with the heavy wet snow falling. Power outages/tree issues were also found in other areas of west-central Montana.  On Sunday March 15, Polson Rural Fire District responded to numerous calls including downed trees and powerlines and a vehicle slide-off. According to Mission Valley Power there were several power outages in their area including Melita Island Rd/Wilderness Valley, Rocky Point/Kings Point areas, and Hellroaring Road.  |There were lots of downed power lines in Rocky Point where power was out for over 30 hours.  Blackfoot Communication reported telephone lines and power were out 6 miles east of St. Ignatius on Saturday March 14.  Snow totals from CoCoRaHS for March 13-14 (Fri-Sat) were 3 to 4 inches in the Flathead, 8 inches in Polson, and 7.5 inches in Ronan.  Much of the power outages and trees down occurred with the heavy snow Friday night March 13.

Montana Department of Transportation required chains for Lookout Pass on Interstate 90 on two occasions: 0530MST and again at 1843MST.  The interstate was blocked in both directions by a semi trailer.  On the morning of March 14, Lookout Pass Ski Area had reported 35 inches of new snow in 48 hours, 49 inches in 72 hours.

Wet, heavy snow snapped tree limbs which fell on power lines, causing several power outages in the Missoula and Bitterroot valleys.  Missoula COOP reported 2500 customers without power on the night of March 13.

This storm was a major snow producer.  Montana Department of Transportation cited severe driving conditions and chains required on Highway 12 over Lolo Pass.  Storm total snow for Twin Lakes SNOTEL on the Bitterroot Crest was 43 inches, with 8.10 inches of snow-water equivalent.  Lost Trail Pass got 43 inches, and the Lolo Pass Visitor Center reported 59 inches.

Montana Department of Transportation required chains for MacDonald Pass on Highway 12 overnight on March 13, and severe driving conditions on Highway 141 on the morning of March 14.  Missoula Electric COOP reported over 223 customers without power, with one broken power pole.

Montana Department of Transportation reported severe driving conditions on MT Highway 83 from milepost 14.0 to 47.8, Seeley Lake to Condon due to blowing and drifting snow, heavy snow.  There was a slide-off accident on Highway 83 south of Seeley Lake.  Obstructions blocked travel on Highway 200 and Interstate 90 on the morning of March 14.  Missoula Electric COOP reported 2500 customers without power at 0930 MST March 14 plus a major infrastructure failure: two main feeders from the Clinton substation were damaged, cutting power to 505 members.  Some storm total snow amounts were 26.7 inches in Seeley Lake, 16 inches at Clearwater Junction, 14 inches at Lubrecht Forest, and 32.6 inches at the Ovando CoCoRaHS.
Elk Butte SNOTEL recorded  2.80 inches of snow-water equivalent since 0000 PST March 11, 18 inches of snow.   Crater Meadows SNOTEL two feet of storm total snow.

Montana Department of Transportation (on the east side of Highway 12) reported severe driving conditions.  Lolo Pass Visitor Center reported 59 inches of storm total snow. Rock slides occurred between Grangeville and Elk City. A power outage event was reported in Elk City.
Montana Department of Transportation reported severe driving conditions due to freezing roadways on MT Highway 141 and Interstate 90 between 2056MST and 0056MST.
Over 160 people in the Lakeside to Angel Point area of Flathead Lake were without power. A tree was reported in the power line at Angel Point.

Strong winds with gusts to 57 mph were recorded between Lolo and Hamilton. There was an unconfirmed report of a gust to 72 mph between Blodgett Canyon and US-93 with damage to a greenhouse. A large Ponderosa pine tree fell onto a garage located one mile north of Pinesdale. On top of Mount Sentinel at 5,000 feet MSL, wind gusts reached 62 mph at 1345MST. A flipped trailer was reported south of Florence.
MacDonald Pass recorded a wind gust of 57 mph, while Deer Lodge saw a gust to 48 mph. A power outage impacting over 51 customers was reported in Hall.

Precipitation began as a frontal passage that moved through around 0700MST on April 2, bringing snowfall rates of nearly two inches per hour to the Discovery Ski Area. Snow continued into April 3, resulting in storm total accumulations of ten inches at Discovery and five and a half inches northwest of Anaconda. Roadway conditions deteriorated, leading to significant travel impacts on April 3. At 0239MST, chains were required for towing units on Interstate 90 between mile markers 228 and 241. A crash resulted in a right lane closure on US Highway 12 westbound at mile marker 29.5 at 0305 MST (indirect). Additionally, spun-out semi-trucks forced a right lane closure on Interstate 90 eastbound at mile marker 232 around 0355MST (indirect). At Georgetown Lake, snowfall began around 0600MST on April 2, accompanied by wind gusts near twenty miles per hour and road temperatures dropping to thirty-two degrees, before tapering off by 0300MST on April 3. Snow eventually tapered off at Homestake Pass by 0830MST.
There were about 600 people without power on the northeast side of Flathead Lake.  The Department of Transportation also reported a power line across a road in Bigfork.

Winds were gusting to 50 mph when the power went out in western Mineral County around 3:13am MST on March 12. There were a lot of power outages in western Sanders County from Thompson Falls to Heron.  There were still people without power as of 2:00 am MST March 13.   Northern Lights also had 10,265 members affected, as of 1:00 am MST March 13, 6,085 have been restored. Still 4180 without power.  Schools were closed in Noxon, resulting in Picture Day needing to be rescheduled.

Missoula County roads crews reported sending crews up to the Seeley Lake area where other crews in that area were being overwhelmed by downed trees.  Damage was worst in the Seeley���Swan Valley, where approximately 480 members are without power. There was a downed powerline near mile marker 57 along Highway 83.

There were over 1800 people without power from Yaak to Bull Lake.  Multiple trees were blocking roads as of 6:54am March 12.  There was a downed power line across Highway 56 creating a total road blockage.  Trees fell on a garage and house in Libby.|There were 52 power poles down south of Libby.
There were about 150 people without power.

Snow Squall.  Metars from Ronan Airport, K7S0, indicate a drop in visibility from 9 statute miles down to less than 1/4 statute miles in 20 minutes at 1435MST.   A 3 degree (F) drop in temperature accompanied the drop in visibility.  Temperature dropped from 30 to 27 degrees.  A member of the public called to report that they were driving through whiteout conditions and could hardly see the car in front of them at  1450MST.   Another member of the public reported 12-14 inches of snow from this event in St. Ignatius.

Snow Squall. A snow Squall hit the Highway 200 corridor between 1930MST and 2020MST.  An NWS Missoula employee was between Greenough Hill and Clearwater Junction. About 1 inch of snow fell with the squall. Easterly winds developed with the squall with temperatures falling due to the Arctic cold front that pushed westwards.  He reported that several people left the camp at 1930MST and encountered snow and low visibility on their drive back to Missoula.

The most significant impact occurred south of Orofino, where a large landslide blocked US-12 between mile markers 44 and 45. The initial slide occurred around 1539MST on Friday, March 13. While crews worked to clear the route, a second slide occurred at the same location at 0920MST on Saturday, March 14. The highway remained closed in both directions until Saturday afternoon. Additional landslides and rockslides were reported on Lower Fords Creek Road, Grangemont Road, Sunnyside, and Bobbitt Bench. Heavy traffic diverted to Sunnyside Road caused that secondary route to begin failing under the saturated conditions.||In Orofino, the urban drainage system reached maximum capacity and overflowed, flooding residential areas. In the Riverside area (115th Street), rushing water surrounded homes and filled basements. Significant damage occurred at the Joint School District 171 bus garage when a nearby creek (likely Flume Creek) blew out, flooding the facility. While officials successfully moved most of the fleet, one school bus and a neighboring food pantry were inundated and suffered major damage.||Small streams and creeks, including Jim Fords Creek and Freeman Creek, crested their banks, threatening homes and washing out culverts. Near Weippe, a creek overflowed onto the roadway, causing significant rutting. The Clearwater River at Orofino saw a dramatic rise of over 8 feet, increasing from 5.78 feet on Thursday to a crest of 13.96 feet on Saturday night���staying just below the 16-foot flood stage, though the high water contributed to the drainage backup in the city. Total rainfall between March 10 and 15 included 3.57 in Orofino, 4.00 in Peck, and 4.50 at the Pierce SNOTEL.

Eight and a half inches of snow fell at Java East, with four inches reported at the West Glacier COOP. Two and seven tenths inches of snow accumulated at Shed 4. A disabled semi truck blocked the eastbound lane of US Highway 2 at milepost 184. Power outages were also reported during the event, totaling around 400 customers.

Six inches of snow accumulated at Lolo Pass. Five inches of snow fell in the Painted Rocks area and at the Nez Perce SNOTEL. Six inches of snow was also reported at the Daly SNOTEL. A few power outages were noted near Painted Rocks Reservoir. Winter driving conditions were common over the passes.

Eight inches of snow fell at Garnet Ghost Town. Five inches of snow accumulated in Potomac, and three inches fell in Clinton. Two vehicles had to be towed out after getting stuck attempting to drive to Garnet.

Ten inches of snow accumulated at the Basin Creek SNOTEL south of Butte. Six to eight inches of snow was estimated in Philipsburg, while 6.4 inches fell seven miles west of Anaconda. MacDonald Pass and Homestake Pass were covered in snow, requiring chains for travel. Multiple semi trucks spun out, blocking the eastbound lanes of US Highway 12 on MacDonald Pass.

There were a few power outages were reported southwest of Victor, snow amounts ranged from 2 to 7 inches in the Bitterroot Valley. Snow covered roads were reported on US 93. Impacts were limited in the Missoula Valley, where snowfall amounts were generally less than 1 inch.

Fifteen inches of snow fell at the Mountain Meadows SNOTEL. Six inches of snow accumulated at Lolo Pass, and 3.6 inches fell at Dixie. Downed trees were reported on the way to Red River Hot Springs due to the heavy weight of the snow.

At Lolo Pass, snow started around 0400MST on April 2 and lasted through 0200MST on April 3, accumulating approximately seven inches. Air temperatures dropped to twenty-eight degrees, with peak snowfall intensities of two inches in three hours occurring midday on April 2. At Lost Trail Pass, rain changed to snow around 0330MST, with air and road temperatures dropping into the mid-twenties, leading to a possible road freeze-up. Winds gusted to twenty-nine miles per hour throughout the day, and snow transitioned back to light rain around 0830MST on April 3. Moose Creek observed snowfall starting around 0700MST on April 2, with snowfall rates averaging one inch per hour from 0800 MST to 1100 MST, accumulating a total of six inches before ending at 0200MST on April 3.

Snow started around 0400MST on April 2nd at Lolo Pass, lasting through about 0200MST on April 3rd. Approximately seven inches of total snow fell, and air temperatures dropped as low as twenty-eight degrees. Peak snowfall intensities occurred midday on April 2nd, with two inches accumulating in three hours. At Elk City, rain changed to snow around midnight Pacific Standard Time.

Localized hard freezing conditions impacted areas north and southeast of Salmon. A weather station southeast of Salmon at an elevation of 4,058 feet recorded a low temperature of 25 degrees Fahrenheit, remaining at that temperature for over two hours on the 25th. Temperature in Salmon dropped into the upper 20s to near 30 degrees Fahrenheit on the mornings of the 25th and 26th.

Multiple locations recorded low temperatures in the lower 20s, with some dipping to 19 degrees Fahrenheit. A station west of Fortine at 3,087 feet fell to 19 degrees Fahrenheit and remained at 25 degrees or colder for over six hours. In the Eureka area, the Hollenback Circle station observed 24 degrees Fahrenheit, while other nearby stations recorded 21 degrees and 23 degrees Fahrenheit. A station in Trego at 3,200 feet dropped to 23 degrees Fahrenheit, and a station near Troy measured 22 degrees Fahrenheit.
Snowfall in the Kootenai region was relatively uniform, with accumulations falling comfortably in the 3 to 5-inch range.

Twelve inches of snow accumulated just above the town of West Glacier at an elevation of 3,600 feet. Five to six inches of snow fell in the town of West Glacier. Four inches of snow accumulated six miles north of Polebridge.

In Elk City, temperatures fell to 24 degrees Fahrenheit on April 25 and 22 degrees Fahrenheit on April 27. Another nearby station recorded a low of 24 degrees Fahrenheit on April 26 and 22 degrees Fahrenheit on April 27, recording a hard freeze for several hours.
Areas around Elk River and Pierce dropped into the mid 20s on the morning of the 25th and 26th.

A hard freeze impacted the zone on the morning of the 25th, with Finley Point dropping to 31 to 32 degrees Fahrenheit. In the West Valley, temperatures dropped to 23 degrees Fahrenheit for over four hours. Southwest of Kalispell, lows reached 23 to 25 degrees Fahrenheit. Northwest of Kalispell, temperatures hit 24 degrees Fahrenheit. East of St. Ignatius, temperatures reached 25 degrees Fahrenheit. Somers recorded a low of 25.5 degrees Fahrenheit.

A hard freeze occurred on both the mornings of the 25th and 26th. Orchard Homes recorded a low of 24 degrees Fahrenheit. Grass Valley in northwest Missoula also reached 24 degrees Fahrenheit. A station between Lolo and Florence hit 24 degrees Fahrenheit, while the east side of Florence dropped to 23 degrees Fahrenheit. In the Stevensville area, temperatures fell to 23 to 24 degrees Fahrenheit. Areas southwest and east of Charlos Heights recorded lows ranging from 22 to 23 degrees Fahrenheit.
Temperatures dropped into the low to mid 20s for lower elevation sites such as just west of Lolo, around Sula, and along Rock Creek on the mornings of the 25th and 26th.

A 60 MPH wind gust was recorded at the Stevensville Airport, with frequent gusts exceeding 50 MPH and sustained winds of 42 MPH observed later in the afternoon. Peak wind gusts of 55 MPH were recorded at the Missoula International Airport. The Hamilton airport measured a 49 MPH wind gust. A 48 MPH gust was observed at the Stevensville RAWS.

A 53 MPH wind gust was measured at Montana Tech. Fifty-two mile per hour gusts were observed at Avon North. MacDonald Pass and Deer Lodge both recorded 51 MPH wind gusts. A 49 MPH gust was observed at the airport in Butte. The Yankee Flat RAWS measured a 48 MPH wind gust at an elevation of 6000 feet. Wind gusts of 46 to 48 MPH were reported near Georgetown Lake. The strong winds resulted in 265 power outages across Powell County.
Heavy snow fell from Lemhi to Tendoy with amounts of 6 to 11 inches of snow reported.

Heavy snow fell across southwest Montana with 6 to 13 inches of snow reported from Philipsburg to near Butte. Montana Highway Patrol responded to 11 weather-related crashes in the area between 200 AM and 330 PM.
Heavy snow fell over the southern part of Lemhi County with 6 to 12 inches of snow reported from Tendoy to Leadore. Local gusty north winds caused reduced visibility from blowing snow.

Heavy snow fell over southwest Montana. At the lower elevations 6 to 7 inches of snow fell at Butte and Philispburg, with 8 to 14 inches of snow over the higher terrain. Gusty north to northeast winds caused reduced visiblity from blowing and drifting snow.
Wind gusts estimated between 40 to 52 mph caused tree and power line damage in the Salmon area. Scattered power outages were reported from Salmon to Elk Bend.

Flathead Electric Company reported a cottonwood tree blown down onto a mobile home on Evergreen Drive near Kalispell, causing damage to a side wall and the roof of the home.  Trees were also reported down onto power lines in Foyes Lake with 14 power outages in Flathead County.  Wind gusts of 45 to 50 mph were recorded from wind sensors in Flathead County.
Trees were reported down on power lines in West Glacier. Wind gusts of 45 to 50 mph were reported from local weather sensors.
Five metal sheets were lost from a roof.  A few cottonwood trees were reported down on West 9-Mile Road.
Ravalli County Road Department reported wash-outs on Middle Bear Creek Rd. (SW of Victor), Pleasant View Dr. (W of Victor), and Red Crow Rd. (SW of Victor).
Ravalli County Road Department reported wash-outs on West Side Rd. (SW of Hamilton), West Hills Way (NW of Hamilton), and Camas Creek Loop (SW of Hamilton).

Snow amounts between 6 to 12 inches were reported in the valleys, with up to 15 inches falling over the higher terrain.  Additionally, local northeast sustained winds of 20 mph with gusts up to 33 mph were recorded. Reduced visibility due to blowing and drifting snow was reported on areas roads.

Snowfall amounts between 5 and 8 inches were reported.  In addition, winds from the northeast sustained up to 20 mph, gusting up to 45 mph, lowered visibility to near zero periodically. The DOT reported severe driving conditions along US Highway 2 over Marias Pass due to snow and blowing snow reducing visibility.

Snowfall was difficult to measure due to the blowing and drifting nature, but estimates were anywhere from 3 to 7 inches.  The main impact came from strong east to northeast winds measured at sustained 20 mph gusting up to 40 mph.  Visibility down to near zero was reported in many locations due to the blowing snow.  Many area roads were closed, including Highway 35 between Polson and the junction with S-206 where many trees were blown down onto the road from strong winds.  One person was killed on this road when a tree blew onto his vehicle. Two other vehicles were also damaged from falling trees.
Snowfall accumulations between 9 and 15 inches were reported.  Sustained northeast winds up to 18 mph with gusts up to 30 mph caused blowing and drifting snow, lowering visibility on local roads.
Eight to twelve inches of snow was reported with north winds sustained at 20 mph gusting up to 35 mph.  Lolo and Lost Trail Passes had reduced visibility due to blowing and drifting snow.

Snowfall accumulations between 6 and 8 inches were measured by storm spotters. Automated observing stations reporting north winds sustained at 20 to 25 mph with gusts up to 40 mph.  Severe driving conditions were reported by the DOT along Interstate 15 between Glen and Butte.

Snow accumulations between 7 and 10 inches was reported by local storm spotters.  Winds were sustained up to 20 mph with gusts up to 30 mph.  The DOT reported low visibility along Highway 83 between Clearwater Junction and Condon due to blowing and drifting snow.
Up to 6 inches of snow fell over the lower elevations, while up to 12 inches fell over the higher terrain.
Nine to twelve inches of snowfall accumulations reported, including over Lolo Pass.
Windchills dipped down to 26 to 36 below zero in Polebridge and Essex.

Windchills between 20 and 25 below were reported at several observation sites.

Snow accumulations ranged between 6 to 12 inches.
Eight to eleven inches of snow accumulation reported by several spotters.

Severe driving conditions were reported by the DOT on Interstate 90 between Lookout Pass and St. Regis.  Twelve vehicle accidents were reported along this route over night on the 17th. Storm total snow accumulations between 8 and 12 inches was reported by spotters in the area.
