They also reported 6 snow drifts. The MT DOT reported blowing and drifting snow on I-90 between Frenchtown to US-93 interchange at 6:17 am MST. Heavy snow bands affected portions of the Bitterroot and Missoula Valleys between Jan. 30 to 31. A multiple vehicle accident occurred on I-90 between the Orange St. and Van Buren St. exits in Missoula around 10:47 am MST on Jan. 31. Moderate to heavy snow with slick roads were reported at the time of the accident. Three day total snowfall include: 7.5 South Hills of Missoula, 5.6 Missoula International Airport, and 1 Hamilton COOP.

A trained spotter located 1.5 miles south of Condon reported heavy snow from 9 am to 1 pm MST on Jan. 29. When the arctic cold front moved through by 1 am MST Jan. 30, the MT DOT reported snow-covered, blowing and drifting snow on MT-200 from Greenough to Helmville. A person from the public located 1.5 miles south of Condon reported 18 of heavy snow 24 hours ending at 8:47 am Jan. 30. An injury occurred associated with an automobile accident in Bonner around 5:52 pm MST Jan. 30 and the MT DOT road reports at the time indicated moderate to heavy snow. Other three day snowfall totals include: 19.6 Seeley Lake Ranger Station COOP, 19 Snowbowl Ski Resort, 14 5 miles ESE Evaro and 10 Potomac.

The Lost Trail Ski Resort reported 6 of heavy snow by 10:23 am MST on Jan. 29. The MT DOT reported snow, blowing and drifting snow at Lost Trail during the afternoon and evening hours on Jan. 29. According to the Saddle Mountain SNOTEL located 1 mile west of Lost Trail Pass on US-93, 16 of total snow with 1.90 snow water equivalent fell between Jan. 29-30. The Lolo Pass SNOTEL recorded 20 of total snowfall with 2.30 of snow water equivalent between Jan. 28-30.

The MT DOT sensor reported moderate to heavy snow that fell with the arctic cold front just before midnight Jan. 30. Chains were required for towing units for both MacDonald and Homestake Passes during much of the morning on Jan. 30. MT DOT indicated blowing and drifting had occurred along I-90 from Drummond to Phosphate Junction and also at MacDonald Pass. Snowfall amounts included 8 6 miles southeast Philipsburg, 6.5 Elliston,  6 Drummond, 5 Anaconda and 3.5 3 miles west of Deer Lodge.

The Lolo Pass SNOTEL recorded 20 of total snowfall with 2.30 of snow water equivalent between Jan. 28-30. It reported heavy snowfall between 6 am and 1 pm PST on Jan. 29. The Dixie COOP reported a storm total snowfall of 14.4 with 0.92 liquid equivalent.

The Lost Trail Ski Resort reported 6 of heavy snow by 10:23 am MST on Jan. 29. The MT DOT reported snow, blowing and drifting snow at Lost Trail during the afternoon and evening hours on Jan. 29. According to the Saddle Mountain SNOTEL located 1 mile west of Lost Trail Pass on US-93, 16 of total snow with 1.90 snow water equivalent fell between Jan. 29-30. Salmon saw 7 of heavy snow that mainly fell on Jan 29. The Salmon School District closed early because of the snow loading concerns with their aging roofs. Other total snowfall amounts include: 6 Carmen and 3 in May.

The Pierce observer reported a three day snowfall total of 16.5 with 2.26 of precipitation. The Crater Meadows SNOTEL located 25 miles east-northeast of Pierce measured 28 of total snowfall with 4.40 of snow water equivalent.

At 7:34 am PST on Jan 29., the Idaho State highway patrol reported freezing rain at Cottonwood. A weather spotter located 3 miles northwest of Ferdinand measured a thin coating of glaze on their patio. Anywhere from 5 to 10 inches of snow fell in the vicinity of Orofino between Jan. 29-30.

The COOP observer located 30 miles south-southeast of Libby at 3,440 ft., recorded a low temperature of -40 deg. F on the morning of Feb. 6. This breaks the all-time coldest temperature for the month of February for this station since continuous records began in June 1949. The previous record was -39 set back on Feb. 2, 1996. Other low temperatures include: -34 Olney and -29 Yaak 9 NNE. During the first surge of arctic air on Jan. 3, 2 to 4 inches of snow fell along US-2 from Libby to Kila causing slick roads.

The MT DOT sensor located at milepost 179.9 on US-2 near Essex recorded a wind chill of -47 deg. F at 8:02 am MST Feb. 6. The air temperature was -21.5 and the wind was 14.9 mph from the south-southeast direction. The HADS sensor at Marias Pass measured an air temperature of -40 deg. F at 6:15 am MST on Feb. 6.

The Ronan Airport AWOS recorded a low temperature of -38 deg. F at 5:15 am MST on Feb. 6, and a power outage was reported in Ronan.  The Glacier Park International Airport located north of Kalispell saw extreme wind chills between Feb. 4-6 and saw its coldest wind chill reading of -30 at 5:55 am MST Feb. 6. The Polson Kerr Dam COOP recorded -22 on Feb. 6, which makes it the coldest all-time temperature for the month of February since records began in March 1951. Other low temperatures recorded include: -42 St. Ignatius 5 north, -28 St. Ignatius, -24 Whitefish, and -23 Creston. On Feb. 5, the Bigfork school districts closed due to dangerous wind chills. On Feb. 6, the St. Ignatius schools closed due to extreme cold and wind chills.

A trained spotter located in Columbia Falls reported brief episodes of near white-outs, blowing snow with northeast winds gusting to 27 mph during the early morning hours of Feb. 3. The Polson COOP observed 3 of snow on Feb. 3, which according to the DOT fell mainly during the early morning hours. Easterly winds over 40 mph were observed by the Flathead Lake Biological Station Yellow Bay Point sensor on the morning of Feb. 3. Other snowfall amounts include: 4 Ronan and 3 Arlee.

Lookout Pass Ski Resort shut down due to the extreme cold between Feb. 4-5. During this period the Mullan Pass ASOS recorded wind chill values as low as -42 deg. F. On the morning of Feb. 6, a COOP observer in Alberton recorded a low of -22 deg. F while the COOP located one mile west of Haugan recorded -28 deg. F.

The spotter located 2.7 miles north-northeast of Evaro measured 5 of snow. The Montana Highway Patrol reported an 8 motor vehicle pile-up on the bridge that crosses the Clark Fork River, 3 miles west of Tarkio on I-90 around 12 pm MST. It was reported that whiteout conditions and slick conditions contributed to the accidents that caused a three mile traffic jam that lasted for 3 hours. One person was taken to the hospital for minor injuries. Other snowfall amounts include: 8 Lookout Pass Ski Resort, 5 Thompson Falls and 3.5 9 miles northwest of Thompson Falls.

The Missoula International Airport ASOS reported wind chills less than -20 deg. F during this period.  The coldest wind chill reading recorded was -37 deg. F at 8:53 am MST on Feb. 6 when the temperature was -23 and wind was 4.6 mph. On the morning of Feb. 6, a power outage occurred on the east side of Florence where minimum temperatures had reached -32 deg. F. The Stevensville school district closed due to power outages caused by the extreme cold. The Stevensville COOP recorded a low temperature of -21 on Feb. 6.

The Seeley Lake Ranger Station COOP recorded low temperatures in the mid-20s below zero Fahrenheit for 4 days straight. The coldest low temperature recorded was -41 deg. F on the morning of Feb. 6. This COOP also observed its coldest maximum temperature of -1 on Feb. 6 which broke the all-time February coldest maximum temperature of 2 degrees set back on Feb. 8, 1994, since records began in Oct. of 1936. The Snowbowl ski area closed down due to a power outage and dangerous wind chills between Feb. 4-5. The Point 6 RAWS sensor at 7,905 ft., recorded a wind chill of -63 deg. F at 7:59 am MST on Feb. 5. Other coldest minimum temperatures include: -37 Potomac, -34 F Condon, -33 F Greenough Hill, -32 F Condon and -31 F 3 miles northeast of Bonner.
The COOP observer located 14 miles northeast of Sula measured a minimum temperature of -39 deg. F while a weather spotter in Sula reported -41 degrees on Feb. 6.

The Bert Mooney Airport ASOS located south of Butte reported wind chills below -20 F from early morning on Feb. 4 through the morning of Feb. 7 with the coldest wind chill value of -50 deg. F observed around 6:53 am MST on Feb. 6. The MT DOT sensor located 8 miles north of Avon on Highway 141, measured a wind chill of -59 deg. F from 7:45 am through 8:16 am MST on Feb. 6. Also a wind chill of -57 F was observed in Elliston via the mesonet. The Discovery ski area closed due to the extreme cold between Feb. 5-6. The coldest minimum temperatures recorded during this period were: -37 F 3 miles west of Deer Lodge, -36 F Philipsburg and Bert Mooney Airport, -34 F Anaconda and Elliston.

The COOP observer located one mile north of Dixie observed a minimum temperature of -31 deg. F on the morning of Feb. 6. Other cold temperatures observed include: -33 Elk City (ITD highway sensor) and -23 F at Lodgepole (RAWS).

The Grangeville 911 dispatch estimated that 8 inches of snow had fallen in a period of 24 hours and several vehicle slide-offs had occurred due to steady snow early on Feb. 4. The coldest day for Grangeville was Feb. 6 when the the high only reached 10 degrees while the low was -13 F.

The ITD road sensor located 1 mile east of Gilmore Summit on Highway 28 at 7,018 ft. MSL reported extreme wind chill as low as -43 F during the morning of Feb. 6. Minimum temperatures reported during this period include: -34 F Leadore, -27 F Gilmore Summit, -25 F 2 miles south-southeast of May, -24 F at the Salmon Airport and -19 F at Salmon.
The COOP observer located one mile west of Haugan measured 11 of snowfall between Feb. 9-10. Other snowfall reports include 6.5 one mile north-northwest of Evaro and 3.2 4 miles northwest of Noxon.

The Missoula International Airport saw a total storm snowfall of 7.2 with 0.24 of precipitation. Other snowfall reports: 8 Hamilton, 6.5 one mile south of Lolo, 5.3 4 miles east of Corvallis and 3.5 2 miles north-northwest of East Missoula.
A person from the public located 4 miles south-southeast of Clinton estimated 7 of snow. Six inches of snow was reported by the public in Potomac.
A person from the public estimated that 13 of total snowfall fell while the COOP located 14 miles northeast of Sula measured 11.2 of snow.
The COOP observer located 3 miles west of Deer Lodge measured 7 of total snowfall with 0.26 of liquid equivalent.  Other reports include: 4.3 7 miles south of Butte and 4 in Anaconda.
Trained spotters located from Orofino to Grangeville reported anywhere from 3 to 5 inches of total snowfall.
The ITD reported up to 14 inches of snow had fallen along Williams Creek and locations near Salmon to Leadore reported anywhere from 5 to 8 inches of snowfall.

The Pike Creek SNOTEL located 1.6 miles southeast of Marias Pass reported heavy snow during the morning of Feb. 13. It recorded a total snowfall of 5 inches with 0.50 of snow water equivalent. During the afternoon and evening hours of Feb. 13, the MT DOT required chains on towing units over Marias Pass. The Fielding RAWS located 4 miles southwest of Marias Pass reported wind gusts to 48 mph during the morning of Feb. 13 which most likely caused blowing snow. A moderate avalanche cycle was reported in the JFS Canyon the day before but didn't affect US-2.

A weather spotter in Troy reported at 8:51 am MST on Feb. 13 that there had been 4 vehicle accidents, especially on Bull Lake Road and US-2 due to very slick conditions. Rain fell on top of a frozen ground which worsened untreated road surfaces. Temperatures during the daytime were able to rise into the 40's and lower 50's but plummeted to the 20's at night helping to freeze up slush and cause slick conditions.
Glacier Park International Airport saw a period of freezing rain because of cold surface temperatures.

The COOP observer located one mile west of Haugan reported 6 of snow between Feb. 11-12. The Lookout Pass ski resort reported 9 of snow that fell in 24 hours between 6 am and 6 am MST on Feb. 12, but a total of 17 between Feb. 11-14. Freezing rain was reported along I-90 and MT-200 especially during the morning hours on Feb. 12. There were a few accidents and slide offs, and the event was a moderate impact to travel.

Strong warming aloft with above normal moisture brought light snow that changed to light freezing rain across the Missoula Valley during the morning hours of Feb. 11. The Missoula International Airport ASOS reported freezing rain from 7:46 to 8:20 am MST. Several motor vehicle accidents were reported during the morning between Stevensville and Missoula. Freezing drizzle was reported again on the morning of Feb. 12 and freezing rain caused very slick secondary roads on Feb. 13 with enough impact that the Hamilton, Victor, Florence, Corvallis and Frenchtown school districts all had two hour delays.

The combination of anomalous warmth with temperatures approaching 50 degrees F, rain and rapid snow-melt on frozen ground, caused lowland flooding across the Bitterroot Valley. Just before noon on Feb. 12, a National Weather Service employee reported water covering up to three-quarters of US-93 just south of Florence. They also reported ponding of water at the Florence IGA store parking lot and fire hall. More flooding was reported on Feb. 13 and the Ravalli County EM reported that home owners in Victor and Corvallis had already experienced ponding of water around their homes and water running down the streets in Victor. At least one homeowner did experience water in their basement.

The MT DOT reported 2 to 4 inches of snow that fell along MT-83 during the morning of Feb. 12. The MT DOT also reported freezing rain from Clinton to just west of Drummond and also from Condon on MT-83 to the junction with S-209 at 7:47 am MST on Feb. 13.
The Snowbowl Ski area had to close both chair lifts due to strong winds.

A warm occlusion brought a transition from snow to rain during the morning hours of Feb. 12 to elevations below 7,000 feet. Strong warming aloft associated with a plume of moisture with subtropical origins most likely nixed the ability for the formation of stellar dendrites; therefore, heavy snow wasn't able to materialize in these areas as such is common with heavy up-slope westerly flow events. Nonetheless, moderate impact was experienced during the nighttime and morning hours as light to moderate snow made road surfaces slick. Both Lolo and Lost Trail Passes saw around 4 of total snowfall while total precipitation amounts ranged between 1 and 1.80 in the Bitterroot Mountains.

The Peterson Meadows SNOTEL at 7,200 ft. MSL, located 4.6 miles south-southwest of Georgetown Lake reported 5 of total snowfall. A weather spotter reported a period of heavy snow at 8:14 am MST while the Georgetown Lake MT DOT sensor indicated southwest winds gusting up to 34 mph at times.  Light freezing rain with a thin glaze of ice was reported by a weather spotter one mile west-southwest of Deer Lodge at 8:54 am MST on Feb. 13. The MT DOT also reported freezing rain from Deer Lodge to Warm Springs on Interstate 90 at 8:54 am MST on Feb. 13. The MT DOT sensor located 8 miles north of Avon on Highway 141 reported snow showers that helped to bring gusty winds to 58 mph at 10:28 am MST on Feb. 11, to 50 mph at 3:12 pm MST on Feb. 10 and to 52 mph at 2:57 am MST on Feb. 13. A brief heavy snow shower brought wind gusts as high as 47 mph at the Bert Mooney Airport south of Butte between 11:30 to 12 pm MST on Feb. 11.

Lolo Pass saw around 4 of total snowfall while total precipitation amounts ranged between 1 and 1.80 in the Bitterroot Mountains. Due to the perceived high avalanche threat, the Idaho Transportation Department closed U.S. 12 between mileposts 100 and 161 from 12:46 pm PST Feb. 12 to 10:50 am PST Feb. 13. The COOP located one mile north of Dixie at 5,740 ft. MSL, reported a 2 day snowfall total of 8.2 with 0.87 of precipitation.
A person from the public located one mile north of Dixie estimated a storm total snowfall of 8.
Snowfall amounts in the Grangeville area ranged from 4 to 6 inches.

events.cz_name: LOWER HELLS CANYON / SALMON RIVER REGION
events.event_narrative: Snowfall amounts in the Grangeville area ranged from 4 to 6 inches while Pollock at 2,500 ft. MSL received 2.5 inches which is relatively rare for them to receive snow.
A weather spotter reported 4.5 of snow fell 7 miles south of Williams Lake.
Total snowfall reported by the Pierce COOP came in at 6.7 with 0.32 of precipitation.

Lost Trail Pass received around 4 of total snowfall while with a total precipitation around 1.00 according to the Saddle Mountain SNOTEL. Light snow fell in the Salmon area on Feb. 12 with one inch of total snow reported. Williams Creek saw 5.5 of snow through 8:53 am MST on Feb. 12. A weather spotter located one mile north-northwest of Salmon reported snow at 4:30 am MST on Feb. 13 that turned to freezing rain before 7 am. They reported that sidewalks and other surfaces were slick.
The National Weather Service handar located one mile north of Grangeville at the Idaho County Airport reported a high wind gust to 59 mph.

The Lookout Pass SNOTEL reported 0.10 or more SWE (snow water equivalent) per hour through this period. Web cams confirmed that snow was falling at a good clip and the MT DOT required chains on towing units from 7:52 am to 9:28 pm MST. The SNOTEL reported a total of 1.50 of SWE which could have equated to over a foot of snow.

The Lolo Pass SNOTEL reported 7 of total snowfall with 0.80 of snow water equivalent while the Saddle Mountain SNOTEL near Lost Trail Pass measured 5 of snow with 0.30 of liquid. The MT DOT required that towing units have chains at Lolo Pass during the evening of Feb. 17.
Glacier Park International Airport reported a total snowfall of 1.8 inches that caused roads to become snow covered and icy.

The COOP located at 9 miles north-northeast of Yaak at 3,075 ft. MSL reported 10.5 of snow with 0.66 liquid equivalent. The Garver Creek SNOTEL located 11.3 miles north-northwest of Yaak in the Purcell Mountains at 4,250 ft. measured 9 of snow with 0.70 liquid.
The Lookout Pass Ski resort reported 14 of heavy snow in 12 hours while the MT DOT required chains for towing vehicles from 7 pm Feb. 18 through 5:30 am MST on Feb. 19.
The Lolo Pass SNOTEL reported 7 of total snowfall with 0.60 of snow water equivalent.

The MT DOT sensor at MacDonald Pass on US-12 milepost 27.9 at 6,325 ft. MSL reported a cold front passage around 1 am MST with light to moderate snowfall and winds sustained around 25 mph with gusts between 30 and 40 mph. MT DOT required chains for towing vehicles from 2 to 6:30 am MST at the pass due to blowing and drifting of snow.

Very strong wind gusts nearing 50 mph occurred after a cold front went through during the early morning hours of Feb. 19 near Marias Pass. This combined with 4 to 6 inches of new transportable snow caused reduced visibility, blowing and drifting snow and severe driving conditions 7 miles west of Marias Pass to Marias Pass on US-2. There were reports of 3 foot drifts near Marias Pass and US-2 east of Marias pass was closed between 10 am and 2:30 pm MST.

The COOP located 30 miles south-southeast of Libby at 3,440 ft. reported a two day snowfall total of 7.1 with 0.39 of precipitation. The Lincoln County sheriff dispatch reported slick roads with black ice on the morning of Feb. 21. During the evening of Feb 20, a motor vehicle slipped on the slick conditions on Granite Lake Road near Libby and went off a 30 foot embankment causing injuries.
The West Glacier COOP reported a storm total of 6 with 0.20 of snow water equivalent. A person from the public located 6 miles southwest of Marias Pass reported an estimated 6 of total snowfall.

At 4:25 am MST on Feb. 21, Montana DOT reported heavy snow, snow covered and icy conditions on US 93 from Arlee to Polson, on Highway 212 4 miles north of Dixon and Moise and Highway 211 junction fo US-93 at Ronan west to Hot Springs. A heavy snow band had parked itself over this area for several hours as noted on radar imagery.

A NWS employee reported that snow was falling at least 1 per hour rates during this time period from Haugan to Lookout Pass. The MT DOT reported that several semi-trucks had spun out and jack-knifed due to the snowy conditions. Interstate 90 was closed for a period of time around 3:34 pm MST. The NWS employee reported again at 4:20 pm MST that probably small cars had no chance to travel near the Lookout Pass area due to the deep snow on the sides.

Snow bands brought heavy snowfall rates between 1 to 2 per hour across portions of Sanders and Mineral Counties. Montana DOT reported heavy snow along I-90 and MT-200 at times throughout the morning hours. Mineral County dispatch reported periodic power outages due to the heavy snow in Superior and also in St. Regis. The St. Regis schools were closed due to the heavy snow and slick roads. Heavy snow brought whiteout conditions from Tarkio to Frenchtown on I-90 around 11 am MST.

The Missoula International Airport received 5 inches of snow in 5 hours from a heavy snow band that was over the Missoula Valley. A weather spotter located one mile north of Florence reported 7 of snow in 8 hours at 5:36 am MST. A weather spotter located 2 miles west of Charlos Heights estimated that 10 of snow fell in 12 hours ending at 6:36 am MST. Multiple motor vehicle slide-offs and accidents were reported from Missoula south to Hamilton due to the snow.

A CoCoRaHS observer located one mile north of Greenough measured 11 of snow due to the heavy snow bands. The COOP located in Seeley Lake reported 9 of total snowfall with 0.50 of precipitation. A Missoula County deputy reported driving through a foot of snow on MT-200 from Seeley Lake to Missoula around 7 am MST. Very slick driving conditions were experienced in the afternoon and evening hours on I-90 from Bonner to Bearmouth with numerous accidents reported by the MT DOT.
The COOP located 14 miles northeast of Sula observed 6.5 of snow with 0.30 of precipitation. The COOP at Lolo Hot Springs measured 5 of snow with 0.35 of precipitation.

The Granite County dispatch reported 4 of heavy snow in Drummond 4 hours ending at 7:13 am. MT DOT required chains for towing units on MacDonald Pass on US-12 from 6:10 am to 8:27 am MST. A SNOTEL located 11 miles north-northeast of Bearmouth reported 8 of snow with 0.50 snow water equivalent. Nine slide-offs were reported from Bearmouth to Drummond throughout the day.

The COOP at the Polson Kerr Dam reported a storm total snowfall of 8 with 0.30 of precipitation. Other snowfall amounts include: 7.5 Bigfork 2.6 SSE, 7.3 Ronan 4.1 NE, 6.5 Columbia Falls 7.7 S, and 6 Creston. Strong gusty winds brought blowing snow and reduced visibilities at Bad Rock Canyon. The St. Ignatius schools, Salish Kootenai College and Two Eagle River high school in Pablo closed on Feb. 24 due to the weather. The Arlee, Dixon and Charlo schools had a two hour delay. Multiple reports of vehicle accidents and slide-offs were reported especially in the Mission Valley.

An avalanche buried two snowmobilers in the West Cabinet Range, about 17 miles southwest of Troy or about two miles north of Spark Peak. One person survived after being partially buried while the other person, a 49 year old male, died after being buried under 4 to 6 feet of compacted snow. The avalanche was classified as a D3 sized avalanche which means that it was a soft slab remotely triggered by a snowmobile.

The COOP located one mile west of Haugan measured a storm total snowfall of 14 with 0.84 of precipitation. Other snowfall reports include: 11.4 Evaro .7 miles north-northwest, 10 Thompson Falls 9.3 miles northwest, 7.5 Alberton, 7 Thompson Falls and 5.2 Heron 2 miles northwest.  Fifteen motor vehicle slide-offs were reported mainly occurring on I-90 between Superior and Alberton. A motor vehicle accident near mile-marker 82 on I-90 west at 12:48 pm MST on Feb. 23, resulted in an injury after a semi-truck lost control at the Nine Mile bridge. On Feb. 24 because of the weather, the Superior and St. Regis school systems closed while the Alberton schools had a 2 hour delay. Montana DOT reported blowing and drifting snow causing limited visibility at Evaro Hill.

A NWS employee reported heavy snowfall in Florence by noon on Feb. 23. Snow was falling in the Missoula area at this time in the form of small crystals, most likely due to the influence of the strong easterly winds breaking up the dendrites. It was apparent watching webcams and observations in the Stevensville and Florence area that weak northerly winds, a shallow arctic air mass and overrunning moist Pacific air allowed for the heaviest snowfall. A person from the public from Stevensville posted 13 of total snowfall on a local media's Facebook page. Other storm snow totals include: 12 at both Florence 3.7 SE and foothills near Victor, 9 Hamilton, 8.8 Corvallis 4.2 ENE, and 4.6 at the Missoula International Airport,. On Feb. 24, Missoula Valley Christian, Darby and Victor schools closed while the Charlo, Stevensville and Frenchtown schools were delayed for 2 hours due to the weather. Numerous motor vehicle accidents were reported especially between 2 and 6 pm MST on Feb. 23 when the heaviest snow fell in the area.

A period of light snow fell on Feb. 22 causing US-93 to become slick. Three persons died, while two were injured in an automobile accident around 5:30 pm MST near Trader Brothers on US-93 south. According to the Montana Highway Patrol both speed and the road conditions were a factor in the crash.

The COOP located at Lindbergh Lake or 8 miles south-southwest of Condon reported a storm total snowfall of 21.2 with 0.79 of precipitation, which happens to be the highest snow total reported across western Montana during this event. Other snowfall reports include: 20 Seeley Lake, 14.2 Greenough 2 NNE, and 10 in Potomac. Montana DOT reported periods of snowfall, poor visibility, blowing and drifting snow along MT-200 Greenough Hill to Helmville and also I-90 east of Missoula near Bonner. The Potomac schools had a 2 hour delay on Feb. 24. At 5:42 pm MST on Feb. 23, a weather spotter in Seeley Lake reported 2.5 per hour snowfall rates. At 3 am MST on Feb. 24, a car slid off the road and caused a mini-avalanche east of Bonner at mile-marker 3 on Highway 200 partially burying the vehicle and roadway. Traffic was backed up for 2 hours while crews and several plows worked to clear the snow.
The Lolo Hot Springs COOP reported a storm total of 10 with 0.57 of precipitation. A weather spotter located 7 miles south-southeast of Hamilton reported a storm total snowfall of 11.5.

The COOP located 3 miles west of Deer Lodge reported a storm total snowfall of 17 with 0.49 of precipitation. The atmospheric conditions of being just to the north of the arctic frontal boundary that brought an intensification of snow near the Deer Lodge area may have been similar to what had happened near the Florence & Stevensville areas. Other snowfall amounts include: 8.2 Anaconda 7.4 NW and 4.6 Philipsburg. Montana DOT reported snow, blowing and drifting snow from MacDonald Pass west to portions of I-90 near Garrison Junction to Drummond. Numerous automobile accidents and slide-offs were reported especially between 2 and 6 pm MST on Feb. 23. Chains were required for towing vehicles on MacDonald Pass for a period of time between Feb. 23-24.
The COOP located one mile north of Dixie measured a three day total snowfall of 16.9 with 1.21 of precipitation.

The COOP located one mile south-southeast of Headquarters reported a three day snowfall total of 13.1 with 1.57 of precipitation. The COOP in Pierce observed 8.6 of snowfall with 1.75 of precipitation.

The CoCoRaHS observer located 0.4 southwest of Grangeville reported a four day storm snow total of 11.6 with 1.31 of precipitation. Other snowfall amounts include: 6 at the Fenn Ranger Station and 8 two miles west-southwest of Cottonwood.

The Missoula International Airport received 5.5 of snow in 5 hours, but received a total of 6.8 from this particular storm event with 0.29 of precipitation. The heavy snow fell during the later part of rush hour traffic and the secondary roads became congested with many vehicles being stuck in deep ruts. The main roads were being plowed, but the melted snow from earlier had frozen into a sheet of ice exacerbating road conditions. Many school systems in the Missoula and Bitterroot Valleys had delays on the morning of Feb. 26.

Montana DOT reported heavy snowfall with snow-covered roads during the evening hours of Feb. 24. They also required chains for towing units on Interstate 90 from St. Regis to Lookout Pass. It is a rare occasion for chains to be required from St. Regis to Saltese. A weather spotter 9 miles northeast of Thompson Falls measured 4 in 3 hours from 6 pm to 9:08 pm MST. Similarly, a weather spotter located at Evaro Hill measured 4 during that same time-frame.

Montana DOT reported heavy snowfall that affected I-90 and MT-200 from Bonner to Greenough Hill to Helmville. They also reported periods of blowing and drifting snow from Greenough Hill to west of the Helmville Junction. A CoCoRaHS spotter in Bonner measured 1.5 of snow in the 65 minutes ending 10:30 pm MST on Feb. 24. Potomac schools had a 2 hour delay on Feb. 25.

Montana DOT reported snowfall along I-90 from Drummond to Homestake Pass and MT-1 through Georgetown Lake through this period. They also reported snow along US-12 over MacDonald Pass where chains were required for towing vehicles during the early morning hours of Feb. 25. There were no reports of heavy snow in these areas, and it seemed that the snow was more steady and moderate impact was felt.
The COOP located at the Eureka Ranger Station reported 1.1 of snow on Feb. 28. Light snow was reported across the area during this event keeping roads slick at times.

A person from the public in Hungry Horse reported whiteout conditions through Bad Rock Canyon due to blowing and drifting snow. Also extreme wind chills to -21 deg. F were reported from Essex to Marias Pass.

A spotter reported whiteout conditions 2 miles west-southwest of Columbia Falls. Winds were gusting to 50 mph during the event. Their best estimation of the snowfall was 4 inches. Snow bands developed during the day and brought the heaviest snow to the Ronan area where a storm total of 8.5 fell as measured by a weather spotter. The Columbia Falls schools closed on Feb. 28 due to the weather. A weather spotter located 8 miles east-southeast of Rollins reported a wind gust of 53 mph at 10 pm MST on Feb. 28. The Northwestern A divisional basketball tournament in Kalispell was postponed as well. As a side note, freezing rain fell on Feb. 27 between 1 and 4 pm MST from Arlee to Ronan causing slick conditions.

Freezing was the first impact to cause black ice on I-90 between St. Regis and Frenchtown with a few accidents reported earlier on Feb. 27. The rain changed to moderate to heavy snow by nightfall. A NWS employee located one mile north of Alberton  reported 11 of snow at 5 am MST Feb. 28. Montana DOT reported blowing snow along sections of I-90 from Frenchtown to Alberton and also at Evaro Hill. Other reports include: 9 Evaro and 8 Haugan 1 west.

A person from the public reported whiteout conditions just to the west of Hellgate Canyon where they estimated wind gusts to 50 mph at times. They had a tough time driving the streets in their four wheel drive vehicle. There were 1 to 2 foot drifts on the streets with up to 9 foot drifts in some parking lots. Numerous businesses delayed  opening, and several closed for the day as employees could not make it to work.  Many vehicles became stuck and were temporarily abandoned in downtown streets.  All public and private schools in Missoula were canceled. The Missoula International Airport storm total snowfall was 9.1 with 0.70 of precipitation. Freezing rain was reported on Feb. 27 from Hamilton to Missoula before it changed to snow by the evening hours. It caused very slick conditions in places, especially side streets. There were numerous motor vehicle slide-offs and accidents reported throughout the event. The Missoula snowfall total for the month of February was 40.2 and became the 2nd highest on record since 1894.

Montana DOT reported high winds, snow, reduced visibility from Bonner to Greenough Hill area. A CoCoRaHS observer in Bonner measured 2.1 of heavy snow that fell in 2 hours ending at 11:30 pm MST on Feb. 27 with a total of 6.2 through 5 am Feb. 28. Other snowfall amounts: 14 Snowbowl Ski area, 9.5 Seeley Lake and 8 1 mile south of Condon. The spotter in Condon reported wind gusts to 30 mph on Feb. 28 with snow falling. The Lindbergh Lake COOP saw 59.7 of snow for the month of February which breaks the previous all-time record of 47 set back in 1966. Records go back to Feb. 1960 for that station.

Freezing rain fell from 4 to 9 pm MST on Feb. 27 along I-90 from Drummond to the Butte area and also along MT-1 from Anaconda to Hall. As the arctic air moved in combined with falling moderate to heavy snow, blowing and severe drifting developed. This contributed to the Montana DOT listing I-90 from Phosphate to Warm Springs, MT-1 Drummond to Hall as Severe Driving conditions from 12 am MST to 10:30 am MST on Feb. 28. It also reported severe driving conditions on I-90 from Gold Creek to Warm Springs from 8 to 11 am MST on March 1. Extreme wind chills to -29 F were reported at 8:24 pm MST 7 miles north of Helmville on Feb. 28. Thirty-eight slide-off and motor vehicle accidents were reported during this event. There were 11 reports of stranded vehicles as well.
Montana DOT reported freezing rain from Lolo Pass to Lolo on US-12 during the afternoon on Feb. 27. The Lolo Pass SNOTEL reported around 5 of total snowfall that mainly fell on Feb. 28.
Freezing rain was reported by the MT DOT during the afternoon of Feb. 27 at Lolo Pass. The Lolo Pass SNOTEL reported around 5 of total snowfall that mainly fell on Feb. 28.
The COOP located in Headquarters reported 6.2 of total snowfall with 0.75 of precipitation. The COOP in Pierce reported 4.5 of snow with 0.64 of precipitation.
A spotter located 7.5 miles east-southeast of Kooskia reported a total storm snowfall of 3. Other amounts include: 1 at both Cottonwood 2 west-southwest and Fenn RS.

Near record snowfall for the month of February and strong easterly winds associated with an arctic air mass intrusion, caused severe wind loading on the western slopes of Mount Jumbo between Feb. 27-28. A snowboarder triggered a hard slab avalanche on a west facing, 35 degree slope of Mount Jumbo during the late afternoon of Feb. 28. The snowboarder was caught and carried for several yards before he was able to get out by himself. The avalanche traveled at approximately 80 to 100 mph and caught two children, ages 8 and 10, who were playing in their backyard as it slammed into and destroyed a two story wood frame home built in 1975. One child was partially buried  up to their armpits but not injured while the other was completely buried under 3 feet of snow. This child was later rescued, taken to the hospital and sustained only  minor injuries. The two residents of the destroyed home, a 66 year old male and his 68 year old wife were inside their home when it was hit and both were buried under several feet of snow and debris. Live power lines and broken natural gas lines complicated the rescue. The 66 year old male was rescued, had multiple injuries and lived. The 68 year old wife was rescued, but later died on March 3 from traumatic injuries. Three rental homes, 8 vehicles and an apartment building were also damaged by the avalanche. The avalanche width was 658 ft., depth was 2.5 to 4 ft. and the distance that it traveled from crown to terminus was 2,200 ft. Information courtesy of the West Central Montana Avalanche Center. The National Weather Service Missoula calculated a rough property damage estimate of $319K.

A weather station located 4 miles north of Kila reported a wind chill of -26 deg. F at 8:08 am MST on Mar. 1. Another station located one mile east-southeast of Marion reported -23 deg. F at 4:48 am MST on Mar. 1.

The Fielding RAWS station located 4.4 miles southwest of Marias Pass reported extreme wind chill values that peaked around -40 deg. F during the evening hours of Mar. 1. The MT DOT near Essex reported a wind chill of -35 F.

The Glacier National Airport located 8 miles north of Kalispell reported wind chill values between -20 and -30 deg. F while winds were ranging between 10 and 31 mph mainly blowing out of Bad Rock Canyon.

The Missoula International Airport reported the coldest wind chill value of -24 deg. F at 9:09 am MST on Mar. 1. Winds were gusting as high as 35 mph at the airport, but were probably over 50 mph near Hellgate Canyon.
At 12:33 pm MST on Mar. 1, a local newspaper reported that a large tree blew onto a car near the intersection of Cooper and Scott Streets in Missoula due to the wind.
A weather sensor located 4 miles east of Mullan reported the coldest wind chill of -21 deg. F. A weather sensor located three miles north of Ninemile reported -20 deg. F.

The MT DOT sensor located near Helmville reported a wind chill of -41 deg. F at 8:06 am on Mar. 1. Other cold wind chill values include: -40 Garrison, -37 Elliston and -32 at both Georgetown Lake and Bert Mooney Airport near Butte.

Montana DOT reported heavy snow overnight between Mar. 2-3 and estimated that 8 to 12 inches had fallen along Highway 2 south of Libby. They remarked that this was the heaviest snow event for the season. Montana DOT plow drivers in Troy estimated 12 fell there as well. Other snow amounts include: 12 Rexford 7 NNE, 8 Olney, 8.5 Yaak 9 NNE and 6.3 1 E Eureka.

An avalanche forecaster located in Essex reported a storm total snowfall of 16 with just over an inch of snow water equivalent. The West Glacier COOP measured a storm total snowfall of 13 with 1.01 of precipitation. A person from the public located 6 miles southwest of Marias Pass reported an estimated 2 per hour snowfall rates at 9:11 pm MST on Mar. 2. Montana DOT reported severe driving conditions from Blacktail to Marias Pass for a period due to the heavy snow. Wind chills in the beginning of the event were ranging between -30 to -40 F through the US-2 corridor as temperatures were below zero with winds gusting to 30 mph out of the easterly direction. Because of the heavy snow and strong winds, an avalanche was released one mile north of Blacktail covering the BNSF train tracks. Because of the elevated avalanche threat, train service was shut down for period.

Glacier Park International Airport reported a storm total snowfall of 10 with 0.47 of precipitation. Other snowfall totals include: 7.5 Whitefish, 7 Columbia Falls 1 NW, 6.3 Bigfork 13 S, 8 Polson Kerr Dam and 6.5 Polson. A weather spotter located in Columbia Falls reported snow-covered roads and were pretty bad during the afternoon of Mar. 2. An above normal amount of vehicle slide-offs and accidents were reported during this event from the Flathead to the Mission Valleys; 20 were crashes, 22 were slide-offs and 2 were stranded vehicles.

The Lookout Pass Ski resort reported 17 of heavy snow in 24 hours. Montana DOT required chains for towing units over Lookout Pass and labeled the I-90 stretch from St. Regis to Lookout Pass severe driving conditions due to heavy snow, poor visibility and icy roadways. Six snow slide-offs were reported between mile-markers 10 and 33 on I-90 by the afternoon of Mar. 3 which closed the westbound lanes from 3 to 5 pm MST. All east and westbound lanes were closed due to avalanche danger at 5:47 pm and traffic was re-routed to Hwy-200 until 4 pm MST on Mar. 4. Thirty vehicle incidents were reported by the MT DOJ in the two day period; 9 were crashes, 13 were slide-offs and 8 were stranded vehicles. Other snowfall amounts include: 18 Haugan 1 W, 10.7 Heron 2 NW, 10 Thompson Falls and 5 Alberton.

The COOP Seeley Lake Ranger Station reported a storm total snow of 11.6 with 0.84 of precipitation. A trained spotter located one mile south of Condon estimated 11 of snow 24 hours ending at 9 am on Mar. 3.

A CoCoRaHS observer located 4 miles east-northeast of Corvallis reported freezing rain with a temperature of 16 F at 3:42 pm MST on Mar. 2. A weather spotter located one mile north of Florence reported 6 of snowfall at 5:30 pm MST on Mar. 2. Freezing rain caused a glaze up to a 0.10 in thickness to develop across portions of the Bitterroot Valley. Missoula, Corvallis and Hamilton public schools closed due to the icy conditions on Mar. 4. Fifteen slide-offs, 4 crashes, and 3 stranded vehicles were reported by the MT DOJ.

The DES coordinator for Sanders County reported that the Little Bitterroot River flooded with 2 to 3 feet of water observed in places. The Little Bitterroot Road from Anderson's Corner to Sloan's Bridge was closed for 4 days. According to a river gauge located at one of the river's headwaters, Mill Creek, the discharge rate peaked at 238 cubic feet per second at 3:15 pm MST on March 6. In 31 years, this value surpassed the previous record of 53 cubic feet per second set back in 1986. A local rancher reported that this was the worst flooding he had ever seen. In terms of damage, the Little Bitterroot Road experienced minor damage with several culverts that needed to be replaced while homes were spared. Observations were sparse in the region, but a COOP observer located 2 miles northwest of Heron reported a 48 hour precipitation total of 1.99 between March 9-10. The combination of above normal snowfall that fell across western Montana in February, warm day and night-time temperatures and the rainfall contributed to substantial snow-melt in this event.

Above normal snowfall in February resulted in an unusually high snowpack across the Bitterroot Valley at the beginning of March. The Hamilton COOP reported a snow depth of 16 on March 2 which disappeared by March 9. Weather spotters in the Florence area reported well over a foot of snow at the beginning of March. This snowpack combined with 0.50 to 1 of mild rainfall and temperatures well into the 50's caused rapid snowmelt and subsequently overland flooding in the Bitterroot Valley. A person from the public in Florence off Hidden Valley Rd. reported a damaged fence, multiple homes with water damage and several windows broken. The MT DOT reported heavy water on the roadways S-203 2 miles east of Florence, near the junction with US-93. They also reported heavy amounts of water on S-203 10 miles north of the Stevensville Junction with S-269. The Ravalli County DES coordinator remarked that this was the worst flooding he had seen in 41 years in these areas.
Several days of moderate to heavy rainfall contributed to rock slides across northwest Montana. One in particular blocked a lane on Montana 37 north of the Libby Dam for a few hours.

Due to the large amount of precipitation between 1 and 2 inches in the mountains with high freezing levels, natural avalanche releases were reported between Essex and Marias Pass. A BNSF avalanche forecaster reported very large avalanche releases during the early morning hours on March 6. The MT DOT reported that US-2 between Essex and 7 miles west of Marias Pass was closed from 2 to 4:30 MST on March 6 due to avalanche mitigation. Both freight and passenger train service was shut down for an estimated 24 hour period between March 6-7.
The Idaho Transportation Department reported that many snow slides had blocked US-93 south of Lost Trail Pass. One of the avalanches was reportedly 700 feet in length.
A driveway was completely washed out by a flood, presumably caused by snowmelt and very warm temperatures.

A 27 year old male died as a result of asphyxia after being buried by a hard slab avalanche on a westerly slope above Altoona Lakes, in the Flint Creek Range or about 11 miles east-northeast of Philipsburg.  The crown was located at 8,512 feet, slope angle was 35 degrees plus, length was 1,324 feet on the ground and the estimated horizontal length of the crown was 2,100 feet. An investigation made by the West Central Montana Avalanche Center found that dry & cold weather during the early winter and a shallow snowpack had created a very weak faceted layer near the ground was 10 inches in depth. The skier broke through the weakness near some rocks which allowed for the season's snowpack to slide at once.
A weather spotter located 7.4 northwest of Anaconda reported 6.5 of snowfall in 18 hours.

The USGS Bitterroot River gauge at Darby reported a peak discharge rate of 8,590 cubic feet per second at 915 am MDT 5/24 and a peak height of 7.84 feet (7.5 ft. is the minor flood stage) at 8 am MDT 5/24. A gravel county road, Ross Lane, located just to the west of the Bitterroot River in Florence experienced minor flooding. The fishing access in Florence was totally inundated but was also closed due to construction. Also a few fields were flooded between Florence and Lolo.

The USGS Bitterroot River gauge at Missoula reported a peak height of 11.11 feet (11 ft. is the minor flood stage) and peak discharge rate of 17,300 cubic feet per second at 8:30 pm MDT on May 25. A NWS employee reported field flooding between Lolo and Missoula.

The USGS Bitterroot River gauge at Darby reported 5 instances where the river height surpassed the 7.50 ft. flood-stage: 7.84 ft. 8 am MDT 5/24, 7.57 ft. 8 am MDT 5/26, 7.76 ft. 815 am MDT 5/27, 7.63 ft. 8 am MDT 5/28 & 7.67 ft. 815 am MDT 5/29. It also reported a peak discharge rate of 8,590 cubic feet per second at 915 am MDT 5/24. Field flooding was reported by a NWS employee between Lolo and Florence.

An official observer at the Glacier Park International Airport observed a funnel cloud approximately 8 miles to the northwest. They reported that it didn't seem to reach the ground and only lasted for a minute. Radar and lightning data confirmed that the funnel cloud was attached to a cumulonimbus cloud(thunderstorm). Due to strong deep layer southwest wind shear ranging between 40 and 45 knots and with the relative location of the precipitation shaft to the base of the storm, the thunderstorm could have been supercellular. The Glacier National Park ASOS observed high relative humidities and south to south-southeast winds between 13 and 17 knots which added low-level wind shear. The appearance of the thunderstorm cloud base was relatively low which is another favorable atmospheric condition for funnel cloud development. Thanks to James LaDue from the NWS Warning Decision Training Branch for his added contribution to this report.

A 41 year old man heading west on U.S. Highway 12, lost control as he crossed an icy bridge deck over Lolo Creek near mile-marker 7 and shortly died thereafter. Another vehicle heading eastbound had to swerve into a ditch attempting to avoid a collision but still was side-swiped by the bike.

A COOP observer reported a 4 day precipitation total of 4.25 during this event which was the highest manual observation. Other total amounts include: 4.20 Bigfork 3.2 miles east-northeast, 4.08 Columbia Falls 7.7 miles south, 3.52 Kalispell 1.7 miles northwest, 3.23 Olney, 3.22 Ronan 4.1 miles northeast, 3.01 West Glacier and 2.50 Thompson Falls 9.3 miles northwest.  Kintla Lake Rd. in Glacier National Park was closed for a period of time due to water over the road and caused a campground crew to be stranded.

The National Park Service at Glacier National Park measured a 3 day snowfall total of 20 at the Sperry Chalet located at 6,580 ft. A person from the public in Essex reported 2 of snow with some damage to small trees and vegetation. They also reported that an estimated 4 fell at Marias Pass.

A person from the public located 8 miles northeast of Bigfork on Foothill Road at an elevation of 3200 ft. reported that the rain changed to wet snow with some mixture with rain. Other locations that saw a trace of snow were Whitefish, Columbia Falls, and Olney.
A person from the public located 3.4 miles southeast of Marion near Rogers Lake and at 4,063 ft. reported that just over 3 of snow fell.
The spotter at the Leadore Ranger Station reported dime to penny size hail.

The Glacier National Park RAWS reported 0.76 of rainfall in one hour. Other heavy rainfall reports include 0.78 40 min. ending 4:10 pm MDT 3 miles east of Creston and 0.65 in one hour via Hungry Horse RAWS at 6:11 pm MDT.
The weather spotter at the Leadore Ranger Station reported 0.40 of rainfall that fell in less than an hour.
Weather observer reported 1.27 of rainfall.
A person from the public reported dime to nickel size hail along with heavy rain. Pea-size hail was reported in Philipsburg.

The mesonet station EW4329 located 1 mile west-northwest of Elliston reported 0.74 of rain in one hour while the mesonet station TT234 located 7.7 miles north of Ovando reported 0.50 of heavy rain in an hour.
A person from the public reported 0.50 of rainfall that fell in 15 minutes. A person from Florence measured 0.74 that fell in 15 minutes as well.
A trained spotter estimated that 1 hail fell during the thunderstorm.
Law enforcement reported trees down near Marten Creek Bay area.
Several 6 inch diameter limbs blown down from a tall and very sturdy tree in the location of the inflow of a supercell thunderstorm.
A spotter reported multiple power poles down, along with power outages.
The forest service located in Rexford reported that multiple trees had fallen down or snapped off.

A single lightning bolt struck small crab-apple trees at a ranch located on Tin Cup Road, killing all 45 cattle crowded together. The Black Angus cattle consisted of cows, calves and a prize bull that died. A conservative damage estimate calculated by the NWS Missoula office is around $100,000.

A trained spotter estimated thunderstorm winds between 50 to 60 mph that caused tree damage and power outages in the area. The wind developed 10 to 12 minutes before brief heavy rain fell. They reported that the wind caused 4 big healthy fir and one yellow pine tree with a diameter of up to 2 feet to fall over.  They also observed a few cottonwood trees with their tops blown off. A 200 person awning from a wedding was damaged while a part of the roof trim from the Bull Lake Fire Department blew off as a result of the wind. Timing is based on reports and post-radar analysis.
The Lincoln County Emergency Manager reported that thunderstorm winds downed numerous trees and power lines in the Troy area.
Law enforcement reported a tree down which blocked the south bound lane of highway 56 between mile marker 23 and 24 for a period of time.

The emergency manager from Lincoln County reported that numerous trees and power lines were down with roads blocked in the Libby area. The Zonolite RAWS located at 4,200 feet MSL reported a 51 mph wind gust at the 21:06 MST observation time.
A law enforcement office reported mostly 1 hail but a few were up to half-dollar size. The hail accumulated up to 12 inches in places.

One tree, possibly a yellow pine, twisted off 20 to 30 feet above the ground. A 2nd yellow pine smashed into a vacant trailer house while a 3rd yellow pine was uprooted from the high winds. The severe winds combined with large hail also peppered the sides of a few farming structures.
A law enforcement officer estimated that between 1 and 2 inches of rain fell and caused a nearby creek to swell to 3 feet in width and a couple feet in depth.
The COOP observer measured 1.66 inches of rainfall for the 24 hours ending at 7 am Aug. 15. Most likely this rainfall amount was associated with the supercell thunderstorm that tracked over the area.

A farmer reported major property and crop damage due to both large hail and wind. The property damage included 5 rental home roofs, siding from 3 homes, several windows, and 12 garage doors that either were dented or destroyed. Approximately 75% of his spring wheat crop, approximately 450 acres, was decimated by the wind and hail. In the 67 years that he has lived there, there was only one other storm that was comparable to this one. Back in 1963, a similar storm decimated his dad's crops.

A farmer reported around 12 trees (pine and red fir) broke between 6 and 16 feet above the ground. A bull pine near 3 feet in diameter at the base, broke off around 6 feet from the ground and destroyed a trailer house.

The USDA reported that at least 400 acres of hard red spring wheat were destroyed and 700 acres were damaged.  They also reported that 183.6 acres of soft wheat were destroyed and 189.2 acres were damaged. All in all, the total crop damage tallied at $425,000.

A COOP observer located 2.4 miles northwest of Heron reported strong gusty winds that caused the top 30 feet of a 70 year old sub-alpine fir to topple over a power line near their house. They also reported that approximately 5 trees located within a quarter of a mile of their home were damaged by the wind. Most of those trees broke off about 30 to 40 feet up and fell in a eastward direction. Their community was without power for about 23 hours after the event.

About 20 ponderosa pine trees fell down onto the main Salmon River Road while one pine tree smashed the USGS river gauge on the Salmon River.  Evidence revealed that debris flows occurred at Boulder Creek, Owl Creek, Colson Creek and at an unnamed gulch. The unnamed gulch produced a large debris flow with rock onto the main Salmon River Road. A man-made dam located near the delta of Colson Creek was damaged.

A heavy thunderstorm produced heavy rains and severe mudslides along the Magruder Corridor mainly between Scimitar Creek and the CCC Camp. There were about 6 washouts reported with large trees and rock debris making the road impassable. Timing was based on radar data.

A person from the public west of Deer Lodge estimated that quarter size hail fell during this event. Also a trained spotter located 1 mile west of Deer Lodge measured pea size hail and reported that large amounts of it had fallen.
A trained spotter measured 0.80 of rainfall in 20 minutes due to a thunderstorm.

According to a spotter 1 mile west of Deer Lodge 0.80 of rain fell in a time span of 20 minutes. This rain resulted in street flooding in the town of Deer Lodge with water lapping doors of many businesses. The Powell County fair and rodeo were impacted by the flooding especially the fairgrounds exhibition center. Prisoners from the state prison were summoned to help setup sandbags to help mitigate the flooding.
A trained spotter reported 1 size hail south of Butte.
Debris flows were reported in Club Gulch in Flat Creek, Pardee Creek and at Shaw Gulch with moderate road damage.
The Hoodoo Basin SNOTEL at 6,050 ft received 8��� of snow and 0.80��� of snow water equivalent.

events.cz_name: LOWER HELLS CANYON / SALMON RIVER REGION
events.event_narrative: This was the first measurable snowfall for central Idaho for the 2014/2015 winter season. According to road sensors at Whitebird Grade, road temperatures were above freezing before snow began to fall after 12 pm PST. This contributed to a flash freeze scenario causing extremely slick conditions. A snow plow struck a sheriff's cruiser around 1500 PST which caused Whitebird Grade to close for several hours, opening up around 1745 PST. The Idaho State Police reported multiple semi-trucks that had jack-knifed and 2 vehicle slide-offs. These impacts, along with the fact that this was the first winter weather for the area, justified the classification as a high impact event.

Several farms and orchards in the Missoula Valley saw damage to corn, tomatoes, squash, pumpkin and basil. A winery saw 25% loss to their grapes despite attempts at mitigation via watering and helicopter operations. The official low temperature at the Missoula International Airport was 25 degrees which broke the old daily record of 28 set back in 1988. It was also the 3rd coldest low in the first 15 days of September since records began in 1893.

Several inches of snow fell across the region as an arctic air mass pushed in from east of the Divide. The Going-to-the-Sun Road was closed from Big Bend on the west side to Jackson Glacier Overlook on the east side of Glacier National Park due to wind, snow, ice and limited visibility. At Marias Pass on US-2, snow fell with visibility being reduced to 1/2 mile at times. A weather spotter located nine miles north-northeast of Polebridge reported 7 inches of snow at 841 am MDT on the 11th. The COOP station in Polebridge saw a low of 16 degrees on the morning of the 12th.

The arctic cold front pushed through during the evening of the 10th and brought several hours of light to moderate snow to MacDonald Pass and subsequently snow-covered roads. This front continued its way south affecting Homestake Pass on I-90 and also the Butte area. A trained spotter located 6 miles south-southwest of Butte at 5900 feet measured 3 inches of snow through 744 am MDT on the 11th.

A spotter located in Ronan reported a tree with a three foot diameter base damaged by strong winds. Winds between 35 to 45 mph were reported from the Flathead to Mission Valleys as the cooler and more dense modified arctic air mass pushed southward. Flathead Lake saw choppy waves from the strong north to east winds causing the water to slop over into parking lots in Polson.

A powerful arctic front made its way over the Continental Divide bringing damaging winds along highway 2 and to Glacier National Park. In Glacier National Park, about 20 structures were hit by large falling trees including a vehicle and six homes. No injuries were reported as a result of the damage.

As the powerful arctic front made its way through Bad Rock Canyon, it brought damaging winds and blizzard-like conditions to Columbia Falls, MT and Kalispell, MT. Trees falling on power lines left 9000 Flathead Electric Cooperative members without power on Saturday, Nov 29. The ASOS at Glacier Park International airport recorded wind gusts of 48 mph, with 40 mph gusts being common for 11 hours and wind chill values down to -20 degrees F. Snowfall totals were estimated at 7 inches for Columbia Falls and 5 inches for the Kalispell airport. Roads conditions around the area reported blowing and drifting snow and ice.  Between early Saturday morning and Sunday afternoon, Montana Highway Patrol responded to more than 40 crashes in Flathead County alone.

The Glacier Park International Airport observers reported a storm snowfall total of 5.3 with 0.44 melted liquid and temperatures only rising from the mid-teens to the lower 20's during the event. The reports of freezing rain on top of snow were mainly found from the southern half of Flathead Lake and points south. Other reports include: Near 9 of new snow 5 miles north of Bigfork, 7 at Lake Blaine, 6 near Polebridge, 6 east of Polson towards the Mission Mountains, and 5 north of Whitefish. A 17 year old boy died as a result of a head-on crash between Bigfork and Somers on Montana Highway 82 on Dec. 4. The crash happened on a curve where road conditions were particularly slick and the Montana Highway Patrol commented that the boy was driving too fast for the conditions.

The Missoula International Airport received 1.7 of snow, sleet and freezing rain during the event. It initially started as snow with temperatures at 23 degrees and then started to mix with sleet by 6 am MST on Dec 4. It then changed to light freezing drizzle and rain by the evening hours causing black ice on side roads. The Bitterroot Valley saw an earlier change to freezing drizzle during the early morning hours. An observer in Florence reported 0.8 of snow before it changed to freezing drizzle. The slick conditions caused several vehicle slide-offs and accidents in the area.

A power company reported that downed power lines closed Interstate 15 at mile-marker 123 which is at the Rocker Interchange. The Bert Mooney Airport south of Butte reported a peak wind gust to 45 mph at 4:03 pm MST with the cold front passage.

A power company reported a power outage in the southern Hamilton area most likely due to strong wind gusts. Valley observation stations reported wind gusts between 40 to 50 mph while a few higher elevation stations reported wind gusts to 58 mph.
The Moss Creek SNOTEL reported 12 of snow. Impact-wise, difficult travel was reported by hunters and back-country users.
The North Fork Jocko SNOTEL at 6330 ft reported 8��� of snow, and the Stuart Mtn SNOTEL at 7400 ft reported 12��� of snow.

Lolo Pass DOT called after the event to report that 6-7��� of snow fell at the pass, which was a significant impact for them since they had not yet started full winter staffing. The Skalkaho SNOTEL at 7250 ft reported 7 of snow; the Twelvemile Creek SNOTEL reported 6 of snow.
The Mountain Meadows SNOTEL at 6360 ft reported 10��� snow, and the Savage Pass SNOTEL at 6170 ft reported 7��� of snow.
The Warm springs SNOTEL reported 5 of snow with frontal passage.
The Crater Meadows SNOTEL at 5960 ft reported 11��� of snow, and the Cool Creek SNOTEL 6280 ft reported 8��� of snow.

A spotter estimated strong arctic winds gusting to 30 mph near Essex, MT. Glacier Park International Airport saw a peak gust of 48 mph when the arctic air began to spill into the Flathead Valley, and this wind likely topped 50 mph in the Bad Rock canyon region. Police dispatch reported wind knocking down multiple trees in West Glacier, MT. An additional hazard was rain, which fell before the arctic cold front. The flash-freezing of this water on roads contributed to very slick road conditions, as reported by spotters.

Glacier Park International Airport saw a peak gust of 48 mph when the arctic air began to spill into the Flathead Valley. At the airport, sustained 32 mph winds with gusts to 40 mph were commonplace, and visibility down to 0.75 mi was reported at times. These winds caused multiple trees falling across roadways in Whitefish and Kalispell. Power outages and ���treacherous��� road conditions impacted many and were reported by weather spotters. ASOS reports of rain before the cold winds explained why a weather spotter in Columbia Falls tweeted that there was a solid sheet of ice beneath the snow.
Accidents, slick roads, and whiteout conditions reported along I-90 by DOT partners and county sheriffs. The Kraft Creek SNOTEL at 4750 ft reported 7��� of snow.

The MDT reported that the quick transition from warm to cold with the quick freezing of rain under snow presented crews with a difficult challenge in keeping roads navigable, and they had over 30 weather-related accidents. Slick roads and whiteout conditions reported by county sheriffs. Icy roads caused a very slow commute for NWS employees and workers across Missoula.

The Butte DOT reported being extremely busy, with semi trucks stuck on Homestake Pass being a major impact for them. ASOS wind gusts at Butte's airport measured as high as 52mph. Farther north, a trained spotter reported 5 of snow in Deer Lodge, MT.
The Essex DOT sensor reported temperatures of 1 F and winds gusting to 17mph causing wind chills as low as -15 F.
The Glacier Park International Airport ASOS recorded Wind chills as low as -10 F, but winds were not as strong as expected, with the single digit air, leading to only modest chill values.
Winds of 16 mph and temperatures in the mid single digits lead to prolonged wind chills near -12 F over 5 hours on the morning of the 11th.
The ASOS sensor in Butte, MT recorded wind chills to -23 F on the 11th and -35 F on the 12th.
The RAWS near Clearwater Junction reported wind chills as low as -17 F through the mornings of the 11th and 12th.

An arctic front spilled over Evaro Hill which brought snow to Missoula and Bitterroot Valleys. Due to warm road temperatures, snow initially melted then refroze. Icy road conditions led to over 30 slideoff incidents being reported by the DOT.

There were reports of whiteout conditions by numerous spotters. A St. Regis hotel estimated a storm total snowfall of 6 inches. In addition, multiple accidents occurred along I-90 due to the slick road surface.

Law enforcement reported 10 crashes due to ice with at least 1 rollover. Over half of these accidents had injuries associated with them. Multiple trained spotters reported slippery roads with a couple reporting the roads as ice rinks.
Libby, MT law enforcement reported roads as a solid sheet of ice overnight. Local businesses also reported icy roads throughout Lincoln county.

Snow became heavy over Homestake Pass around noon and was closed due to 12 semi-trailer trucks stuck on the pass. DOT officials reported 8 to 10 inches of wet heavy snow throughout this event and at one point they had 4 snow plows out at Homestake Pass. There were approximately 14 crashes/slideoffs from around 9 am to 10 pm within the area.  This includes two jack-knifed semis, both on Homestake Pass.
A semi-truck slide off occurred on Hwy 2 near Essex, where 4 inches of snow fell overnight on the 26th. There was also a snow report of 8.5 inches at Swan Lake.

The park service reported a large tree down across Hwy 83, with 11 inches of snow being reported by a weather spotter in the Seeley Lake area. Power outages and 8 inches of wet snow were reported by the public in Greenough.

Over 2500 people in the Bitterroot Valley were without power for over 6 hours after 5 inches of extremely wet snow fell in and around Darby. Hamilton spotters reported 3 to 4 inches. Snow ratios were near 5:1 for this event. A local fire chief near Darby said it was the worst he's seen it in over 50 years in regards to call volume and number of broken tree limbs.

The Butte area saw steady snow for 24 hours and the spotter report amounts ranged from 8 to 14.5 inches. An additional hazard was the layer of ice below the snow due to the preceding rainfall in some places. In the morning school buses were stuck in uptown Butte delaying their arrival. Tens of weather-related accidents occurred in the Silver Bow county area. An emergency manager said this was definitely an above normal impact event for the Silver Bow County.

Anywhere from 6 to 10 inches of snow fell across the higher elevations of western Lemhi County during this event. The heaviest fell with the frontal passage in the late evening hours potentially catching any back-country person off-guard.

A person from the public reported up to 5 inches of snow in the higher terrain in the vicinity of Carmen Creek area. According to nearby sensors, this snow fell in a short amount of time associated with the cold front passage.

As of 6:30 am on the 24th, MDT reported 12 to 14��� of snow between Coram and West Glacier. On top of the morning snowfall report, the Pike Creek SNOTEL located 697 feet above Marias Pass reported an additional 11��� after this time-frame. Pike Creek saw a total snowfall of 17���.  MDT later reported that there were times when they had a hard time keeping up with this snow event.

A storm spotter from Olney reported 12 inches of snow over 24 hours with periods of 1/4 mile visibility at times during this holiday weekend.  Another spotter from Marion reported around 8 inches of snow on the 28th.

A storm spotter reported 13 inches of snow in Essex over 48 hours with periods of blowing and drifting snow when the arctic air moved through. Also, the MDT reported periods of moderate to heavy snow during this event along US-2 and also mentioned that there were times when they had a difficult time keeping up with the snowfall.

As snow began to fall over the Flathead Valley, reports of crashes and slide offs began to increase sharply around 5 pm on the 27th. By the next morning, a storm spotter in Colombia Falls reported 13.5 inches of snow during this event. Over the Mission Valley, storm spotters reported 13 inches of storm total snow in Polson and 9 inches in Ronan. Strong winds associated with the arctic cold front caused numerous power outages over the Flathead Valley. Sustained winds of 43 mph over Flathead Lake near Yellow Bay was recorded by mesonet sensors for several hours.

As the arctic front continued to move through western Montana, a snow band developed near Missoula and eventually made its way over Interstate 90 between Frenchtown and Superior. Multiple accidents and slide offs were reported with whiteout conditions under the heavy snow band.

A heavy snow band developed along the arctic frontal boundary and caused numerous accidents between Frenchtown and the west end of Missoula valley. This resulted to the shutdown of the westbound lanes on Interstate 90 for a couple of hours. An observation of 3.3 inches of snow was reported at the Missoula International Airport from this band which lasted around 2 hours.
Lost Trail Pass received 14 inches of snow and 10 inches of snow fell at Lolo pass over a 24 hour period. Periods of blowing and drifting snow also occurred at Lost Trail pass.

A moist weather system brought heavy snow and dangerous back country conditions to the Seeley Lake region. Local media reported 4 snowmobilers were buried in an avalanche in the North Fork Bowl area, but were able to ride out on their own. 8 inches of snow was measured by a SNOTEL 6 hours before the avalanche.  A spotter from Condon also reported 14 inches of snow over 24 hours.

Pierce ranger station SNOTEL reported 14 inches of snowfall for this event with periods of heavy snow during the afternoon on Saturday and on early Sunday morning. Pierce COOP reported 16.5 inches of snow from Dec 28th through the 30th. Shanghai Summit SNOTEL reported 13 inches of snow during this event.
The Dixie Cooperative Observer (COOP) reported 11.1 inches of snow over 2 days. Other SNOTEL observations include Savage Pass with 9 inches of snow and Lolo Pass with 10 inches.

Lookout Pass ski resort reported 17 inches of snow over a 24 hour period. Out of the 17 inches, 14 inches of snow fell between 4 pm MST Saturday and 5 am MST Sunday. MDT required that towing vehicles use chains after 5 pm on the 27th.

Montana Highway Patrol reported road conditions were so slick that tires on some vehicles could not get traction and they became stranded. Traffic backed up from approximately 6:54 pm through 10 pm MST because of the accidents. A Greyhound bus and a number of semi-trucks jack-knifed across the highway while several vehicles ended up in the ditch.

The MDT reported that between 11 to 16 inches of snow fell between Marion and Happy's Inn, up to 20 inches between Libby and Happy's Inn on US-2. They reported that the snow changed to freezing rain at times later on Jan. 5 through the early morning hours of Jan. 6. The Lincoln County Emergency Manager reported a few downed power lines and brief power outages. A weather spotter just southwest of Libby measured 18 inches of snow while Troy receive 11 inches.

The BNSF avalanche forecaster reported a storm total snowfall in Essex of 20.4 inches with 1.40 inches of snow water equivalent. They reported that the snow changed to freezing rain on Jan. 6 and then the second push of arctic air froze everything up solid. A large avalanche covered US-2 10 miles north of Essex while a second avalanche occurred around 920 am on Jan 5, two miles north of Swan Lake. The West Glacier and West Valley school systems were closed on Jan. 6.  Blowing snow was reported at Bad Rock Canyon and at Marias Pass.
The MDT reported that a snow slide affected Highway 83, two miles north of Swan Lake. Except for traffic being diverted to one lane, no further information was provided on the size of the avalanche.

The MDT reported an avalanche that blocked both lanes of US-2 located 10 miles west of Essex near the Blue Rock Cut or at milepost 168.6. It was approximately 30 to 40 yards long, 3 feet deep on down hill side, and 5 feet deep on the uphill side. One lane was opened up after 1.5 hours while the other lane took an additional hour to clean up.

A foreman with the Idaho Transportation Department reported that 13 avalanches occurred during this period. One of them crossed both lanes of US-93 at milepost 349.5. and was 12 feet high, 110 feet long and 12 feet wide. It took around 1 hour to clear one lane and another 2 hours to clear the remaining snow.

A person from the public located one mile south of Condon measured 12 inches of heavy snow that changed to freezing rain by the morning of Jan. 5. They also reported that the power went out starting at 6 pm MST on Jan. 4. At one point Highway 200 east bound lanes east of Bonner were closed for several hours due to a snow slide. MDT also reported severe driving conditions along Highway 200 due to icy conditions and freezing rain. The Seeley-Swan school system was closed on Jan. 6 because of the freezing rain.

The MDT estimated 18 inches of snow fell at Lolo Pass through the morning of Jan. 5. Snow changed to rain by the afternoon and by nightfall road surfaces became slick again. The MDT foreman in charge the Lolo Pass stretch mentioned that a small car would have had a tough time due to the very heavy snowfall rates. A 43-year-old man was killed on Highway 12 west of Lolo when his vehicle hit ice on a curve. Other factors involved included alcohol and not wearing his seat-belt.

The MDT reported severe driving conditions from 9 pm Jan. 5 through 1 am MST Jan. 6 over MacDonald Pass due to heavy snow. A snow slide occurred near the intersection of Highways 200 and 141 closing one lane of traffic around 1 pm on Jan. 5.

Glacier Park International Airport reported 19.2 inches of storm total snowfall which became the 6th highest 2-day snowfall on record. Several families were stranded at their homes until they were plowed out because of the heavy snow. Most schools closed on Jan. 5 and also on Jan. 6 except for portions of the Mission Valley where 2-hour delays were common. The Kalispell City Manager reported that there were some roads that were impassable without 4WD vehicles. Weather spotters reported trees down in Bigfork and also over Highways 35 and 83. Other notable storm total snowfall totals include: 26.5 3 miles north of Bigfork, 23 Woods Bay, 21.5 Bigfork, and 8.5 4.1 miles northeast of Ronan.

MDT reported severe driving conditions from Superior to St. Regis and Lookout Pass during the late evening on Jan. 4. They reported that it was so heavy at times that the snow plow drivers couldn't keep up. Chains were required over Evaro Hill for towing vehicles from roughly 5 am to 9 am MST on Jan. 5 which is a rare occurrence. Storm total snowfall at Lookout Pass was 21 inches while Heron saw 17 inches.

After 6 inches of snow fell in the Missoula area, freezing rain developed and caused up to 0.25 of glaze to form on untreated surfaces. Numerous school delays or cancellations were made for the Missoula and Bitterroot Valley school systems. Roads were especially bad due to the fact that previously plowed streets became very slick with the glaze of ice on them. Buses were not able to drive off the main roads in Florence and Victor due to the icy roads.
The COOP observer reported 12.1 inches of total snowfall while 10 inches was reported in Orofino.

A person from the public in Dixie reported that 2.5 feet of snow fell between 9 pm PST on Jan. 4 through 4 pm PST on Jan. 5. In Elk City, 2 feet of snow was reported before it turned over to freezing rain and rain. The Crater Meadows SNOTEL reported 4.50 of snow water equivalent with 18 inches of total snow. The ITD also estimated 18 inches of snow at Lolo Pass and they remarked that small cars would have had a hard time driving during the heavy snow.

Periods of moderate to heavy snow fell mainly during the early morning hours affecting Lookout Pass. Around 11 inches of snow fell which caused snow-covered roads and slick conditions. No crashes or slide-offs were reported during this period by the MT Department of Justice.
A rockslide was reported along US-2 just east of West Glacier, MT. The eastbound lane was blocked by softball-sized rocks. Road crews cleared debris and the road was usable again an hour later.

Heavy rains led to a large boulder falling and blocking the west-bound lane of US-12 during the early morning hours of February 10th, 2015. The slide happened 14 miles west of Lolo, MT. The mountain pass road was closed to any through-traffic for over a day and a half as officials hired a crew to inspect, blast, and remove large rocks. Truckers reported losing thousands of dollars per day as they could not use the route. Road crews noted that this is one of the largest slides they could recall. Full traffic flow resumed 2 days later.

Heavy rain caused a rockslide on February 7th that closed the westbound lanes of I-90 west of St Regis, MT. Several hundred small rocks and boulders had to be cleared from the road surface. No accidents were reported. Westbound lanes were closed for 2 days as traffic was forced to divert to the north via MT Hwy 135 and MT Hwy 200, thus increasing travel distance. By the afternoon of Feb 9th, one lane, two-way traffic had been set-up, ending the interstate re-route.

Temperatures up to 48 F on February 6th, 2015 and above-freezing temperatures near 44 F overnight led to rapid snow melt which caused Salmon, ID area creeks and rivers to rise rapidly on February 7th. Temperatures reached up to 56 F that day, with rain runoff further complicating issues. The main flooding occurred near Kitz Creek and its confluence with the Salmon River. Four homes sustained minor flood damage in Salmon, ID. Additionally, the Salmon County Airport was shutdown for the day due to water on the runway.

Due to the nature of this system, it was a major change to road conditions and most likely caught some travelers off-guard. Three main areas saw the highest impacts with the storm: The first area was around Georgetown Lake. Snowplow crews barely could keep up with the heavy snowfall even with extra equipment they had to bring in to mitigate. The second area included the Racetrack Interchange to Warm Springs along Interstate 90. Heavy wet snow caused deep slush on the road which contributed to a three vehicle car accident in that stretch. The third area that saw impacts covered a stretch of I-90 east of Butte to Homestake Pass. Blizzard-like conditions were reported by the MDT and the sharp temperature drop from the 40s to the 20s caused road temperatures cold enough for snow to stick. Weather sensors reported wind gusts to 38 mph while snow amounts up to 6 inches were estimated in the higher terrain including Homestake Pass. Two jack-knifed vehicles caused Homestake Pass to be closed for a time around 415 pm MDT.

The MDT section manager in the Hot Springs area reported heavy snow and gusty winds to 25 mph causing severe drifting and blowing snow. The one to two foot drifts formed continually throughout the evening especially between 830 and 1030 pm MST on highway 28 between the 10 to 19 mile-markers. Another impact was snow that melted then froze to an ice layer under the snow causing treacherous conditions. They received anywhere from 1 to 5 inches. The manager had to call in extra help from another area to mitigate the conditions.

Moderate to heavy snow fell along Interstate 90 ahead of an arctic cold front during the evening of the 2nd. The snow melted and then turned to ice as colder air filtered south causing road conditions to become very slick. The MDT and a NWS employee reported very icy roads during the morning of the 3rd. Alberton received 4.5 inches of snow.

Even though a few places saw a melt and re-freeze scenario with slick roads, the majority of the Missoula and Bitterroot Valleys saw low impact. Around a half-inch of snow fell in Frenchtown which froze after sunset causing roads to slicken up. A 57-year-old man was injured in an accident in which he slid and rolled off I-90 near Frenchtown.
