The MDT reported periods of moderate snow with gusty winds and drifting snow in the Hamilton area.

MDT reported 6 inches  of snow fell at Lost Trail Pass on US-93 while in the higher valley northeast of Sula 4 to 5 inches fell. The snow began around 5:20 pm on the 2nd at Lost Trail Pass and caused road conditions to become slick throughout the evening. Webcams revealed some blowing and drifting snow.

MacDonald Pass on US-2 began accumulating snow with deteriorating conditions with blowing snow by 3 pm MST on the 2nd. MDT reported around 3 inches of snow at the pass while only 2 inches were reported at Discovery Ski Resort. The Butte ASOS reported light snow with strong gusty winds to 35 mph with the arctic cold front.
The MDT reported snow that melted and froze causing slick areas along I-90 near Clinton to Bearmouth. Around 2 inches of snow fell in the Clinton area.
A person from the public reported persistent rain and hail between 6:30pm to 7:30pm. They estimated the largest hail were quarter size.

An NWS Employee experienced torrential rainfall and 0.50 inch hail while driving on I-90. The hail lasted 5 min, and rain rates were so high cars on the 75 mph interstate slowed to around 25 mph for a few minutes due to reduced visibility. A nearby RAWS weather station reported 0.55 inches of rain from the storm shortly before it crossed I-90.
A trained spotter reported mostly 0.50 inch to 0.75 inch hail, with a few nickel-sized hailstones (0.88 in). Winds were estimated to be gusting at 50 mph with the storm's passage.
The Montana Mesonet weather station near St. Regis reported 0.80 inches of rain in one hour, from 2:02pm to 3:02pm local time.
A trained spotter reported penny-sized hail in Superior, with 0.50 inches of rain falling in 30 min. Winds estimated at 40 to 50 mph accompanied this report.
The public reported half dollar sized (1.25 in) hail that fell in the woods near Headquarters, ID. Pictures confirmed the size of hail.
Trained spotter reported heavy rain with 0.5 inches of accumulation, pea size hail, and estimated 50 mph winds.

A cluster of thunderstorms brought heavy rain just west of Anaconda. Edward from Anaconda reported 0.59 inches of rain and his friend who lives to the west recorded 1.13 inches of precipitation. The intense rain caused mud run off into a basement.
A tree fell on a house bringing damage to a power box. Another large tree fell and downed multiple power poles. The power outage affected 5000 homes.
A fence with 5 x 5 inch posts was blown down. Wind estimates near 60 mph.

A macroburst brought damaging winds to the city of Missoula. A 74 mph wind gust was measured at the Missoula airport, but a majority of the damage occurred towards the |South Hills area. Major power lines and large trees were knocked down, and some residents were without power for four days. A local power company reported that several power poles, rated at 80 mph, were snapped in half. Over a million dollars in damages is estimated for this event.
NWS employee reported a power outage, and tree limbs 5 to 6 inches in diameter broke off. Estimated winds of 50 mph.
Multiple downed trees in Turah. Also the highway sign for Bonner was broken off by the wind. Wind speeds of 60 mph estimated.
Power lines and trees were downed by the wind. One of the trees that was knocked over was 18 inches in diameter.
Public tweeted image confirms at least quarter size hail.
Trained spotter estimated 59 mph wind gust. A person from the public on Facebook estimated wind gusts were over 65 mph in Darby.

KREM news reported The Lawyer Complex has burned 42 homes and 75 other buildings, according to Northern Rockies Incident Management Team.  The National situation reported  118 structures lost (as of the last report 9/10/2015) with the cost of fighting the fire at 25 million dollars. The Idaho County Sheriff's Office says a woman died preparing for evacuations due to the Lawyer Complex Fire. She died Friday evening after falling and hitting her head.
Forest service employee reported that 2 forest service structures were burned from the fire.  Total cost of the fire is estimated at 5 million dollars.

Roads were reported to have slushy accumulations of 3 to 6 inches in Butte, with at least 5 slide-offs accidents influenced by weather. Widespread storm accumulations of 3 to 6 inches were reported, with a highest estimated snow report of 7.0 inches 7 miles southeast of Butte, and the highest measured report of 6.5 inches 7 miles south of Butte. Additionally, the public reported 7 - 9 inches of snow over Homestake Pass.
The Bert Mooney Airport in Butte, MT had to divert a flight at 9am and cancel a flight at 12pm due to observations of 1/2 mile visibility along with overcast skies at 1000 feet.

During the overnight hours, law enforcement staff were overwhelmed by number of vehicle slide-offs. More than 12 weather-related crashes occurred in the vicinity of Butte. They needed to call in multiple off-duty staff members to assist in accident clean-up and in helping stranded motorists.  MDT road crews reported severe driving conditions on I-15 south of Feeley Hill interchange, with ice under the fresh snowfall. Chains were required for towing units, with lane blockages due to semi-trucks being unable to summit pass. One snow plow drifted off road in heavy snow conditions.  A storm spotter reported 7.0 inches of snow 7 miles southeast of Butte, MT over a 24 hour period.
The wind sensor at Idaho County airport recorded sustained wind speeds of 44+ mph, with occasional gusts of 50 to 60 mph. The maximum measured gust was 61 mph at 6:55 pm PST.

A barn, with roof dimensions of approximately 40 by 50 feet, was blown off and traveled 100 to 150 feet to the east-southeast blocking both lanes of McIver Road.  Based on the damage, the wind gusts could have been 75 mph.

Zonolite RAWS reported wind gusts of over 50 mph for 5 hours, with a peak gust of 66 mph. The strength of winds in valleys was likely not quite to this level, but based on damages, localized mountain waves likely caused winds of nearly this magnitude in valleys overnight.

Power outages affected many communities in Lincoln County. Trees took out power lines and a 4 power poles.  Several pine, elm and spruce trees were blown down and blocking area roads. Prior rainfall contributed to helping push the trees over. One hotel had severe roof damage, and a few houses lost their metal roof, although these roofs were old and reportedly not up to code. Debris was widespread in county. Cell service was down from 7 pm 11/17 through 4 pm 11/18. In Troy, they lost power overnight. The winds in Libby were worse than measured at the nearby Libby airport.

At 1:30 am, the Missoula International Airport ASOS reported a wind gust of 59 mph. Tens of Ponderosa Pine and other deciduous trees in town were blown down overnight, and several limbs were blown off. A trained weather spotter estimated 60+ mph winds in southern Missoula around 1 am 12/18, additionally reporting roof damage to house due to 8-inch diameter limb falling off tree. An apartment complex in the hills of southern Missoula sustained heavy roof damage as well.

A personal weather station a few miles southeast of Lolo, MT measured a 66 mph wind gust at 3600 ft around 8pm on 12/17. Trees downed power lines, which cut out power to 3500 people in Ravalli county. The power returned during the afternoon on 12/18.

The public reported 60 mph winds in Anaconda Overnight. A personal weather sensor between Anaconda and Butte reported a 52 mph gust. One home in Anaconda sustained siding damage, while another lost part of a metal roof (the roof was not well-constructed). Emergency managers reported a street light blown down in Anaconda, with multiple trees down in the area. Additionally, a tree smashed a parked car in Butte, causing thousands of dollars of damage.

Snow combined with high winds over Homestake Pass lead to a traffic jam of semi-trucks during the early morning hours as road conditions became hazardous. Over 30 semis were stuck at a time, with most issues due to failure to chain-up.

Montana road crews reported 8 to 10 inches of snow overnight at Marias pass, with heavy snow at times. Lower elevations, such as West Glacier, MT reported 2 to 3 inches. Multiple trees were blown down over both lanes of US-2 near Essex, MT. High elevation RAWS sites reported winds gusts in the 50 mph range, causing dangerous back-county conditions for hunters.

Snowfall intensity increased during the evening at Lolo Pass with winds gusting to an estimated 50+ mph. Roads crews reported snow-covered roads with high winds overnight, with the Deer Mountain RAWS at 7300 ft reporting 63 mph gusts in the early morning hours.

Light snow at high elevations combined with winds gusting 50-84 mph made for hazardous back-country conditions for hunters. The Point 6 RAWS at 8000 ft reported a wind gust of 84 with light snow, while the 6250 ft N Fork Elk Creek SNOTEL also reported light snow.

The Savage pass SNOTEL at 6200 ft reported 6 inches of new snow overnight, with heavy snow from 11pm to 1am 11/18. Nearby RAWS sensors showed wind gusts of 40 to 60 mph, making for blizzard-like conditions for anyone in the high terrain.
The Morgan Creek SNOTEL at 7600 ft reported light snow overnight, with nearby winds at Skull Gulch gusting to 56 mph, making for dangerous back-country conditions.

The Saddle Mountain RAWS at 7900 ft reported 4 inches of snow overnight, with the nearby Deer Mountain RAWS reporting wind gusts of 63 mph during the early morning hours, making for dangerous back-country conditions.

A trained spotter in Troy reported 4 inches during the morning hours. Another spotter reported 3.5 inches of snow north of Noxon, MT. Roads crews reported black ice on roads causing hazardous driving conditions.
The public reported 4 inches of snow in Coram, and 3 inches in West Glacier. Winds gusting into the 30+ mph range cause blowing snow and low visibility at times.

Trained spotters reported between 3 to 5.8 inches of snow in Kalispell during the day, with drifts up to a foot and a half deep. Winds at the Glacier Park International Airport ASOS gusted to around 40 mph during the morning and afternoon, peaking at 41 mph in the late morning. Roads became very slick by the afternoon. Local law enforcement reported that snow and wind had caused over 60 vehicle accidents or slide-offs in the Flathead Valley.

Lookout Pass recorded 5 inches of snow during the event. A trained spotter reported a brief period of freezing drizzle before snow started. Seven slide-offs were recorded in the area throughout the day. Hwy 200 was especially bad during this storm, with several accidents and one semi truck getting stuck.

There were widespread spotter reports of 3 to 4 inches of snow in Missoula during the afternoon and evening of 11/24. The highest report was 7.2 inches in the upper South Hills neighborhood of Missoula. The Missoula County Sheriff's office requested emergency travel only due to extreme hazardous weather conditions. This is their highest level of travel alert, and a significant impact to travel during the evening commute. The general travel ban lasted 3 hrs, and during this time, vehicles and buses were unable to drive up to houses in the hills around Missoula due to slick roads. Over 40 accidents and slide-offs occurred in Missoula & Bitterroot Valleys during this time frame. Many schools cancelled class the next day due to continued slick roads.
Nine inches of snow fell at Lolo Pass during the event, with snow-covered roads and slick driving conditions.

Heavy snow began falling during the late morning. Along I-90, a fatal accident occurred when a pickup truck lost control on the icy roads and went into a fence. Trained spotters reported between 5.3 to 3 inches from Anaconda to Butte.

The public reported an estimated 6 inches of snow with this storm near Potomac. Highway 200 was snow-covered and slick, with multiple slide-offs. Area SNOTELs reported between 2 to 7 inches of snow, depending on location.

A trained spotter measured a wind gust of 52 mph in the Flathead Valley around 7pm. A personal weather sensor measured a wind gust of 49.3 miles per hour on the north shore of Flathead Lake, near the Bigfork, MT.  Estimated sustained winds were 45 mph based on damages. That evening, power was lost by about 8000 customers, as over a dozen power poles were blown down.

For 9 hours, from 4pm 12/17 - 1am 12/18, the Pardee RAWS recorded gusts of around 40 mph, with a peak gust of 45 mph at 10pm. Sustained winds in the valleys were estimated at 45 mph based on damages. The relatively uncommon SSE wind direction likely contributed to tree damage with this storm. Five large trees fell near Alberton, MT, one which briefly blocked an interstate lane overnight. Additionally, Superior, MT schools were cancelled on 12/18 due to power outages.

The MDT reported severe driving conditions starting at 11:25 pm on the 3rd and closed Interstate-90 from Haugen to St. Regis from 11:55 pm on the 3rd through 8 am on the 4th because of ice. MDT also reported severe driving conditions along Highway 200 from the Idaho border to Dixon. There were 47 automobile wrecks reported from Missoula to St. Regis according to a Facebook report.  Ice accretion amounts generally were around a tenth of an inch or less from St. Regis to Lookout Pass. The St. Regis, Superior and Trout Creek schools were closed due to the highway closures.
Widespread severe driving conditions were reported for much of the overnight hours due to freezing rain. A spotter in Libby reported a thin glaze of ice coated on the driveway at 844 am on the 4th.

Widespread severe driving conditions were reported for much of the overnight hours due to freezing rain except for the Mission Valley. There was a spotter report at 11:45 pm on the 3rd that Kalispell was reporting freezing rain. The Bigfork schools were closed due to the driving conditions.

Widespread severe driving conditions were reported for much of the overnight hours due to freezing rain except for the Mission Valley. The MDT reported that Marias Pass also received freezing rain and slippery conditions in this event, which is rare because they usually report snow.

Very strong winds took three power poles down, some of which were splintered, along Maclay Ranch Rd. south of Trader Brothers three miles south of Lolo. A nearby resident south of the power pole report experienced tiles being blown off their roof. A south Missoula resident located near the Linda Vista area reported 5 rows of roof shingles lost. A private weather station located southeast of Lolo at 3632 ft. reported at wind gust of 57 mph at 11:38 am and 59 mph at 12:39 pm MST.
The Deer Lodge AGRIMET sensor reported a wind gust to 65 mph around 1:30 pm MST. The Bert Mooney Airport located south-southeast of Butte reported a gust to 55 mph at 107 pm MST.

On Dec. 7 at 2pm MST, a Lemhi County official reported that area roads were very slick due to freezing rain. Salmon schools were closed on Dec. 8 because side roads were very slick. The local newspaper reported that there were road closures. The COOP observer in Salmon reported a 2-day rain total of 0.53 which is fairly significant for that area. Where the rain didn't freeze in the afternoons, it appears that the water on the smooth ice surfaces exacerbated the conditions.
Two inches of snow fell at Pierce while higher elevations saw 5 to 9 inches. Web cams during the event showed snow on roadways (i.e. Grangemont on Highway 11).

Higher elevations SNOTEL sensors reported anywhere from 6 to 12 inches of snowfall with this event. The SNOTEL at Lolo Pass only reported 5 inches.  The Elk City web cam revealed snow covered roads by 5 am on the 13th.

events.cz_name: LOWER HELLS CANYON / SALMON RIVER REGION
events.event_narrative: The web cam and weather sensor at White Bird Hill revealed light to moderate snow that brought slick conditions.
Williams Creek received 12 to 16 inches of snowfall during this period. Blowing snow was also reported.

Lost Trail Pass received 21 inches of snow with periods of blowing snow during this event. Wind gusts to 25 mph were reported at 10 pm MST on the 12th which contributed to lower visibility from the falling and blowing snow. Snow plows had a hard time keeping up at times at Lost Trail Pass. Seven and a half inches of snow fell in the Salmon area while 4 to 6 inches fell in the Leadore area. Gilmore Summit saw strong gusty winds to 42 mph at times with blowing snow and slick conditions.

Heavy snow with with blowing snow caused by wind gusts to 30 mph and low visibility created hazardous conditions at Lookout Pass. Nine inches of snow was reported at the pass.  Chains were required for towing units at Lookout Pass and also from Taft to Haugen on Interstate 90.

Lost Trail Pass received 21 inches of snow with periods of blowing snow during this event. Wind gusts to 25 mph were reported at 10 pm MST on the 12th which contributed to lower visibility from the falling and blowing snow. Snow plows had a hard time keeping up at times at Lost Trail Pass. Lolo Pass only received around 5 inches of snow with this event.

Periods of heavy snow combined with blowing snow created hazardous travel along US-12 between Elliston and MacDonald Pass. At MacDonald Pass 22 inches of snow was estimated while 10 inches was measured in Elliston. A person from the public reported 16 inches, 7 miles southeast of Elliston. An estimated 18 inches of snow fell in Maxville while 8 inches was reported at deer Lodge.
In Potomac, 4 inches of snow was reported while 2 inches fell in Seeley Lake.
A spotter located in Weippe reported 5.5 inches of heavy snow and web cams at Greer Grade on Highway 11 revealed very low visibility and intense snow.
A person from the public located northeast of Glenwood off of Road 100 in Idaho County reported an estimated 8 to 10 inches of snow.
A spotter located 3 miles northeast of Orofino reported 7.5 inches of snow that fell in 5 hours.
A weather spotter reported heavy snowfall with reduced visibility and snow covered Highway 35 near Bigfork. A weather spotter located 8 miles north of Finley Point measured 4.5 inches of snow.

Lookout Pass on Interstate 90 saw heavy snow that caused reduced visibility. The ski resort by the pass reported 7 inches total snowfall for this event. MDT reported snow and blowing snow with reduced visibility between Tarkio and Alberton. A person from the public reported very slick conditions in the St. Regis area with several vehicle slideoffs reported. There were reports of freezing rain towards Missoula and a tractor trailer spun out in the driving lane of US-93 at Evaro Hill before daybreak.

Light freezing rain with slick roadways were reported between Lolo and Missoula on US-93, on the Eastside Highway between Stevensville and Florence. Also freezing rain was reported in Condon along Highway 83. Snow amounts across western Montana included 8.2 Seeley Lake, 6 Bull Lake, 4 Greenough and 3 in both Libby and Stevensville.

A person from a gas station in Pierce remarked that it snowed so much that they had to constantly shovel at their house. They received an estimated 10 inches in the overnight period. The Crater Meadows SNOTEL at 5960 ft. reported 15 inches of snow during this period while 8 inches was reported in Elk River.

Lolo Pass saw periods of moderate to heavy snow throughout this period. Moderate snow showers were felt into the afternoon of the 22nd. Lolo Pass saw a total of 8 to 10 inches from this storm. The Savage Pass SNOTEL reported 18 inches of snow in 24 hours with the heaviest falling from 7 to 10 am on the 22nd.
A spotter located 6 miles northeast of Heron measured a storm total snowfall of 13 inches. Other amounts include 12 inches a few miles north of Libby, 7 inches at Troy and 6 inches in Libby.

Anywhere from 6 to 12 inches of snow fell across the Flathead to Mission Valley according to MDT. Up to 12 inches was reported along highway 206 between the junction with MT-35 and old US-2. Glacier Park International Airport observers measured a storm total snowfall of 9.5 inches.

Lolo Pass on US-12 & Lost Trail Pass on US-93 saw periods of moderate to heavy snow throughout this event. Moderate to heavy snow showers caused intermittent high impact into the afternoon of the 22nd. Lolo Pass saw a total of 8 to 10 inches from this storm while Lost Trail saw 8 inches. A tree fell across US-12 about 24 miles west of Lolo which caused a lane blockage, power line damage and power outages from approximately 834 pm through 3 am on the 22nd. A NWS employee reported 1 inch per hour snow rates at Lolo Pass at 12 pm on the 22nd.

Heavy snow fell at Lookout Pass with 16 inches being reported by the nearby ski resort. Chains were required for all towing vehicles from Saltese to Lookout Pass on I-90. Several semi-trucks became stuck which caused lane blockage and subsequent road closure and delays around 8 pm on the 21st. Snow plows had a tough time keeping up with the snow.

Anywhere from 3 to 15 inches of snow fell along US-2 from West Glacier to Marias Pass according to the MDT. Chains were required for towing units for this region during the event. A railroad avalanche forecaster measured 15.6 inches of snow in the Essex area from this storm. Despite the remote extreme amounts, hardy folks reportedly were used to these amounts.

MDT reported multiple slide-offs and jackknifed semis. Interstate 90 was categorized as Severe Driving Conditions by MDT at 4:57 AM between Tarkio and Alberton. Much of the rest of the zone had roads reported as either ice/black ice or snow covered. Due to the slick roadways, nearby schools were delayed for 2 hours in the morning.

Trained spotters in Bigfork, Montana reported 3 inches of very heavy, wet snow. Tree branches were being weighted down significantly, and people were unable to plow with an ATV due to the snow being very heavy. Power outages were reported around the area.

Noisy Basin snotel recorded 2 feet of snow in 24 hours with 19 inches of it coming down in 12 hours. 3.2 inches of snow water equivalent was recorded in the Swan range which prompted the Flathead Avalanche Center issuing an Avalanche Warning.

NWS employee reported heavy, intense snow with little to no visibility over highway 93. Widespread 3 to 4 inches of snow with pockets of 4 to 6 inches of snow were reported along highway 93 near Big Arm. Multiple semi trucks were stuck on the side of the road and the highway was briefly shutdown due to severe driving conditions.

During the early morning hours, snow started falling over Lookout Pass and portions of I-90 in Mineral county. Around 10am, conditions reached a point where the MT Department of Transportation declared severe driving conditions for the section of I-90 from Lookout Pass to St. Regis, MT. These conditions lasted until the early afternoon.
South Fork RAWS reported 0.50 inches of rain over the 7 days preceding the event. The greatest 1 day rainfall was Feb 15, when 0.23 inches fell.
Fenn Ranger Station RAWS reported 2.21 inches of rain over the 7 days preceding the event. The greatest 1 day rainfall was Feb 15, when 0.81 inches fell.
Red River RAWS reported 1.08 inches of rain over the 7 days preceding the event. The greatest 1 day rainfall was Feb 14, when 0.48 inches fell.

A strong thunderstorm unleashed a small microburst that caused hundreds of trees to either snap in half or blow over at the Denna Mora Rest Area on Interstate 90 east of Lookout Pass.  Two large fir and spruce trees with diameters up to 3 feet wide fell onto the eastbound lanes just to the northwest of the rest area obstructing the road at night. Approximately an hour later around 10 pm MDT, several vehicles hit the trees causing car damage, injuries and one fatality. A 21 year old male died after his vehicle collided with the topmost of the crisscrossed trees.

Between 4 to 6 inches of rain fell within 24 hours causing Spoon and Duck lakes to spill out onto Lake Drive and North Fork Road, and ending up near the Blankenship Road intersection as culverts were unable to handle the extra runoff. Rabe Road also  experienced flooding from water originating from the Tea Kettle Mountain area.  A private sensor located east-northeast of the Tea Kettle North Mountain or about 3 miles northwest of Coram, measured 6.29 inches of rainfall. The flooding closed North Fork Rd and Rabe Rd which impacted 25 to 30 residents. At least fifteen structures including basements and shop garages were flooded. One unfinished garage saw water that rose to near the ceiling. A fire chief with the Blankenship Fire Department who lives just off of North Fork Road outside of Columbia Falls reported that over three thousand gallons of water flooded his finished basement during this event. On May 23rd, more intense rain developed just north of Columbia Falls resulting in Trumble Creek coming out of its banks. This placed water around seven homes, but did not cause much damage or prevent residents from access. Glacier National Park closed the Going-to-the-Sun-Road at the Apgar Loop Junction due to a culvert washout in the afternoon of May 23rd.  Another reason why the culvert was overwhelmed was due to beaver dams breaking up higher in the drainage. At least two portions of the Forest Service road 895 past the Hungry Horse Dam were washed out on May 23rd including Beta Creek. Forest service road 316 from the 6.3 mile marker on North Fork Road to the Canyon Creek area also experienced several washouts.
Gem Mountain, located west of Georgetown Lake, reported 15 inches of heavy snow.

Up to 6 inches of snow fell across the higher terrain of southwest Montana including Georgetown Lake and in the Butte area. Power outages were reported during the evening of May 9th in the Philipsburg area.

The Flathead Lake Biological Station Narrows sensor reported an increase in northerly winds gusting to 41 mph at times by 8 pm MDT. Winds could have peaked closer to 50 mph over the open water towards the center of the lake. This northerly wind caused waves to grow over 26 miles of fetch reaching an estimated 6 to 8 feet at times. The waves knocked a shipping container off the stern of the barge and eventually the vessel sank. The bow of the barge was nosed onshore while the stabilizers were extended into the mud. With time, the waves hammered the legs down into the silt over time swamping the barge.
Spotter estimated the hailstones were up to 2.00 inches in diameter.

A person from the public who lives 3.5 road miles west of Syringa, observed strong west-northwest winds that caused five Ponderosa Pine trees to snap in half and fall onto US-12. The Ponderosa Pine trees were tall but with small diameters. Based on an eye-witness report of a twisting white cloud coming up from the river, the damage could have been a result of a short-lived gustnado.
A member of the public in Troy reported one inch hail at around 4:46 pm.

A member of the public located 5 miles west-southwest of Lupfer reported ping pong size hail, which dented 3 vehicles and broke the windshield of 1 vehicle. There were also many plants defoliated by the hail.
Public estimated 1.25 inch hail with wind gusts to 25 mph.

The Deer Mountain RAWS reported a max wind gust of 50 mph between 12:06pm MST and 1:06 MST. Other locations above the valley floor gusted in the 40 to 50 mph range, including the Little Rock Creek RAWS with 45 mph gusts.

A utility company reported via social media that a power outage affected a maximum of 2700 customers. Within 3 hours, all but 206 customers had power returned. These 206 customers regained power by the evening. Local media reported on the power outage shortly after the initial utility company report came out.
A business in Saltese, MT reported quarter or larger size hail. Winds blew down some tree limbs, and the hail dented cars. The worst part of the storm lasted about 15 minutes.

Larger than quarter sized hail was reported at residence north of MT-35 bridge over Flathead River. The hail punched larger than golf ball-sized holes in plastic chicken coop roofing, destroyed residence���s surveillance camera, and dented their metal barn roof.
The public reported quarter-sized hail from a thunderstorm west of Kalispell, MT.
The public sent a photo showing multiple hailstones as large as quarters in Kalispell, MT.
The public reported 1-inch hail via social media 3 miles south of Columbia Falls, MT.
A 25 foot power pole was snapped by the wind in Charlo, MT. The wind was strong enough to make it difficult for resident to open his front door.
A resident in Charlo, MT reported 0.80 inches of rain in 10 min with minor street flooding.
The Montana DOT weather sensor north of Avon, MT reported a gust of 60 mph between 9:38pm MDT and 9:45pm MDT. Sustained winds at this time were 49 mph.
A co-workers friend reports quarter size hail.
NWS employee  reports quarter size hail.

The weather station at the Anaconda, MT airfield reported a wind gust to 53 mph between 8pm and 9pm MDT, likely as the line of storms arrived around 8:45pm. County officials reported small branches down and one tree knocked over as well, but there was no known damage to property.
A person from the public observed a prominent dust devil in northern Missoula. It formed ahead of showers that were tracking south to north in a very unstable environment. No damage was reported.

The Missoula dispatch reported a lot of tree limbs down around town with numerous power lines down. A couple of lightning strikes started fires with one strike to a house in Missoula and a field in Florence. A private weather sensor located southeast of Lolo recorded a wind gust to 60 mph ahead of the main thunderstorm cells.

A person from the public reported a small metal building had been thrown across a ranch, ending up in the ditch near the corner of Long Road and US-93. The Lemhi County Sheriff reported a few trees down around Salmon. One of the larger trees was deemed unhealthy. A person from the public located 5 miles ESE of North Fork reported  the winds blew the roof off of a chicken house and a 15 foot tall tree fell over the Fourth of July Creek Road.

The Lemhi County Airport AWOS measured a 64 mph wind gust at 3:35 pm MDT. The local media from Salmon reported that a 100 year old American Elm tree, up to 3 feet in diameter, had been knocked down from the winds. Multiple mature Cottonwood trees were also knocked down west of downtown Salmon.
A spotter in Elk Bend reported golf ball sized hail that smashed approximately 6 car windows.
The Lemhi County dispatch reported ping pong ball-sized hail with the storm.
A spotter measured the half dollar hail after all the lightning stopped, so it could have melted down a bit.
Penny size hail reported on the south side of the Roaring Lion Fire.
A trained spotter estimated that some hailstones were bigger than quarters.

Glacier Park International airport located north of Kalispell recorded winds sustained between 40 and 44 mph with gusts to 55 mph between 6:45 and 7:25 pm MDT. Wind gusts were estimated near 60 mph towards Bad Rock Canyon near Columbia Falls. A boat charter on Flathead Lake estimated 5 foot waves in Lakeside where his boat was docked. Several trees were knocked down in Kalispell with some power outages. The mid-lake buoy recorded a peak wind of 46 mph at 7:30 pm MDT.

Two transmission poles located in the South Hills area of Missoula were knocked out by the wind which caused a power outage. Multiple trees were pushed over by the wind including a 50 foot Ponderosa Pine tree that fell onto a home. A NWS employee reported that a Maple tree was snapped in half at the corner of Mount and Brooks Street.

A person from the public located in Missoula tweeted a photo of hail that appeared to be quarter size. There were multiple reports of nickel sized hail with some damage to gardens and vegetation. Intense rainfall was also produced by this storm, and the greater impact may have been street ponding.
A COOP located 2 miles northwest of Heron reported very strong ENE winds that uprooted several trees, caused metal roofing to be torn off a barn, and caused a power outage that lasted for 43 hours.
One inch hail was reported just south of Rock Creek.
A member of the public reported one inch hail, which caused small damages to vehicles.
Idaho county sheriff reported quarter size hail, some trees down, and minor flooding on main street.
One inch hail was reported by a member of the public.
A hotel employee reported lots of hail ranging from dime size to quarter size. The storm lasted about 10 minutes and was accompanied by gusty winds.
Weather spotters in Weippe and Headquarters reported between 7.5 and 8 inches of new snowfall accumulations respectively.
Between 6 and 9 inches of new snow fell at Polebridge and along the US Highway 2 corridor between Essex and Marias Pass.
The COOP observers in Pierce and Elk City reported 10 inches of new snowfall accumulations from this event.
The COOP observers in Powell and Dixie reported 8 and 9 inches of new snowfall accumulations, respectively, from this event.

The Idaho road department reported that Lost Trail Pass received 12 inches of new snowfall accumulations from this event. Also, the Moose Creek weather station received 9 inches of new snowfall accumulations from this event as well.
The Idaho and Montana road departments reported 11.7 and 12 inches of snow at Lolo and Lost Trail Passes, respectively.

The Lookout Pass Ski Resort reported 8 inches of new snow. The Montana Department of Highways website reported 7.8 inches of new snowfall accumulations at Lookout Pass. A weather spotter in Heron reported 16 inches of new snow.
Low temperatures fell below freezing across northwest Montana including 25 deg. F at Eureka, 22 deg. F at Yaak and 29 deg. F in Libby.
Yaak, MT temperature sensor reported a low of 22 F.
Libby, MT temperature sensor reported low of 29 F.
A temperature sensor in Trout Creek reported a low of 25 deg. F while in Thompson Falls, the temperatures fell to 27 deg. F.
Thompson Falls, MT temperature sensor reported low of 27 F.
Kalispell International Airport temperature sensor reported a low of 27 F.
Kalispell International Airport saw a low of 27 degrees while a temperature sensor in Ronan recorded a low of 25 degrees Fahrenheit.

The local media in Missoula reported that local farms took steps to harvest tomatoes, lettuce, and squash early because of the forecast sub-freezing temperatures. Temperatures dropped to 30 deg. F at the Missoula International Airport and to 28 deg. F in Stevensville.

Media reported on local farms in the Missoula Area taking steps to harvest tomatoes, lettuce, and squash early. Temperatures only dropped to 30 F in Missoula proper, but farmers were impacted even by just below freezing temperatures.

The RAWS sensor in Seeley Lake reported a low of 21 degrees F. Spotters from the Potomac and Greenough areas reported heavy frost with temperatures dropping to 20 degrees F and possibly lower in the early morning hours.
Spotters from the Potomac and Greenough, MT reported heavy frost with temperatures dropping to 20 F and possibly lower in the early morning hours.

Flathead County Search and Rescue personnel reported a large avalanche on the back side of Big Mountain Ski Resort. Two skiers were killed and one was injured. The avalanche was initiated by another skier who was skiing out of bounds in an area closed to skiing.

Lolo Pass was closed to all but emergency travel during this event. The road crew that plowed the highway to Lolo Pass reported seeing the worst white out conditions in 10 years. The Lodgepole weather observation site reported wind gusts to 38 mph. Red River Hot Springs reported wind gusts to 23 mph. Savage and Lolo Pass received 9 and 8 inches of new snow respectively from this event.

Weather spotters at Essex, West Glacier, and 10 miles north of Columbia Falls reported 6 to 8 inches of new snow over a 12 hour period. In addition, weather observation stations at Fielding, Essex, and Swan Lake reported gusty winds between 28 and 33 mph.

Lolo Pass was closed to all but emergency travel during this event from heavy snow and poor visibility. Wind gusts to 66 mph were recorded at the Little Rock Creek weather observation site which blew down 10 large trees. Lost Trail Pass received 6 inches of new snowfall accumulations over a 12 hour period.

The Montana Department of Transportation reported 10 inches of snow at Marias Pass and multiple trees down on Highway 2 due to heavy wet snow and strong gusty winds. The Going to the Sun Road was also closed due to the snow.
Libby and many other areas in the region reported temperatures in the mid to upper 20s.
Thompson Falls and many other valleys reported temperatures in the mid to upper 20s.
Missoula ASOS and many other valleys reported temperatures in the low to mid 20s.
Weather obs reported temperatures down in the low to mid 20s for valleys in Western Lemhi County.
Salmon reported a temperature of 21 degrees and other valleys also reported temperatures in the low to mid 20s.

The Montana Department of Transportation reported around 5 inches of new snow with considerable blowing and drifting along Highway 37. Highway 56 was also slick with some blowing snow. Snotel sites around the area reported 6 inches of snow.

Whitefish Mountain ski resort reported 7 inches of snow with wind gusts of up to 45 mph. Due to the strong winds and very cold wind chills, several ski lifts were forced to close. Other higher elevation sites such as Hornet RAWS also reported high winds of up to 40 mph.

Glacier Park International Airport and the Montana Department of Transportation reported widespread blowing snow around the Kalispell area with wind gusts of 30 to 40 mph. Over on the Flathead Lake east side highway, wind gusts of over 50 mph were recorded on the the Mid Lake buoy.  Due to the strong gusty winds, 2 foot drifts were common in the valleys, along with visibility reductions, due to the blowing snow.

The Montana Department of Transportation reported widespread areas of blowing snow with periods of moderate to heavy snow during the day. A fair amount of slide offs were reported and a fatal crash was also reported on highway 12 several miles west of Avon.
Montana Department of Transportation reported widespread 4 to 8 inches of snow for the valleys of northwest Montana.

Montana Department of Transportation reported widespread 6 to 12 inches of snow during this event. Due to the winter storm, Glacier Park International Airport had some flight cancellations and delays, and Dixon schools were also on a 2 hour delay.

Freezing rain over Interstate 90 caused severe driving conditions between Lookout pass and St. Regis. The combination of snow and freezing rain also caused 2 snow slides on Interstate 90, which briefly blocked some lanes. In the Noxon area, the Montana Department of Transportation reported 12 to 16 inches of snow.

The combination of snow and freezing rain caused slick roads and led to numerous accidents across the area. Due to the road conditions,  an emergency travel alert was issued for Missoula county. The emergency travel was eventually lifted the next morning but more freezing rain led to severe driving conditions around Missoula and parts of the Bitterroot valley.  Many schools, businesses, and flights were delayed or cancelled because of this winter storm.
Montana Department of Transportation reported severe driving conditions due to freezing rain between Bonner and Potomac.  Schools in Bonner and Potomac had delayed starts to their day.
A Spotter reported 10 inches of snow over the previous 24 hours and 13 inches for the storm total at Essex.

Montana Department of Transportation reported severe driving conditions on highway 56 to Bull Lake, and black ice on highway 37 and 93 going to Eureka. Due to the slick roads around northwest Montana, Troy High School cancelled all after school activities.

Montana Department of Transportation reported freezing rain and black ice across most areas in the lower Clark Fork region. Severe driving conditions were also reported near the Noxon and Trout Creek area, and schools were cancelled at Trout Creek due to the road conditions.

The Lolo Pass SNOTEL reported a storm total snowfall of 13 inches with 1.40 inches of snow water equivalent(SWE). Temperatures cooled down into the lower teens at Lolo Pass and -8 F in Dixie which contributed to icy conditions on the morning of Dec. 5th. The Dixie COOP reported 12.2 inches of snow with 0.86 inches of SWE.

Moderate to heavy snow fell across portions of Clearwater County above 3000 feet during the event. Total snowfall amounts ranged from 3.4 inches in Pierce to 17 inches at the Shanghai Summit SNOTEL at 4500 feet. The temperatures plummeted from the 20's and 30's to the teens by Monday morning which kept roads slick. Gusty winds in the higher terrain caused dangerous conditions for hunters in blowing snow and near-zero wind chills.

Anywhere from 2 inches in the valleys to 8 inches in the mountains fell with this event. The cold front moved through on the evening of Dec. 4th which created gusty winds between 20 and 36 mph, falling temperatures, and blowing snow with below zero wind chills at Williams Creek Summit. The single digit temperatures in the valleys created slick driving conditions.

Anywhere from 2 inches in the valleys to 8 inches in the mountains fell with this event. The cold front moved through on the evening of Dec. 4th creating gusty winds between 20 and 36 mph, blowing snow, and below zero wind chills at Bannock Pass and other ridge-top locations. The single digit temperatures in the valleys created slick driving conditions.

Lost Trail Pass received 8 inches of snow while Lolo Pass saw 13 inches of snow during this event. A strong cold front moved through between the afternoon and evening of Dec. 4th which initiated gusty winds and temperatures dropping into the teens at Lolo Pass and single digits at Lost Trail. The combination of fresh snow, dropping temperatures and wind chills approaching 15 degrees below zero caused dangerous conditions in the back-country for hunters.

Moderate to heavy snow fell in the valleys and mountains during this event: 21 inches at Stahl Peak at 6000 feet east of Eureka, 12 inches north of Kila at 4000 feet, up to 12 inches in the Eureka area and 4 to 10 inches in other valley locations. Temperatures plummeted to the teens and single digits in the mountains with gusty winds to 35 mph which created dangerous conditions for back-country users.

Moderate to heavy snow contributed to severe driving conditions along Interstate 90 by the afternoon of Dec. 4th which continued through the nighttime hours. Lookout Pass received 16 inches with this storm. Gusty winds and falling temperatures into the teens and single digits after the cold front passage contributed to hazardous conditions in the back-country.

A trained spotter located near the Blankenship Bridge between West Glacier and Columbia Falls reported near whiteout conditions from heavy snow.  A business in Essex reported that 18 inches of snow had fallen with the storm.

Road conditions became slick as snow melted and then refroze during the evening of Dec. 4th continuing into the following morning. The South Hills, including the Miller Creek area of Missoula, saw several slide-offs and accidents due to the slippery roads. This resulted in the local police stating that emergency travel only was advised around 10 pm on the 4th.

Periods of light to heavy snow fell during this event. A few places did mix with rain in the afternoon of Dec. 4th. While over a foot of snow fell in the mountains, Lindbergh Lake saw 11.6 inches and Seeley Lake saw 3.7 inches of total snowfall. Once the cold front passed through later Sunday, temperatures fell into the teens by Monday morning causing slick spots on the roads. The combination of fresh snow and cold temperatures created dangerous conditions in the back-country.

A person from the public tweeted that Interstate 90 eastbound of mile marker 145 was snow and ice covered at 9 am on Dec. 5th. Light snow fell during the evening of Dec. 4th with the cold front passage and temperatures fell into the teens and 20's making road mitigation difficult.

Lookout Pass had reported 21 inches of snow in 20 hours ending noon on Dec. 12th. Over a foot of snow was estimated towards Haugan. A person from the Montana Department of Transportation reported that it was an extremely busy weekend with almost non-stop snowfall.

A trained spotter from Condon reported 7 inches of snow while a COOP observer from Lindbergh Lake recorded a storm total of 11.3 inches of snow with 0.87 inches snow water equivalent. Other areas along Highway 200 and Interstate 90 saw anywhere from 1 to 3 inches of snow that brought slick and snow-packed roads.

Anywhere from 9 inches of snow by Marias Pass to 13.5 inches at West Glacier fell with this storm. An Arctic cold front plowed through Marias Pass which caused temperatures to drop from the middle 20's to single digits below zero in a matter of two hours. Combined with winds gusting near 30 mph, the wind chills ranged between -20 and -30 degrees. Blowing snow was reported by MDT during the night along US 2. The Arctic cold front lost steam as it made its way toward Columbia Falls and the Flathead Valley where only 2 to 3 inches of snow fell.

Several heavy snow bands, with snow rates up to 5 inch per hour, developed during the day of Dec. 4th then a weak Arctic cold front tracked south during the evening causing widespread snow. As this front lost its steam towards Flathead Lake a heavy snow band formed and impacted much of Highway 35 towards the northeastern Mission Valley. Above freezing temperatures during the day contributed to a snow-over-ice situation by the evening, and very slick conditions lasted into the next morning. Total snowfall amounts include: 9 Columbia Falls, 5.5 Bigfork, 4.6 Glacier Park International Airport.

A combination of moderate to heavy snow, snow-covered roads, and low visibility created high impact to travel. The poor visibilities were caused by vehicles stirring up the very light snow on the surface. Total snow amounts include 13 at Darby and 2 miles WNW of Stevensville, 8 at Hamilton, 7.5 3 miles east of Florence, 7 in the South Hills of Missoula, and 6.3 at the Missoula International Airport.

A combination of moderate to heavy snow, snow-covered roads, and low visibility created high impact to travel. The poor visibilities were caused by vehicles stirring up the very light snow on the surface. Chains were required for US-93 to Evaro Hill during the morning commute on the 15th. Total snow amounts: 5.3 at Alberton, 4 at Haugan and Evaro Hill, and 3 at Thompson Falls.

A combination of moderate to heavy snow, snow-covered roads, and low visibility created high impact to travel. The poor visibilities were caused by vehicles stirring up the very light snow on the surface. Multiple vehicle slide-offs were reported, and there was a snow plow that slid off the road near Bonner. Total snow amounts: 10 Lindbergh Lake, 6.4 Seeley Lake, 6 Bonner and Clinton, and 4 Greenough Hill.

A combination of moderate to heavy snow, snow-covered roads, and low visibility created high impact to travel. The poor visibilities were caused by vehicles stirring up the very light snow on the surface. The snow fell heavy enough that there was barely one lane on Interstate 90 at times. Snow amounts: 9 Deer Lodge, 7 Georgetown Lake, 6 Elliston, and 3 Anaconda and Ovando.

Between 8 and 14 inches of heavy snow fell from the Polson area east to Highway 35 on the east side of Flathead Lake. Also a combination of moderate to heavy snow, snow-covered roads, and low visibility created high impact to travel in the Mission Valley. The poor visibilities were caused by vehicles stirring up the very light snow on the surface. Other snow amounts include 4 NW of St. Ignatius, 2.4 at Glacier Park International Airport and 2.2 at Ronan.

Moderate to heavy snow created slick conditions with low visibility across the Camas Prairie. Gusty winds between 30 and 40 mph caused blowing and drifting snow on top of the benches above Orofino making some driveways to be impassable. Total snow amounts include 13 on Crow's Bench at Ford's Creek Road, 10 three miles NE Orofino, 8 four miles E Orofino, 7.4 six miles NNW Kamiah, 5 in Orofino, and 4.8 in Ahsahka and Grangeville. Clearwater County schools closed because there was a communications problem due to a power failure that occurred during the storm.
Periods of moderate to heavy snow fell with snow amounts including 5 in Powell, 7 at Lolo Pass, and 8 in Dixie.

events.cz_name: LOWER HELLS CANYON / SALMON RIVER REGION
events.event_narrative: The Idaho Transportation Department reported that 6 to 8 inches of snow fell between Lucille and Riggins. They said that the snow rates were probably 1 to 2 inch per hour rates. Blowing snow from passing vehicles created very low visibility which contributed to the travel danger. The schools in Kooskia closed due to the weather.

Moderate to heavy snow caused power issues that affected school communications in Clearwater County resulting in school closures on December 15 and 16. Snowfall amounts generally ranged from 5 to 10 during the event.

Moderate to heavy snow caused slick roads and low visibility during this event. Total snow amounts include 13 at Lost Trail, 10.5 five miles east of Sula, 9.5 fourteen miles northeast of Sula, and near 6 west of Lolo.
Heavy snow was reported between North Fork and Salmon during the storm where up to 7 inches of snow fell. The Salmon schools were closed due to snowy road conditions.

Moderate to heavy snow with amounts between 9 and 12 inches combined with wind gusts near 50 mph to generate blowing and drifting snow between Essex and Marias Pass. The Montana Department of Transportation stated that there were severe driving conditions in the aforementioned area along US-2.
The Pierce COOP reported 4.2 inches of total snow while over a foot of snow fell in the mountains.

Lolo Pass received 13 inches of snow during the event, and there were reports of whiteout conditions in blowing and drifting snow. A worker at the pass reported that it was the worst conditions he had seen in 13 years. The winds were so strong that a tree had blown into the west bound lane north of the pass.

Moderate to heavy snow combined with strong gusty winds to create blowing and drifting snow on the higher benches of the area including near Greer. Winds gusted to 59 mph at the Grangeville Airport at 715 am PST.

Lookout Pass received 12 to 14 inches of snow with strong gusty winds near 40 mph during the event. Freezing rain was reported in sections of Sanders County causing road conditions to be treacherous at times. Portions of Mineral County also saw several hours of freezing rain.

Lolo Pass received 13 inches of snow during the event, and there were reports of whiteout conditions with blowing and drifting snow. A worker at the pass reported that it was the worst conditions he had seen in 13 years. The winds were so strong that a tree had blown into the west bound lane north of the pass.

Sustained winds of 45 mph with a gust to 62 was measured by the MDT sensor located north of Avon. A trained spotter located two miles north of Deer Lodge reported wind gusts over 60 mph.  Also there was a short period of blizzard conditions around 5 pm at MacDonald Pass when the cold front went through.

Very strong winds caused a sale barn from the Lemhi County Fairgrounds to collapse during this event. A person who lives near the fairgrounds observed that the windows of his trailer home flexed during the high winds. No sensor was nearby to record the wind speed, but there is a sensor located to the west about a thousand feet above town that recorded a gust to 53 mph.

Severe driving conditions were reported from noon to 3 pm from Lookout Pass to St. Regis due to blowing and drifting snow, reduced visibility and slick conditions. Lookout Pass Ski resort reported 18 inches of storm total snowfall in 24 hours.

Periods of moderate to heavy snow combined with frequent wind gusts to 32 mph to generate blowing and drifting snow along US-2 between West Glacier and Marias Pass. By the morning of the 28th, the Montana Department of Transportation reported severe driving conditions leading up to Marias Pass. Total storm snowfall ranged from 6 to 10 inches.

Lolo Pass and Lost Trail Pass both received close to two feet of snow during this event in 24 hours. A trained spotter remarked that the snow was falling very hard at Lost Trail Pass during the evening and this was the worst he had seen in several years. Gusty winds brought blowing and drifting snow to the passes.

A person from the public who lives in Lowell estimated that a foot and a half of heavy snow fell there. This is an unusually high amount for this low elevation station. Lolo Pass experienced near 20 inches of snow from this event. Gust winds created blowing and drifting snow at the pass.

Strong winds sustained at 35 mph with gusts to 50 mph combined with falling snow and over a foot of existing transportable snow to create blizzard conditions on the Camas Prairie. At least 5 vehicles and one snowplow became stuck on US-95, and tow trucks were unable to give assistance because of heavy drifting in the morning. Because of the whiteout conditions, US-95 from Grangeville to Cottonwood, Red Rock Road, Highway 162, and Highway 7 were closed for much of the day, and were not fully opened back up until the morning of the 28th.

A person from the public estimated that southerly winds along Highway 95 between Grangeville and Whitebird Hill were gusting up to 70 mph. This stretch of highway is oriented southwest to northeast and several vehicles were blown across the road. The roads were slick at the time with snow on the road with whiteout conditions. Near Fenn located northwest of Grangeville, a few vehicles were reportedly stuck in snow drifts. Recent snow storms had deposited at least a foot of transportable snow which contributed to the hazardous conditions.
Idaho Transportation Department reported slick roads due to freezing rain and black ice. Roads were also closed south of Salmon due to the threat of an avalanche.

The Hamilton AWOS reported up to 4 hours of quarter mile or less visibility due to moderate and heavy snow. A trained spotter reported 8 to 10 inches of snow in Hamilton. The combination of heavy snow and warm afternoon road surfaces led to icy road conditions during the evening commute.

The Hamilton AWOS reported up to 4 hours of quarter mile or less visibility due to moderate and heavy snow. A trained spotter reported 8 to 10 inches of snow in Hamilton. The combination of heavy snow and warm road surfaces during the afternoon led to icy road conditions during the evening commute.
Trained spotters reported 7 inches of snow in Anaconda, and 6 inches of snow in Butte with snow drifts up to 2 feet. Discovery ski resort reported 9 inches of new snow in 24 hours.
Trained spotters reported 7 inches of snow in Anaconda and 6 inches of snow in Butte with snow drifts up to 2 feet. Discovery ski resort reported 9 inches of new snow in 24 hours.
The Emergency Manager of Clearwater County reported secondary roads were like an ice skating rink due to freezing rain. Due to the icy roads, all schools in the district were closed.
A trained spotter reported 7.3 inches of new snow 5 miles north of Grangeville. He also mentioned roads were atrocious.  A spotter in Kooskia reported 6 inches of new snow as well.
An intense band of snow brought heavy snow to Lookout Pass for several hours during the evening of the 4th which caused the Montana Department of Transportation to issue severe driving conditions.

Heavy snow showers with two inch per hour rates brought low visibility and a short period of slick roads. An NWS Missoula employee reported zero visibility with snow-covered roads during the event. Anywhere from 3 to 7 inches of snow fell with this band, but due to the fact that it occurred during a relatively quiet period on a Sunday morning, the impact was mostly moderate.
A Greenough spotter reported that one inch of snow had fallen in only 30 minutes and it was still snowing. Seeley Lake received two inches during this event.
Web cams revealed periods of heavy snow with the slow moving front from Ovando south to Butte. The Bert Mooney Airport reported moderate to heavy snow between 7 and 735 pm MST on the 5th.

Difficult travel due to heavy snow occurred from Lookout Pass to Haugen along Interstate 90. Montana Department of Transportation listed Taft to Lookout Pass as severe driving conditions between 948 pm on the 7th to 522 am MST on the 8th.
The Lolo Pass Visitor center reported up to 18 inches of snow during the event while Lost Trail Pass saw up to 6 inches.

Snowfall amounts during this storm include: 5 to 8 inches in the Seeley and Swan valleys, 3.3 inches in Condon and 11 inches at the top of Snowbowl Ski Resort. Roads conditions were mainly snow and ice.

Snow and freezing rain fell across northwest Montana with snow totals ranging from 3 inches in Troy, Libby, and Eureka to 6 inches in Stryker. A person from the public reported on Facebook that snow, ice, and slush made Highway 37 terribly slippery on the morning of the 10th.

Blowing and drifting snow was reported between West Glacier and Marias Pass during the night-time hours. Snowfall amounts include: 18 inches at Marias Pass, 15 inches in Polebridge, and 8 to 10 inches at the Devil's Creek area located east of Essex.

Snowfall amounts ranged from 3 inches in Polson to 9 inches in Columbia Falls before changing to freezing rain before daybreak. The freezing rain became absorbed in the fallen snow therefore lessening the impact.

Very slick conditions were reported in the Bitterroot Valley which caused vehicles to have a hard time stopping. The slush caused by mild road conditions overnight solidified with new snow falling causing the icy conditions. Most schools in the Bitterroot Valley were delayed due to the conditions. Snow amounts include: 4.3 inches at the Missoula International Airport, 6 inches at Frenchtown, 6 inches south of Missoula, and 8 inches east of Stevensville.

Very slick conditions were reported across southwest Montana while 4 to 9 inches of snow fell during the event. Multiple vehicle slide-offs, jack-knifes and crashes were reported by the Department of Justice between 7 and 10 am on the 10th from east of Drummond to Homestake Pass on Interstate 90.

Snow amounts ranged from 4 inches in Huson to 6.5 inches in Alberton to 8 inches at Lookout Pass. Conditions were reported to be slick but compared with the other areas there were no school delays and accident reports were low.

Heavy wet snow contributed to multiple rock slides with one covering Mount Idaho Grade Road southeast of Grangeville. Due to the already saturated ground, the heavy precipitation downed multiple trees and power lines. Widespread power outages were reported with one spotter reporting 8.5 hours without power east of Kooskia. Snowfall amounts ranged from 4 inches in Grangeville to up to 10 inches across the northern Camas Prairie. Mud slides, washed-out culverts and streams that were bankful contributed to Clearwater County declaring a State of Emergency on the 10th.

Several locations along US-12 experienced flooding, mud and debris on the road which caused it to close for 10 hours. Three inches of rain with snow-melt occurred a week before this event contributing to saturated soils. A nearby sensor in Lowell recorded 1.23 inches of rainfall 24 hours leading up to the flooding. Multiple culvert washouts and other mudslides were reported through March 24 along the following roads: Cedar Creek, Big Cedar and Cove. Idaho County declared a state of emergency because of all the issues.

Abundant rain and low elevation snow melt in the upper portions of Orofino Creek near Pierce led to high stream flows on the 15th, followed by minor flooding on the 16th. Multiple homes and property were sandbagged to prevent flooding across southwest portions of the county. Jim Ford Creek flooded multiple properties in the Weippe area. Clearwater County declared a state of emergency because of all the mudslide, debris and river issues. Although the most severe flooding occurred on or near the 16th, another culvert gave way and caused Grangemont Road to shut down mile-marker 22 on March 25th lasting until April 5th. Total estimated cost of road repairs was 3 million dollars due to landslide failures.

The Clearwater County Emergency Manager reported rain freezing on already frozen back roads, leading to additional glazing overnight. This caused cars to have difficulty in gaining traction, especially on driveways. Even vehicles with chained tires had difficulty navigating during the event.
The Idaho Transportation Department reported widespread ice on Hwy 14 leading to Elk City, ID. At higher elevations, heavy snow fell, with the public reporting 15 inches of snow at Lolo Pass.

Warm weather and rain helped prime conditions for multiple snow slides that covered roads in Lemhi county. The Idaho Transportation Department reported one 100 ft wide and 10 ft high snow slide on Hwy 93 north of Salmon, ID that completely blocked the road for 1.5 hours. Four other smaller slides caused roads to be reduced to one lane, and heavy equipment was needed to clear snow.

At least four trailer homes in Troy were directly impacted by water that had flowed over US-2 from an unauthorized channel that had overflowed. In Libby, a home cellar was flooded, the Libby Elementary School saw minor issues and Education Way was closed due to flooding caused by a clogged drainage. Silver Butte Creek south of Libby filled with debris causing it to re-route and surround a house with water during the early morning hours of the 19th. Several culverts had to be replaced due to washouts.

White Pine Creek, located 12 miles northwest of Thompson Falls overflowed and damaged White Pine Creek road so bad that one resident was isolated from getting back to their home. Elk Creek road near Heron sustained damage during this event.
An ice jam on the Big Hole River at the Dickie Bridge caused water to back up and flood a land owner to the west of the bridge.

The Montana Department of Transportation reported Severe Driving Conditions with blowing and drifting throughout the afternoon and evening of Feb. 3, lasting through the early morning of Feb. 4. They use this label sparingly, only when road conditions are treacherous. Road conditions improved by 7 am MST on Feb. 4. Glacier National Park officials estimated 8 inches of snow in West Glacier, MT between noon and 8 pm on Feb. 3rd, which translates to 1 inch or greater per hour snowfall rates.

Severe driving conditions were issued at 3:22 pm on Feb. 3 for a 33 mile stretch of I-90 leading up to Lookout Pass. Webcam images showed heavy snow throughout this time period. The Montana Department of Transportation reported at least two snow slides, one of which was at milepost 7, blocking individual lanes during the event. Highway patrol reported semi trucks stuck blocking lanes throughout the event, as well as semi truck accidents.

Severe driving conditions were declared by the Montana Department of Transportation during the early morning hours of Feb. 4, due to snow-covered roads with blowing and drifting occurring. Freezing rain was also reported from Conner to Stevensville during the late evening of the 3rd.

The emergency manager for Lincoln County estimated 30 to 36 inches of snow had fallen within 48 hours in Libby, MT. A Reverse 911 message went out to all citizens to warn them of this event. Schools were cancelled on Monday Feb. 6. This decision was made a day in advance of the predicted snowfall, which is extremely rare. The Eureka, MT AWOS showed visibility of less than 1 mile for over 8 hours during the peak of the event with periods of less than 0.25 mi visibility. Public reports put 2 day snow totals at 20 to 30 inches in Eureka, MT, depending on which part of town. Also there were reports of blowing and drifting snow between Kalispell and Eureka. The Fire Department in Bull Lake suffered a partial roof collapse from the heavy snow load. This trapped a type 6 fire engine within the building. The damage listed was an estimated amount. During the morning of the 5th there were reports of freezing rain on US-93.

US-2 over Marias Pass was closed by the Montana Department of Transportation due to impassable conditions. Severe driving conditions were issued for most highways in this portion of northwest Montana. MDT plow drivers estimated a three day snow total of 48 inches in Essex, MT. Ten foot drifts were seen in the vicinity of roads near Glacier National Park. The Flattop Mountain weather sensor in Glacier National Park reported 26 inches of snow in 24 hours. Another Department of Transportation weather sensor in Essex, MT recorded steady 30 mph winds with frequent gusts into the 40 mph range throughout the event. US-2 at milepost 153 near West Glacier was closed during the early morning hours of the 6th due to heavy snow and drifting.
An avalanche covered the BNSF railway that runs parallel to US-2 near Marias Pass. Avalanche warnings and rail and road closures continued for days after the storm ended.

Glacier Park International Airport had to cancel two flights due to intense snowfall, with rates of up to 1.5 inches per hour. Winds combined with snow made it nearly impossible to de-ice planes before departure. The ASOS weather sensor at the airport recorded winds 30 mph gusting into the 40 mph range overnight. The peak wind speed was 33 mph sustained with 44 mph gusts. One airport fire crew employee was unable to get to work on time due to getting stuck in a snow drift. Ground blizzard conditions caused widespread travel impacts. A trained spotter reported glazed ice surfaces in Columbia Falls with freezing rain during the beginning of this event. The public reported very slick side roads due to freezing rain around Kalispell. This initial freezing rain made subsequent snowfall more dangerous to travelers. The US Postal Service did not deliver mail in some portions of the Flathead Valley on the 6th.

events.cz_name: LOWER HELLS CANYON / SALMON RIVER REGION
events.event_narrative: Truck drivers sent pictures of multiple semi trucks stuck on Whitebird Hill during the periods of heavy snow.
A spotter reported 5 inches of new snow at the highest elevations along Grangemont Road in Clearwater County, ID. Two cars had to be pulled from ditches during this spotter's commute.

Freezing rain prompted a local official in Eureka, MT to encourage all to stay at home during the evening of Feb. 8 unless there was an emergency. Public reports mentioned several cars in ditches along US-93 south of Eureka, MT. Fortine and Eureka schools were open on a 2 hour delay on Feb. 9. with no bus service. Plow crews reported being unable to keep up with sanding area highways given the large areal coverage of freezing rain. Trained spotters reported 8 inches of new snow in Bull Lake, MT, while other spotters reported 5 to 6 inches of snow in Libby, MT. Power went out in Bull Lake for 6 hours during the early morning hours of Feb. 9. The Bull Lake Fire Chief's basement was flooded with 6 of water due to the fact that the snow-pack was so deep and the falling rain had no where to go.

US Hwy 2 from Essex to East Glacier, MT was closed during this event due to the threat of avalanches with 6 inches of new snow on top of the 30 to 50 inches of snow earlier in the week. An avalanche did occur between Essex and Devils Creek spilling over US-2 in the morning. The Montana Dep. of Transportation listed US-2 with Severe driving conditions during the day.

Many reports of freezing rain came in during the morning hours of Feb. 9. A trained spotter in Bigfork, MT sent images of 0.13 of ice accretion on his vehicle. Another spotter in Columbia Falls, MT sent an image of completely glazed roads. Airport crews were unable to clear runways at Glacier Park International and the airport was temporary closed until late morning. The Montana Department of Transportation issued Severe Driving Conditions for portions of the Flathead and Mission Valley for 5 hours during the morning of Feb. 9. Highway patrol reported at least 15 slide-off accidents during this time-frame.
Freezing rain lead to Severe Driving Conditions being issued for the Missoula and Bitterroot Valley during the morning hours. School buses were delayed by 2 hours.

A local emergency manager estimated 8 inches of snow in Libby, MT in 24 hours with this event. A public report agreed with this estimate, also stating 8 inches of snow had fallen during the same time-frame, with 15 inches snow depth on ground. Plow drivers stated they had a hard time keeping up with the snow rates. On February 8th, the governor of Montana declared a State of Emergency to help in providing resources for snow removal. The Eureka, MT AWOS sensor, located at the airport, reported multiple hours of heavy snow, with 0.25 mi or 0.50 mi visibility for much of the event.

A trained spotter in Kalispell reported 14 inches of snow during this 21 hour time-frame. Public reports came in reporting the worst driving conditions between Creston and Columbia Falls they have experienced in 30 years. Plow drivers also reported 12 to 14 inches of new snow in Columbia Falls, MT.
The public reported 15 inches of snow in 24 hours at Lolo Pass. Automated SNOTEL sensors suggested intense snowfall throughout the high terrain.

A local ski area reported 35 inches of snow in 36 hours. The Montana Dept. of Transportation reported several accidents along I-90 during this timeframe. Schools were closed due to heavy snow and dangerous travel conditions. The heavy snow also contributed to a power outage that caused the I-90 rest areas to close on the 6th.

The Idaho Transportation Department plow drivers estimated about 12 inches of new snow on portions of area highways. A trained spotter reported 9 inches of snow in Grangeville, ID during this event. Public reports showed snow still falling with 6 to 9 inches of new snow already on the ground in Kooskia and Grangeville. Another public report after the event had ended put the storm total at 14 inches near Kooskia. The Grangeville airport AWOS reported low clouds and reduced visibility for an 18 hour period. During the periods of heaviest snowfall, visibility was as low as 0.25 miles with a cloud deck 300 ft above the surface. Winds were generally less than 10 mph.

A 200 foot wide avalanche occurred between Essex and Devils Creek spilling over US-2 to a depth of 8 inches. This caused the Montana Dep. of Transportation to close to the road because of the avalanche danger.

Ponding water up to 3 feet deep near Saltese, MT on I-90 lead the Montana Dept. of Transportation to close the roadway for much of the day. Antecedent heavy low-elevation snow allowed for this event, as water was unable to drain off the sides of the road. After plows cut breaks in the snow berms, ponding decreased. Roads were reopened during the evening.

An NWS Employee reported extensive ponding in fields and near property in Corvallis, MT. The exceptionally high amount of valley snow-pack allowed for periods of moderate rain combined with relatively warm temperatures to cause unusually extensive areal flooding on Feb. 9 & 10.
An NWS employee reported water ponding on Hwy 12 leading up to Lolo Pass. Snow berms along the road from previous snow events caused a 3-inch deep flow of rainwater on the road surface.
The public reported 12 inches of snow in 24 hours near Lowell, ID.
The St. Regis River at St. Regis peaked at the minor flood stage of 8.06 feet.
The Thompson River gauge near Thompson Falls peaked at 7.15 feet for 4.5 hours.
The Fisher River gauge peaked at 7.8 feet for 8 hours.

Severe weather spotters in Libby and Troy reported 7.5 and 6.5 inches of new snowfall accumulations, respectively, from this event. In addition, gusty winds between 23 and 34 mph were reported in the valley locations.

Severe weather spotters in Ovando reported 6.5 inches of new snow and whiteout conditions during this event. Six inches of new snow was reported in Anaconda. Frequent wind gusts to 37 mph were observed along the Interstate 90 corridor near Deer Lodge.

Weather spotters in Kalispell reported between 6 and 8 inches of new snow. 10 inches of new snow was reported 10 miles north of Bigfork. Winds across the Flathead valley frequently gusted between 33 and 46 mph.
The weather observation site at Lookout Pass and a severe weather spotter in Thompson Falls reported 6 inches of new snow. Winds across the Lower Clark Fork Region gusted between 27 and 35 mph.
Weather spotters in Seeley Lake and Condon reported between 8 and 12 inches of new snow. Wind gusts to 39 mph were observed at the automated weather station at Pistol Creek.

The Montana Department of Transportation declared Interstate 90 emergency travel only due to blizzard conditions. Blizzard conditions were observed at the mouth of Hellgate Canyon by several NWS employees where an automated wind sensor recorded a wind gust up to 70 mph. In addition, several trees were reported to have been blown down by wind across Missoula. One large tree was blown down onto a NWS employee's house in the University District. Wind gusts to 60 mph were estimated in this area with poor visibility in blowing snow.

The Montana Department of Transportation declared Highway 200 from Bonner to Greenough emergency travel only due to poor visibility in snow and blowing snow. Blizzard conditions were observed in areas along this route.
Wind chills to minus 23 degrees were observed at Essex at 01:06 a.m. on January 21. Wind chills to minus 26 degrees were observed at Fielding at 08:42 a.m. on January 21.
Automated weather stations at Avon and Helmville reported wind chills of minus 20 degrees.
Automated weather stations at Pistol Creek and Bearmouth reported wind chills of minus 21 and 20 degrees, respectively.
Wind chills to minus 22 degrees were observed at Tepee Point at 02:09 p.m. on January 21. In addition, Lost Trail Pass Ski Resort was closed due to dangerous wind chills.
Weather spotters in Libby and Troy reported between 14 and 19 inches of new snow. To the north, weather spotters in Yaak and along Lake Koocanusa reported between 16 and 17 inches of new snow.

Severe weather spotters in Essex reported 9 inches of new snowfall accumulations. The automated weather station at Fielding reported 10.5 inches of new snowfall accumulations. Severe weather spotters in Polebridge reported between 8 and 12 inches of new snowfall accumulations between Polebridge and the Canadian border.
Severe weather spotters at Lolo Hot Springs reported 10.5 inches of new snowfall accumulations. The automated weather station at Lolo Pass reported 9 inches of new snowfall accumulations.

Automated weather stations at Lookout Pass and Mullan Pass reported 24 and 29 inches of new snowfall accumulations during this event. A severe weather spotter in Heron reported 6.5 inches of new snowfall accumulations. Lookout Pass reported wind gusts to 32 mph. Pardee and Nine Mile reported wind gusts to 25 mph.

The Idaho Department of Transportation reported 10 inches of new snowfall accumulations between the Elk River and the Clearwater County line. Headquarters received 6 inches of new snowfall accumulations.
The US Highway 12 corridor between Powell and Lolo Pass received between 7.2 and 9 inches of new snow.

Lost Trail Pass received 12 inches of new snow from this event. Significant blowing and drifting snow was reported in Leadore where school was closed for the day due to the winter storm. Wind gusts across the area ranged from 36 mph to 52 mph.

Weather spotters reported 12 and 13 inches of new snow at West Glacier and Essex respectively. In addition, 7 inches of new snow was reported at Fielding and Marias Pass. Long lasting near whiteout conditions were reported along the US Highway 2 corridor between Essex and Marias Pass during this event.

Emergency travel only was declared across Flathead County by the Montana Department of Transportation for this event. Whitefish and Columbia Falls reported between 4.5 and 7 inches of new snowfall accumulations. Whiteout conditions from substantial blowing and drifting snow was reported as well.
A severe weather spotter from Grangeville reported 11 inches of new snowfall accumulations. Schools across the Camas Prairie were closed due to heavy snowfall.
The Montana Department of Transportation declared emergency travel only throughout Flathead County due to Blizzard conditions.
The Montana Department of Transportation declared emergency travel only throughout Flathead County due to Blizzard conditions.
Automated weather stations and cooperative observers reported new snowfall accumulations of 10 inches at Shanghai Summit, 8 inches at Pierce, and 6 inches at Headquarters.
An automated weather station at Lookout Pass reported 11 inches of new snowfall accumulations. A severe weather spotter 9 miles north of Noxon reported 12.5 inches of new snowfall accumulations.
Severe weather spotters in Libby, Troy and Yaak reported between 8 and 12 inches of new snowfall accumulations.
Automated weather stations and severe weather spotters reported between 7 and 10 inches of new snowfall accumulations.

The Montana Department of Transportation declared emergency travel only over Lookout Pass due to poor visibility in snow and blowing snow. The automated weather station at Lookout Pass reported 13 inches, Saint Regis 11 inches, and Mullan Pass 8 inches of new snowfall respectively.

The Montana Department of Transportation declared emergency travel only along the US Highway 93 corridor south of Lolo due to blowing and drifting snow. Wind gusts between 23 mph and 36 mph were observed across the Missoula and Bitterroot valleys.

Weather spotters and automated weather stations reported between 6 and 13 inches of new snow between Lolo Hot Springs and Lolo Pass. Twelve Mile Creek Snotel reported 6.5 inches of new snow. Tepee Point and Sula automated weather stations recorded wind gusts between 32 mph and 39 mph.

The Idaho Department of Transportation reported between 7 and 12 inches of new snowfall accumulations between Pierce and Elk River. In addition, nearby automated weather stations reported gusty winds between 41 mph and 59 mph.

Automated weather stations reported 18 inches at Lolo Pass and 8 inches of new snow at Savage Pass. A cooperative observer at Dixie reported 9 inches of new snow. In addition, gusty winds to 41 mph were reported at the High Camp automated weather station.

The Idaho Department of Transportation reported 1 to 2 feet of new snowfall accumulations at Lost Trail Pass. A severe weather spotter reported 8 inches of new snowfall accumulations at Gibbonsville. In addition, gusty winds between 30 and 45 mph were reported across the county. School in Leadore was closed due to significant blowing and drifting snow.

The Sheriff's Office in Grangeville reported widespread whiteout conditions across the Camas Prairie due to snow and blowing snow. A weather spotter reported substantial blowing and drifting snow. Wind gusts to 59 mph were recorded at the Grangeville Airport.
