The Sheriff's Office in Grangeville and the Idaho Department of Transportation reported widespread blizzard conditions across the Camas Prairie. Several roads were closed due to significant blowing and drifting snow. A wind gust to 59 mph was recorded at the Grangeville Airport.
A RAWS station east of Sula recorded 66 mph winds.
A local resident reported ground covered with quarter-sized hail. A few strikes of lightning accompanied the storm.
The automated weather station at Lolo Pass reported 8 inches of new snow.
The automated weather station at Lolo Pass reported 8 inches of new snow.
The ski area at Lookout Pass reported 9 inches of new snow.
Pike Creek snotel reported 17 inches of snow in less than 24 hours. Additionally, the Department of Transportation reported thick slushy roads, and a few car slide offs.
An NWS employee reported 3 inches of heavy wet snow which caused many tree limbs to break off. Also, a spotter in Evaro Hill reported 5 inches of snow.

An NWS employee reported 4.5 inches of snow up in the Rattlesnake valley and 5 inches just north of Florence. Missoula received 2.7 inches of snow, which caused tree damage power outages lasting several hours. The power outage affected nearly 4,000 people according to Northwestern energy. Additionally, snow rates of 1 inch per hour caused slushy, slick roads in the morning hours.
Lolo and Saddle Mountain snotel recorded 8 to 10 inches of snow.  Many hours of moderate to heavy snow caused slick roads over Lolo and Lost trail passes.

A trained spotter reported 11 inches of snow in the Hills of Butte and at least 8 inches of snow in downtown Butte. The prolonged periods of heavy wet snow caused a few semi trucks to jackknife and resulted in Homestake pass being shut down for several hours. Additionally, Barker Lake snotel reported 22 inches, and Warm Springs reported 11 inches of snow with this system.

A trained spotter reported 4 inches at Twin Creeks and saw 10 to 12 inch diameter trees down at Greenough Hill. Similar reports of damage came from Bonner, where they received 1.5 inches. Additionally, reports were received of 6 inches in Potomac and 3 inches in Greenough.
Lolo snotel reported 10 inches of snow and Mountain Meadows snotel reported 11 inches of snow.  Additionally, a COOP in Dixie reported 5.4 inches of heavy wet snow.

A COOP observer in Pierce reported 4.2 inches of snow which caused power outages and knocked down many cottonwood trees. Shanghai summit snotel just north of Pierce 11 inches of snow with 1.8 inches of Snow Water Equivalent.
The Idaho Department of Transportation reported blizzard conditions across the Camas Prairie. Highway 95 was closed due to significant blowing and drifting snow.

The Montana Department of Transportation reported 8 inches of new snow at Lost Trail Pass and 9 inches of new snow at Lolo Pass. In addition, several automated weather stations in the area reported wind gusts between 24 mph an 36 mph.

A COOP observer in Dixie reported 10 inches of new snow. The automated weather station at Lolo Pass reported 8 inches of new snow. In addition, wind gusts between 29 mph and 50 mph were reported nearby.

Close to seventeen incidents of fallen trees with various damage from strong gusty winds over 50 mph were reported across the Flathead Valley and Flathead Lake areas. Damages included signs, a totaled porch, power lines down and damage to several roofs including one that was partially torn off.
Two incidents of trees blocking the road and two power outages were reported from Libby to Kila due to strong wind gusts.
A local resort in Seeley Lake reported strong winds that caused several trees to fall on their property.

A tree feel onto a transmission line in the Nine Mile area a little after noon causing over three thousand customers to be without power for several hours. Another storm produced strong winds that caused two bull pine trees to fall and damaged part of a roof in the Evaro area around 509 pm MDT.
A trained spotter in Georgetown Lake reported half-dollar size hail.

NWS employee reported quarter size hail 5 miles east of Garrison Junction.  The hailstones were found one hour after the storm had passed. Thus, the hailstones were likely larger when it initially fell.
Large hail of 1��� in diameter was reported by citizen at the Garrison Mercantile in Garrison at 3:57 pm MDT.

The media reported A Montana woman was killed when a tree struck her during a weekend thunderstorm. She was reportedly running back to camp when a tree broke, striking her on the head. She died on the way to the hospital.
The Montana Highway 56 corridor between Bull Lake and Troy received 6 to 8 inches of new snowfall accumulations. Yaak received 8 inches of new snowfall accumulations.

West Glacier received 7.5 inches, Marias Pass received 7 inches, and Swan Lake received 6 inches of new snowfall accumulations from this event. In addition, gusty winds to 35 mph were observed along the US Highway 12 corridor between Essex and Marias Pass.

Whitefish received 8 inches and Bigfork received 6 inches of new snowfall accumulations. In addition, winds across the Flathead and Mission valleys gusted between 21 mph and 31 mph throughout the day.

Severe weather spotters and automated weather stations reported between 6 and 10.5 inches of new snowfall accumulations along the Interstate 90 corridor between Saint Regis and Lookout Pass. In addition, wind gusts in the valleys and at Lookout Pass ranged between 21 mph and 31 mph.

Severe weather spotters reported between 9 and 11 inches of new snowfall accumulations in the areas surrounding Hamilton. In addition, wind gusts between 22 mph and 32 mph were observed across the Bitterroot Valley.

Lolo Pass received 6 to 7 inches of new snowfall accumulations in a 12 hour period. Lost Trail Pass received 10 to 12 inches of new snowfall accumulations during the entire event. In addition, gusty winds between 23 and 37 mph were observed throughout the mountains during the event.

Frequent wind gusts between 40 mph and 50 mph caused significant blowing and drifting snow along US Highway 12 between Garrison and McDonald Pass and also along Montana Highway 200 between Ovando and Lincoln. Whiteout conditions were observed on webcams at Avon and McDonald Pass.

Severe weather spotters 8 miles west of Clearwater Junction on Highway 200 and 10 miles east of Seeley Lake reported between 6 and 10 inches of new snow. In addition, blowing and drifting snow was reported. The automated weather station at Pistol Creek reported wind gusts to 27 mph.
Weather observers in Pierce and Elk River reported 8 to 12 inches of new snowfall accumulations. In addition, nearby automated weather stations reported wind gusts between 20 mph and 29 mph.

The weather observer at Powell reported 9 inches of new snowfall accumulations. The automated weather station at Lolo Pass reported 6 inches of new snowfall accumulations. In addition, nearby automated weather stations reported wind gusts to 29 mph.
The police department in Grangeville reported whiteout conditions across the Camas Prairie from blowing and drifting snow.

The police department in Grangeville reported whiteout conditions across the Camas Prairie througout the night. In addition, the automated weather station in Grangeville reported wind gusts to 62 mph. US Highway 95 was closed to travel.

The Idaho Department of Transportation reported 10 to 12 inches of new snowfall accumulations along US Highway 93 between Gibbonsville and Lost Trail Pass. In addition, automated weather stations across Eastern Lemhi County reported wind gusts between 28 mph and 45 mph.

The automated weather station at Lookout Pass reported 14.5 inches of new snow. A severe weather spotter in DeBorgia reported 8 inches of new snow. In addition, wind gusts between 20 mph and 36 mph were observed at serveral weather observation sites in the area.

The Montana Department of Transportation reported 10 to 12 inches of new snow at Lost Trail Pass. The automated weather station at Lolo Pass reported 7 inches of new snow. In addition, wind gusts between 20 mph and 40 mph were observed at serveral weather observation sites in the area.

Weather observers in Elk River and Pierce reported 12 inches and 8 inches of new snowfall accumulations, respectively. In addition, several automated weather stations nearby reported wind gusts between 23 mph and 29 mph.

The Idaho Department of Transportation reported between 7 and 9.2 inches of new snowfall accumulation between Powell and Lolo Pass. In addition, several automated weather stations nearby reported wind gusts between 23 mph and 29 mph.

The Idaho Department of Transportation closed US Highway 95 to emergency travel only over the Whitebird grade due to whiteout conditions. In addition, 6 to 8 inches of new snowfall accumulations were received in Cottonwood.

events.cz_name: LOWER HELLS CANYON / SALMON RIVER REGION
events.event_narrative: The Idaho Department of Transportation closed US Highway 95 to emergency travel only over the Whitebird grade due to whiteout conditions.

Automated weather stations in the Glacier National Park area reported wind gusts to 25 mph and wind chills that were between -20 degrees and -27 degrees. In addition, a weather observer in Essex reported 6 inches of new snowfall accumulations.

Local emergency manager reported flooding at the Oregon Bar campground 7 miles north of Salmon. Also an NWS employee reported minor flooding in the Elk Bend area, where water was flowing over yards and into outbuildings.

The USGS river gauge Salmon River at Salmon reported minor flooding on May 31st. The river continued to rise and reached moderate flood stage in the first half of June. See June storm data report for more information.

Resident reported mostly nickel-sized hailstones, with a few quarter-sized hailstones mixed in. No evidence of damage to property was seen. Resident estimated wind speeds with the storm outflow at 40 to 50 mph. Frequent lightning was also reported.

The USGS river gauge Salmon River at Salmon reported possible minor flooding (stage height of 7.5-8.5) on May 31st. The river continued to rise and reached moderate flood stage (stage height of 8.5-9.5) from June 2nd through June 10th. Multiple roads in the area lost shoulders due to the water level coming right up to road surfaces. A few acres of farmland along the river were flooded for about a week. Additionally, the park near the bridge in Salmon, ID saw water reach the bottom of structures.
The public sent a photo in to local media showing hails stones up to approximately 1.5 inches in diameter. Photos of hail damage to cars in the vicinity also came across social media feeds.

Road crews, the public, and the county emergency manager all had reports of damage from the strong winds during the late evening. Power companies reported outages to approximately 600 customers due to trees on power lines. A storm spotter in the area reported losing a few shingles, while another resident lost a stove pipe off the roof on the west side of Salmon, ID. Road crews reported downed Cottonwood trees on US-93.
Multiple reports of tree damage and a localized power outage occurred southeast of Kalispell and Evergreen according to a call to the NWS office and via Twitter reports.
A person from the public reported nickel to quarter size hail along Highway 41 on Twitter.
A resident on Z Bar T Road estimated hail smaller than golf balls but larger than quarters which caused tree branches to break and dented a camper.
Nickel to quarter size hail fell causing Aspen tree leaves to tear off and destroyed a bird feeder.

Multiple trees of varying thicknesses were either blown over or snapped in the Lake Alva campground. One spruce tree larger than 20 inches in diameter fell lengthwise onto a camper, totaling the trailer but sparing an infant in a bassinet. Another camper was also damaged as a tree fell lengthwise onto it but no one was injured. Property damage of both campers was estimated to be sixty thousand dollars.

Multiple trees fell due to the severe wind in the Florence area with up to 6 inch diameter bases. One large tree fell onto a house and broke the sky light. Another tree hit a power line on Ambrose Creek causing a fire. Over three thousand customers were without power for four hours after the thunderstorm went through.
A trained spotter estimated 60 mph winds knocking out power for portions of east and southern Missoula County.

There were several reports of very heavy rainfall including one that came from the NWS COOP observer at the golf course: 0.75 of rain in 20 to 25 minutes. Multiple homes experienced flooded basements, man hole covers were lifted off and floated down roads, and Westhill Park road was flooded with a depth of up to 4 feet. The Old Works Golf Course in Anaconda reported the cost to repair flood damage to be $660,000.

The heavy rain had widespread impacts in Ravalli county. RAWS sensors reported between 1 to 3 inches overnight from June 12 to June 13, with Gird Point RAWS receiving 3.67 inches over the 2-day event. Spotters reported water flowing over driveways and local roads near Stevensville, MT. Victor, MT fire department reported flooding at Middle Bear Creek. Water overwhelmed culverts and washed over roads east of Stevensville causing $15,000 of damage for the road department. Homeowners on the east side of the Bitterroot Valley reported damages to garages, driveways, and gardens, with many public roads seeing water over roads. Skalkaho Highway, MT-38, was closed June 13th due to water on roadways.

Granite county saw widespread impacts from the heavy rain. Philipsburg, MT received 3.28 inches of rain in 24 hours from noon 6/12 through noon 6/13. A public report from Georgetown Lake, MT had a measured 3.7 inches of rain over the 2-day event. Fred Burr Creek was particularly hard hit, with private driveway bridges being washed out, thus stranding a couple residents. Many of these same residents had basement flooding as well. USGS stream gauges on Boulder Creek near Maxville recorded 1410 cfs; 1000 cfs begins to cause road flooding issues, and this was much above this impact level. Rock Creek and Flint Creek both saw extremely rapid and high flows, with water spilling into adjacent fields. Georgetown Lake over-topped its spillway for the first time in years. Sapphire Mountain ditch managers narrowly avoided damage to a major irrigation channel feeding the Bitterroot Valley.
Local Firefighters on the Lolo Peak wildfire reported quarter sized hail with no damages.
A spotter reported a pine tree with a diameter of 2.5 feet snapped in half from the strong wind. They estimated the wind gust to be 60 mph. Also power was reported out for 13 hours.

Up to 4 inches of snow fell across the higher terrain during this event causing snow and slush to cover parts of Skalkaho Pass and backcountry roads. Fire personnel from the Lolo Peak wildfire were cut-off from any access to the mid and upper part of the fire due to snow. Temperatures fell from the 70s and 80s in the higher terrain earlier in the week to the upper 20s to lower 30s by the 15th.

Very heavy snow fell over parts of southwest Montana above 6000 feet. A person from the public located one mile east-southeast of Seven Gables Inn in Georgetown Lake measured 14 inches of total storm snowfall from this event. By the morning of the 16th Homestake Pass and MacDonald Pass were snow-covered with slick conditions.

Sixteen to eighteen inches of heavy snow was reported in the foothills southeast of Leadore. Visibility reduced to one half mile or less at Gilmore Summit on Highway 28 due to snow during the morning and afternoon hours on the 15th.
The Marion area saw lows in the middle to upper 20s for four hours while the Yaak area saw a low around 21 degrees.
Glacier Park International Airport reported a low of 27 degrees while Hot Springs saw a low of 29 degrees Fahrenheit. Both locations experienced around six hours at or below freezing.
Lookout Pass received 15 inches of snow within 12 hours and this created hazardous conditions. Montana Department of Transportation closed I-90 for 6 hours from 1 am to 5 am MST.

A significant number of trees were blown on to power lines around the communities of Libby, Troy, and Eureka which resulted in power outages lasting up to 12 hours in those communities. Falling power lines also resulted in several new wildfires starts around the communities mentioned earlier. Wind gusts to 50 mph were common across the area with winds estimated to 70 mph by Forest Service officials in Libby.

Strong winds caused multiple trees to fall throughout Glacier National Park stranding hikers and campers for several hours. Quarter Circle Bridge Road and Inner North Fork Road were closed within the park so that rangers could clear away the trees. A vehicle parked at the Rocky Point trail head, located on the northwestern shore of Lake McDonald, was damaged by a fallen tree.  Downed trees and power outages were also reported near Hungry Horse, West Glacier, and Essex. Recorded wind gusts to 50 mph were common across the area.

Downed trees and power lines resulted in 15,000 members of Flathead Electric COOP to be without power in 150 separate outages which were primarily in West Valley, Whitefish and Columbia Falls. Six new wildfires were reported from downed power lines. Wind gusts to 55 mph were common throughout the Flathead and Mission valleys causing damage including a totaled billboard near the junction of Highway 40 and US-2.

Considerable power outages were reported from Florence to Victor in the Bitterroot Valley leaving thousands without power. Fallen trees were reported on roadways around Stevensville. The Missoula International Airport ASOS sensor measured a wind gust of 59 mph at 6:50 pm MDT.

Montana Department of Transportation (MDT) reported trees were falling on highway 56 north of Noxon due to the weight of the snow. Snow amounts were very impressive for early November with Libby reporting a storm total of 11 inches. Spotters also reported 10.4 inches near Marion and 12.1 inches near Kila.

The media reported 8 to 10 inches of snow in Hungry Horse and 12 inches of snow in West Glacier over 24 hours. Marias pass saw less snow than the valleys with 5 inches being reported. Fielding RAWS station reported an easterly wind at 10 gust 18 mph, and this may have contributed to lower snow ratios at Marias pass.

Montana Department of Transportation declared Severe Driving conditions for US 93 from Polson to Somers due to heavy snow. Roads were closed from about Dayton to Somers. A Spotter in Kalispell reported a 24 hour total of 12.7 inches with a few hours of 1 per hour snow rates. Other spotters in the Flathead Valley reported 7.4 inches in Bigfork and 7.4 inches in Evergreen.

A spotter reported 10 inches of snow in the outskirts of Butte. The heavy snow appeared to play a role in 3 crashes on I-90 near Homestake pass on the evening of November 3rd. Due to the early season nature of this event, Montana Department of Transportation (MDT) was understaffed and overwhelmed from this heavy snow event. An employee from MDT said they already had a winter worth of snow and don't want any more.

Temperatures fell into the upper 20s across the Missoula and Bitterroot Valleys. An NWS employee in Missoula reported that all their pumpkin leaves died while a NWS employee in Stevensville reported sub-freezing temperatures which caused vegetation damage.
Temperatures dipped into the upper 20s across the Bitterroot Valley including the Hamilton area while the Missoula area was a little milder due to some clouds with a low of 32 degrees.
The COOP observer at the KSRA radio station in Salmon recorded a low of 28 degrees.

On the evening of the 29th, the Montana Department of Transportation reported severe driving conditions due to reduced visibility from blowing and drifting snow between Noxon and Bull lake and between Whitefish and Stryker. Libby and Troy reported 6 to 8 inches of snow in 24 hours and 26 inches of snow was reported near Rexford over 3 days. Three feet of snow fell at Bull Lake while two feet was reported at Happy's Inn.

Montana Department of Transportation reported severe driving conditions on Highway 2 near Marias Pass Thursday night the 28th. Conditions deteriorated Friday morning the 29th as the arctic winds funneled through Badrock Canyon, and severe driving conditions were declared from West Glacier to Marias Pass. Periods of severe driving conditions continued through Saturday evening the 30th on US-2. A weather spotter in Essex measured a storm total snowfall of 28 inches over 72 hours. Other snow totals include: 3 feet Swan Lake, between 2 and 3 feet in Nyack, 30 inches Polebridge, 24 inches at Devil's Creek between Essex and Marias Pass and 18 inches at the Hungry Horse Dam. Dangerously cold wind chills dropped down between -35 and -40 degrees Fahrenheit between Essex and Marias Pass during the morning of the 30th.

Montana Department of Transportation declared severe driving conditions between Trout Creek and Heron due to heavy snow. The forest service in Trout Creek reported 21 inches of snow with one inch per hour rates during the evening of the 29th. Lookout Pass reported 17 inches of snow in 24 hours. Total 3 day snowfall amounts included: 35 inches 7 miles southeast of Noxon, 31 inches Lookout Pass, 28.9 inches 2 miles northwest of Heron, 23 inches Haugan, and 10 to 12 inches at Plains, St. Regis, Nine Mile and Alberton.

On Friday afternoon the 29th at 3 pm, Lake county officials declared emergency travel only due to snow drifts which made roads impassable. Also at 4 pm on the 29th, the Flathead County Road Department reported that east and west oriented roads located east and north of Glacier Park International Airport were drifting closed faster than road crews could plow. The Montana Department of Transportation declared severe driving conditions between Whitefish and Kalispell on US-93, Whitefish to Columbia Falls, Polson and St. Ignatius, between Hot Springs and Whitefish from the afternoon into the evening hours on the 29th. Total storm snow amounts between 12 and 18 inches with a few isolated amounts near 2 feet were reported across the Flathead and Mission valleys. Freezing rain caused icy roads on Friday morning in the Mission Valley.

Montana Department of Transportation declared severe driving conditions between the Clearwater Junction and Helmville and also on I-90 between Bearmouth and Drummond. The combination of antecedent wet snow and wet conditions with cold arctic air moving in during the day on Friday the 29th, triggered a flash freeze which caused area roads to become a sheet of ice. Also heavy snow combined with strong gusty winds created blizzard conditions between Potomac and Clearwater on Highway 200 and also along Interstate 90 between Clinton and Drummond. Further north between Condon and Seeley Lake, between 2 and 3 feet of snow fell over the course of 3 days.
Lost Trail pass received 34 inches in 72 hours and Lolo pass saw 22 inches of snow. Freezing rain also developed at Lolo pass on Thursday afternoon.

Between the afternoon and evening of the 28th, snow changed over to freezing rain. Severe driving conditions were declared by the Montana Department of Transportation early Friday morning the 29th between Florence and Stevensville due to black ice and freezing rain. By 9:30 am MST, the Missoula County Sheriff's office issued emergency travel only for Missoula County which was extended through 7 pm that evening. The arctic front brought very strong winds to Hellgate Canyon and surrounding areas. Numerous trees fell down in the Rattlesnake Valley and vicinity of Missoula which was likely a result of the combination of extremely wet snow and strong winds. One tree fell on top of a house and caused considerable roof damage. The ASOS sensor at the Missoula International Airport recorded wind gusts to 37 mph which meant that winds were likely much stronger towards Hellgate Canyon. A NWS employee located northeast of Stevensville measured a total of 0.15 inches of glaze that didn't melt for at least a week afterwards.

Montana Department of Transportation(MDT) reported 12 inches of snow in Drummond with blowing and drifting snow. MDT issued severe driving conditions between Bearmouth and Garrison junction around 2 pm Friday. A spotter 10 miles ENE of Ovando reported 18 inches of snow in 24 hours from this event. Total snowfall amounts included: near 2 feet in the Ovando, Helmville and Elliston areas, 9 inches Hall and 3 inches in the Anaconda area. A weather spotter located 10 miles east-northeast of Ovando reported 3 inches of heavy snow that fell in one hour ending 9:13 am on the 30th due to a transient snow band that set up over northern Powell County.

About 3 feet of snow was reported at Elk River with power outages in the area. For the lower elevations, freezing rain was reported. Also there was minor flooding due to blocked culverts in portions of western Clearwater County.

In Elk City, heavy snow brought down power lines and trees causing an extended power outage that lasted for three days from 11 am PST on the 28th to 10 am PST on the 30th. Heavy wet snow also caused several power outages in the Lower Middlefork, Lowell, Selway and Tahoe areas. The Idaho Transportation Department reported 37 inches at the Powell Shed. Around 22 inches of snow was reported at Lolo Pass, between 14 and 18 inches of snow fell in Elk City and the Dixie COOP reported 11 inches over 3 days. For the lower elevations, Kooskia saw 6 inches of heavy wet snow while freezing rain was reported on highway 12 with several trees down near Lowell.

Spotters reported anywhere from 9 to 18 inches of snow in Libby,  14 inches in Troy and Eureka, and 18 inches at Bull Lake over 48 hours. Scattered power outages were reported throughout the region due to heavy snow on power lines.

Glacier National Park reported 15 to 19 inches of snow over 24 hours from this winter storm. A spotter in Hungry Horse also reported 17 inches of snow in 24 hours.  The Izaak Walton Inn near Essex reported 40 inches of snow over 2.5 days.

A trained spotter reported 11 inches of wet, heavy snow in Kalispell.  Spotters in Bigfork and Polson Bear Hollow reported about 9 inches of snow with this system. The heavy wet  snow produced downed trees and power outages throughout the region. Also, schools such as Columbia Falls , Deer Park, West Glacier, and Whitefish were closed on December 20.

Montana Department of Transportation reported severe driving conditions several times throughout this storm. The first round of severe driving conditions occurred due to freezing rain on the 18th. The second round occurred during the day on the 19th as Lookout Pass experienced 1 to 2 inch per hour snow rates.  Lookout Pass ski resort reported 17 inches in 24 hours and a total of 32 inches in 2.5 days. A spotter near Trout Creek reported 12 inches of snow with this storm.

A trained spotter reported 21.5 inches of snow in Seeley Lake over 2.5 days. A spotter in Condon reported 14 inches of snow. Due to the heavy snow, trees were reported down on MT-83 near mile marker 67.  North Fork Jocko snotel reported a total of 25 inches of new snow.  Lastly, freezing rain was also an issue during the onset of this event.

Due to an increase in snow intensities during the evening commute, Missoula county officials issued an emergency travel only alert from Bonner east to the Missoula/Granite county line along Interstate 90.  NWS employees reported 5 inches of snow near South Hills and 7 inches in Lolo. Numerous accidents were observed between Missoula and Clinton and between Missoula and Lolo.

A Missoula county official issued a MEANS alert for emergency travel only for I-90 between Bonner and the Missoula/Granite county line due to slick roads and blowing snow creating poor visibility and hazardous driving conditions. Numerous slide offs were observed on I-90 on the incident report.

A trained spotter in Anaconda reported 7 inches of snow with this winter storm. Road reports from Montana Department of Transportation reported blowing and drifting snow across portions of I-90 in southwest Montana.

The avalanche moved across Highway 200 for approximately 40 yards in length near mile-marker 55.9 and was 15 to 20 feet deep and 55 yards wide. The cab of a semi-trailer truck was partially buried. Highway 200 was closed until 530 am MST the next morning. Most likely heavy snow and strong easterly winds created severe wind-loading on Mineral Hill contributing to the conditions of the avalanche. According to the Montana Department of Transportation an avalanche of this magnitude had not occurred in this location in over 20 years.
The Montana Department of Transportation reported severe driving conditions for Highway 56 from Noxon to Bull Lake at 6:36 am MST due to freezing rain and ice.
Severe driving conditions were issued for US-2 between West Glacier and Marias Pass and on Highway 83 from Condon to the Junction of S-209 between 5 and 9 am MST due to freezing rain and ice.
The Montana Department of Transportation reported severe driving conditions on Highway 200 between the Idaho state line to Plains between 6 and 8 am MST due to freezing rain and ice.

A period of moderate to heavy snow moved over the region by the evening of the 11th creating low visibility and slick roads. Total snowfall amounts ranged between 6 and 7 inches from Trout Creek to Bull Lake.

An arctic cold front moved west along US-2 past Marias Pass and Essex by noon on the 10th causing wind gusts between 40 and 50 mph and periods of moderate to heavy snow, low visibility less than 500 feet at times, blowing and drifting snow. Snowfall amounts from this first part of the storm included 2 inches at Essex, 4.1 at West Glacier to 7 inches towards Marias Pass. Another 2 to 3 inches of snow fell between the 11th and 12th.

Moderate snow fell across the region while blowing and drifting snow occurred in the Polson area due to gusty north winds off of Flathead Lake. Total Snowfall amounts included 4 to 6 inches in the Flathead Valley and closer to 7 inches in Polson. The Polson schools had a 2 hour delay on the 12th. A 82 year old woman died as a result of injuries sustained in a two-vehicle accident on Montana Highway 40 between Columbia Falls and Whitefish. Slippery road conditions were one of the suspected factors in the crash.

A period of intense heavy snow fell from Lookout Pass towards Haugan along Interstate 90 and also along portions of Highway 200 between the Idaho border and Trout Creek during the evening of the 11th. For observational snow amounts Lookout Pass ski resort reported 7 inches for the day through 7 pm and saw a three day total of 24 inches.

The COOP observers at Lindbergh lake and Seeley Lake reported a total snowfall total of 19.1 and 17.0 inches respectively during this storm. Because of the heavy snowfall rates during the late evening hours of the 11th, tree damage and intermittent power outages were reported in these areas.
Both Lolo and Lost Trail passes saw 14 inches of storm total snowfall during this event. Snowfall rates at Lolo Pass were heavy for several hours during the evening of the 11th.

A person from the public in Elk City estimated over 5 inches of total snowfall while areas along US-12 between Powell and Lolo Pass saw 8 to 15 inches. During the early morning hours of the 12th, heavy snow changed to rain and caused several trees to snap or become uprooted falling onto US-12 near Lowell. One tree was estimated to be 36 inches in diameter and the Idaho Transportation Department reported that the ground has been saturated and not frozen.
Temperatures were in the upper 20s when freezing rain occurred and created slick driving conditions across the Flathead Valley.

An arctic airmass rushed over the Continental Divide the morning of the 3rd, reaching Essex around 11 am and followed the U.S. Highway 2 corridor into West Glacier by 2 pm. Blizzard conditions were observed as falling snow combined with wind gusts of 45 to 55 miles per hour.  A peak wind gust of 57 mph was observed at Essex with gusts over 40 mph for 9 consecutive hours, resulting in an extended period of severe driving conditions.  An avalanche official reported these were the worst conditions he had seen in his 13 years in the Essex area.

An arctic air-mass moved over the Continental Divide into West-Central Montana during the evening of the 3rd, leading to snow, blowing snow, and icy roads. Wind gusts of 35 to 45 miles per hour combined with falling snow led to low visibility and drifting snow.  Widespread snow amounts of 3 to 6 inches were measured with isolated totals to 12 inches.

Snow and blowing snow on the morning of the 5th caused poor driving conditions and numerous accidents during the morning rush hour. The peak wind gust of 39 mph at Glacier Park International Airport occurred at 8:01 am.

A snow slide occurred across State Highway 1 at mile marker 27.5 near Georgetown Lake early on the morning of the 5th.  The northbound lane was impassable with up to 15 inches of snow on the southbound lane.

Heavy rain lead to a fallen tree across U.S. Highway 12 near milepost 52 and subsequent car accident at 4:08 am on the 5th. One person was injured in the incident and the highway was blocked for one and a half hours.

Severe driving conditions were observed on U.S. Highway 2 due to a combination of falling snow and blowing snow as winds gusted to 50 mph. Power outages were also noted around Bad Rock Canyon and Swan Lake due to falling trees.

Severe driving conditions occurred in the Flathead and Mission valleys the evening of the 8th through the morning of the 9th due to snow and blowing snow.  A peak wind gust of 56 mph occurred at Glacier Park International Airport at 4:46 pm on the 8th during the evening commute with minor power outages also noted.

Severe driving conditions occurred in the Flathead Valley due to a combination of snow, blowing snow, and flash-frozen roads. A peak wind gust of 41 mph was observed at the Glacier Park International Airport, along with 4 inches of new snow.

Heavy snow on the 17th was followed by snow and gusty winds late on the 17th into the 18th leading to periods of severe driving conditions.  Snow amounts of 8 to 12 inches were common with 18 inches at Marion.

Severe driving conditions with chains required were reported on U.S. Highway 2 from Columbia Falls to Marias Pass due to snow as well as blowing and drifting of snow.  Essex reported 18 inches of new snow.

Heavy snow on the 17th with rates of 1 to 2 inches per hour were followed by strong winds the evening of the 17th into 18th. Snowfall totals of 12 to 18 inches were common along with wind gust of 35 to 45 mph.  Severe driving conditions were widespread.

Periods of severe driving conditions occurred much of the 17th into the 18th due to heavy snow with some gusty winds.  Twenty-four hour snow amounts included 26 inches at Lookout Pass and 22 inches just west of Trout Creek.

Snow, blowing snow, and a flash freeze led to severe driving conditions late on the 17th into the 18th.  Wind gusts of 30 to 40 mph on the morning of the 18th combined with snow to produce greatly reduced visibilities.
Severe driving conditions were observed on major travel routes due to snow and blowing snow. Wind gusts of 50 to 60 mph were common creating localized ground blizzard conditions.

Numerous slide off crashes and jackknifed semi trucks occurred on Interstate 90 due to snow and blowing snow.  Widespread snowfall amounts of 8 to 12 inches were common with wind gusts of 35 to 45 mph.

Significant impacts were felt on major travel corridors. Interstate 90 was blocked several times due to jackknifed semi trucks in addition to periodic severe driving conditions. A 24 hour snow amount of 25 inches of snow was reported at Lookout Pass.

Severe driving conditions occurred on U.S. Highway 2 from late on the 4th to early on the 5th due to a combination of freezing rain, heavy snow, blowing snow, and icy roads. Snow amounts of 4 to 8 inches were common with wind gusts to 35 miles per hour.

A band of heavy snow developed over Missoula and the northern Bitterroot Valley during the morning commute on the 9th. Numerous traffic accidents occurred on key travel corridors as snow turned to slush and then froze to the roadways.  A total of 5.7 inches of snow was observed at the Missoula International Airport.

Heavy bursts of snow with amounts around 12 inches were common leading to difficult travel over area mountain passes. The highway department noted that it was difficult to keep up with snow rates near Lolo Pass late on the 17th. Also, 24 inches of snow fell at Powell from the 16th through the 18th.

Heavy bursts of snow with amounts around 12 inches were common leading to difficult travel over area mountain passes. The highway department noted that it was difficult to keep up with snow rates near Lolo Pass late on the 17th.
Snowfall amounts of 12 to 20 inches were common from the weekend storm with reports of over 2 feet at Elk River.
Snowfall rates of 2 to 3 inches per hour were observed on U.S. Highway 12 between Lowell and Bald Mountain with general amounts of at least a foot. Heavy snowfall made travel difficult.

Blowing and drifting snow were a significant impact as wind gusts to 40 mph transported newly fallen snow late on the 23rd into the 24th. Snow drifted across U.S. Highway 95 west and south of Grangeville leading to treacherous road conditions.

A second round of blowing and drifting snow occurred on the 25th with even stronger winds compared to the previous day; a gust to 56 mph was observed at Grangeville Airport. Snow drifted across U.S. Highway 95 west and south of Grangeville, and on State Highway 13 east of Grangeville. County officials took until the 27th to clear drifts of up to 6 feet.
Low temperatures recorded in Salmon, Idaho on January 21, 22 and 23 were -18, -24 and -17 degrees respectively. These cold temperatures resulted in the closure of schools in Salmon and Leadore.
Clearwater Tribune reported that the Idaho State Patrol closed US Highway 95 from mile post 223-259 due to a snow avalanche on Whitebird Hill and blizzard conditions.

Snow and blowing snow across eastern Lemhi County resulted in a period of difficult driving conditions. Wind gust to 40 miles per hour were observed at Gilmore Summit which lofted snow and reduced visibility to near a quarter mile at times. One person who frequents State Hwy 28 described the event as the worst he had ever seen on that stretch of highway.

Heavy snow fell across far northwest Montana with general amounts of 6-10 inches for valleys locations.  The heaviest amounts were observed on Highway 37 south of Eureka, where 18 inches fell over 12 hours.  Travel was difficult to impossible based on public and highway department reports.

Difficult to severe driving conditions were reported in the Kalispell vicinity as well as in Lake County. Numerous accidents occurred due to a combination of ice and reduced visibility in blowing snow.

General snow amounts of 2 to 4 inches with isolated higher totals were observed. The snow combined with much colder temperatures and wind gust of 30 to 40 mph lead to hazardous driving conditions and numerous accidents.

An unseasonably late winter storm brought snow amounts of 2 to 4 inches with isolated higher totals observed. The snow combined with wind gust of 35 to 45 mph lead to reduced visibility and ice, the result was widespread hazardous driving conditions and several traffic accidents.

Increasing river levels and a rising ground water table resulted in flooding around ten homes in the Orchard Homes subdivision of Missoula. The main impacts observed were water covering parts of Tower Street and Kehrwald Drive with adjacent homes being surrounded by water. Some of the affected homes also had basements fill with water. The full details including damages are in the May report.

Increasing water levels in Seeley Lake, as well as a rising water table lead to flooding of 15 to 20 homes. Most of the flooding occurred on the southwest side of Seeley Lake near C Street where water had surrounded 10 to 15 homes.  Several homes in the town of Seeley Lake also had groundwater-filled basements.

Idaho County Free Press reported that the gymnasium roof collapsed under heavy snow loading at the North Idaho Correctional Institution at Cottonwood Butte. 48 inches of snow had accumulated from the recent storm.

Three large snow and debris slides occurred along the Highway 12 corridor. The first slide occurred between 330 PM and 345 PM at mile marker 133.97, large enough to close Highway 12. The second slide occurred at mile marker 133.79 which hit a truck and trailer. The third slide at mile marker 137.06 was large enough to flow into the Lochsa River and dam up the river.
Idaho Department of Transportation reported two avalanches along Highway 12. The first, at mile marker 137.79 pushed a truck into the Lochsa River. The second occurred at mile marker 133.19.

Two avalanches were reported along Highway 12. The first, at mile marker 133.79, covered the highway with 3 to 4 feet of debris and snow. The second, at mile marker 132.48, covered the highway with 23 feet of snow, large trees and debris.

The Clark Fork River north of Missoula reached 13.82 feet and 32,500 CFS on May 11 between 830 pm and 845 pm MDT which goes down as the highest river level since June 1, 1908 when the river reached 17.4 feet. Three mobile homes were washed away and most likely broke up off of Schmidt Road on May 11. Multiple residences and structures in the Orchard Homes area, including those along Tower Street and Kehrwald Drive experienced flood damage. Flooding caused the evacuation of 50 to 60 homes conducted by the Missoula County Sheriff and Northwest Energy had to cut electricity and gas to these homes. Despite the fact that this continuous flooding ended on June 8, the event altered the river channel to the extent flooding occurred well below the established flood stage on June 11 and again with a basin rain event on June 19-25.

Several large trees were uprooted and fell onto two cars and a house. The Missoula International Airport ASOS reported a gust to 48 mph while a sensor on top of Mount Sentinel recorded a 68 mph wind gust. A local power company reported at least 2,000 customers were without power for at least three hours.
Strong winds caused several Ponderosa pine trees to be uprooted. These trees damaged a well house and an all-terrain vehicle.
Hail damaged skylights, air conditioning units and caused leaks in a few RV's at a nearby campground.
The Yaak River reached minor flood stage and affected low lying areas adjacent to the river.
The Blackfoot River reached minor flood stage and mainly low lying areas were impacted.
The Bitterroot River reached minor flood stage causing the Spring Gulch campground and low lying areas adjacent to the river to flood.

With both the Bitterroot River and Burnt Fork Creek running high, damage to the Lee Metcalf Wildlife Refuge and Whitetail Golf Course occurred. Much of the damage included scouring of pavement in these areas.

The Bitterroot River near Missoula reached minor flood stage which caused field flooding on the east side of Highway 93 both north and south of Lolo. Ground water adjacent to the Bitterroot River flooded the Linda Vista Golf course and nearby homeowner's backyards.
Homes and buildings adjacent to Seeley Lake and the Clearwater River were impacted by flooding. Thirteen homes in the Seeley Lake region were under evacuation orders.

Low lying areas adjacent to the Clark Fork River below Missoula to Frenchtown were flooded. The river also flooded numerous homes in the vicinity of Harpers Road from both surface water and groundwater; some homes were evacuated by Missoula County Sheriff's Department. Sandbagging of homes occurred on Mallard Way to keep from flooding.
Low lying areas were flooded by the Clark Fork River between Thompson Falls and Plains.
Several small creeks including Union and Nevada flooded nearby fields.
The Clark Fork River again reached flood stage and caused flooding of the access road to the sewage lagoons outside of Plains.
The Bitterroot River near Missoula reached flood stage and caused flooding in low-lying areas and contributed to high groundwater near the Linda Vista and lower Miller creek areas.

Surface water from the Clark Fork River flooded the county road that accesses the sewage lagoons in Plains. The US Army Corps of Engineers had to construct levees to protect the sewage lagoons and they had to rep-rap county roads along the river to prevent roads from being washed out.

The Bitterroot River near Missoula flooded again and this time reached 12 feet which caused some flooding of farmland and some roads along the river from Lolo to the confluence with the Clark Fork River. Groundwater adjacent to the Bitterroot River flooded Linda Vista Golf course and nearby homeowner's backyards.
The Clark Fork River flooded low lying areas near the river between Missoula and Frenchtown.
Extensive field flooding occurred along the Clark Fork River between Drummond and Garrison Junction. Jens Frontage Road along Interstate 90 had water flowing over it in several places.

Cottonwood Creek overflowed its banks in downtown Deer Lodge on the afternoon of June 19. The excessive runoff flooded basements and surrounded numerous homes as water covered a whole city block. The Clark Street Bridge was over topped and remained closed for over a day.  In addition, Tin Cup Joe Creek and Fred Burr Creek also experienced minor flooding.

Multiple residences and structures in the Orchard Homes area, including those along Tower Street and Kehrwald Drive experienced flood damage. Flooding began the end of April 2018 and continued through June 12.  The event altered the river channel to the extent flooding occurred well below the established flood stage all way through June 12 and again with a basin rain event on June 18-26.

Flooding returned to the Orchard Homes area, primarily on Tower Street and Kehrwald Drive with water into homes, travel was also impacted. An important note is the previously established flood stage was much too high due to changes in channeling from the earlier flooding late April into early June.

This storm produced enough hail to cover the ground several inches in the Hamilton area. There were multiple reports of one inch hail. A lady reported that she would have to replace her roof due to the hail damage. She remarked that she knew of several others who had to get their roofs repaired.

Besides the measured wind report, a spotter in Missoula reported hail sizes between dimes and quarters. Another interesting thing to note is the fact that Point 6 near 8,000 feet received a wind gust to 74 mph.
Hailstones reported varied from marble up to ping pong size during the storm.
Several lodgepole pine trees were blown over and hail up to one inch were reported with this storm.
Approximately fifteen hours after the event, NWS employees found hail near the size of quarters on the side of a building in Hall. There was also evidence of very heavy rain with this storm.

Very heavy rainfall with amounts ranging from 1 to 3 inches combined with snow melt over a several day period led to overland flooding with rock, mud and water along portions of Clear Creek Road, Sally Ann Road, and on State Highway 13 along the South Fork Clearwater River halfway between Stites and Harpster. Plugged culverts were common.

A spotter saw at least three decidous trees that were knocked down along US-12 east of Kooskia. One tree came down onto a trailer at the River Junction RV Park. Two sheds at the park were blown over by the wind gusts. The spotter heard reports of trees down across US-12, farther up the Lochsa River. A large Ponderosa pine tree was uprooted and fell damaging a fence at a baseball field in East Kooskia. Idaho County Light and Power reported one tree was broken off 30 feet above the ground and they lost a power pole up the Selway River after trees began uprooting and falling over. High winds blew down a rotten tree that took out a section of corrugated roofing of the Glenwood Schoolhouse which was 108 years old. The Syringa RAWS at 3377 feet reported a wind gust of 42 mph that occurred between 1152 and 1252 pm PDT. Grangeville airport reported 47 mph wind gust at 1235 pm PDT.
The public reported hail covering the ground southwest of Hall. Golf ball sized hail was the largest stone observed.
Half dollar sized hail was reported by the public at the Deer Lodge Golf Club a few miles west of Deer Lodge.

Pierce set a record high of 101 on August 9th and an all-time record high of 105 on August 10th.  The two day mean maximum temperature of 103 at Pierce was the hottest on record with observations going back to 1963.  Elk River reached a high of 98 on the 9th and then set a record high of 102 on August 10th. Even though RAWS sites have displayed a warm bias, the Dent RAWS in close proximity to the Dworswak Reservoir reached 106 on the 9th and 105 on August 10th.

Cottonwood set record highs of 103 on the 10th and 99 on the 9th. The two day mean maximum temperature of 102 is the hottest two day stretch since observations began in 1976. Grangeville reached 104 on the 10th and 99 on the 9th. Kamiah just inside Spokane's County Warning Area recorded the second hottest two day mean maximum temperature stretch with 109.5. Kamiah set record highs of 109 on the 9th and 110 on the 10th.

events.cz_name: LOWER HELLS CANYON / SALMON RIVER REGION
events.event_narrative: The Pittsburg RAWS reached 116 on the 9th and 119 on the 10th.  RAWS have a well documented warm bias, so these temperatures are difficult to compare to other observations. Nevertheless, in this notoriously hot location, 119 appears to be the warmest in its period of record going back to 1993.  Furthermore, the Slate Creek RAWS reached 113 on the 9th and 114 on the 10th. Finally, Riggins reached 109 on the 10th, one degree shy of the record high of 110, with observations going back to 1896.

Thompson Falls tied an all-time record high of 107 on the 10th and reached 106 on the 9th. The highest two day mean high temperature ever for Thompson Falls occurred on the 9th and the 10th with observations going back to 1956. Superior reached a record high of 105 on the 9th and 107 on the 10th, ranking as the third hottest two day maximum mean temperature stretch with observations going back to 1914.  Heron also set a record high of 102 on the 10th. Even though near-record to record high temperatures were observed on the 9th and 10th, overnight temperatures dropped in the mid to upper 50s at night.

The Libby Dam recorded an all-time high temperature of 108 on the 10th with observations going back to 1986. In addition, a mean two day maximum temperature of 104.5 on the 9th and 10th was the hottest on record. Eureka set all-time record highs of 106 on the 9th and 10th.  The maximum two day mean of 106 is 1.5 degrees warmer than the next hottest two day stretch with observations going back to 1960. Troy also set a record high of 106 on the 10th. Even though record or near record highs were observed on the 9th and 10th, overnight lows still dropped into the mid 50s to low 60s.

West Glacier set an all-time record high of 100 on the August 10th. The two day mean high of 99.5 on the 9th and 10th was the hottest on record going back to 1948. Hungry Horse Dam also set a record high on the 10th of 102. Swan Lake reached 99 on the 9th and set an all-time record high of 106 on the 10th. This two day stretch tied the all-time hottest two day mean maximum temperature stretch with observations going back to 1963. Even with near record to record high temperatures lows were able to drop into the low 50s to upper 50s.

Kalispell reached a record high of 100 on August 10th. Creston also record a record high of 98 on August 10th. The Hot Springs RAWS reached 107 and the Jette RAWS reached 103 on the 10th; however, RAWS sites tend to display a warm bias.  Low temperatures dropped into the low to mid 50s on the morning of the 10th.

Missoula reached a record high of 104 on the 10th. Hamilton and Stevensville recorded near record highs of 97 on the 10th. Even with record to near record highs on the 10th, overnight lows on the 9th and 10th dropped in the low to mid 50s.

Seeley Lake reached a record high of 98 on the 10th and tied a record high of 95 on the 9th. Potomac also set a record high of 100 on the 10th. Low temperatures on the 10th dropped into the low to mid 40s.

Between 6 and 8 inches of snow fell at Marias Pass on US-2 and road crews reported a changeover from snow to rain at about 7 miles west of the pass. Conditions were raw and hazardous in the back-country due to the snowfall.

Light snow of 1 to 2 inches fell during the early morning hours, then melted on roadways.  Gusty winds to 37 mph at KGPI and below freezing temperatures caused wet roads to ice over with numerous traffic accidents reported especially in the city of Kalispell during this early season event.

Heavy showers brought 1 to 3 inches of snow along the Interstate 90 corridor throughout the afternoon hours. Snow partially melted and packed on to the roadway as ice when temperatures dropped into the teens behind a cold front.  The presence of abundant ice and reduced visibility led to numerous traffic accidents.
Supercooled water droplets from fog stuck to freezing surfaces causing black ice on sidewalks and roadways resulting in multiple accidents.
Supercooled water droplets stuck to freezing surfaces causing black ice on sidewalks and roadways resulting in multiple accidents.
Supercooled water droplets stuck to freezing surfaces causing black ice on sidewalks and roadways resulting in multiple accidents.
Periods of heavy, wet snow totaling 6 to 12 inches impacted the Interstate 90 corridor leading to slick roads and travel restrictions on Lookout Pass.

Heavy, wet snow ranging from 3 to 10 inches fell during the morning hours with rates of up to 2 inches per hour. Travel was significantly impacted with minor power outages and a few tree branches pulled down.
Periods of moderate to heavy snow totaling 8 to 12 inches fell during the overnight and morning hours. The main impact was slick roads with travel restrictions on Lolo Pass.

Periods of heavy, wet snow fell during the morning hours leading to difficult travel especially along the Interstate 90 corridor.  Snowfall amounts of 4 to 8 inches were common with rates of 1 to 2 inches per hour for a period of time.
Difficult travel occurred as heavy, wet snow fell during the morning hours. Snowfall amounts of 6 to 10 inches were common with rates up to 1 inch per hour.
A period of heavy snow lead to difficult travel during the morning hours. Snowfall of 4 to 8 inches were commonly observed by the public.
A period of heavy snow lead to difficult travel during the morning hours. Snowfall of 5 to 10 inches were commonly observed by the public.

The area that saw the most ice accretion was along Interstate 90 east of Lookout Pass towards St. Regis where the Montana Department of Transportation listed severe driving conditions and a local weather station measured 0.15 inches of melted precipitation. Impacts include a jack-knifed tractor trailer west of Saint Regis and the St. Regis schools closed because of the icy conditions.
Seven to eight inches of new snowfall accumulations were received along the U.S. Highway 93 route between Saint Ignatius and Arlee during this period.

Trained weather spotters in Pierce and Headquarters reported 12 and 6 inches of new snow respectively over a 12 hour period. In addition, nearby automated weather stations reported wind gusts between 21 and 29 mph.

Weather observers at the Powell Ranger Station and at Lolo Pass reported 7.5 and 10 inches of new snowfall accumulations respectively. In addition, the Lodgepole and Southfork weather stations reported wind gusts to 21 and 29 mph respectively.

Automated weather stations reported between 10 and 12 inches of new snow at Lookout Pass, Noxon, and Evaro. In addition, wind gusts along the Interstate 90 Corridor near Lookout Pass gusted between 23 and 37 mph.

The Montana Department of Transportation reported between 8 and 12 inches of new snow along the Montana Highway 83 Corridor between Clearwater Junction and Condon. Poor visibility from blowing and drifting snow was also reported.

A COOP Observer in Headquarters reported 10 inches of new snow. A weather spotter 10 miles north of Orofino reported 7 inches of snow over a 3 hour period. Another weather spotter 6 miles north of Pierce reported 8 inches of new snow.
COOP observers in Pierce and Headquarters reported between 6.6 and 9.4 inches of new snow respectively.
Automated weather stations at Rexford and Fortine reported 8 and 5.5 inches of new snow respectively. Hawkins Lake received 12 inches of snow.
Weather spotters in the area reported the following new snowfall amounts: 20 miles south of Polebridge, 12 inches, West Glacier 8.5 inches, and Coram 6.5 inches.

A little bit before 4 am MDT, five semi-tractor trailers and one SUV crashed into each other at the bridge near the Quartz Flat Campground on Interstate 90 due to icy road conditions. As a result, two men in their 30s passed away while three other men were injured. The road conditions were labeled as very icy. The guardrails were damaged so much that the Montana Department of Transportation had to close the eastbound lanes for 20 hours after the incident.

A ten hour period of heavy snow brought 12 inches of snow to Marias Pass on US-2. The Montana Department of Transportation hoisted severe driving conditions between 630 and 9 pm in the evening due to zero visibility from blowing and falling snow. Northeast winds gusting between 20 and 30 mph created blowing and drifting snow during this event.

Trained weather spotters near Elliston reported 6 inches of new snow over a 12 hour period. The Discovery Ski Area near Georgetown Lake reported 7 inches of new snow. In addition, several automated weather stations reported wind gusts between 20 and 37 mph.

Heavy snowfall, with accumulations of two to three feet was observed at Lookout Pass. Driving restrictions were enforced the afternoon of the 11th and severe driving conditions were declared during the early morning hours of the 12th between Lookout Pass and Taft on I-90.
A period of heavy snowfall Tuesday evening through Wednesday morning led to snowfall accumulations of up to 14 inches over Lolo Pass and up to 11 inches near Lost Trail Pass.
A period of heavy snowfall led to 12 inches of snow in Pierce and generally 7 to 14 inches elsewhere. Areas of blowing snow were also an issue on Highway 11 near Greer Grade.
A period of heavy snowfall created impacts to travel over Lolo Pass on Highway 12, with up to 14 inches of snowfall being reported.

A period of light freezing rain took place the evening of the 29th ahead of an arctic cold front. The arctic front pushed across the Continental Divide December 30th and a period of heavy snowfall and blowing snow lead to significant reductions in visibility down to a few hundred feet between Essex and Marias Pass. Snowfall between Essex and Marias Pass ranged anywhere from one to two feet along US-2.

Heavy snowfall impacted travel on the I-90 corridor and travel restrictions were enforced over Lookout Pass. Periods of heavy snowfall during the morning of December 30th produced gusty winds and visibility less than a quarter mile.

Snow created tough driving conditions in the Flathead Valley which contributed to dozens of accidents. Winds were gusting over 20 mph towards Columbia Falls which created blowing snow and reductions to visibility. Snow amounts ranged from around an inch in Columbia Falls and Flathead Lake to 1.5 inches near Kalispell.
Widespread snowfall totals between 5 to 10 inches fell overnight into the morning of the 23rd.

Heavy snow ranging from 4 inches near Ronan to up to 13 inches on Swan River Road near Bigfork caused tough travel in both the Flathead and Mission Valleys. Multiple school closures from Whitefish to Bigfork occurred due to the snow.
Widespread 7 to 9 inches of snow was reported from Interstate 90 near Lookout Pass to Highway 200 towards Heron.

Before the bitterly cold arctic winds and snow began, temperatures rose into the 40s and 50s.  The arctic air rushed westward causing temperatures to drop and moisture to freeze on roadways, particularly impacting US-93. The strong winds caused blowing and drifting snow especially north of Whitefish on US-93 on the 3rd. Snow amounts ranged from 3 inches in Libby up to 8 inches along Highway 56 near Bull Lake.

The event started out with freezing rain along US-2 between West Glacier and Marias Pass Saturday night. Strong winds, estimated to 50 mph by an NWS employee vacationing near Essex, ushered in sub-zero temperatures and wind chills between 20 and 40 below zero.  A local ski resort had to close three of their chairs and cancel an outdoor event because of the high winds and cold. This region saw anywhere from 1 to 4 inches of snowfall on top of the freezing rain.

Similar to other areas, freezing rain caused slick travel in the Flathead and Mission Valleys overnight  before the arctic cold front blasted through the area. Winds with the front peaked at 54 mph at the Glacier Park International airport. Besides temperatures  falling into the teens, the strong winds contributed to multiple downed large trees, and severe blowing and drifting snow.  The drifting prompted the Flathead County Sheriff to close Hodgson Road later Sunday. Six foot snow drifts were reported outside of Ronan in the Mud Lake area.  Many schools from Polson to Arlee were preemptively delayed or closed for Monday classes.

Precipitation began as freezing rain ahead of cold arctic winds and heavy snow. Easterly winds gusted to 50 mph at Thompson Falls as temperatures plummeted turning roads to ice. High winds also led to a few downed trees and brief power outages. Heavy snowfall of 6 to 12 inches accumulated by the end of the event.

Light freezing rain proceeded the blast of arctic air and accompanying snowfall.  Winds gusting from 40 to 50 mph were common in the Missoula Valley, accompanied by moderate to heavy snowfall. General snowfall amounts were 2 to 5 inches with higher amounts to 7 inches in the southern Bitterroot Valley. Minor power outages also occurred because of the high winds.

During the height of the winter storm, winds gusted to 50 mph in the Missoula Valley, particularly in East Missoula, with visibilities of less than a quarter mile due to snow and blowing snow.  Minor power outages occurred and a few signs were damaged around Missoula. Travel was also severely impacted with numerous accidents.

Roads froze up with ice as freezing rain proceeded arctic air and snowfall. Although snowfall amounts only ranged from 3 to 7 inches, the icy road conditions followed by snowfall made for treacherous travel over the mountain passes.

Easterly winds came over the Divide ushering in sub-zero temperatures and wind chills between 25 and 40 below zero. The highest wind gust observed was 63 miles per hour at Helmville.  This combined with falling and blowing snow to produce visibilities below a quarter mile at times and treacherous travel conditions. General snowfall across the region ranged between 4 to 8 inches.

Icy conditions were common on area roads as freezing rain proceeded an arctic blast. Once gusty winds arrived, falling and blowing snow combined to produce near zero visibility at times on Interstate 90, making travel nearly impossible.  Snowfall amounts of up to 12 inches were observed.

Sub-zero temperatures and 10 to 20 mph winds combined to produce wind chill values of -30 to -40 for lower elevations on US Highway 2. Extreme values to -63 were observed at the Snow Slip observing site, located near 7000 feet.

Sub-zero temperatures and 10 to 20 mph winds combined to produce wind chill values of -25 to -35 for lower elevations. Extreme values to -49 were observed at the MacDonald Pass observing site, located near 6300 feet.

During the height of the winter storm, wind gusts of 30 to 40 mph with visibilities near zero occurred due to snow and blowing snow.  According to the Montana Department of Transportation travel was severely impacted especially on Interstate 90.
Snowfall of 4 to 8 inches was common, while up to 12 inches was reported at Cardiff Spur. This snowfall led to difficult travel at times along with school closures.
Snowfall of 4 to 8 inches was typical including 6 inches in Orofino and Grangeville. This snowfall led to difficult travel at times along with school delays and closures.

Widespread snow and high winds brought severe driving conditions and significant drifting of snow. Snowfall amounts of 4 to 8 inches were common with wind gusts of 40 to 50 miles per hour with Glacier Park International Airport peaking at 51 miles per hour late Friday evening. Considerable drifting of snow led to several stranded vehicles and to the closure of some west to east roads in the Flathead Valley, especially the north end of the valley.

High winds and widespread snow brought significant drifting of snow and severe driving conditions. Snowfall amounts of 4 to 8 inches were common with wind gusts of 20 to 30 miles per hour. Considerable drifting of snow caused great difficulty for snow plows working on U.S. Highway 2.

Sub-zero temperatures combined with winds of 10 to 20 miles per hour brought wind chills of 30 to 40 degrees below zero in the lower elevations along US-2.  The coldest lower elevation wind chill was 39 below zero at Essex on the morning of the 10th with 64 below zero at Snow Slip located near 7000 feet.

Winds of 10 to 20 miles per hour combined with sub-zero temperatures brought wind chills of 25 to 35 degrees below zero. The coldest wind chill was 53 below zero on the morning of the 9th at MacDonald Pass located near 6300 feet.
Heavy snowfall with rates of 2 inches per hour were common. Two to three feet of snowfall was observed in Libby and Troy and school delays and closures were reported for February 13th.
Heavy snow impacted travel over Marias Pass on Highway 2, with two feet of snowfall being reported. Isolated areas of blowing snow also led to significantly reduced visibility at times.

A prolonged period of heavy snowfall was observed from the evening of the 11th through the afternoon of the 13th. Lookout Pass Ski Resort reported 28 inches of snowfall in a 24 hour period on the morning of the 13th. 39 inches of snowfall was reported in Heron. School delays and closures also were in affect for the 13th.

Heavy snowfall led to multiple avalanches on I-90 near Lookout Pass. Westbound lanes of I-90 were closed at St. Regis through the morning of the 14th as crews cleared several feet of snow off the roadway. A passenger vehicle was partially buried by the avalanche and the driver had to be rescued.
A prolonged period of moderate to heavy snowfall impacted travel on Highway 12 over Lolo Pass were close to 2 feet of snowfall was observed.

A combination of snow and blowing snow brought significant travel impacts across the Camas Prairie. The Idaho Department of Transportation urged travelers to only travel if absolutely necessary on Highway 95 due to impacts from snow and blowing snow. Multiple accidents, including a jackknifed semi truck were reported during the morning of the 12.
Heavy snowfall led to delays and closures of schools on February 20th with 6 to 8 inches of snow being observed in the towns of Orofino, Greer, and Kooskia.

events.cz_name: LOWER HELLS CANYON / SALMON RIVER REGION
events.event_narrative: A period of moderate to heavy snowfall caused travel impacts on US 95 from Grangeville to Riggins. 5 to 6 inches of snow fell on Whitebird Hill and 4 inches of snow was reported in Riggins.

During the afternoon and evening of the 25th, wind gusts over 40 mph and visibility reduced to less than a quarter of a mile in downtown and east Missoula were observed. Significant travel impacts were reported in the city of Missoula, and Missoula County asked citizens to only travel if absolutely necessary. Flights out of Missoula were also canceled or delayed.

A period of intense snowfall during the evening hours of the 25th led to significant accumulations and travel impacts. Chains became required over Evaro Hill on US 95 where  24 inches of snow fell. Heavy snow and blowing snow was observed from Clinton to Ninemile, causing impacts to travel on I-90. 11 inches of snow was observed in Alberton and 8 inches was reported in Huson.

Prolonged snowfall and blustery northerly winds caused significant impacts to the Bitterroot and Missoula Valleys. Widespread accumulations of up to two feet of snowfall was observed in the Bitterroot valley. The City of Hamilton declared a snow emergency February 25, urging drivers to stay off roadways until conditions improve. Areas of snow and blowing snow in the southern part of the Missoula valley and northern sections of the Bitterroot valley led to a period of severe driving conditions and numerous accidents were reported. Many schools in the Bitterroot valley were closed for Tuesday, including Stevensville, Hamilton, and Florence.
Heavy prolonged snowfall impacted travel over Lolo and Lost Trail passes where one to two feet of snowfall was observed.

Heavy snow and blowing snow caused hazardous driving conditions along portions of I-90 and Montana 200 and 83. 17 inches of snow was reported in Potomac, 11 inches in Clinton, and 10 inches in Seeley Lake.

Heavy snowfall and blowing snow led to areas of severe driving conditions and closure of schools, including Butte and Anaconda. According to Butte school district officials, the school closed on February 16 for the first time since 1989. Widespread areas of 9 to 13 inches of snow was observed in Silver Bow county. Up to 30 inches of snow was reported in Anaconda! Numerous accidents were reported on stretches of I-90 near Anaconda and Butte.
A prolonged period of snowfall led to significant accumulations with 18 inches being reported in Lowell, 10 inches in Dixie, and 10 inches near Harpster.

A lengthy period of heavy snowfall brought travel impacts to lower elevations of north central Idaho. 22 inches of snow was observed in Grangeville and schools were closed for Monday and Tuesday, February 25 and 26. In addition, Kamiah saw 7 inches.

events.cz_name: LOWER HELLS CANYON / SALMON RIVER REGION
events.event_narrative: Heavy snowfall impacted travel along US 95 with chains being recommended for all travelers. 6 inches of snow was reported in Riggins.
Heavy snowfall impacted travel over Williams Creek Summit, where 13 inches of snowfall was reported.

Public reported sighting of land spout to news media at around 600 PM MDT. Pictures were taken by three different residents in the area confirming location of land spout touch down between 3 Mile Drive and 4 Mile Drive near Kalispell. A possible secondary funnel occurred farther to the northwest. The Land Spout started from a cumulus cloud around 545 PM, touched down at 550 PM and then dissipated shortly after 600 PM MDT. No damage was reported.

The South Fork of the Clearwater River at Stites, crested at a record level of 10.79 feet on the morning of April 9. This led to flooding of 3 to 5 homes along the west side of the river along North River Road.  A torrent of fast-moving water developed in an unnamed gulch located east of Stites along Stites Grade Road and this led to the closure of Idaho Highway 13 and the flooding of Stites. Approximately 30 to 50 homes were affected by the flooding in the town of Stites with many wells contaminated and the National Guard rescued two people who were trapped in their home. Very large mud-slides caused US-12 to close between Orofino and Kamiah from April 9 to April 13. A home in Syringa was flooded by a debris flow and US-12 between Kooskia and Syringa experienced erosion and water running on the road leading to the closure of Highway 12. Clear Creek, located approximately 2 miles southeast of Kooskia, washed out two private bridges, flooded approximately 5 homes, destroyed a trailer home, and damaged county road Clear Creek Road. The Nez Perce U.S. Forest Service closed Smith Creek Road due to flooding of the Little Smith Creek causing a washout. Numerous other bridges, culverts and roads were washed out across Idaho County.

Because of sub-zero ambient temperatures and wind chill temperatures, Blacktail Ski Resort closed on March 2. Snow amounts ranged from 2 inches in Eureka to 5.3 inches in Marion. The Boorman RAWS weather sensor near Marion saw wind gusts between 20 and 30 mph at times Friday evening March 1 through early morning Saturday which caused blowing and drifting snow with low visibility along US-2.

Severe driving conditions were reported for MT-83 between Condon and Ferndale due to blowing and drifting snow. While only a trace of snow feel between West Glacier and Marias Pass, bitterly cold temperatures followed the arctic cold front passage in those areas. Other snow amounts ranged from 4.5 inches near Swan Lake to 8 inches at the Hungry Horse Dam.

Emergency Travel Only, was issued for Lake County due to blowing and drifting snow with low visibility. Numerous accidents and slide-offs caused tow service to be backed up as much as three hours during the event in the Flathead Valley. While new snowfall ranged from two to four inches with up to 5.8 inches in Whitefish, the main cause of the high impact was more due to the combination of existing one to two feet of snow on the ground with strong winds sustained between 20 and 33 mph with gusts over 40 mph. The GPI airport recorded a peak wind speed of 43 mph at 7:41 pm on March 1.

Though minimal new snowfall amounts only ranged from a trace up to 1 inch, pre-existing transportable snow on the ground combined with strong wind gusts in constricted areas such as eastern Thompson Falls, generated blowing and drifting snow for a period. The Thompson Falls airport had a peak wind of 42 mph around midnight March 2.

Poor visibility due to heavy snow bands was followed by blowing and drifting snow caused by strong arctic easterly winds. At 9 pm, a MEANS alert was issued by the Missoula County sheriff's office to tell the public about poor driving conditions. Around midnight, Severe Driving was declared by the Montana Department of Transportation between Lolo and Missoula due to poor visibility from blowing snow and drifting on US-93. Snow drifts, approximately several feet in depth, were reported from the Rattlesnake, Missoula and Lolo locations. While new snowfall amounts between a half an inch at the Missoula Airport up to 5 inches in Lolo were observed, the antecedent transportable snow on the ground contributed to most of the low visibility and heavy drifting during this event. By the evening of March 2, wind chill temperatures ranged between 10 and 20 below zero.
A NWS employee located in Lolo reported 5 inches of snow that fell in only 3 hours under the snow band that also affected Highway 12 west to Lolo Pass.

Around 9 pm on March 1, the Missoula County sheriff department issued a MEANS 911 alert for Emergency Travel Only from Interstate 90 at Hellgate Canyon to Revenna just west of Bearmouth. They stated that there were multiple accidents due to white-out conditions. Between 20 to 30 inches of snow were already on the ground before the strong arctic winds pushed through causing the blowing and drifting snow.

Severe driving conditions were reported in two separate areas, along Highway 141 between Helmville and Highway 200, and on Interstate 90 between Phospate and Deer Lodge due to slick roads and poor visibility from blowing and drifting snow.

A Montana Department of Transportation weather sensor in Essex reported air temperatures of 10 to 20 below zero with sustained winds of 10 to 20 mph which produced wind chill values between 30 and 48 degrees below zero.
Wind chill values between 20 and 28 below zero were reported by the Glacier Park International Airport ASOS during this event.
Bitterly cold wind chill temperatures between 25 and 30 below zero were measured at Garrison Junction and Elliston and as cold as 40 below zero at both MacDonald Pass and Anaconda.

The USFS Eureka Ranger Station COOP recorded 23 below zero which made it the coldest temperature there since 1961. An unofficial temperature of 40 below was reported in Marion and 34 below at MacGregor Lake. The Yaak COOP reported 30 below zero.

The Polebridge RAWS and the Marias Pass HADS sensor both recorded a low temperature of 38 below zero. The Seeley Swan high school had a two hour delay and the Special Olympics at the Big Mountain Resort delayed an event due to the extreme temperatures.

Air temperatures ranged from near 20 below in St. Ignatius and Kalispell to an unofficial 40 below zero in Lone Pine. A rancher in Lone Pine lost two calves due to the cold. While Ronan school buses were delayed, the Charlo buses did not run because of the extreme cold.
A pair of Frenchtown school buses filled with students, became disabled due to temperatures in the teens below zero.
Air temperatures ranged from 22 below in Maxville to 30 below in Butte and the coldest spot reported by 34 below in Georgetown Lake.
A low of 28 degrees was recorded in Grangeville which is right at the threshold for compromising potential blossom drop in some fruit trees.

events.cz_name: LOWER HELLS CANYON / SALMON RIVER REGION
events.event_narrative: A low of 29 degrees was recorded just south of Riggins which is near the threshold for compromising potential blossom drop in some fruit trees.
The Potomac COOP recorded 37 below zero. A temperature of 30 below was reported at both the Seeley Lake RAWS and Clearwater Junction RAWS with an unofficial temperature of 32 below near Condon.

Flooding was observed in the Orchard Homes area of Missoula as the Clark Fork River rose above minor flood stage beginning midday on the 14th. The Clark Fork River's flow peaked at 9.15 feet late on the 18th, and finally fell below flood stage late on the 21st with residential flooding coming to an end.  Observed impacts included flooding on the north end of Tower Street and on Kehrwald Drive with some water into basements of adjacent homes.

High winds from a thunderstorm along with wet soil conditions lead to considerable uprooted trees in East Kamiah.  The greatest damage occurred along a two mile stretch of US-12 from Rock Road to the Kamiah Bridge. Trees fell across US-12 resulting in traffic disruption, in addition one residential trailer and one travel trailer were also damaged by falling trees.

Strong winds were observed during the evening of the 6th in Salmon as well as in the neighboring foothills west and south of town. The peak gust of 59 mph was measured by a trained spotter just west of downtown Salmon with other sites measuring wind gust to 50 mph.  Several large trees and branches came down, damaging vehicles and blocking local roads briefly. Power outages were also noted.
Hail stones from penny to nickle size still on the ground a day after the thunderstorm passed through. Minor damage to tree leaves and plants also noted.
Hail drifted up to two feet deep off of roofs with some minor vegetation damage.
Nickel to quarter-sized hail was reported in the town of Harpster, Idaho.
Quarter to ping-pong-sized hail was reported in Hamilton. Quarter-sized hail was also reported in Corvallis.
