A severe thunderstorm moved over southern portions of Grangeville, Idaho and areas along U.S. Highway 95 southwest of the city. Large amounts of hail created hazardous driving conditions, causing a vehicle to slide off the highway. Ping-pong-sized hail was reported along the highway, 5 miles southwest of Grangeville, with nickel-sized hail being reported in the city itself.
A line of decaying thunderstorms produced a 65 mph wind gust at MacDonald Pass.
A line of thunderstorms produced 40 to 55 mph winds in Deerlodge with minor tree damage reported. Further south, a 67 mph wind gust was recorded north of Racetrack.
A thunderstorm produced nickel to quarter-sized hail in the town of Bonner during the afternoon of the 13th.
Penny to half-dollar-sized hail was reported in the town Seeley Lake. Half-dollar-sized hail was reported by a boater on Seeley Lake.
A severe thunderstorm dropped hail up to two inches in diameter on a small rural community in the Rock Creek drainage.
Quarter-size hail was reported in the rural community of Quigley, Montana.
A thunderstorm produced half-dollar-sized hail in Ovando, with a truck sustaining hail dents on the roof of the vehicle.
A strong thunderstorm dropped ping-pong-sized hail over the town of Helmville, Montana during the afternoon of July 14th.
A strong thunderstorm produced quarter-sized hail a few miles south of Butte, Montana during the early evening hours of July 30th.
Ping-pong-sized hail was reported in Victor as a thunderstorm moved off the Bitterroot divide and into the valley.
Quarter-size hail was reported in Dewey, Montana during the evening hours of July 16th.
The Spot Mountain Lookout in the Bitterroot National Forest reported quarter-size hail during the morning hours of July 3rd, as a line of thunderstorms moved through the area.
The Bert Mooney Airport ASOS reported a peak wind gust of 62 mph.
Mostly egg-sized hail with up to baseballs fell between Slate Creek and Riggins, Idaho and damaged greenhouse roofs, fences, pump house tanks, PVC pipelines, windshields, vehicles and orchards.

A severe thunderstorm put down an inch and a half of rain in 30 minutes over the canyons near Lucile. This caused large debris flows in Fiddle Creek, Sheep Creek and Chair Creek that covered US-95 with up to a 4 feet deep of mud. More than a dozen vehicles became stuck in the mud. The highway was closed until the next day when one lane was opened up. The highway opened up totally by Monday, three days later. The flooding also damaged Cow Creek Road and John Day Road.
A debris flow occurred above the Hot Springs ranch road south of the Tower Creek area. The Idaho Department of Transportation cleaned it up with a grader.
A local business near the 4th of July Creek estimated the hail that fell to be the size of quarters.
One spotter measured quarter-sized hail while another estimated the largest hailstones to be up to tennis ball size.
Hail size was estimated to be the size of quarters.
A business reported a very tall ponderosa pine tree snapped in half in their yard and they heard of several other trees down in the area. The hail was mostly dime-sized.
Besides the golf ball-sized hail, the storm produced torrential rain which caused motorists to pull off to the side of Interstate 90.
The spotter measured one inch hail in Butte.
Two different reports of golf ball-sized hail in the St. Regis area.
Estimated winds to 60 mph caused waves to 4 feet on Flathead Lake and power outages in the Dayton area.

Multiple thunderstorms collided together just south of Flathead Lake and produced a severe gust front that tracked north to the Flathead Valley. Multiple observers reported that the strong winds lasted for up to 15 minutes. Dozens of toppled trees, damaged power poles, transmission and distribution lines were reported from Bigfork up to Columbia Falls from strong winds. Power outages lasted for 24 hours. The golf course in Bigfork reported losing 59 trees, mostly spruce from 20 to 30 feet tall with diameters between 18 inches and 2.5 feet. The restaurant at the golf course lost all their food due to the power outage.

General rainfall of 1 to 2 inches fell across parts of the Flathead and Mission valleys eastward to the Continental Divide. Heavier amounts of 3 to 4 inches fell locally on the east side of Flathead Lake and in the Mission Mountains, which were near record 2-day totals for the month of September. Also, minor debris flows were noted on Hwy 35 between Bigfork and Polson with some water into the Bigfork after-school building.

Numerous trees fell on power lines resulting in power outages, especially during the predawn hours. Damage was concentrated on the east side of Highway 93, particularly the Eureka neighborhoods of Glen Lake, Indian Creek Road, Graves Creek Road, and Burma Road. Also, tree and power line damage occurred in Stryker and Star Meadows. In addition, cell phone service was unavailable for all of Lincoln County Saturday afternoon and evening because of wind damage to cell towers.

Wind damage to tree and power lines was concentrated in and around Lake Blaine, Swan Lake, and the eastern shore of Flathead Lake. The strongest wind gust were estimated near 60 mph in these areas. Power outages began early Saturday and lasted into Sunday evening for some with thousands of customers impacted. Thirty trees and five power lines were reported down across Highway 35 which resulted in the road being closed to only local traffic. A conservative estimate of a couple hundred downed trees occurred in populated areas. On the west side of Flathead Lake, significant boat and dock damage occurred as waves reached over 6 feet. At the Dayton Yacht Harbor, 2 sailboats sank due to damage sustained from impacting a dock with another 5 boats destroyed. In addition, another dozen boats were damaged at the Somers Bay Marina.  Only intermittent cell phone service was available in Flathead and Lake counties due to cell phone towers damaged by falling trees.
General snow amounts of 4 to 8 inches fell above 4000 feet with some locations above 6000 feet, experiencing over 12 inches of snow. Difficult travel was experienced by the backcountry users.

General snow amounts of 4 to 9 inches fell above 4000 feet with some locations above 6000 feet, recording over 12 inches of snow. Also, wind gusts to 40 mph were observed on the higher terrain. Difficult travel was experienced by backcountry users with periodic slippery, snow-covered, primary roads such as Highway 12 at Lolo Pass.

Snow amounts of 4 to 8 inches were observed above 4000 feet with some locations above 7000 feet, recording over 12 inches of snow. Also, wind gusts to 30 mph were observed on the higher terrain. Backcountry users experienced difficult travel.

Snow amounts of 4 to 8 inches were observed above 4000 feet with some locations above 7000 feet, reporting over 12 inches of snow. Also, wind gusts to 35 mph were observed on the higher terrain. Backcountry users experienced difficult travel with periodic slippery, snow-covered, primary roads such as Highway 93 at Lost Trail Pass.

Snow amounts of 2 to 4 inches fell in the valleys with 5 to 10 inches in the higher elevations, local amounts to 20 inches were observed at the Hawkins Lake SNOTEL. Also, wind gusts to 35 mph were reported in the higher terrain, locally over 50 mph at the western base of the Whitefish Range. Backcountry users experienced difficult travel.

Heavy snowfall was focused near the Continental Divide with 2 to 3 feet common.  Social media videos from near Marias Pass indicated up to 4 feet of snow fell along with drifting snow as winds gusted to 40 mph.  Further west in the Whitefish Range, general snowfall was 4 to 8 inches with wind gust to 50 mph at Big Mountain. Periods of hazardous travel were common on Highway 2, especially near Marias Pass due to the combination of snow, wind, and low visibility.

Snow amounts of 1 to 3 inches fell in the valleys with 5 to 10 inches in the higher elevations. Also, wind gusts to 40 mph were reported in Thompson Falls and on some of the higher terrain. Difficult travel was experienced by backcountry users with periodic slippery, snow-covered, primary roads such as Interstate 90 at Lookout Pass.

General snow amounts of 4 to 8 inches fell, locally up to 12 inches. Also, wind gusts to 35 mph occurred. Difficult travel was experienced by backcountry users with periodic slippery, snow-covered, primary roads such as US-93 at Lost Trail Pass and US-12 at Lolo Pass.

Snow accumulations ranged from 6 to 10 inches leading to difficult backcountry travel and occasional slick, snow-packed, primary roadways. Strong winds brought down numerous trees on local trails used by outfitters especially around Upper Holland Lake which significantly slowed packing operations.

Periodic snow and gusty winds brought considerable travel impacts due to slick, snow-covered roadways and reduced visibility. Traffic accidents were common on Interstate 90, especially west of Butte on Sunday morning with chains required on Homestake Pass for a time. Snow accumulations of 4 to 10 inches were common which also limited backcountry travel.

Light snowfall of 1 to 2 inches fell in the Missoula and Bitterroot valleys with up to 6 inches on the south side of Hamilton. While impacts were limited, this was an unusually early snowfall for valley locations.

A wind shift from the east, beginning at 8 am the 8th, signaled passage of the frontal boundary. Snow rates of greater than 1 per hour were experienced for 3 to 4 hours. Widespread snow amounts of 3 to 4 were observed, while Marias Pass had an estimated total (from water equivalent measured by HADS site) of 12. The DOT roads report described driving conditions with 'high winds' and a tree down at 8am, on the 9th. A private citizen tweet described driving conditions as limited vis, heavy snow, and tough driving conditions.

Chains were required on both Homestake and MacDonald Passes as early as 9:45 pm mdt (MacDonald Pass). There were snowfall reports of 10 south of Butte, 3-4 at Anaconda, with estimates of 13-14 on Homestake Pass. Winds observed on ASOS up to 30 mph were common. The Eastbound Lane of I-90 was completely blocked by multiple stuck semi-trailers.
There were reports of power outages in the St Regis area, and a reported 640 people were without power in the Alberton area.

Gusts to 40 mph were observed for multiple hours at the Narrows bouy weather station, and gusts to 30 mph were measured at the Yellow Bay Hill weather station. Mission Power reported 13 people without power at 7am on the 9th.

At 5:26 am mdt on the 9th reports of snowfall amounts and hazardous driving prompted issuance of an advisory. Charlo Heights reported 6 of snowfall, while other locations in the southern Bitterrroot reported 2 to 5. Multiple slide-offs were reported in Hamilton  by the emergency manager of a federal facility.
Wind gusts to 43 mph caused whiteout conditions with multiple car slide-offs. Snow in the valley produced generally light amounts, but the USFS office in Leadore did measure 7.

Road conditions rapidly changed as wet roads quickly became snow covered and icy. Car accidents numbered 22 by noon on the 28th according to DOT road reports. An NWS volunteer reported large pine trees down on MT-35, visibilities dropping from 7 miles to a 1/4 with wind, and their car being pushed around on road.
Multiple slide offs (reported by MT DOT) prompted County officials to urge the public to travel only if necessary at 3:30 pm mdt. Highway 271 was closed due to semi-trailers blocking roadway.
Due to numerous road accidents, Granite County Sheriff urged the public to drive only as necessary.

Due to a rapid freeze up of roads, blowing snow, and low visibilities, the Missoula Police Department sent an alert requesting essential driving only.  Approximately an hour later, Missoula County Emergency Management issued a MEANS (Missoula Emergency Activation Notification System) Alert for Emergency Travel Only both directions on Interstate 90 through Missoula County.|An NWS Missoula employee witnessed school buses having difficulty driving without slipping while driving at a speed of less than 5 mph.

A SNOTEL station at Crater Meadows reported 17 of snow. Mountain passes like Lolo and Lookout, received approximately 4 of snow, but due to warm ground conditions,  accumulations melted rapidly. Lost Trail Pass measured around 7 of snow. One car was reported abandoned by Clearwater County dispatch during the storm.

A power company in northwest Montana reported infrastructure damage including a dozen poles along the western foothills of the Whitefish Range between Ksanka Peak and Marston Mountain. They estimated 40 to 60 mph wind gusts brought the fir and pine trees down. They also remarked that the strong winds swirled from the northerly direction, which probably contributed to the tree damage.
A power company reported trees on power lines with 14 separate power outages in the Flathead Valley.
Marias Pass received 4.9 inches of snow during this event. Roads became slick as temperatures fell below freezing.

Rain made roads wet before freezing up when the arctic air moved west across the Continental Divide. Snow on top of this freeze created icy conditions which contributed to several vehicle accidents on Interstate 90. Several snow bands brought white-out conditions from snow and gusty winds which worsened travel and road conditions. Highway 1 between Drummond and Georgetown Lake were also affected by ice, as reported by MDT.

A person from the public sent in a photo of Interstate 90 west of Bearmouth which portrayed icy conditions. They said they saw several roll-overs west of Drummond on their way to Missoula. A news report in the evening reported multiple vehicles in ditches between Turah and Clinton after a passing snow band caused white-out conditions.

There were multiple locations along the western foothills of the Whitefish Range that were impacted by the high winds. At the end of Burma Road, residents estimated at least 5 acres of pine and fir trees were blown down. This caused some roof damage to several homes. A metal roof partially peeled off of a trailer home located due west, across US-93 on Acres Lane. Billboard signs were blown down between Eureka and the Canadian Border. The utility company reported two power poles damaged, and power was out for 20 hours. In the Glen Lake area, five miles east of Eureka, countless trees were strewn all over the roads, especially along Stevens and Therriault roads. At one point, emergency vehicles couldn't immediately get to a person who was on oxygen. A power company reported that they lost 8 span of power line and 8 power poles in the Graves Creek drainage area, where they reported that at least 1500 yards by 500 yards of trees blown down. They were cleaning up the damage for a few weeks after the event. They estimated that 20 log truck loads would come out of there. Multiple trees in the Dickey Lake area also had fallen on power lines. The highway department reported dozens of trees down five miles south of Troy, or between mile-markers 30 and 32 on Highway 56. A tree fell on a utility truck in this area, but no one was hurt.

A thunderstorm moved over the Camas Prairie and the Whitebird Grade, producing accumulating heavy snow. Four inches of heavy wet snow was received in 1 hour and 45 minutes in Grangeville, with a total snow accumulation of 4.6 inches reported by spotters in 3 hours. Very slippery conditions caused vehicles to spin out over the Whitebird Grade, blocking traffic on U.S. Highway 95 between 6 PM to 725 PM, when the highway was temporarily closed. Idaho County Sheriff reported other vehicle slide offs and accidents due to the heavy wet accumulating snow.

A local utility remarked that this was one of the most damaging storms they've ever experienced. The owner of a tree farm, located north of Echo Lake, stated to a local newspaper that he had never seen such damage since 1958. The Echo Lake area was one of the most hard hit: four houses had minor structure damage, one truck and trailer were totaled, and one mobile home had moderate to severe damage. Dozens of trees, mostly pines and firs, some estimated to be 100 feet tall and three feet wide, were reported to have fallen in this area. One resident was sleeping when a tree fell onto his house into his bedroom, but escaped unharmed. Sporadic tree damage and power outages were reported in the Columbia Falls to Lake Blaine areas. There were dozens of fallen large trees, as well as broken power poles and lines, along Highway 83 between Ferndale and Swan Lake. One resident reported at least 10 fallen trees on their property, with one 80 foot tree damaging their garage. Multiple trees, some snapped in half and some uprooted, went down over Highway 35 between mile-markers 19 and 23, causing damage to telephone and power lines. This also caused the highway to be closed for two hours. Several homes were damaged and in one case, a large tree smashed through the roof and lower room of a home, but didn't cause any injuries. Three large trees, up to three feet in diameter, took out a power line on Finley Point.

Moderate snowfall during the evening of December 12th into the morning of December 13th lead to slippery conditions on I-90 over Lookout Pass. Several semi trucks spun out traveling over Lookout Pass, leading to the closure of the interstate at 1132 pm December 12th to approximately 430 am on December 13th. Only 5 inches of snow was reported at Lookout Pass Ski Area. Temperatures were in the low 30s at pass level, and the nearby Mullan Pass ASOS only briefly reported visibility down to 1/2 mile.

Widespread snowfall of 2 to 4 inches was reported across the Kootenai/Cabinet region. Snow transitioned to freezing rain briefly during the early morning hours of December 20th causing pockets of slick conditions due to a light glaze of ice accumulation.

Snowfall quickly transitioned to freezing rain across lower elevation valley areas in the Lower Clark Fork region. A light glaze of ice accumulation caused slippery conditions on Highway 200 and I-90. Five inches of snow accumulated at Lookout Pass causing the Montana Department of Transportation to require chains on towing units over the pass during the evening of the 19th into the morning hours of the 20th.

Heavy snowfall was reported across northern areas of eastern Lemhi County. Salmon was impacted by 8 inches of snowfall while areas along US 93 between Gibbonsville to Lost Trail Pass saw 12 inches. Blowing snow also caused significantly reduced visibility on Idaho Highway 28 between Leadore and Gilmore Summit.

Snow squalls impacted travel on I-90 between Superior and Ninemile with visibility well below 1/4 mile. Travel was significantly impacted over Evaro Hill on US 93. Several accidents caused travel to come to a stand still and lead to chains being required for towing units over Evaro Hill.
A snow squall lead to heavy snow with visibility well below 1/4 of a mile between Frenchtown and Missoula. The rapid change in visibility caused difficult driving conditions and accidents on I-90.

A snow squall caused dangerous driving conditions on I-90 between East Missoula and Clinton. Heavy snow lead to visibility well below 1/4 of a mile. An overturned semi truck was reported near Clinton due to slick roads and poor visibility.
A relatively long lived snow squall caused dangerous driving conditions on US 93 between Missoula and Lolo. Visibility well below 1/4 mile was observed with snowfall rates of two inches per hour.
A snow squall created dangerous travel conditions east of Missoula on I-90.
A snow squall created dangerous travel conditions on I-90 between Bearmouth and Drummond.

Three snowmobilers were involved in an avalanche approximately 1 mile northwest of Lake Dinah, or about 12 miles northwest of Seeley Lake. The riders were caught and carried a short distance; two were fully buried, and one extricated himself after being separated from his snowmobile. The dimensions of the avalanche were 560 feet long, 100 feet wide, and an average of 6 feet deep. The two riders who were fully buried could not be saved, thus two fatalities occurred as a result of the avalanche.

Strong wind gusts to 50 miles per hour in the valleys and to 70 miles per hour on the terrain were observed. Several areas experienced power outages including a stretch of US Highway 2 from West Glacier to Essex, as well as in the town of Hungry Horse, and the south end of Swan Lake.

Snowfall totals of 12 to 18 inches were common on US Highway 2 between West Glacier and Marias Pass. Travel was difficult to impossible at times. Also, several hundred people were without power up to four hours in West Glacier as heavy snow caused power lines to snap.

Hazardous travel due to heavy snow occurred on Interstate 90, leading to multiple semi truck slide offs and lane blockages near Lookout Pass. Peak 24 hour snowfall was 21 inches at Lookout Pass ending the morning of the 7th.

Strong winds and falling snow made for hazardous travel on the Camas Prairie. A peak wind gust of 59 miles per hour was reported at the Grangeville Airport the afternoon of the 6th which resulted in the total loss of a local drive-in movie theater screen. A semi truck and trailer was also blown off US Highway 95 about 5 miles south of Grangeville. The highest snow total reported was 12 inches in Cottonwood.
Snow totals ranged from 12 to 18 inches from Potomac to Seeley Lake. Travel was very difficult at times, especially on the morning of the 7th.
Snowfall amounts of 1 to 2 feet were common on the higher benches with 2 to 3 feet at Cardiff Spur and Pierce.  Periods of hazardous travel occurred.
Although snow amounts were only 2 to 4 inches, strong winds up to 60 miles per hour led to periods of very low visibility.  Travel was very difficult during the critical evening commute hours.

Easterly winds gusting to 35 miles per hour and heavy snow of 10 to 18 inches resulted in periods of severe driving conditions on US Highway 2. In addition, wind chills dropped to -30 degrees at Marias Pass.  Snow bands led to isolated areas receiving nearly 3 feet of snow on North Fork Road between Columbia Falls and Polebridge.

Periods of heavy snow led to severe driving conditions on Interstate 90 from Saint Regis to Lookout Pass. Several public schools were forced to operate on a delayed schedule the morning of the 13th as well.

As a snow squall moved over I-90 east of Missoula, a motorist reported visibility reduced to 200 yards and a NWS employee reported 0.25 to 0.50 mile visibility between Clinton and Bonner. A personal weather station in Clinton recorded temperatures dropping into the 20s which contributed to roads icing up.

A heavy snow band moving south over Evaro Hill on US-93, resulted in low visibility and slick conditions. Montana Highway Patrol alerted drivers to a stuck tractor trailer 2016MST and there were reports of slide-offs near the US-93 and I-90 junction, at 2036MST. A weather spotter at Evaro Hill, reported 3 inches of snow in just 2 hours, between 1830 and 2030MST.

After a snowband moved south and east of Missoula, a NWS employee driving along I-90 near Clinton, reported 0.25 mile visibility and dangerous travel conditions. In response, a snow squall warning was issued and re-issued an additional hour at expiration. Impacts observed were slide-offs at 2030MST and a crash with injury at 2130MST. During the subsequent day, a snow report of 8 inches for the event was tweeted from Clinton, MT and a Bearmouth, MT wind sensor measured winds of 15 to 25 MPH between 2200 and 2225MST.

A snowband that had been steadily moving south began to back-build over south Missoula, encompassing a stretch of Highway 93 called the 's-curves', which are highly susceptible to impacts from snow accumulation. Snowfall totals were variable over short distances near the airport: areas northwest of Missoula received 3.3 inches, while 5 miles south of the airport 9 inches were observed during the 5 hour event. An NWS employee considered their commute to work in the top 10 worst winter commutes they've experienced in the area. Finally, there was a multi-car accident just north of the s-curves on Highway 93, around 0600MST.

Radar measured up to 30 dBZ reflectivity at 20 thousand feet MSL in a band parallel to a cold front over Highway 93 from Lost Trail Pass south to North Fork, ID. After a tweet reported whiteout conditions at the pass, a snow squall warning was issued, which was an upgrade to the previous special weather statement. In addition, Idaho Transportation Department cameras confirmed whiteout conditions at the pass.

As the cold front advanced south, the snow band stayed organized via radar, therefore a snow squall warning was issued for the city of Salmon, ID. A known observer and snow plow operator called in whiteout conditions and reported snowfall accumulations of 2.5 inches. The AWOS at the Lemhi County Airport measured winds changing from SE at 5 kts to NNW 22 kts, gusting to 30 kts in 30 minutes.
The same squall line with the cold front continued to progress southward in Lemhi County. Whiteout conditions were reported along Highway 28.

A line of heavy snow in front of a cold front developed in Anaconda, MT, which moved towards I-90. An AWOS weather station in Anaconda measured a reduction in visibility to less than 0.25 of a mile in 30 minutes along with winds increasing from 13 mph to 25 mph gusting to 43 mph. Also there was reported whiteout conditions.

Radar observed returns of 50 dBZ and a good KDP signature in a snow squall out in front of a cold front. A Montana Department of Transportation road sensor located at MacDonald Pass, reported winds of 40 mph gusting to 57 mph, while whiteout conditions were observed via their webcam. Additionally, thundersnow was reported just to the west in Elliston, MT.

Taking into account previous snow squall reports, as the front advanced eastward towards Butte, MT., a snow squall warning was issued for a radar reflectivity of 30 to 35 dBZ with impressive KDP. The ASOS at the Bert Mooney Airport, south of Butte, reported heavy snow and winds 24 mph gusting to 49 mph. The visibility sensor at the airport was not working at that time. The Montana Department of Transportation hoisted severe driving conditions at Homestake Pass during this event.

Winds gusted as high as 60 mph in Hungry Horse and up to 62 mph at Marias Pass. High winds caused downed trees on US-2 between West Glacier and Marias Pass, but particularly at Nyack or at mile-marker 164. The winds also damaged power lines and transmission lines, causing power outages for approximately 9 hours. A tree fell onto a cabin 7 miles west of Marias Pass. A local ski resort, Whitefish Mountain Resort, had to close two chair lifts and a T-bar due to high winds. A rock slide occurred at mile-marker 154 on US-2 and MDT remarked that they had to remove 6 loader buckets of large boulders.

While wind gusts between 40 and 50 mph were common, gusts near 60 occurred near Hot Springs. Downed power lines were reported by MDT, 4 miles south of Lakeside on US-93 at 1200MST.  Multiple trees were reported down and the media tweeted photos of a large tree that was uprooted in Kalispell.

Winds were measured between 30 and 40 mph with wind gusts up to 75 mph during the event. The highest measured wind gust in the valley was 75 MPH, located southeast of Stevensville. Mount Sentinel, which is situated at 5000 feet MSL, recorded a gust to 96 MPH at 1330MST. Winds blew down power lines, blew over a semi-truck on US-93 in Stevensville, MT, which closed all 4 lanes of traffic and caused trees to fall over and total a truck in Stevensville. Also the Missoula County Sheriff issued a shelter in place and emergency travel only between Lolo and Stevensville because of the wind threat. Local utilities estimated an excess of 2800 customers without power. A utility remarked that this was major impact to them and stated that trees had fallen into power lines in at least 20 locations in Florence and east Carlton Creek area was the hardest hit with 50 trees down including 2 foot in diameter Ponderosa Pine to smaller Lodgepole trees.

Winds gusted from 53 to 58 mph from Georgetown Lake to Deer Lodge and Avon. These winds resulted in part of the roof of the Deer Lodge Hotel being blown off, multiple power outages, and trailers flipped on I-90 around Butte, MT.
Wind gusts over 50 mph near Clinton, contributed to power outages to an estimated 800 customers from Bonner to Helmville. An area ski resort had to close down due to the high winds.

An estimated 2 to 4 feet of snow fell in higher elevations, while the Dixie COOP measured a single day record of 30 inches. In addition, as lower elevations warmed, snow changed to rain which caused mudslides on US-12 between mile-markers 93 to 97, which are 17 to 21 miles east of the Kooskia area.

There were widespread snow accumulations of 10 to 20 inches, with up to 3 feet of snow that fell at the Williams Creek Summit over a 2 day period. Schools were closed for the first time during the 2019-2020 winter.
Interstate 90 was closed down to emergency travel only from Warm Springs, MT to just south of Opportunity, MT. This was due to blowing and drifting snow and poor visibility.
At least 750 people lost power in the Essex, West Glacier and Hungry Horse areas, as a result of tree debris falling onto power lines.

While most of the wind gusts were in the middle to upper 40s mph, a sensor located in higher terrain northeast of Hot Springs reported a gust to 61 mph around 0645MST. There were a 100 people without power in the Bigfork and Wood's Bay areas.
A private sensor, located 5 miles southeast of Stevensville, recorded the strong wind gust at 1549MST. No damages were reported in Ravalli County.

Most of the wind gusts were in the 40s during this event. There were a few instances of winds gusting over 50 mph along the Continental Divide, including: 61 mph north of Avon around 1154MST, 58 mph MacDonald Pass at 0949MST, 52 mph Montana Tech in Butte at 1430MST and 51 mph at the Bert Mooney Airport south of Butte at 1451MST. No damages were reported.
There was a MDT road report of a tree down at 0609MST on Highway 56, one mile north of the junction with Highway 200. The tree was on a guardrail, blocking the northbound lane.

Approximately 30 percent of tall spruce trees in a 20 acre swatch fell over due to the high winds at the mouth of Deep Creek Canyon, located 3 miles ENE of Fortine. Multiple trees were reported down with power outages in the following areas: Glen Lake, Grave's Creek, and Farm-to-Market Road in Whitefish. A chain-linked fence was damaged at a private residence in the Deep Creek area. Power crews were unable to mitigate initially due to the hazardous conditions.

The mesonet station FW5910, located on Lake Blaine reported multiple wind gusts to 70+ mph between 1800 and 1900MST on the 13th. Widespread wind damage was reported from along the western foothills of the Swan Range and also of the Mission Mountains. Multiple large trees fell over, and 5 power poles were snapped in half along Highway 35 from mile-markers 5, 8, 9.7 to 25. This resulted in road closure between Polson and Bigfork from 1600MST on the 13th to late morning on the 14th.  Also, multiple power outages occurred in these areas that lasted well into the weekend. In this area along the eastern shore of Flathead Lake, several trees had fallen onto rooftops, and one fell on a car. A Lutheran camp, located 4 miles SE of Lakeside, reported a dozen trees down with damage to 3 cabins, a shed, and a new deck. A personal cup anemometer situated on the roof, located 8 miles east of Rollins, measured a gust to 69 mph at 1300MST on the 13th. A reporter for the Daily Interlake reported 10 large trees down near Lake Blaine. What made this wind event more difficult is that the high winds lasted longer and occurred more frequently, which made it tough for mitigation.

A local utility company remarked that the Red Owl area was one of the worst areas hit by the high winds. There was so much damage that it took 3 or 4 days to clear up the tree debris. They said it was difficult to mitigate during the event because there were trees falling all around them. A local said that they often get these winds coming down out of the canyon where the Red Owl Trail starts. Multiple trees had also fallen along Meadow Lake Road, Whitetail Road, and Landmark Lane downwind or west of Bear Creek Canyon. Approximately 6 trees fell across South Ferndale Road with dozens of trees down towards Highway 83. A local remarked that these were 100 year old trees that were laid down from east to west. A man was injured when a tree fell on him, near the northern part of Swan Lake.

Multiple trees were damaged by high winds in Missoula proper and also in the Rattlesnake area. Just before daybreak on the 14th, a 24 inch diameter tree fell onto Rattlesnake Drive, causing damage to a vehicle and blocking part of the road. A 60 to 70 foot tree snapped off about 6 feet from the base in Greenough Park, located in the Rattlesnake area, north of Missoula. Winds were gusting up to 84 mph on top of Point 6 Mountain, north of Missoula which contributed in a local ski area closing for two days straight.
Trees were reported down between mile-markers 6 and 7 on Highway 200 in Heron.
Strong winds tore the roof off a trailer home.

Montana Highway 12 from Garrison Junction, MT to Avon, MT was closed to emergency travel only due to blowing, drifting snow and poor visibility. Sustained winds of 30 mph gusting up to 37 mph was reported at Garrison Junction during this time. Interstate 90 was closed down for emergency travel only from Phosphate, MT to Warm Springs, MT including the town of Deer Lodge, MT due to blowing and drifting snow with poor visibility.

Lolo Pass Snotel Observation reported 8.2 inches of storm total snow. The snow plow crew at Lost Trail Pass reported 8.5 inches of storm total snow. The Combination Snotel observation reported 9.5 inches of storm total snow.

Weather spotters reported 7.0 inches of new snow 1 mile northwest of Butte, 7.0 inches 8 miles south of Butte, and 9.6 inches snow in Anaconda, MT. Montana Department of Transportation reported 9.5 of storm total snow along Montana Highway 141 from Avon, MT to the Highway 200 junction.

Troy dispatch reported numerous trees down, including at US-2 mile-marker 5, Old Highway 2 near the state line and 508 near Yaak.  US-2 was also closed at mile-marker 89 for a period. Multiple power outages were reported from Troy to Libby and trees fell on cars and a mobile home in Libby.
Spotter at 2 miles north of Evaro reported 6.5 of storm total snow.

Idaho Department of Transportation snow plow crew reported 7.0 inches of storm total snow accumulation at Bannock Pass, ID. At Lemhi ridge, located 500 feet above the pass level, 10 inches of snow was reported by an automated snow reporting station.

Snow totals ranged from 3 to 6 inches across the Seeley-Swan and Potomac valleys and along the I-90 corridor east of Missoula. Little travel impact was noted on Montana Highway 200 and 83 and along I-90.

Heavy snowfall and blowing snow was observed on U.S. Highway 12 and Montana Highway 141. Travel was difficult on Highway 12 and Montana Highway 141 as 6 to 10 inches of snow fell. Lesser snow amounts were noted on I-90 from Garrison Junction to Butte. Wind gusts up to 30 mph led to blowing snow and reduced visibility for travelers going over MacDonald Pass.
Light snowfall and gusty easterly winds impacted travel on U.S. Highway 2 over Marias Pass the evening of April 10 through the morning of April 11.

Gusty north and east winds were felt across the Flathead Valley and Flathead Lake with gusts over 40 mph being observed. A downed tree damaged power lines on Echo Lake Road northeast of Bigfork. Flathead Electric noted 400 customers lost power during this strong northeast wind event.

Heavy, wet snowfall of up to 12 inches, fell at Georgetown Lake during the morning hours. A few power outages also occurred because of the weight of the snow on powerlines. Higher elevations adjacent to Georgetown Lake reported up to 18 inches of snow.

Overbank flooding was reported along much of the North Fork of the Flathead River, from the North Fork and Camas Road intersection, north to the Canadian border. While much of the adjacent areas are rural, flooding did occur on North Fork Road and other local roads around Polebridge through June 1.

Swollen small streams brought flooding to fields and low-lying areas in the Bitterroot Valley. A few homes were surrounded by water and reported water in basements. Local and county roads, along with a small section of Eastside Highway north of Stevensville, experienced water flowing across roadways. A Forest Service campground south of Darby was also closed because of the stream flooding.  In addition, the Bitterroot River rose enough to flood ranch fields around Lolo.

The Clark Fork River flooded the Orchard Homes neighborhood in Missoula. Neighborhood streets turned into streams, with 10 to 15 homes sandbagged and surrounded by flood water. Flooding continued through the second week of June.

Widespread high winds were reported as a line of thunderstorms, in the form of a squall line, moved north-northeastward across the region. While wind gusts of 50 to 60 miles per hour were common, a person from the public in Kila reported a measured peak wind gust of 78 miles per hour, and the ASOS at Glacier Park International Airport  recorded a peak wind gust of 69 miles per hour. Numerous trees were either snapped in half or uprooted,��which resulted in over 200 power outages and 37,000 customers without power. Several houses and vehicles were destroyed as trees fell onto them. Highway 2 and Montana Highway 83 were both covered by fallen trees for a time. A local electric coop remarked that this wind event may be the largest, most damaging outage event in our history.
Numerous tree damage led to power outages and blocked roadways. Damage was noted on both sides of Flathead Lake, but damage was most concentrated near Polson, Dayton, and Finley Point.

Widespread power outages, slick roads with low visibility, and extensive tree branch damage was reported. Total snow amounts included 16 inches in Walkersville, between 8 and 10 inches in Butte, and 8 inches in Deer Lodge.

Sustained winds between 40 to 50 mph with frequent gusts between 50 and 63 mph occurred during the event. Uptown Butte sustained the most roof damage with blown-off shingles, partially due to the older style homes found there. Multiple trees and power lines were damaged which resulted in power outages. Isolated reports of damaged trees and power lines were found from Anaconda to Deer Lodge. Downed power lines caused two separate fires: a quarter acre grass fire located four miles south-southwest of Butte, and a two acre grass and timber fire southwest of Homestake Pass along Blacktail Canyon Road.
Strong winds from a thunderstorm damaged power lines and brought power outages to the west Hamilton area.

Up to two feet of snow fell near Williams Creek Summit, which caused numerous trees to break or fall over the road, making travel impossible for much of the day. Approximately 14 inches of wet snow fell at Lost Trail Pass adversely impacting travel.

The Darkhorse Lake SNOTEL reported 19 inches of total snowfall with this event, while 9 inches fell at Schwartz Lake. The Schwartz Lake SNOTEL reported a 24 hour precipitation total of 1.80 inches which is the highest amount reported for any time of the year, going back to 1995. Gilmore Summit saw heavy snow that covered the road with several inches of slush.
A photo on social media showed several hailstones that were a little larger than a quarter. Also hail was reported to have accumulated several inches in the storm's path.

A photo was received via social media of a hailstone that appeared a little larger than a golf ball in Kila. Damage to cars, trailer and roof in Kila was also reported. Half dollar hail was reported in Kalispell and just south of Whitefish.

Significant power line and power pole damage was reported by the power company, due to multiple, downed trees. A photo on social media showed a large pine tree on top of a car. Power was out in the area for almost 24 hours.

Between 28-30 June 1.67 of rain was measured at the Riggins COOP (45.42/ -116.31). Around 10 AM on the 3rd a rockslide was reported near mile marker 188 on US Route 95 in Idaho. This slide closed both lanes of the highway. A bypass was built and opened on the 9th, however instability in the slope continued to hinder repair (which continued through much of the summer).
A strong thunderstorm dropped large hail on U.S. Highway 93 between Conner and Sula. Quarter to half dollar size hail was reported near Sula, MT.
Valley lows in the lower to mid 30s caused damage to sensitive vegetation.
Widespread valley lows in the upper 20s to lower 30s caused damage to sensitive vegetation. The lowest reading was 29 degrees in downtown Salmon.
Widespread valley lows from the lower 20s to lower 30s caused damage to sensitive vegetation. The coldest readings were around Marion and Olney with 21 degrees.
Widespread valley lows from the upper teens to lower 30s caused damage to sensitive vegetation. The coldest reading was at Polebridge with 18 degrees.

Widespread valley lows from the upper teens to lower 30s caused damage to sensitive vegetation. Damage was reported to an above ground waterline just west of Kalispell with a morning low of 19 degrees.
Widespread valley lows from the upper 20s to lower 30s caused damage to sensitive vegetation. The coldest reading was at Trout Creek with 27 degrees.

Widespread valley lows from the upper 20s to lower 30s caused damage to sensitive vegetation. It was noted that only gardens that were sufficiently covered, survived the cold temperatures. The coldest reading was at Stevensville with 27 degrees.
Widespread valley lows from the mid to upper 20s caused damage to sensitive vegetation. The coldest reading was 24 degrees at both Avon and Georgetown Lake.
Widespread valley lows from the mid 20s to lower 30s caused damage to sensitive vegetation. The coldest reading was 26 degrees at Seeley Lake.

Going to the Sun Road was temporarily closed from the Avalanche Creek parking lot to the Logan Pass parking lot due to an early season snowfall. The snowfall and freezing temperatures made for icy and hazardous road conditions. Snowfall around Logan Pass ranged from 2 to 4 inches, primarily on the morning of the 7th.

Damaging north to northeast winds began in the Lake Blaine area early in the morning then moved southward to Flathead Lake. A peak wind gust of 75 mph led to several houses losing shingles around Lake Blaine, a roof blown off a shed, and multiple power outages. Further south, downed trees and associated power outages were focused around Flathead Lake, especially along Finley Point. Several docks were damaged or destroyed on the south and west side of Flathead Lake by waves of up to 6 feet, and  one pontoon boat was torn apart. Power outages impacted several thousand customers.

Strong wind gusts estimated at 50 to 55 mph caused numerous downed trees from Thompson Falls northwestward to the Idaho border along and adjacent to Highway 200. Power outages were common.  At least 2 vehicles were damaged, as was a fifth wheel trailer.
Gusty north winds to 50 mph brought down a few trees around Victor, Hamilton, and Darby. Brief power outages were noted due to falling trees.
Gusty winds brought brief power outages around Essex. Also, a Remote Automatic Weather Station was blown over at Spotted Bear Ranger Station.

Appropriately 40 mature Ponderosa pine and Douglas fir trees were blown down along 4th of July Creek Road northeast of Carmen. Several campers were trapped by the falling trees. In addition, around 20 cottonwood and aspen trees were either uprooted or had tops snapped out along Carmen Creek.  Isolated tree damage was noted around Salmon. Power and phone outages occurred because of downed trees.
Downed trees were reported along Highway 12 from Lowell to the Montana border. Sporadic power and phone outages occurred at Lowell. Wind gusts were generally 40 to 45 mph.

Winds gusting to 45 mph caused trees to fall on power lines, and this in turn sparked several wildfires near Orofino. These fires spread quickly in the low humidity and windy environment. Later named the Sunnyside Complex, an initial damage assessment included 13 homes, 31 outbuildings, and 27 vehicles destroyed. Highway 12 was also closed for a time.

Downed trees were reported southeast of Eureka near Glen Lake, Marion, Dickey Lake, near Yaak, and also Troy. Power lines were damaged with isolated power outages near Eureka, more widespread power outages occurred around Troy and Yaak. A common theme from spotters was a few trees down on their property but not widespread tree damage. Though damage occurred, locals noted that this event was far less impactful than previous wind events last fall and winter.

Intense early morning snow showers, accumulating up to 5 inches at Butte and Homestake Pass on Interstate 90, resulted in a couple of tractor trailer spin-outs and a road closure that lasted for approximately 5 hours.

Widespread, downed trees over power lines were reported by a local utility across the Flathead Valley. West Valley on the west side Kalispell was especially hit hard. At 7 p.m. up to 53,000 members were out of power. A personal wind sensor in Kila measured a gust to 57 mph. In Hot Springs, the RAWS sensor reported a gust to 58 mph.

Several trees toppled from the winds in the Missoula area. In one case, the tree fell onto a parked car on 3rd Street. In Missoula, up to 1,900 people were without power for a period of time.  Fallen trees were also reported in the Bitterroot Valley, especially in Hamilton and  in Stevensville. Approximately 1,200 people lost power in the Bitterroot Valley.

Winds gusting up to 75 mph were observed in the higher terrain across west-central Montana. While no damage was reported, this was considered a high impact event due to the fact that hunting season occurring and the winds could have caused tree-fall in the backcountry.

The COOP station located 32 miles south of Libby recorded 13 inches of snow which would be the all-time one day record for the month of October. Other snow amounts include: 10 inches 2 miles southwest of Marion, 8 inches in Libby and 2 inches in Eureka. A person on Twitter remarked that Highway 2 became a sheet of ice between Libby and Kalispell.

Wind gusts of 50 to 60 miles per hour were common, with a peak gust of 73 miles per hour, measured just northwest of Grangeville. At least 3 power poles were snapped in half, adding to up to 1000 customers without power. In addition, trees were blown down, debris blown through windows and across roads, and blowing snow occurred early in the event causing 'near-zero' visibility as reported by the Idaho Department of Transportation.
Snow rates of 1 to 2 inches an hour developed by 8:30 pm. Heavy snowfall amounts fell around the Missoula Valley, with at least 1 weather-related accident.
A employee from the Montana Department of Transportation reported a storm total snowfall between 4 and 6 inches from West Glacier to Devil's Creek along Highway 2.

Very heavy snowfall fell in the Mission Valley with reports of strong gusty winds causing blowing and drifting issues around Flathead Lake. The peak wind at the Flathead Lake Bio station was 46 mph at 4 am, and around that same time a large tree fell over blocking highway 35 near milepost 20. Snow amounts in inches include: 14 Hot Springs, 13 Arlee, 12 St. Ignatius, 11 located 8 miles south of Wood's Bay, 10.5 Ronan, and 5 in Kalispell.

Very heavy snowfall caused difficult travel through the region with several automobile accidents and slide-offs. Snow amounts in inches include: 17 Plains, 14 St. Regis, 12 Haugan, Superior, Alberton and Thompson Falls, 11.9 Evaro and 11 in White Pine. The unofficial amount of 12 inches in Haugan blew away the previous all-time one day total of 7 inches when compared with the COOP records.

The COOP observer reported a whopping 18 inches of total storm snowfall on the 24th. This COOP station has not been continuous, but during the period of 1965 to 2009, the highest 24 hour snowfall was 6.8 inches measured on October 21, 1975. The Seeley Lake COOP reported 11 inches on the 26th which makes it the highest 24 hour amount, topping the 9.6 inches observed on Oct. 31, 1942. Other snowfall amounts in inches include: 18 near Garnet Ghost Town, 17 Placid Lake, 15 five miles NW Seeley Lake, 14.3 Seeley Lake, and 10.9 Clinton.

A storm total of 13.8 inches fell in two days in Missoula, ranking second highest for a two day total in October, behind 15 inches that occurred on October 5-6, 1914. Other snowfall amounts in inches include: 12 Corvallis and Conner, 10.5 three miles NNE Lolo, 10 Lolo and Victor, 8 Hamilton, and 7 Stevensville.
Lolo Pass received 15 inches of total snowfall from this event.  Other amounts in inches include: 14 Skalkaho Pass and Twelvemile Creek SNOTEL, 12 Lost Trail Pass, and 7 fourteen miles NE Sula.

Heavy snow combined with gusty easterly winds ranging between 15 and 35 mph caused blowing and drifting snow from Ovando, south along the Continental Divide towards Deer Lodge. Sixteen and a half inches fell at Avon, and this is not far below nearby Elliston's two day record of 18.9 inches that occurred Oct. 4-5, 1914 (Elliston did not submit an observation for this 2020 event). Additional snow totals in inches include: 16 Edwards Gulch near Drummond, 15 MacDonald Pass, 14.5 three miles SW Ovando, 11 Drummond, 8 Georgetown Lake, 6 Anaconda and seven miles south of Butte, and 5.8 Butte.
Fifteen inches of heavy snow was reported at Lolo Pass during the event. Other snow amounts include 7.5 inches at Selway Lodge and 3.1 inches in Dixie.

Early season heavy snow fell in the mountains causing dangerous conditions for hunters and other recreationists. Total snowfall in inches included: 15 Crater Meadows SNOTEL at 5,960 ft., 12 Shanghai Summit at 4,570 ft., and 3.4 Pierce.

A half a dozen trees, mostly evergreen, were damaged by heavy, wet snow, causing  power outages in western Clearwater County. Total snowfall in inches included: 7 Rudo Rd. Grangemont, 6 three miles NE Orofino, 2.3 Woodland, and 1.5 Grangeville.
Snow bands, observed on radar from Lookout Pass east along I-90, brought snow rates high enough to reduce visibility and cause rapidly changing road conditions.
Snow rates of 1 to 2 inches per hour were observed. Additionally, total accumulations of snowfall were reported as 10.5 inches in Clinton and 9.2 inches in Bonner MT.

Severe driving conditions were declared for Homestake Pass, from Avon to MacDonald Pass along US-12, and Avon to Nevada Lake along HWY-141 at 11 pm on the 7th. Chains were required for towing units on Homestake Pass at 11:45 pm on the 7th.

A spotter west of Grangeville measured 10.9 inches of snow with drifts as deep as 3 feet. There were additional reports in the Camas Prairie area of 10 to 12 inches. Idaho County Light and Power also reported multiple outages due to lines down.

A snow squall impacted US highway 12 from MacDonald Pass to Garrison and the I-90 corridor from Drummond through Deer Lodge. Department of highway officials reported a flash freeze of roadways as road temperatures dropped from the mid 30s to upper 20s. Visibility below one quarter of a mile and wind gusts in excess of 20 mph where observed. Highway officials reported 3 to 5 inches of snow in less than two hours from Garrison to Deer Lodge.

Whiteout conditions were observed from Whitefish to Eureka on US Highway 93 as a snow squall moved southward. Roadways quickly became snow-covered and icy as temperatures dropped from the mid to upper 30s into the upper 20s to low 30s. Visibility less than one quarter mile and wind gusts in excess of 20 mph were observed. A trained spotter, located 4 miles northeast of Rexford, reported 2 inches of snow in a one hour period.

A snow squall impacted the Flathead Valley during the morning hours of December 22. Roadways quickly became snow-covered and icy as temperatures dropped from the mid 30s to the upper 20s. Heavy snowfall with visibility down to 100 yards and gusty northeast winds in excess up 25 mph were observed. The Glacier Park International Airport temporarily closed and trained spotters in the Flathead Valley reported 2 to 3 inches of snowfall.

A snow squall impacted the US Highway 2 corridor during the morning hours of December 22. Roadways between Hungry Horse and West Glacier quickly became snow-covered and icy as temperatures dropped from the upper 30s to mid 20s. Visibility below one quarter of a mile was observed along with northeast wind gusts in excess of 20 mph. Two to three inches of snowfall was observed in Hungry Horse and West Glacier during a two hour period.
Periods of moderate to heavy snowfall impacted the southern Clearwater Mountains. Total snowfall amounts included 7 inches in Lowell and 4 inches at Lolo Pass.
A light glaze of freezing rain was reported in Libby and vicinity. Lincoln County dispatch reported icy and slick roads.

Roadways between Orofino and Weippe on US Highway 12 and Idaho State Highway 11 became treacherous due to snowfall rates of 1 to 2 inches per hour at times. Snowfall amounts include: 3.5 inches Orofino, 6 inches on bench above Orofino, 6 inches 2 miles northeast of Kamiah and 8 inches 3 miles southeast of Weippe.

Heavy snow impacted the northern Clearwater Mountains during the evening hours of December 30 and during the morning hours of December 31. Pierce reported 9 inches of snow. Furthermore, a foot of more of snowfall was observed in higher elevations in areas off and away from Idaho State Highway 11.

A glaze of ice due to freezing rain led to the closure of I-90 from Lookout Pass to St. Regis. I-90 was closed for approximately three hours. Cold ground temperatures allowed for ice accumulation to occur.

events.cz_name: LOWER HELLS CANYON / SALMON RIVER REGION
events.event_narrative: An Idaho Department of Transportation employee reported this event to be moderate to high impact due to staffing numbers this early in the season. At 5:40 pm, an Idaho Department of Transportation sensor at Whitebird Hill reported 'very slick' road conditions.

Heavy snow developed at Lookout Pass by late evening, and continued through daybreak on the 3rd. The Montana Department of Transportation labeled the stretch of Interstate 90 from Lookout to Taft as severe driving conditions from 7 am to around 10 am MST. The Lookout SNOTEL reported 1.50 inches of snow water equivalent during this event, which equates to 12 to 14 inches of snowfall at the pass.

This was a very widespread wind event for northwest Montana. Countless trees were either blown down or snapped in half in many locations, causing numerous road blockages. At least 2 dozen trees were blown over along Bull Lake Road, 10 miles north of Heron. One power company reported that they had 51 broken power poles, and experienced extensive power line and cross arm damage during the event. Winds were gusting up to 80 mph at the Zonolite station which is situated 2,000 feet above the Libby area. Wind gusts between 66 and 70 mph were reported in the valleys in the Idaho Panhandle and based on the fact that trees were down all over Lincoln County, these wind speeds are a good estimate of what happened. At least 15,000 people were without power by mid-day on the 13th, and some outages lasted through the following weekend. One utility that covers part of the Idaho Panhandle and northwest Montana reported over one million dollars in damages.

Winds gusted between 50 and 65 mph in the lower elevations, causing mature trees to fall over or snap in half.  In Martin City, a mature tree snapped three feet from the ground and destroyed a small outbuilding. Power lines were reported down across Highway 83 about 4 miles northwest of Swan Lake. On top of Mount Aeneas, located in the Swan Range at nearly 7500 feet, winds peaked at 101 mph. The winds forced one ski resort to close the top half of their mountain. Several thousand people were without power, and the West Glacier School closed because of the high winds.

Multiple locations in both the Flathead and Mission valleys reported frequent gusts between 50 and 65 mph. An employee with the Montana Department of Transportation, who had lived in the area for over 40 years, remarked that he had never seen such widespread tree damage before. Many primary and secondary roads were blocked or closed for a time during the windstorm due to downed trees or powerlines down. One power company reported over 16,000 customers without power with 153 distinct outages from Libby to Essex at 3 pm MST on the 13th. Power was not restored for some people until 5 days later. A large pine tree crushed a pickup truck and damaged another vehicle on Elk Park Road in Columbia Falls.

The Thompson Falls airport observed a peak gust to 58 mph at 10:02 am MST. A trained spotter located 2 miles west-northwest of Belknap observed several 90 year old trees uprooted by the wind. Other reports include: widespread power outages, roof damage in Plains, several buildings damaged in Thompson Falls, 2 ponderosa pine trees down in St. Regis, a fallen tree across a vehicle in De Borgia, a tree down on part of Interstate 90 near mile-marker 22, and multiple large trees across Prospect Road in Thompson Falls.

Damaging winds were observed from the Missoula Valley to the central Bitterroot Valley. The Missoula International Airport recorded a gust of 59 mph, while a station 2 miles east-northeast of Stevensville registered peak winds up to 67 mph. Multiple large ponderosa and fir trees, as well as powerlines, were reported down across the area.  Close to 10,000 customers were without power at one point during the storm. One electric company reported 38 power poles broken in Missoula County.

Volunteer groomers for the Chief Joseph cross country trails had to clear an estimated 100 downed trees. They remarked that there was a tree down almost every 100 yards. The U.S. Forest Service reported that a couple of their radio repeaters were blown down in the Bitterroot Mountains. The Little Rock Creek RAWS located at 5500 feet, just south of Lake Como, reported a peak wind of 58 mph. A wind sensor on top of Mount Sentinel (north end of the Sapphire Mountains) recorded a peak wind speed of 125 mph at 10:45 am MST.

The Clearwater RAWS reported a peak wind of 63 mph at 11:30 am MST. A private weather station in east Bonner reported a peak wind of 54 mph, and a Montana Department of Transportation sensor at Bearmouth reported a peak wind of 59 mph. Several thousand customers were without power from Condon in the north, through| Seeley Lake, to Bonner and Clinton in the south. Multiple downed trees were reported between Condon and Clearwater Junction. One electric company had to use a helicopter, in tandem with employees hiking in, to replace a power pole near Cramer Creek off of Interstate 90.

During this event a Montana Department of Transportation wind sensor, located north of Avon, observed an incredibly extended period of high winds from 9 am to 3 pm MST. Power outages were observed from Ovando to Helmville to Avon and also in the Anaconda area. Peak wind speeds observed during the event included: 80 mph Avon North, 78 mph at MacDonald Pass before the sensor stopped reporting, 67 mph Deer Lodge, and 59 mph Bearmouth.

Besides frequent gusts above 60 mph in the Grangeville area, wind gusts up to 55 mph were observed at Greer in western Clearwater County. Power outages were observed during this event due to multiple trees down in the vicinity of Orofino and Grangemont.  Trees and power poles were reported down on the Old Dent Bridge Rd. and on Grangemont Rd. between mile-markers 10 and 16. A smaller window of high impact occurred between 8am and noon PST on the 12th when southerly winds between 50 and 60 mph caused severe cross-wind on US-95 south of Grangeville and caused a tractor trailer to tip over on Whitebird Grade.

Heavy wet snow fell generally above 3000 feet with rates over 1 inch per hour at times. General snow totals of 10 to 14 inches were common with 10 inches in Elk River, 11 inches at Cardiff, and 12 inches at Pierce. Periods of difficult travel were observed.

Heavy snow fell above 3000 feet with rates over 1 inch per hour at times. Snow totals of 10 to 18 inches were common with 15 inches in Elk City and 18 inches at Red River Hot Springs. Periods of difficult travel were observed.

Widespread snow, wind, and dangerously low wind chills were observed. Snow amounts generally ranged from 5-14 inches with 22 inches reported near Marias Pass. Easterly wind gusts of 30-40 miles per hour resulted in blowing and drifting snow with wind chills of -15F to -30F at lower elevations and -35F to -55F at higher elevations. Dangerous avalanche conditions developed because of the wind and snow with one avalanche related fatality reported in the Swan Range near Wildcat Lake. This winter storm also created significant challenges for plow crews along US Highway 2.

Heavy snow, gusty winds, and snow bands brought difficult driving conditions. Snow amounts ranged from 2-4 inches in the Missoula Valley with 6-10 inches in the Bitterroot Valley. The southern Bitterroot Valley experienced the heaviest snow with 13-14 inches reported around Conner and Darby. Gusty winds and cold temperatures resulted in wind chills as low as -15F.

Snow bands created severe driving conditions as reported by the state highway department near Lolo Pass and Lost Trail Pass. Snow totals ranged from 9 to 21 inches with wind gusts to 25 miles per hour.

Wind and heavy snow resulted in difficult driving conditions and natural avalanches in the backcountry. Snow totals ranged from 10-20 inches with the greatest total of 23.5 inches just east of Seeley Lake. Wind chill values of -10F to -20F were also observed.

Snow, wind, blowing snow, and low wind chill values were all observed. A flash freeze occurred late on the 5th into the morning hours of the 6th causing icy conditions on Interstate 90. Periods of severe driving conditions were also reported by the state highway department through the morning of the 7th. Total snowfall ranged from 10-20 inches with the highest amount of 24 inches near Avon. Wind chills of -20F to -35F were noted as well.

Wind gusts of 20-30 miles per hour and well below zero air temperatures resulted in extended periods of wind chills of -30F to -50F. The coldest observed wind chill was -70F at the Snowslip sensor above US Highway 2.
Wind chill values of -25F to -35F were observed as winds gusted to 40 mph with air temperatures near zero.
An extended period of wind chills ranging from -35F to -55F was observed.
Wind chills bottomed out at -30F during the early morning hours in the Missoula Valley.
Wind chill values of -30F to -40F were common through the period.

events.cz_name: LOWER HELLS CANYON / SALMON RIVER REGION
events.event_narrative: Hazardous driving conditions because of snow and blowing snow caused the state highway department to recommend chains on US Highway 95 from Grangeville southward to the Idaho County line. Very slick road conditions were reported on Whitebird Grade. Meanwhile, the lower elevations along US Highway 95 experienced 3-7 inches of snow which is significant for those elevations.

Two distinct periods of wind and snow occurred, early on the 22nd then again the evening of the 22nd into the early morning hours of the 23rd. Fifty mile per hour wind gusts and snowfall rates of 1-2 inches per hour caused periods of severe driving conditions with chains required from near Essex to Marias Pass on US Highway 2.

Multiples periods of snow added up to 12-24 inches. Specific totals included 14 inches in Pierce and an estimated 24 inches at Elk River. Most of the impactful snow occurred above 3000 feet leading to difficult travel for much of the region.

General snow totals of 6-18 inches occurred with the heaviest totals at Lolo Pass with 21 inches. Chains were also required for towing units over Lolo Pass with snow covered roads all the way to Lowell.

Widespread hazardous driving conditions occurred due to heavy snow, even at the lowest elevations such as Orofino. Snowfall of 11-15 inches was typical resulting in school and public services closure. Lesser snow amounts were noted on the Camas Prairie with around 6 inches of accumulation.

A combination of heavy snow and falling trees (around 30-40 trees) caused power outages and blocked roads throughout the zone. The area from Lowell to just west of Bald Mountain on US Highway 12 received 18 inches of heavy snow, which was very significant for these lower elevations. Also, driving was very difficult on Mt. Idaho grade and in the Dixie area where they received 17.8 inches from the storm.

Snow and blowing snow led to hazardous driving conditions with chains recommended on US Highway 95 from Grangeville southward to the Idaho County line. The heaviest snow amounts were around the Camas Prairie with 5-7 inches along with wind gust to 20 miles per hour.

The highest observed wind gust of 43 mph was measured at the Dent RAWS along the northern shore of the Dworshak Reservoir. A power outage north of Weippe resulted in approximately 27 customers losing power.

More than 600 customers were affected by power outages in an area from Grangeville to Elk City to Dixie, ID. In the mountains, there were multiple measured gusts in the 40s mph, while Hells Half RAWS (elevation of 8100 feet) measured the highest gust of 57 mph.

Widespread wind gusts between 50 and 60 mph were observed during this storm with the peak wind gust of 66 mph occurring just northwest of Grangeville. Close to 4000 customers lost power during this event. Additionally, the Idaho Department of Transportation reported a few trees down on ID-12 east of Lowell, ID.
With widespread measured wind gusts from 50s to 60s mph and the highest measured of 86 mph at Kriley creek RAWs, close to 1000 customers lost power during the event.

Greater than 400 customers lost power during this wind event. In general, the highest winds were in the mountains with a peak recorded gust of 52 mph at Zonolite. In populated locations, gusts into the 40s were common with a peak gust of 49 mph at Kila, MT.

High winds caused a downed tree in the Coram area which resulted in a power outage. The highest wind recorded in the valleys was 58 mph in Hungry Horse.  The highest gust, measured at 98 mph, reported by the Tunnel Ridge Snow avalanche monitoring station (high elevation). Less than 100 customers were without power during the storm.

Between 200-500 customers lost power during the event. There was at least 1 report of a tree down north of Lakeside, MT. Winds were relatively uniform with widespread gusts into the 40s mph and a couple of reports in the low 50s mph.
With wind gusts into the 40s mph, impacts were constrained to 200 or fewer customers without power.

Widespread wind gusts between 40 and 50 mph with a couple of gusts in the 60s occurred during this event. Overall, impacts were constrained to around 400 customers without power and a single report of a blown-over shed in Stevensville.
Although wind gusts in the mountains ranged from 60 to 75 mph, the impacts were few in the sparsely populated areas with less than 100 customers without power at one time during the storm.

High wind gusts were common with gusts to 63 mph west of Butte and 57 mph at Georgetown Lake. Additionally, brief heavy snow, rapidly falling temperatures, and strong gusty winds contributed to slick road conditions, especially between Butte and Anaconda.

A band of heavy snow set up across southern portions of the Bitterroot Valley during the morning hours of April 19 following the passage of a Canadian cold front. The spring snow led to school delays and closures, with Corvallis cancelling school. Snow was measured at 5-9 inches during this event.

A period of moderate snow impacted travel across Lolo Pass on US Highway 12 and across Lost Trail Pass on US Highway 93 from the evening hours of April 18 to the morning hours of April 19. New snow of 3-4 inches was reported by area SNOTEL sites.

Winter driving conditions were observed on US Highway 2 from Essex to Marias Pass due to the combination of gusty northeast winds and moderate to heavy snowfall. Montana Department of Transportation officials reported 3 inches of snow on roadways at Devil Creek. An estimated 7-9 inches of snow fell at Marias Pass.

Strong winds behind a fast moving cold front led to several downed trees and numerous power outages in the vicinity of Troy, Bull Lake, and in the Yaak. The Northern Lights COOP reported more than 2400 customers without power from north of Bonners Ferry to the Canadian border and into northwest Montana through Troy, Bull Lake, and the Yaak.
Strong northeast winds led to power outages on the East Lakeshore of Whitefish Lake, in Bigfork, and at Lake Blaine.  Two trees were snapped in half in the Lake Blaine area.

Sanders County Dispatch reported numerous trees and power lines down along Highway 200 between Thompson Falls and Trout Creek. Trees fell across power lines in five areas along Blue Side Road between Thompson Falls and Trout Creek, igniting a few small wildfires. Power outages were also observed in the Heron area from fallen trees.
Impacts were difficult to find. However, 12 customers lost power, and a max gust of 64 mph was measured at the Skull Gulch RAWS.
Idaho Free Press employee took picture of funnel cloud over Grangeville.
Northwest Montana Border Patrol and public reported funnel cloud between Rexford and Eureka, MT.
Heavy snow reported at Georgetown Lake. Five inches of snow was received by 2 PM on 5/22/2008 and eight inches total by 7 AM 5/23/2008.
A downburst wind from a rain shower coupled with a strong pressure gradient, produced an estimated wind gust to 60 mph. One small aluminum shed was blown to over 20 feet into the air and damaged.

Strong southerly outflow winds of 45 to 60 mph downed hundreds of live trees, primarily ponderosa and larch varieties. Most of the trees were uprooted but a few had tops blown out.  The main area of damage extended from Salmon Lake to the Seeley Lake area with isolated areas of damage around the Morrell Falls trailhead and near Condon. Multi-hour power outages were common along with several vehicles damaged by fallen trees. In addition, hikers were stranded by fallen trees for a time at the Morrell Falls trailhead.
Reports of dime to quarter sized hail in Libby. Some trees lost leaves but no other damage was noted.

Several live trees were uprooted as thunderstorm outflow winds moved from southwest to northeast across the Mission Valley. Power outages and one report of minor vehicle damage from a falling tree branch were reported.

Thunderstorm outflow winds caused a few downed trees and tree branches which resulted in several power outages around Flathead Lake northward to Whitefish. The main power outages were centered on Woods Bay, Echo Lake, and in the Whitefish area with around 1000 customers without power for a time.
Outflow winds from nearby thunderstorms knocked down 20 to 25 mature trees and blew siding off an outbuilding.

Two firefighters, a 25 year old woman and a 29 year old man, members of the Flahtead National Forest were struck by lightning while finishing up a mop up of a prescribed burn west of Whitefish, MT and heading back to their vehicles. The lightning directly hit two nearby trees and injuried the firefighters. The two firefighters were taken to the hospital and listed as in stable condition.

Estimated wind gust to 75 mph from a rain shower over the Rangitsch Brothers Home Center flipped one trailer over in the sales lot. Two additional trailers were moved. Major damage was observed to the trailer that was flipped over. Minor damage was observed on one other trailer.

A sensor at Marias Pass reported 12.8 inches of snowfall from this event. Heavy snow occurred between 12 AM to 4 AM and also between 10 to 12 pm MST on the 20th. Gusty northeast winds between 20 and 35 mph were also observed. Snow amounts decreased substantially west of the pass where up to 1 inch of snow was estimated in Essex.

Power outages occurred in the Sula area and points east due to snow loading on power lines. The COOP observer located 14 miles northeast of Sula reported 5.1 inches of total snowfall while the Skalkaho Summit SNOTEL reported 8 inches.

Heavy wet snow fell over the southern Bitterroot Valley. Total snow amounts ranged from 1 inch in Corvallis to 2.3 inches located 2 miles east-northeast of Grantsdale and up to 4 inches in the Conner area. A power outage was reported in the Conner area most likely due to snow loading to power lines.

Heavy wet snow caused several power outages in the Potomac and Seeley lake regions. Snow totals included: 11 inches located 3 miles east-northeast of Clinton on Wallace Creek Road at five thousand feet, 6 inches near Potomac and 3.7 inches in Seeley Lake.
A period of wet snow fell across portions of southwest Montana. Snow amounts ranged from 2 inches in Butte, to 3 inches in Anaconda and up to 4 inches, 7 miles south of Butte.
Water from the Clark Fork River flooded the north end of Tower Street and also Kehrwald Drive. The peak gage height occurred at 2230 PM May 28 and was 7.98 ft.
Montana Department of Transportation weather station on Highway 141 near Avon recorded peak wind gust of 63 mph.
A weather spotter 2 miles north of Wise River, MT reported several 8 to 10 inch diameter trees blown down by thunderstorm winds.
Law Enforcement and a weather spotter reported that a roof blew off a trailer house and several large tree branches were down on Highway 93 in southern Lemhi County.
Highs temperatures reached from 100 to 110 degrees Fahrenheit with overnight lows in the upper 60s to lower 70s. Orofino peaked out at 112 degrees on the 29th.
Overnight lows only dropped into the 60s after daytime highs reached 100 to 110 degrees at the lower elevations.
High temperatures ranged from the upper 90s to 107 degrees at lower elevations with overnight lows in the 60s.

events.cz_name: LOWER HELLS CANYON / SALMON RIVER REGION
events.event_narrative: High temperatures ranged from 100 to 110 degrees with overnight lows generally in the 60s. There were some exceptions, such as the observation site at Pittsburg Landing reaching 115 degrees on the 29th with a morning low that day of 78 degrees.
High temperatures ranged from 100 to 110 degrees Fahrenheit in the lower elevations with overnights in the mid 50s to low 60s.
Overnight lows ranged from the mid 50s to low 60s, while daytime highs were from the upper 90s to 106 degrees in the lower elevations.
Flood waters impacted the north end of Tower Street and also Kehrwald Drive. The peak gage height occurred at 1245 PM June 5 and was 8.19 ft.

An outflow wind from a northerly moving thunderstorm produced strong to severe winds from roughly 6-7 pm MDT, with a peak gust of 64 mph at Missoula Intl. Airport. These winds caused downed trees and powerlines, and also damaged a roof. The outflow boundary snapped a tree north of Seeley Lake at 7 MDT. The first reported downed tree happened at 5:52 pm MDT in the Mullan Trail area. Additionally, a homeless camp in South Missoula suffered ripped tents.

A local apple orchard owner reported that 'a massive amount of flood water', overflowed the Bitterroot irrigation canal after heavy rain. This flood water carved 18 ditches through about 3 rows of his orchard. In addition, hail shredded some leaves of trees and strong winds toppled a 20-year old pine tree. After assessing the damage he felt there would be no crop of apples in 2021.

By 7:10 pm PDT, the Idaho Department of Transport began to receive reports of water, rocks, and mud on US-95 between mile marker 196-204, centered on MM200. This slide briefly closed both directions of the highway.
A severe thunderstorm developed close to Clinton, MT, and began a slow movement to the northeast over the next hour and 30 minutes. During that time two different spotters reported 1 hail.
A long-lived severe storm continued to produce 1 hail east of Seeley Lake. Additionally, it was reported the storm was producing heavy rain and winds up to 40 mph.

This particular thunderstorm developed off the outflow boundary from a previous severe storm affecting Missoula and Powell Counties. The FBAN on the Anderson Hill Fire reported large hail and heavy rain had fallen on the fire. In fact, he said sufficient hail had fallen to cover the ground white. The storm continued to Monture Ranger Station where a ranger reported 2 hail and damage to vehicle windscreens (unknown number of vehicles).

Backpackers camping at the edge of Lake Ellen Wilson in Glacier National Park were awakened by torrential rainfall and the clapping of thunder around midnight. Bias-corrected radar data estimated over half an inch of rain fell in one hour through 1 am on the 11th. The rain continued at moderate intensities for a few more hours and ended by late morning with an radar estimated total rainfall amount of over 2 inches. The campers reported boulders rolling down Mount Jackson into the lake throughout the night with 6 new waterfalls cutting off their exit trail towards Sperry Chalet. Three backpackers had to bed down at Gunsight Pass for an extra night due to all the rock slides and fast-moving water through the trails.

Law enforcement reported heavy rainfall led to street flooding in the Uptown District of Butte, Montana. Further, road department officials reported several clogged storm drains resulted in areas of minor street flooding.

The Boulder 2700 fire spread quickly during the early morning hours of August 1st in the presence of strong downslope winds and dry conditions. The fire ran down the west slope of the Mission Mountains, crossing Montana Highway 35, reaching the east shore of Flathead Lake. Damage surveys confirmed the loss of 14 primary structures and 17 outbuildings.

The Idaho Department of Transportation reported numerous rock and mudslides blocking US Highway 93 between Elk Bend and Ellis as a result of heavy rainfall. The roadway was closed for a period of time to allow for crews to clear roadways. Area gauge measurements suggested half an inch of rain fell across the US Highway 93 corridor over a 3 hour period.

Salmon-Challis National Forest officials reported a 30 feet wide by three feet deep sand and dirt debris flow across Salmon River Road, 1.5 miles west of Panther Creek. Another debris flow was reported from the Dutch Oven Creek drainage and was three feet wide, by four feet deep, including two to three boulders. The Salmon River Road was impassable from Panther Creek to Dutch Oven Creek through the morning hours of August 2nd. The Skull Gulch RAWS, located a few miles northwest of Panther Creek, reported 0.24 inches of rain from 1500 to 1600.
A trained spotter reported 1.3 inches of rainfall during a 45 minute period in Big Sky Lake. Excessive runoff washed out a resident's driveway along Big Sky Lake.

Multiple trees were reported down, some damaging power lines, due to high winds along US-2 and US-93. A Facebook dashcam video showed a vehicle hitting a falling tree during the storm. Several thousand citizens were without power for close to 12 hours after the event.
